[p. 10]

Peter Abelard and his disciple Peter Lombard. It is divided into three ages, of which the first, in the opinion of some, began about the middle of the eleventh century and was carried down to the middle of the twelfth. At that time there flourished Abelard; Lombard, called the Master of the Sentences because he expounded the sentences collected from the ancient Fathers; Gilbert de la Porrée, Peter Comestor, and John of Salisbury. The second period runs to about the year 1330; it was made illustrious by the geniuses of Albert the Great, St. Thomas Aquinas, and St. Bonaventure. The third lasted until letters and the arts were restored; in which age Durandus, Ockham, and Cardinal Pierre d’Ailly were renowned.

33 Among the Scholastics, or new Peripatetics, three more illustrious sects are reckoned: namely those of the Thomists, the Scotists, and the Nominalists. The first follow as their leader St. Thomas, born in the year 1224 in the Castle of Aquino, who afterwards professed the Rule of the Order of Preachers, and on account of the purity of his morals and the excellence of his doctrine was justly and deservedly distinguished with the title of the Angelic Doctor. Among the Thomists are celebrated Dominic of Flanders, Francisco de Vitoria, the Most Illustrious Melchor Cano, Domingo de Soto, Medina and very many others, whom it would take long to recount.

34 The second School acknowledges as its chief John Duns, who, whether he was a Scot by country (a surname that is still given to him even now and is carried over to the sect founded by him), or was born at Dunstan in Northumberland, or in the village of Duns in Ulster (for the Writers are not agreed about this), entered the Order of Minors and flourished chiefly at the beginning of the fourteenth century. His subtle wit, and the Wisdom answering to it, brought forth the title of Subtle Doctor; and both together brought it about that, while he held the Theological Chair at Oxford, thirty thousand Scholars and more flocked together to hear him. Among the followers of Scotus there excelled Francis of Meyronnes, who had received the doctrine while his Master was still living, John Punch, Bartholomew Mastrius, Martin Meurisse, and Claude Frassen, a celebrated Scotist, who was taken from among the living in the eleventh year of this century (m).

35 The third sect is that of the Nominalists, who contended that names and words are the object of Logic, and whose Doctor was William of Ockham, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, and a disciple of Scotus. The Scholastics are also divided into Realists and Nominalists. The matter of this disagreement, moreover, was furnished by the treatment of universals, since the former contended that universal natures exist, as it were, in reality, while the latter affirmed that they are constituted only in words.

§. IV.

(m) Wadding, in the Bibliotheca Minorum.

[p. 11]

§ . I V.

Innovators in Philosophy who Revived the Ancient Doctrine.

36

About the middle of the seventeenth century Galileo, the excellent

Mathematician of the Grand Duke of Tuscany (n), shook off the yoke of the custom grown inveterate in the Schools and tried new paths. Following in his footsteps, very many Men outstanding in learning restored the Mechanical philosophy.

37 Pierre Gassendi, Royal Professor of Mathematics in the Academy of Paris, was born in the year 1562. He put together a system of the Epicurean Philosophy, rejecting those things which could not well be reconciled with Religion. And indeed the tenets of Epicurus as emended by him so commended themselves to the Learned that from this eminent restorer the Gassendist sect arose.

38 Certain men devised a new kind of Philosophy, called the Philosophy of the Christians. Of their number is Thomas Burnet in the Sacred Theory of the Earth, where he busies himself with interpreting Moses, but most wretchedly distorts the Mosaic narrative. To him must be joined the Theory of Whiston; both of these, however, were refuted by learned Men. To the same class belong Edmund

Dickinson in his Physica vetus et nova, and John Comenius in his Physica ad lumen divinum reformata. His hypotheses were for the most part retained by Johann

Bayer in the Work entitled Ostium et atrium naturae.

39 At this point mention must now be made of the restored Philosophy of the Chemists, and of those who as it were dug it out of the ashes, cultivated it, and rendered this discipline Experimental, by laboriously scrutinizing nature, subjecting bodily things to trials, and putting useful experience in place of the sterile speculations of others. That the origin of metallurgical Chemistry is most ancient is shown, among others, by the celebrated Boerhaave (o). Paracelsus is said to have revived the Chemical art, chiefly among the Germans, whence he is also called the Father of the Chemists. That part of this discipline which comprises metallurgy was cultivated, after Georg Agricola, by Lazarus Ercker, Joachim Becher and Johann Kunckel. Chemistry was made useful to Medicine and Physics by

Boyle, Slare, Homberg, Geoffroy, Lémery the Younger, Hoffmann, and the celebrated Hermann Boerhaave, who brings forward these and others.

¶¶¶¶¶ 2                           §. V.

(n) Born at Pisa in the year 1564.

(o) Elements of Chemistry, vol. 1, pt. 1, On the History of the Art.

[p. 12]

§ . V.

The Newer Eclectic Philosophy, with Bacon of Verulam as its

Author.

40

Of the newer Eclectic Philosophy, namely of that which has gained not only approvers but also cultivators, the parent is held to be Francis Bacon of Verulam, born in England in the year 1561. Others throughout England, stirred by the lead of this Man, cultivated the Philosophy sketched and shaped by him. The chief were

Boyle, Wilkins, Willis, Christopher and Matthew Wren, from whom the Royal

Society of England took its origin, founded under Royal auspices in the year 1660.

And this Eclectic manner of philosophizing held sway among the English almost until the times of Newton, by whose authority it passed into a sectarian one.

41 The same thing happened in France: for Descartes, born in the year 1569, after he had passed through the philosophical course in the College of La Flèche and had completed journeys through various provinces, published the system of his doctrine that he had worked out, and found adversaries by far the fiercest, but also adherents and vigorous champions, who, spread far and wide, formed a sect named

Cartesian from the name of its Author. Among these the chief are held to be

François Bayle, Antoine Le Grand, Jacques Rohault, Nicolas Malebranche, D. de

Molières, Hartsoeker, Purchot and others. This, however, must here be noted: that by the lead, or the example, or the counsel of Descartes the manner of philosophizing was changed, and the Mechanical sect flourished.

42 In England, as far as the Cartesian manner of philosophizing had penetrated, another Philosophy was inaugurated by Isaac Newton, who was brought into the light in the forty-second year of the last century; and it afterwards passed into a sectarian one, and is today defended with great zeal by very many. That eminent

Man, namely, rejecting the hypotheses of Descartes and conjectures of every kind, established new rules of philosophizing, holding that nothing ought to be admitted in Philosophy except what either experiments or reasons invincibly demonstrate.

He set out the foundations of his doctrine partly in the excellent work which he entitled Mathematical Principles of Philosophy, illustrated with Commentaries by the most celebrated Le Seur and Jacquier, partly in the Opticks. In these he everywhere uses the greatest moderation, professing that natural things are considered by him only mathematically, and that their physical causes are not inquired into: wherefore he made use of certain general terms, by which he designated abstract notions after the manner of Geometers.

43 This sect numbers celebrated Men, men who for their skill in experimenting [p. 13] and in making calculations are especially illustrious: so that it is for this reason called

Newtonian from the name of its Author, but Mathematical on account of its method of treatment. It is pleasing, for honor’s sake, to name in particular Keill, Roger Cotes, ’s

Gravesande, Musschenbroek, Clarke, MacLaurin, Jurin, Desaguliers, Krafft; and, to say nothing of others, the theory of Newton finds plain favor with the more recent

Astronomers.

44 In Germany an Eclectic-Exotic kind of Philosophy unfolded itself through

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, born at Leipzig in the year 1646. He praised the

Scholastics’ manner of philosophizing; and, having undertaken to restore to its former standing their authority, hitherto shaken and all but trampled underfoot, he also touches in his works on what pertains to rational and moral Philosophy; but he accomplished greater things in the higher Mathematics.

45 He published a natural Philosophy mixed with the principles of Descartes, comprising it in two little books, a New Physical Hypothesis and a Theory of Abstract

Motion; he was, moreover, the first to lay down the distinction of forces into living and dead, and to teach that the former must be estimated in a far different way from the latter. In Metaphysics he showed himself exotic in the highest degree, by introducing the principle of sufficient reason, asserting monads and a pre-established harmony, and defending the perfection of the world far too much. The principles of Leibniz were cultivated by Christian Wolff, famous in this our age for the volumes he has published, in which he comprised universal Mathematics, Logic, Metaphysics, Ethics and

Physics. I do not care to list the adherents of either of the two, since they have neither greatly distinguished themselves by their writings nor propagated the doctrine more widely.

§. VI.

The Efforts of the Moderns in Cultivating the Parts of Philosophy.

46

It remains for us now to weave together the history of those who, after the restoration of the study of letters, whether within private walls or by the combined labors of many, emended and illustrated particular parts of Philosophy. In doing this, the names chiefly of the Moderns will be brought forward, including those Authors whom we have so far placed in no sect; at the same time, however, it will be necessary to recall to mind those also whose efforts have already been made plain before.

47 Rational Philosophy, besides Lorenzo Valla, Rudolph Agricola, Juan Luis Vives,

Bacon, Descartes, Gassendi and Hobbes, whom their differing periods set apart, some more widely, others less, was taken up for emendation by Peter Ramus, born in

France in the year 1515, with such success that the Ramist Dialectic commended itself exceedingly to many [p. 14] on this account, that, rejecting empty subtleties, it referred that discipline to the use of the courts and of life, and above all to the reading of the ancient Writers. Hence it came about that it gained both numerous disciples and eminent men as patrons: in France, Omer Talon; in Germany, Franz Fabricius, Sturm, Chytraeus.

48 Among the Cartesian Writers on Logic there stand out the Author of the Art of Thinking (L’Art de penser), whether he was Arnauld or someone else (p), and Malebranche, who treated at length the art of seeking the truth. There were also those who deduced the precepts of Logic from Mathematical principles; a work of this kind was published by Erhard Weigel, entitled in this form: Analysis Aristotelica ex Euclide restituta, etc. Likewise Walther von Tschirnhaus, in the book whose title is Medicina mentis. To the same class belongs the Logic of Christian Wolff, which he composed by the Mathematical method, illustrated with higher examples. Those Writers on Logic who seem to deserve the name of Eclectics are generally reckoned to be these: John Locke; Christian Thomasius; Mariotte; Poiret; Jean Le Clerc; Jean- Pierre de Crousaz; Andreas Rüdiger; Fortunato da Brescia; Antonio Genovesi; the celebrated Luís António Verney, who also published at Valencia a Method of Studying under the feigned name of Father Barbadiño; Honoré Fabri, Dominique Buffier, Noël Regnault, Cochet, and others.

49 Metaphysics and Logic, since they lend each other mutual service, have been joined together by most of the authors of Logic just indicated. Morhof says that Descartes and Honoré Fabri were reformers of Metaphysics; he then brings forward Henry More’s Enchiridion Metaphysicum and Thomas White’s Euclides Metaphysicus, and in the latter he censures the method. Finally, he commends the little book of Juan Luis Vives On First Philosophy. As for others, a great many may be counted who treated parts of this discipline. Ontology, Cosmology, Psychology and natural Theology were expounded in ample volumes by Wolff, following the doctrine of Leibniz. Nor were the studies of others lacking, although they pursued these several subjects in a somewhat different way, and also less expressly. Among the rest there were renowned Clauberg, Du Hamel, Le Grand, Régis, Buddeus, Le Clerc, Purchot, Corsini, Cudworth, Clarke, Nieuwentyt, Derham, and all those who, by fighting against the Atheists, deserved best of natural Theology. To their number must be joined, more recently, the celebrated Antonio Genovesi. The doctrine, moreover, of first truths, as a particular part of Metaphysics, was unfolded as vigorously as it was elegantly and skillfully by the celebrated Verney and by Father Buffier.

50 But some have abused this most excellent and most useful part of Philosophy, while either, granting too much to the soul and to ideas, they rushed headlong into

Idealism,

(p) Some say the Author of this work is Nicole, others D. de Trigny, others several men of Port- Royal.

[p. 15]

Idealism and Egoism, like fanatics and enthusiasts; or while, on the opposite side, not separating the mind from the affection of the body, and wrongly disparaging the excellence of the noblest being, they entangled themselves in the foul error of Materialism. Most impudently, and at the same time most unskillfully of all, this matter was handled by Benedict Spinoza, whom one may call an abortive vagabond of Philosophy, and something viler than a man.

51 Many increased moral Philosophy by their writings, but not all advanced it equally as its dignity deserved. For Hobbes and Spinoza indeed contaminated this doctrine with principles full of poison. As for the rest, namely Montaigne, Grotius, Pufendorf, Buddeus, Selden, Heineccius, Cumberland, Wolff and others, what is to be thought of them beginners must necessarily learn from their own masters in this discipline. Here again the most learned Buffier performed excellent service, comprising a treatise On Civil Society in four books, to which he added his remarks on the moral doctrine of Aristotle, Cicero, Gassendi, Pufendorf, Silvain Régis, Pierre Charron and the Scholastics. The Ethical precepts of the rest, such as Du Hamel, Purchot and Corsini, are in any case in everyone’s hands. Likewise the celebrated Genovesi comprised Moral philosophy in the Work entitled Diceosina: ovvero Filosofia del Giusto, e dell’Onesto.

52 The Mathematical disciplines, bound to Physics by an intimate agreement and serviceable to the life and society of men, have been cultivated by a great many of the Moderns. It is by no means our purpose to review them one by one, since we know that this has been done, among others, by the celebrated Wolff (r). We shall bring forward only the chief ones, and those who cannot be unknown to a Philosopher.

53 And of Astronomy, indeed, there were eminent restorers in the fifteenth century of Christ: Georg Peurbach; Johann Regiomontanus; Copernicus; Tycho Brahe, famed for his arrangement of the world system; Kepler, Galileo; Huygens; Hevelius; de la Hire; Newton; Cassini, etc. It would take long to bring together all those who developed the various parts of Mathematics. Among others, these too claim a place here: Christopher Clavius, Paul Guldin, Scheiner, Grimaldi, Claude Milliet de Chales, Riccioli, D. de la Caille, D. Clairaut, Guido Grandi, Father Cametti, Abbot of Vallombrosa, and D. La Lande, who last of all, but above all, has treated of Astronomical matters.

54 Finally, with how great accessions the Studious searchers of Nature have enriched natural Philosophy cannot be defined in a few words. For who could comprise in a page the manifold discoveries, the perfection added to the discoveries of the ancients, the number, manner and elegance of the experiments, and in them the accuracy, the attention, the selection? We shall briefly sketch both the restorers of Physics and the new form of this discipline.

After

(r) Elem. of Mathematics, vol. V.

[p. 16]

55 After those already named before, namely Bacon, Gassendi and Descartes, there followed exceedingly illustrious Men: Galileo of Florence. He undertook to treat the doctrine of motion by a clear method; he demonstrated the weight of the air, or held up a light to the others for discovering it; to him is also attributed the discovery of the Astronomical telescope, of the sunspots, and of the Satellites of Jupiter, although others will have it that the former were detected earlier by Father Scheiner, the latter by Simon Marius.

56 This master of his was followed in advancing Physics by Evangelista Torricelli, from whom the use of tubes adapted to measuring the weight of the air took its origin. What shall I say of the remaining discoverers and discoveries? Andrea Cesalpino,

Chief Physician to Clement VIII, Supreme Pontiff, illustrated Physics by having detected, or explained, the circulation of the blood, although the English attribute this to Harvey, others to the Spaniard Gómez Pereira, others to others.

57 Pecquet, in the last century, first detected the receptacle of the Chyle. And how much did others toil in the various parts of natural science? Boyle, Digby,

Homberg, Lémery, Boerhaave in Chemistry; Grew, Sam. Morland, Camerarius,

Vaillant, Morison, Hermann, Ray, Rivinus, Tournefort, Linnaeus in Botany? Indeed

Mariotte, by means of trials made on motion, on plants, waters, colors, etc.; Pascal, by investigating the weight of the air and weighing the equilibrium of liquids;

Newton, by his optical observations and the bringing of Geometry over to natural science; Otto Guericke, by the invention of the air pump, won great light for Physics and for themselves a matching name in the republic of letters. To say nothing now of the efforts of Richer, of both Cassinis, of Picard, Maraldi, Maupertuis and his

Companions; of the microscopical secrets of Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Power,

Hartsoeker, etc.; of the Electrical experiments of Jallabert, Watson, Waitz, Bose,

Nollet, Musschenbroek, Franklin, Beccaria, Paulian; of the various studies of

Hauksbee, Fermat, Carré, Petit, Sauveur, Malézieu, Ramazzini, Dodart, Santorio,

Feuillée, Hales, Cotes, Ozanam, Desaguliers, Borelli, Malpighi, Redi, both Bernoullis,

Varignon, Hermann, Bülfinger, Poleni, Euler, Grandi, Teichmeyer, Krafft, Verdries,

Sturm, Wolff, and very many others, whose memory will very often recur in the

Physics.

## §. VII

The Academies of Sciences, Usefully Established.

58

Further, how great are the accessions that natural Philosophy owes to the

Academies of Sciences, not one of the learned is unaware. Nor [p. 17] is it our intention, however, while we present these, to list all the Gymnasia and public Schools established in various places from Charlemagne onward; still less does it please us to enumerate the private little gatherings of a few, which were, namely, of short life and hardly fitted for the public utility. The name of Academy was given, while Paul II, Supreme Pontiff, governed the Church, to the College of those residing at Rome who had undertaken some restoration of the fallen ancient learning.

59 In the same city celebrated Academies afterwards opened, namely: that of the Humorists, founded by Paolo Mancini, a Roman nobleman, so called from the rain falling from the clouds, because this was their Emblem, with the motto Redit agmine dulci [it returns in a sweet stream]. The other was that of the Lynxes; they took this name from the gift of the Lynx, which excels in sight, so as to intimate their perspicacity in scrutinizing the works of nature; and this Academy, founded either by Federico Cesi or by Angelo, son of Federico, cultivated chiefly Chemistry, and produced illustrious men, Galileo Galilei, Fabio Colonna, and others. There were likewise several Colleges at Rome, such as those of the Ordinati, the Delfici, the Incitati, the Partenii, the Rinnovati, etc. (s); at Venice the Veneta Academy flourished, and also another, of the Incogniti. At Padua the Academy of the Eterei took its origin from Scipione Gonzaga; another comprised the Animosi Academicians. Nor did the other parts of Italy lack their Academies: at Naples, Siena, Ravenna, Ferrara, Verona, Milan, Bologna, etc.

60 In Tuscany, at Florence, besides the Academy of the Bran-Sifters, or della Crusca (so named because in their disputations the Academicians separated the purer flour, namely the food of minds, from the bran, that is, from errors, being nevertheless intent with their chief care on imparting elegance to the Italian language), there shone forth the Experimental Academy, or del Cimento, by the munificence of Leopold, Grand Duke of Tuscany: by which it came about both that outstanding Philosophers were associated in it, and that spirit, aids and opportunities for setting up experiments were furnished to the Academicians. Britain followed the example when, about the year 1663, the Royal Society of England was erected at London by the authority of King Charles II. France, stirred by the rise of the Academies of Italy and England, and moved also by the happy successes of her own (namely of the French Academy (Académie Françoise), instituted in the year 1637 by Louis XIII through the agency of Cardinal Richelieu, and likewise of the other Academy, of Sculpture and Painting, which unfolded itself in 1664), saw the Academy of Sciences born under the auspices of King Louis XIV in the year 1666, which in the year 1699 received a new rule by the King’s will. In Germany, although a beginning of the German College of the Curious of Nature was made in the year 1652, it must nevertheless be confessed that it long remained stuck in its infancy, on account of the distance between its Colleagues, the lack of patrons, etc.

¶¶¶¶¶¶                                 61 For

(s) Giovanni Ferro, in the Theater of Emblems.

[p. 18]

61 For this reason the Emperor Leopold the Great in 1670 added spurs to the

Academicians, holding out to them the hope of his patronage, so that they might devote their efforts to promoting this business. And indeed the studies of the Academy of the Curious of Nature answered the wishes of so great a Prince; for in that same year, namely 1670, they began to publish the Miscellanea Curiosa. In the year 1690 an

Academy of Philosophers was formed at Bologna, who were to share among themselves the sciences pertaining to Mathematics and Physics; it afterwards, in the year

1712, took on another face through the favor and gifts of Count Marsigli, and was named the Institute of Sciences and Arts of Bologna. Frederick, King of Prussia, established the Academy of Berlin; Peter, Emperor of Muscovy, that of Petersburg. In our own Spain, moreover, besides the Royal Academy of Seville and the Cantabrian, there is no lack of others for the cultivation and increase of the Sciences and Arts. Now, what and how great advantages have flowed, chiefly into Physics, from the

Academies established by the favor, liberality and care of Princes, and what are to be expected hereafter, is easily seen. The former the books of the Physicists declare; the latter the industry, sagacity and ardor of the Academicians promise.

## §. VIII

The Institution of Literary Journals.

62

What, finally, do we judge it to be that the newer Physics owes to the institution of Journals, or literary acts? In the sixty-fifth year of the last century (for before this the learned world lacked these aids) a man of great mind and most zealous for the promotion of letters, Monsieur Sallo, Senator of the Supreme Court at Paris, formed the plan of preparing universal Journals; this he himself also first carried out, and he entitled the work Diarium Eruditorum (Journal des Sçavans). In the year 1666

the celebrated Gallois took over the author’s labor, laboriously compiling the Journal continuously week by week up to the year 1674; and it was afterwards carried on by the celebrated de la Roque. The History and Memoirs of the Royal Academy of

Sciences (Histoire & Mémoires de l’Académie des Sciences) are communicated annually to the learned world.

63 Next, in the first year of this century, under the auspices of the Duke of

Maine, the Acta Trivoltiensia (Mémoires de Trévoux, pour servir à l’Histoire des Sciences, &

des beaux Arts) began to appear. Italy too, in the year 1668, published learned Journals

(Giornale de’ Letterati). In Germany certain men of letters from the Electorate of

Saxony, with joint labor, produced about the year 1682 the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig, or Journals. Holland, not suffering its own industry to be found wanting here, brought out at Amsterdam in the year 1684 the Excerpta Reipublicae Literariae

(Nouvelles de la République des lettres).

[p. 19]

64 In the thirteenth year of this present century the Diarium Literarium (Journal Litteraire à la Haye) appeared at The Hague, several men joining their labors. I pass over the transactions of the English Society (Transactions Philosophiques), published from the year 1665; the Literary Journals of Great Britain at the beginning of this century; the Bibliotheca Germanica, published in the year 1720, or the literary History of Germany and its Regions. In the year 1737 there began to be brought out in our Spain el Diario de los Literatos, an excellent work indeed; and would that it had been carried on down to this day.

65 Nor do I mention the Acta of the Institute of Bologna, the Petersburg and the Swedish, the Learned Mercuries (les Mercures Sçavans), etc. In this class must be placed the monuments of those who have collected the History of nature; the way being led (after the example of Aristotle and other more ancient writers) by Gaius Plinius Secundus, or the Elder, who, famous in the age of Vespasian and Titus, compiled thirty-seven books of natural History; he was followed by Solinus and Dioscorides; likewise by Claudius Aelian, author of seventeen books of the History of animals, in the time of the Emperor Hadrian. With these, I say, leading the way, the following treated this subject: Conrad Gesner, born in Switzerland in the year 1516, a distinguished Physicist and Philologist, and for this reason given the surname of the German Pliny, who, besides other things, comprised a History of animals in four volumes; Rembert Dodoens, born in Brabant in 1517, Physician to the Emperors Maximilian II and Rudolph II, famous for the Histories he published of plants, flowers, etc.; Ulisse Aldrovandi, celebrated for having written a natural Dendrology, a Museum metallicum, a history of Monsters, of Serpents, and also of Dragons.

66 To these must be added Bacon’s Sylva sylvarum, or Ten Centuries of natural History, and the Works on Natural History of M. de Buffon (Description du Cabinet du Roy). What Physics in particular owes to these aids too, there is no leisure to relate one by one. For how many heads of this science have been called into examination? How many phenomena of nature discovered? How many errors wiped from minds, doubts uprooted, opinions emended? These things are treated at greater length by Regnault, who shows diffusely that Physics has in these last centuries been rendered more perfect in every part: I. By bringing the conjectures of the ancients to examination. II. By scrutinizing nature itself. III. By treating the discipline according to the laws of method. IV. By requiring observations, repeating experiments, inventing useful instruments. V. By establishing Academies. VI. By instituting Journals.

67 And with this it has pleased us to conclude the History of Philosophy: which indeed, if you compare it with the lengthy works of Laertius, Gassendi, Horn, Stanley, Jonsius, Vossius and Brucker, you will understand to be nothing other than an Epitome; you will find it, however, arranged on this principle, that the chief heads of this subject have been treated thoroughly, the rest touched upon, and, finally, nothing omitted of those things which pertain to, and suffice for, the first instruction of Philosophers.

## OF THE NEWER PHILOSOPHY

## PA RT I . ELEMENTS OF LOGIC

[p. 1]

## ELEMENTS

O F T H E N E W E R P H I L O S O P H Y.

P RO L E G O M E N A .

hilosophy, whose principal parts we shall set forth as it were in a nut1

P          shell, is the knowledge of the true, the good and the honorable, acquired by

the light of nature alone and by reasoning drawn from it. Reasoning, or right reason, is the ready faculty of eliciting truths from other truths with which they are connected. From this it is easily seen that Sceptical philosophy, since it professes that nothing can be known with certainty, does not deserve the name of Philosophy, whereas Dogmatic philosophy does.

2 Nor is it obscure that this name is not to be attributed to a knowledge of the true and the good which we have either received from our elders, handed down from hand to hand, or draw from the precepts of some learned man.

Hence Traditionary and Sectarian Philosophy are banished, since neither of them is derived from right reason. For the first rests wholly on the authority of the elders, the second on the authority of one man, who is an oracle to his sectaries. Hence the divisions of Philosophy that are commonly offered are less than accurate; for you would no more accurately call Sceptical and Sectarian philosophy Philosophy than call a statue a man.

3 As for that Eclectic Philosophy, in Latin Elective, it is the one in which we seek wisdom by reason alone, and govern reason by the experiments of the senses and by observations, by inner consciousness, by reasoning, and by authority in those things that cannot be known by any other way. In this manner of philosophizing one does not ask who said a thing, but how rightly, that is, how conformably to reason. That one must philosophize in this way is splendidly demonstrated by Lactantius, whose passage I shall give whole; for it is most worthy of being read.

4 “Wherefore,” he says, “in that matter above all in which the conduct of life is at stake, each man ought to trust himself and rely on his own judgment and his own senses for investigating and weighing the truth, rather than, by believing, be deceived by the errors of others, as if he himself

A [p. 2] were devoid of reason. God has given wisdom to all according to each one’s share, so that they might both search out things unheard and weigh things heard. Nor, because our elders went before us in time, did they also go before us in wisdom; for if wisdom is given to all equally, it cannot be seized beforehand by those who came first. It cannot be diminished, like the light and brightness of the sun: for as the sun is the light of the eyes, so wisdom is the light of the human heart. Wherefore, since to be wise, that is, to seek the truth, is innate in all men, those deprive themselves of wisdom who without any judgment approve the discoveries of their elders and are led by others in the manner of cattle. But what deceives them is this: once the name of elders is set before them, they do not think it can happen either that they themselves are wiser, because they are called younger, or that those others were foolish, because they are named elders.”

5 All these things are to be understood of the natural sciences, such as, for example, Philosophy is. For of him who most arrogantly, with his brief human reason, insults the authority of God, that is, the highest reason, what else am I to say than that he casts off all reason? He who does this is not a Philosopher; he is not even rational. In natural science, therefore, we commend that freedom which approves no estrangement from the Church, none from her dogmas. This is the Eclectic Philosophy, to which I judge you must apply yourselves with all care and all zeal. For it is that philosophy, to speak with Tully, whose study, if anyone disparages it, I truly do not understand what it is that he thinks worthy of praise.

6 Since, further, Philosophy is designed for the true utility of man, and the end is of the same kind as the means: it follows that the subtler speculations of the Peripatetics about things that either cannot be searched out by human reason, or at least can bring no profit to the human race, will belong to the study of wisdom the less, the less they are joined with the true happiness of man, which, with the Theologians of better note, we judge to consist in knowing God, the founder of nature, and the beginning and end of everything true, good and honorable.

7 Since, finally, Philosophy consists in the knowledge of the true and the good: that part of Philosophy which prepares the mind for the knowledge of the true is usually called Instrumental, or Logic; that which imbues it with that knowledge, Theoretical; and that which finally leads it to the true good, Practical. The Theoretical, since it imbues the mind with the knowledge of the true, either inquires into truths about God, spirits and being, or investigates what is true concerning the causes of natural things. In the former case it is called Metaphysics, in the latter Physics. Finally, since the Practical shows the way to the good: it is either what is good in general, or in particular what is just, becoming, or useful, that it

[p. 3] teaches. Of the good in general Ethics treats; of the just, the honorable and the becoming, Natural Law; of the useful, Politics and Economics. But since the narrowness of time does not allow me to linger too long in explaining all the parts of Philosophy, I shall explain Logic, Metaphysics and Ethics somewhat more briefly, perhaps, than was fitting; Physics much more fully.

8 But before I begin the work, I humbly invoke God, the Creator and Governor of all things, and I beg him not to fail me as I write, but to flood my mind with his light, lest I go astray in these lucubrations; rather, that I may hand down such precepts as will lead the minds of boys not only to a thorough understanding of these things contained in the visible world, but also (what we ought most of all to care for) in some manner to those heavenly things and to the blessed vision of the Maker; and that he not permit anything alien to the Roman Church or to the sanctioned Laws to slip from us unawares.

9 But if through human infirmity we shall have erred, whatever we have said we condemn: and we most willingly submit ourselves and all that is ours to the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff. And if at times we shall praise some heretical author, we praise the man’s learning and detest his wickedness, nor do we propose him for reading except to those to whom the most grave judges whose office it is have granted leave to read.

10 But you, most excellent Young Men, I both admonish and exhort humbly to call upon God, that he may grant you a good mind, and earnestly to pray to the Angelic Master St. Thomas Aquinas, that he may obtain for you from God, Best and Greatest, sharpness of understanding. For unless you first imbue your mind with the precepts of God, never (believe me) will you attain the true Philosophy. God grant that, just as I undertake a labor of this kind for your sake and to lead you to the best studies, you in turn may answer to me and to my efforts.

## OF THE ELEMENTS

## OF THE NEWER PHILOSOPHY

PA RT I . B O O K I .

## ELEMENTS OF LOGIC

## CHAPTER I

On the nature and constitution of Logic. 1

Since Philosophy is the knowledge of the true, and Logic prepares the intellect for that knowledge, it can very well be defined as the Discipline that refines the mind so that it may attain the truth in every place and time, or more briefly: the

Science of finding and setting forth the truth. And since the truth is established either with certainty or only probably, the Logician must be concerned with both.

2 And although all men, unless hindered by disease, are strong in right reason, that is, in the faculty of reasoning, so that it cannot be denied that there is a natural Logic, it does not follow from this that the Artificial is to be neglected; for art perfects nature, and the intellect must be furnished not only with the faculty but also with readiness in reasoning, and indeed with method in arranging thoughts and reasonings. For man enjoys, for example, the faculty of counting under the guidance of nature alone, and the power of dancing, of speaking, of persuading; and yet no one doubts that Arithmetic, the Art of Dancing, Grammar and

Rhetoric are most useful. The utility of Logic in every kind of learning is therefore altogether to be admired. For what other end of all our studies do we set before ourselves than to find the truth and, having found it, to communicate it to others?

3 Zeno of Elea, to whom the origin of this science is commonly credited, once cultivated Logic with great care. The Megarians, Stoics and Epicureans also cultivated it. We shall apply ourselves to it with keen zeal, [p. 5] so that we may set forth all the best precepts that we have received as handed down by the Moderns, in the order that seems to us most suited to the nature of this discipline; and it seems most convenient to consider first the nature of the human intellect, then the nature of truth, and finally to inquire how truth is to be found and set forth.

## CHAPTER II. On the Nature of the human intellect, and on the operations of

the mind.

The intellect is occupied rather with the True, the will with the Good. Since, therefore, Logic teaches the method of finding and setting forth the truth, it is easily seen that it cannot be taught unless we have thoroughly examined the powers of the mind, or human intellect, and its operations.

5 This living being which we call Man consists of Body and Spirit. In the body all these are found: extension, divisibility, solidity, figurability, mobility of parts, etc. Spirit, on the other hand, is that which is in man and is not body, nor is seen by anyone: we infer, however, that some incorporeal directing principle is present from the things, conspicuous enough, that take place in the bodily machine; while as for the internal operations of the mind, these are established, in the end, by the innermost conviction of man himself. For we experience that there is in us something that knows and wills. For we both know our friends and wish them well, and we turn our limbs at our pleasure. For I know for certain that I move my arm if I will to, and do not move it if I do not will to. Accordingly, there is something in me that presides over this machinery and rules and governs it.

6 In turn, if our body is affected by the impact of an external body, the mind feels it by means of those organs of our machinery which are called senses: for if you bring fire near the skin, this affection of the body is felt by the mind. Likewise I feel pain when a thorn pricks my finger. The body, therefore, obeys the mind and carries out what the mind commands, and in turn the mind itself feels whatever is perceived by means of the senses. But that the one

[p. 6] is moved by the other and depends on it, this is the very thing that is called the complexion, or commerce, of the mind and the body.

7 Whatever, then, that may be which understands and wills (of which we shall have to speak in another place), this much is certain: that there is in man something which knows and wills, which we call the soul, the mind, the rational soul, the spirit, etc. Finally, it is certain that body and mind are two altogether distinct substances. The mind perceives the forms of things, discerns, judges, reasons, feels, is stirred by passions, etc., things which no one would attribute to the body except foolishly: the soul, therefore, is not body.

8 We have also found that our mind has this peculiar to it, that it understands, so that in understanding it elicits one cognition after another rightly and in order, and also that it acts freely. That is to say, when the mind makes an object present to itself, it perceives it. But what an idea is, and what a perception, is a matter of great disagreement. (a) In order, however, that all equivocation be removed, we lay down first that by the name of idea we mean any perception whatever of any thing whatever. Every notion, therefore, or comprehension, or perception, whatever it may be, is called by us an idea. Hence, e.g., the notion or perception of a figure, a plant, an animal, a pleasure, etc., is an idea.

9 We perceive the external things that affect our sense organs. Now this is the law of sensations, that whenever some change is produced by a sensible object in a duly

constituted

(a) There are those who hold that ideas and perceptions are the same thing, and say that they consist in motions of the senses and of the brain. So Hobbes, Leviathan, pt. 1, ch. 3, 4, and in Elem. Philosoph. ch. 25, art. 2. There are those who say that ideas and perceptions are the same cognition of the mind, yet in such a way that the same cognition, inasmuch as it is referred to the mind which perceives, is called perception; inasmuch as it is referred to the object of which it is the image, and which is perceived, idea. So Arnauld and Locke, Essai sur l’Entendement Humain, in the Preface, and bk. 2, ch. 8, §. 7, 8. Others altogether separate perceptions from ideas, and think that God impresses the ideas of things on the human mind. So Malebranche, Recherche de la Verité, bk. 3. Lastly, others say that material ideas are affections of the senses and of the brain, while intellectual ones, which correspond to the material, are perceptions of material things. So Wolff, from whom the Scholastics do not dissent, though they call the material idea an intellection. Amid so great a disagreement among the most learned men, it would be arrogant to wish to put forward anything as certain. [p. 7] constituted sense organ, so often there arises in the soul a certain particular sensation corresponding to this change. Thus the motions of the senses affect the brain and impress something on it, from which the mind perceives the things that strike the sense, (b) as Haller (c) confirms with very many examples in his notes to Boerhaave. This perception of the mind is called an idea.

10 When the intellect acquires simple ideas, that is, when it makes an object present to itself and perceives it without referring it to another, e.g. when it knows the sun, or a horse, this cognition is called simply perception, or, as the Scholastics put it, Simple apprehension, that is, a cognition affirming or denying nothing; but when the intellect compares two ideas with each other, refers one to the other, and perceives that it agrees with the other, or not, e.g. when it says The sun is bright, The sun is not a horse, this cognition is judgment, or the act of the intellect by which we affirm or deny something of an object. When the intellect compares three ideas with one another, it is said to Reason. Reasoning, or discourse, is the action of the mind by which we put together several ideas, of which one depends on another, so as to uncover what lay hidden. The question is asked: is air heavy? This is not at once clearly apparent; I therefore use reasoning in this way: whatever, placed on a scale-pan, presses it down is heavy; air placed on a scale-pan presses it down: therefore air is heavy.

11 Further, our mind puts together several ideas of things very different from one another, as when it joins a lion’s body and wings to a human head and feigns a new animal. Sometimes, on the contrary, the mind as it were disjoins one idea from another: as when we think of the whiteness of a wall without thinking of the wall. Sometimes it arranges its thoughts and reasonings in order, the more easily to see whether one ought to proceed from some to others. This operation of the mind is called Method. Sometimes, after the matter has been argued and disputed on both sides, and it is not clearly understood

on

(b) That this is so is plainly shown even from this: that a very acute disease of the head, or a fracture of the skull, or diseases of that kind which have occurred in the brain and the head, have sometimes destroyed all memory of things, and sometimes taken away the understanding of things. This also happens in the demented and the insane, who through a defect of the brain speak incoherently and senselessly. And since the mind neither falls sick nor is changed, because these affections are bodily, it remains that something is impressed in the brain, from which we perceive the forms and ideas of things.

(c) Vol. 4, §. 581. [p. 8] on which side the truth stands, the mind doubts, or suspends judgment. Finally,

to pass over other things, when the mind perceives a thing again and is moreover conscious that it had known that same thing long before, this operation is called Memory.

12 From this it becomes manifest that there are more operations of the mind than the common Aristotelian Logicians suppose; and by them the intellect is rightly defined: the faculty of the mind which perceives, judges, reasons, disposes, etc. One must, however, keep well in mind the force and the variety of the names that signify faculties of the mind and occur here and there. Phantasy, or

Imagination, is that power of the mind by which we represent to ourselves all things expressed by a bodily image. Ingenuity is the mind’s skill in discovering and devising. Judgment is the faculty of selecting the things that are right and of using them according to the worth of the matter. And indeed the things that ingenuity composes do not always exist in reality. For I can easily join in my mind the ideas of gold and of a mountain, and form for myself the image of a golden mountain, which nevertheless does not exist outside thought. Ideas of this kind are called chimerical, or beings of reason.

13 From this, moreover, it is plain that these beings of reason are not to be confused with non-beings, which are not objects of the mind at all, since nothing can be thought about them. Thus a square circle is a non-being, because nothing whatever can even be thought about it. Since, therefore, the things that ingenuity composes do not always exist in reality, there is need of judgment to distinguish accurately the thing from the shadow, the chimera from the reality itself. Hence the more correct a man’s judgment is, the fitter he will be for finding and setting forth the truth. Hence it is also clear why those who are very strong in ingenuity are generally not so in judgment: for ingenuity is occupied in devising and composing anything whatever, whereas judgment is occupied in separating the right from the not right, which differ widely from each other.

## CHAPTER III

How are the senses related to the acquiring of ideas?

14

Although not all ideas whatsoever proceed from sense, as Locke holds (d), it is nevertheless true, if we speak of the greater part of them, that the senses are the windows of the mind, through

(d) Essai concernant l’Entendement Humain, bk. 1. [p. 9] through which the first notions enter into it, and by which it understands the other things that are outside it. But since how easily this comes about cannot be known unless we have some rough idea of the construction of the senses, we shall set down beforehand a very few things to pave the way for what follows.

15 There are five senses of the human machine, by which the ideas of things are communicated to the brain and to the mind: Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, Touch, by which names we designate five different organs. And to begin with sight: the eyes, by which it is perceived, have a peculiar and wonderful structure, which it is not the place here to elucidate minutely; let us say only that the eye is a globe composed of three principal membranes, namely the cornea, the uvea and the retina, each of which encloses its own humor. The humor that is in the middle, which is called the crystalline, is convex on both sides and has the shape of a lens. The rays of light reflected from the object body are refracted while they pass through this lens, and paint an inverted image (e) of the object on the back of the inner membrane, which they call the retina. The retina is an expansion of the innermost medullary part of the optic nerve, which reaches as far as the common sensorium, as Winslow (f) explains very well in his anatomical exposition of the human body.

16 When, therefore, the eye has been struck by light, and this impulse has been impressed on the brain by means of that nerve, there is at once an idea and perception, e.g. of a triangular figure, or of a square one, etc. These perceptions are followed by the judgment by which I declare that there exists a body of triangular figure, or of square, etc.; and this judgment follows upon the other perceptions of the senses as well.

17 The organ of Hearing is like a snail’s shell, at the bottom of which is a certain stretched membrane, which they call the Tympanum. Behind the tympanum are four movable little bones, and air within a certain twisted case which has two openings leading to the labyrinth, that is, to a tortuous passage hollowed out in the very substance of the bone; in the far part of this labyrinth the fibers of the auditory nerve spread out, and this nerve extends to the brain. Suppose you strike some piece of bronze: the motion and vibration of the bronze strike the outer air.

B                                            The

(e) That this little image contributes nothing to vision insofar as it is an image, the Modern Philosophers had, already in the age of Descartes, not only suspected but all but proved. For René Descartes himself asks: by what other little eye, then, is the aforesaid little image to be seen?

(f) Cours d’Anatomie, vol. V.

[p. 10]

The air, thus struck and compressed in the cochlea, is carried to the tympanum of the ear and sets it in motion. The tympanum in turn strikes the little bones and the air, which, entering the labyrinth, communicates that very tremor to the fibers of the auditory nerve; and this nerve makes the same impression in the brain. Here you have the idea of sound, which varies according to the different tremor of bodies. The celebrated Bernard Nieuwentyt (g), from whom we have taken these things, reports innumerable others about the ear.

18 Willis, who treats of flavors at length (h), thinks that Taste is situated chiefly in the upper surface of the tongue. Now the tongue is wrapped in certain membranes: an outer one, which is called the Epidermis; a second, which is pierced with many holes; a third, which is sprinkled with very many papillae, which pass through the second and end in the epidermis. These prominences are certain expansions of very fine nerves; and it is in these papillae of the tongue that flavor is perceived, which is explained by most Anatomists in roughly this way, and so it comes about. Saline particles, and likewise a certain very thin spirit, with which all flavorful bodies abound, strike with their sharpness the sensitive nerves of which those papillae consist. This motion is communicated to the brain. Hence the mind feels this motion, that is, has the perception of flavor.

19 In like manner Smell: that villous membrane which lines the inner part of the nostrils is woven of very many nerves stripped of epidermis, which is the reason why it is of so exquisite a sense that, when barely touched, it produces a great commotion. And this is the organ of Smell: for the very fine particles, both of oil and of volatile salt, as they call it, which are exhaled from bodies, running into that membrane, twitch the nervous papillae in one way and another; and this titillation is impressed on the brain through the nerves, and so is felt.

20 Finally, this is proper to Touch, that it does not have a definite place, as the other senses do, but is in the whole body: so that whatever part of the body we scratch, the contact of a body is felt. Nevertheless, touch resides in a peculiar manner in the tips of the fingers of the hand, for distinguishing very many things. Further, under the cuticle or epidermis, that is, under the outer membrane of the flesh, there extend the reticular membrane and the skin, which is sprinkled with innumerable nervous papillae; and these papillae, rising out of the skin like very fine little brushes, touch the epidermis itself. Hence when you touch flesh you touch a nerve, and since all the nerves

are

(g) L’Existence de Dieu demontreè par les merveilles de la Nature, Contempl. XIV.

(h) De Anima Brutorum, ch. 12. [p. 11] are led from the brain, or from the cerebellum and the spinal marrow, they very easily excite the same motion in the brain, from which the mind perceives the contact, that is, acquires the idea of touch, as Haller, Faye and Verdier (i) explain very well.

21 Hence it becomes manifest that the office of the organs is to receive the impression of bodies and to transmit it to the brain, and to do so by means of the nerves, which are most apt for accomplishing this; but that it is the mind which elicits the ideas of things according to the variety of the senses. We say, however, that the eye sees, the ear hears, etc., which is not so. For the eye only receives, together with the image, a certain motion, so to speak, which it communicates to the brain; while the mind, prompted on the occasion of such a motion, forms for itself the idea of the thing seen. But since the perception of the mind follows that motion of the organ, we therefore confuse the two, and think that the eye sees, etc.; although it is altogether hidden from us how the affections of the senses reach the brain, and how our mind perceives those motions that are impressed in the brain. Thus in almost all sensations, as Malebranche (j) very well notes, four things, though different, are confused, namely because they take place together, and as it were in one point of time.

22 The first thing that is confused is the action of the external body, that is, in heat, for example, the impulse and motion of the particles of the wood against the fibers of the hand. The second is the passion of the sense organ, that is, the agitation of the fibers of the hand arising from the impulse of the particles of fire, which agitation reaches all the way to the brain. The third is the sensation, or perception of the mind, that is, what anyone feels when he approaches the fire. The fourth is the judgment by which the mind judges that what it feels is in its hand and in the fire.

23 These four, as may be seen, are very different, and yet they are not commonly distinguished; yet there is no one who, attending to the matter, does not see that of these four, which take place in us when we are affected by some external body, the first two pertain to the body, the last two to the mind alone. These things having been said in passing, we shall have to consider somewhat more accurately how our mind forms for itself clear, distinct and adequate ideas.

## The Division of Ideas. 24

An idea, as we have already said, is the genuine image of any object whatever, which the mind contemplates immediately, or any thought whatever about any thing. Sometimes we perceive a thing in such a way that, when it presents itself again, we easily distinguish it from others; this is called a clear idea: if I cannot so distinguish a thing from another, the idea is confused. Thus, e.g., everyone, even among the common people, has a clear idea of the Moon, but not likewise of Jupiter, Mars and Saturn, stars which a man of the people will easily confuse with the fixed stars.

25 But even if I easily distinguish some thing from others, it sometimes happens that I am able to enumerate one by one all the marks that separate the thing from the rest, and sometimes not; in the first case the clear idea is distinct, in the second indistinct. E.g., when I know that a triangle can be distinguished from other figures by the number of the lines by which it is enclosed, I am said to have not only a clear but also a distinct idea of it. On the other hand, if, seeing that a magnet draws iron to itself, I separate the magnet from other stones by this mark, but cannot enumerate one by one all the other marks that set the magnet apart from other stones, I have a clear but confused idea of the magnet.

A distinct idea therefore expresses more than a clear one, and a clear idea is rightly divided into distinct and confused.

26 But if I not only have the thing and its marks enumerated, but also have a distinct idea of those very marks which enter into that distinct notion, this idea will be adequate; where it is otherwise, the idea will indeed be distinct, but inadequate. Thus, e.g., the marks by which I discern fire from other materials are light, heat, the power of setting on fire, etc. If anyone has a distinct idea of all these things, he will have an adequate notion of fire; if not, an inadequate one.

An adequate idea therefore expresses more than a distinct one; nor can we acquire adequate ideas of all things, for we do not have a distinct idea of all the adjuncts of which each thing consists; indeed, very few adequate ideas can be obtained in this life, as Wolff rightly warns on this point.

Moreover

[p. 13]

27 Further, ideas are either of Substances, or of Modes, or of Relations. For all the things we know either can exist apart from each single mode, and this we call substance; or they are modes of some thing, and these we call accidents, or modes; and among modes, again, there is something that is conceived as referred to another, and this we call relation. This division is adequate; for it is plainly impossible that there be any perception which is neither a perception of substance, nor a perception of a mode, nor a perception of some relation.

28 The whole is made clear by an example: a square piece of wood is a thing that can exist apart from the square figure, for it can be made round; and this we call substance. On the other hand, you will nowhere find squareness and roundness separately in natural bodies, and this we call an accident, or mode of substance; and if I conceive squareness as a mode proper to a body, it necessarily leads me to the knowledge of the body, and this we call relation.

29 From what has been said it becomes manifest that we do not have a clear and distinct idea of substance, but a very obscure one. For the ideas we have of particular substances are acquired by sense; but the senses reach only the modes that adorn the substance, not likewise the nature of the substance: hence substance cannot be clearly separated from other things. E.g., iron offers us the idea of a heavy, hard body, which is melted only by a great fire, which is consumed by rust, and which is altogether suited to cutting bodies, etc.; and however much we try to know the nature of iron thoroughly, we shall achieve nothing. For this idea represents nothing other than the modes of iron. Who indeed would dare to say that he finds anything else in iron besides these? Therefore the idea of iron that we have is composed of the ideas of all its modes. Since, however, we know for certain that those adjuncts can be changed, e.g. the square figure into a round one, etc., and that iron can become harder and better suited to splitting wood, without the very nature of iron being changed, we conclude that there is something in iron besides its adjuncts and properties, which we call substance and subject. But what that is, and in what it is distinguished from other things, we do not know.

30 Thus the notion of substance, as Locke rightly warns, is the idea of a thing altogether unknown to us, or the idea of a most obscure thing, which we feign to be the subject of accidents. But the idea of particular substances, as of iron and of wood, is an idea composed of the ideas of all their properties. Those, therefore, philosophize badly who hold that the nature of a thing is fully known from the properties we know. For even if we know some properties, we cannot affirm with certainty that no properties remain which are not known to us. Wherefore from the properties which we know

[p. 14] we can separate things from one another, and the more properties we discern, the more nearly we approach the knowledge of the nature; yet this is far removed from a clear and distinct perception of the essence, or nature, and much farther still from an adequate one.

31 Relations, as we have said, are ideas of which one refers to the other in such a way that one cannot be understood without the other, or that the consideration of the one involves the consideration of the other. From this we infer that those err not a little who affirm or deny something absolutely of a relative idea, and do not duly weigh the foundation of the relation. How useful this observation is for avoiding logomachies, and indeed for calming the sadder passions, cannot be told. Thus many grieve that they are poor, though they lack nothing necessary. And why so, unless because they take very rich men as the foundation of the relation, compared with whom they seem to themselves very poor? Elegantly says Seneca, (k)

To bear the lot that all men suffer

No one refuses.

No one believes himself wretched, though he be.

Take away the fortunate, take far away

The rich in gold, take away those who

Cleave rich fields with a hundred oxen;

The poor man’s downcast spirits will rise.

No one is wretched, except by Comparison.

C H A P T E R V.

On singular, particular and universal ideas, where also of the five predicables. 32

Some ideas represent to us the thing itself in the individual, e.g. Alexander; others what the thing has in common with certain others, e.g. his royal dignity; others what the thing has in common with all things of the same nature, e.g. humanity. Ideas of the first kind are called singular, of the second particular

(k) In Troad. V. 1016. [p. 15] particular, of the third universal. Universals, therefore, are not outside the mind,

or, as the Scholastics put it, a parte rei [on the side of the thing]. Universal man is nothing but an idea; for the men who exist are singular.

33 The Peripatetics, following Porphyry, made five classes of universals:

Genus, Species, Specific Difference, Property and Accident. Genus is defined by

Porphyry as a universal notion which is predicated of many things differing in species, when it is asked what a thing is: e.g. animal is the genus of man and of horse, because it designates the notion common to both, and it is what is usually offered by one who answers someone asking what a man, what a horse is. Species is a universal notion which is said of many things differing in number, as their whole essence, as man, which is predicated of Peter, and Paul, and the other individuals of human nature. An Individual, moreover, is that which cannot be divided into several things such as it is itself: e.g. Peter. Specific Difference is a universal notion which is said of many things differing in number, as a metaphysical form, determining the genus to such a species, e.g. rationality.

34 Property is said in four ways: first, what belongs to one species alone, but not to the whole of it, as to be a Physician. Second, conversely, what belongs to the whole species, but not to it alone, as to be two-footed. Third, what belongs to one species alone and to the whole of it, but not always, as in man to be conversing. Fourth, what belongs to the whole species, and always: such in man is the faculty of discourse, or of conversing; for, as Cicero excellently says: for in this one thing above all we excel the beasts, that we converse with one another, and that we can express our thoughts by speaking. Accident is a universal notion which can be present to or absent from many things while their nature remains intact, or, as the Scholastics put it: that which can be present or absent without the corruption of the subject; such in Peter is whiteness. It will be enough to have indicated these things for the present.

## CHAPTER VI

On the Antepredicaments and the Categories of the

Peripatetics. 35

The Peripatetics call the categories, or Predicaments, a philosophical Dogma, which cannot be called into doubt in Philosophy. Nonsense! For the predicaments are nothing other [p. 16] than a nomenclature, which shows by what name Aristotle named certain beings: in actual fact it is an inept division, as we shall show below; but first we shall explain a few things about the antepredicaments.

36 Aristotle counted four Antepredicaments: Univocals, Equivocals, Analogues and Denominatives. Univocals are things whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is altogether the same in all. Those words altogether the same signify not identity, but likeness. Equivocals are those whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is altogether different. A common example is Dog, which is taken for the domestic animal and for a star. Analogues are things whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is partly the same, partly different, or belongs properly to one, improperly to another; thus laughter is analogous with respect to a man and to a meadow. Denominatives are those which are derived from some name, as brave from bravery, etc. And these are the antepredicaments. But if we consider the things themselves, we shall understand without effort that all ideas can be reduced to three classes, as it were: Substance, Adjuncts, Relations, as we also said above.

37 Aristotle, however, refers all things that exist to ten classes, which he calls categories, and others Predicaments. One is that of substance, or of a thing that can exist by itself; the others are those of accidents, or of those things that cannot exist by themselves. In the first class he counts two substances. The second is Quantity, either discrete, as numbers, or continuous; and this either permanent, as a body, or successive, as motion. The third is Quality, either of the mind, as virtues and sciences, or of the body, as heat, etc. The fourth is Relation, by which one thing leads to the knowledge of another. The fifth is Action, either that which is in the agent, as love, or that which is received in another, as heating. The sixth is Passion, the contrary of action, as being heated. The seventh is Where, or place, as to be at Rome, to be at home, to be in the country, etc. The eighth is Time, as when, to words signifying time, we answer tomorrow, etc. The ninth is Position, which is expressed by these words: stands, lies, etc. The tenth is Habit, that is, the things that clothe the body, as a cloak, etc. Behold the predicaments. Behold the Philosophical dogma which the Peripatetics judge it rash to call into doubt.

38 Otherwise, however, have the most learned Moderns judged, to whom that division, or distribution, seems to have been devised somewhat too freely; for, as the celebrated Author of the Art of Thinking observes, it came forth from the imagination of some man who had no right to write laws for others, who could, no less than he, use their own right to arrange the objects of their thoughts by whatever method is most in keeping with their own way of philosophizing.

And

39 And in fact such a distribution seems altogether inept, since it certainly contains a great many things that ought to be called not true genera of beings but only extrinsic denominations, as Relation, Where, Time; for if all denominations and extrinsic modes were to be admitted, then not ten but almost infinite genera of beings would have to be admitted. Many things are also missing, e.g. several species of accidents, both of body, as rest, and of spirits, as cognition, etc. It is further faulted in this, that it places man under body as under a genus, although he could equally be contained under mind, and could with no less right be called Mind than Body. It contains things false and conflicting: for it refers length, breadth and weight to quantity, and then the objects of the senses to qualities, although extension and motion also fall under sight, and weight and motion under touch; and so Quantity would be at the same time Quality. To pass over other enormities of this kind.

40 More accurately, therefore, the Modern Philosophers count seven genera, or categories, of beings, so that under the common and supreme genus of being there are contained, in a neat and perfect series, two species of substance, namely body and spirit, or mind, and in addition five species of modes. Hence, in their view,

Mind, Measure, Rest, Motion, Position, Figure

Are, with Matter, the beginnings of all things.

41 For the followers of this Philosophy are persuaded that the whole of nature is exhausted by these seven things. By the name of Mind is understood spiritual substance, as God, the Angels and the rational Soul. Measure signifies quantity. Rest, the permanence of a body in the place in which it is found. Motion is the translation or migration of a body from one place to another. Position signifies the disposition of the parts, above all that which is innermost and which cannot be varied without the substance itself being varied. Figure is that disposition of the parts which appears outwardly, and which can be varied while the substance of the thing remains intact. Matter, finally, signifies body or corporeal substance, whatever in the end may be understood by the name of body or matter. And these seven genera of beings are called the beginnings of all things because nothing can be conceived that is not included in these genera of things; or, finally, no singular substance is found in which several, or even all, of these modes cannot be distinguished or found. But so that everything may appear more clearly, I offer you the following table, as it has been drawn by some of the Moderns.
