## CHAPTER VII

On Definitions and Divisions.

hoever has acquired for himself distinct and adequate ideas of 42

W                 things will now find it easy not only to describe things, but also

to define and divide them. And indeed one who is bound to the study of investigating the truth cannot do without these instruments. For if we have a distinct idea, we can define the thing; if an adequate one, nothing will be easier than to divide it.

43 Definition, then, is a statement so determining a thing that it can always be distinguished from all others. Description differs from definition in this, that although both are true, the former applies to the thing only under certain circumstances, the latter always. E.g. if I say: a clock is a little machine made in this or that way, which, either by a hand or by striking, shows what hour of the day it is, this is the definition of a clock; if I say: it is a round case that hangs from a chain near the bed, this proposition, though clear, is a description of a clock.

44 Since, then, a definition must always apply to the thing, it follows that it must comprehend first that in which the thing agrees with other things of the same nature, and then the idea which belongs primarily to the essence of the thing and by which it is distinguished from all the rest; and so it must consist of genus and specific difference. E.g. a triangle is a figure bounded by three lines. But if I take that specific difference from some mark by which I can always tell the thing I meet apart from all others, that definition will be called nominal: e.g. a circle is a figure whose periphery is everywhere equally distant from the center. If I place the difference in showing the manner in which the thing arises, or how it is possible, a real definition will result; e.g. a circle is a figure described by a radius turned about a point.

45 If, however, the definition of the name is altogether accurate, so that it distinguishes the very thing signified by the name from any other thing whatever, it makes no difference whether such definitions are called definitions of the thing or of the name, as the celebrated Jacquier very well observes. From this it readily appears, first, that a definition ought not to be negative, since in that way a thing is not distinguished from a thing by what belongs to its essence.

Second, that it ought to be reciprocal with the thing defined, or, as the Schools say, that the thing defined and the definition be mutually [p. 19] convertible. Third, that it ought to consist of proper and perspicuous words, or at least of words already defined beforehand. Fourth, that the thing defined should not enter into the definition, that is, that the same should not be explained by the same, e.g. a circle is a circle. Fifth, that the definition ought to apply to all of the thing defined and to it alone; hence that definition of man is faulty: a two-footed animal without feathers. From these rules flow four axioms received in the Schools: to whatever the definition belongs, the thing defined belongs also, and conversely; likewise: to whatever the definition is repugnant, the thing defined is repugnant also, and vice versa.

46 Two things, however, we must take care of here. First, that we define accurately the obscure names that come into controversy, lest we dispute from an ambiguity. Some Philosophers sin against this law, who, because they do not define their terms, wrangle with one another even to abuse and fisticuffs, even if both disputants are saying the same things in different words. Second: that when we define names, we should not think that we are defining the thing itself. Against this rule those very Philosophers also sin: for when they define certain words at their own discretion, they persuade themselves that they thoroughly know and define the natures of the things signified: e.g. ask them, what is a tree? They say it is a living insensitive thing. What is lightning? They answer that it is an exhalation kindled in a cloud, which tends downward. But these explanations declare only what things are signified by those names; they do not lay open the natures of the things, unless I first know distinctly what a living insensitive thing, an exhalation, a cloud, kindling and the rest are. But now let us say a few things about division.

47 Division is a statement that resolves a whole into its parts, so that what it contains may be more easily understood; or better: the resolution of a universal idea into several particular ones. That which is resolved is called the thing divided; the parts into which it is divided, the dividing members. One division is Physical, as when we divide wood into parts; another Logical, as when I divide substance in my mind into body and spirit. These parts are called inferiors.

48 The first law of division is that the dividing members be equal to the whole divided. Faultily, therefore, do the Aristotelians divide being into ten categories, since more can be established. The second, that one member not be contained in another; hence number is not rightly divided into even, odd and binary: for the binary is contained in the even. Let the Logician, therefore, in his wisdom so divide a thing that a clearer knowledge of the thing may be had from it, so that he may define it the more easily and accurately. And let him carefully beware of what we warned above concerning definition, lest, when he divides the signification of a name, he think he is dividing the thing itself: an enormity which Aristotle

C2 [p. 20] himself and some of the Ancients imprudently committed. What we have warned concerning division must be understood of subdivisions as well, although care must be taken that subdivisions are not multiplied beyond necessity. For the more a great rock is ground into dust, the less do we grasp its size with the mind.

## CHAPTER VIII

On Judgments and Propositions, and on the matter, form, quantity and quality of a proposition: on the opposition, equipollence and conversion of propositions.

hen the mind compares two ideas, accurately perceived, with 49

W              each other, and either connects them or pulls them apart, there

arises from this judgment, which is: the perception of the agreement or disagreement that is found between two ideas. Judgment expressed in words is called a Proposition, or enunciation. A proposition, moreover, is: a statement affirming or denying something of something. For it corresponds to judgment, which either connects or disjoins two ideas.

50 Every proposition consists of a subject and a predicate, or attribute, terms which the copula is joins together; although this, just like the subject, often lies hidden in the predicate, and so the whole proposition consists of one or two words, e.g. Peter loves, I die, in which these are understood: Peter is loving, I am dying. The subject is that of which something is said. The predicate, what is said of the subject. The copula is the link, or union of subject and predicate. By the copula, or by the verb is, or is not, the force of judging is signified, that is, it is shown that the predicate is included, or not included, in the subject. For this proposition, God is just, means this: in the idea of God the idea of justice is included. This other, a man is not a horse, means: in the idea of man the idea of horse is not included.

For no affirmative proposition is true except because the whole predicate is included in the subject; no negative [p. 21] one, except because the whole is not included. E.g. when I say I am living, by the pronoun I I designate the complex idea of my individual self, and I mean my individual self is living; which amounts to: in the complex idea of my individual self the idea of living is included.

51 The Matter of a proposition is those words of which the same proposition is composed, as it were of parts. By reason of its matter a proposition is called necessary when the predicate agrees necessarily with the subject, as man is an animal; contingent when it agrees contingently, as John is white; impossible when it is repugnant to it, as Sempronius is a stone. But this too is referred to the necessary: for the former is called necessarily true, the latter necessarily false.

52 The Form of a proposition is the copula itself, which joins the predicate with the subject. By reason of its form a proposition is divided into affirmative, which attributes one thing to another, and negative, which denies one thing of another. Note here in passing that a proposition is negative when the particle not falls upon the verb. It is divided also into Categorematic, which affirms or denies without condition, and hypothetical, which affirms under a condition, as if the Sun shines, it is day. A complex proposition is one that consists of several propositions, as the Master teaches, and the disciple learns.

53 The Quantity of a proposition is the extension of the formal subject to signify more or fewer things. Hence a proposition is universal if the subject is universal, as every man is an animal; particular if the subject is particular, as some man runs; singular if the subject is singular, as Peter runs. To these is added the indefinite proposition, whose subject is common and is not restricted, as man reads; for one does not say every, or some, or this, but indefinitely man reads.

54 The Quality of a proposition is said to be its truth or falsity, because a proposition in general abstracts from being true or false; but if it is taken reduplicatively as true or false, then truth or falsity, being a form that denominates the proposition, belongs to it essentially; whereas to a proposition taken specificatively it belongs only contingently. Those propositions are called modal in which the mode is expressed in which the predicate is affirmed or denied of the subject, as when one says: it is necessary that man be an animal.

55 Hence all propositions are referred to four classes, which the Scholastics express by four letters, A. E. I. O. A, the universal affirmative, as every man is just; E, the universal negative, as no vicious man is happy; I, the particular affirmative, as some vicious man is rich; O, the particular negative, as some vicious man is not rich; but so that these may stick more easily in the memory, they have been comprised in these little verses.

A

[p. 22]

A affirms, E denies, but both universally.

I affirms, O denies, but both particularly.

56 Opposition is the incompatibility of two propositions that consist of the same subject and predicate. Opposition of propositions is commonly held to be fourfold: contradictory, contrary, subcontrary and subalternate. Contradictory opposition is between two propositions of which one is universal, the other particular, one affirmative, the other negative, e.g. every man is white, some man is not white. Singular propositions are also called contradictory when one denies what the other affirms: e.g. Aristotle is the prince of Philosophers, Aristotle is not the prince of Philosophers. For contradiction is the affirmation and negation of the same predicate of the same subject, and at the same time.

57 Of contradictory propositions, one is always true, the other false. Contrary opposition is between two universal propositions, of which one is affirmative, the other negative, as every man is white, no man is white. Subcontrary opposition is between two particular propositions, of which one is affirmative, the other negative, as some man is white, some man is not white. Subalternate opposition (which is not opposition in the strict sense) is found between two propositions of which one is universal, the other particular, but both either affirmative or negative, as every man is white, some man is white; no man is white, some man is not white; and to understand these more clearly, cast your eyes on the diagram below.

A: Every man is white. — E: No man is white. — I: Some man is white. — O: Some man is not white. Above: Contraries. Below: Subcontraries. At the sides: Subalterns. Across: Contradictories.

[p. 23]

## 58 Take, finally, these most certain rules for recognizing opposition: those

which can be neither true together nor false together are contradictories; those which cannot be true together, but can nevertheless be false together, are contraries; those which cannot be false together, and can be true together, are subcontraries. Of subalternate propositions, sometimes one is true and the other false, sometimes both are false, sometimes both true: e.g. every man is an animal, some man is an animal.

59 Equipollence, or equivalence, of propositions is the reduction of opposite propositions to the same sense by means of the particle not, which in contradictories is placed before the subject, in contraries is placed after it, and in subalterns is placed both before and after, as is shown by this little verse:

Before for contradic., after for contra., before and after for subalter.

60 Conversion of propositions is the reciprocal change of the subject into the predicate and of the predicate into the subject, namely when the predicate is put in the place of the subject, and the subject itself in the place of the predicate, the truth of that proposition nevertheless remaining, although sometimes the extension, or quantity, of the proposition is varied. The conversion of propositions, however, is to be gathered from Grammar rather than from Logic.

Here are the mysteries of the old Logicians, explained more accurately than they themselves explain them. We did not wish, however, to omit them, lest the Ancients should perhaps suspect that something useful or fruitful had been snatched away from the youth.

## CHAPTER IX

On Reasoning, or the Syllogism, and the various kinds of argumentation.

easoning, or Syllogism, is the operation of the intellect by which, having set 61

R          up a comparison of two ideas with a third, it learns whether they are to be

joined or to be separated; or, as the Scholastics put it, Reasoning is the cognition that infers another proposition from one or from two propositions. If it infers another from one proposition only, e.g. I think: therefore I exist, it is called an

Enthymeme; but if another is inferred from two propositions, e.g. everything that thinks exists; but I think: therefore I exist, it is called a Syllogism.

Since

[p. 24]

62 Since, then, as we have said, there are three ideas to be compared in a Syllogism, it follows that as soon as we cram four ideas into one Syllogism, a faulty reasoning results; which mostly happens when some word suffers from equivocation. Hence one would reason badly thus: Spirit is a thinking substance; but spirit of wine is spirit: therefore spirit of wine is a thinking substance; for four ideas are crammed into one Syllogism. Those three ideas, if they are expressed in words, are called terms; and the one about which something is asked is usually called the minor term, that which is asked about it the major, and that with which these two terms are compared the middle. E.g. if I wished to know whether air is heavy, and therefore compared these ideas with the pressure of bodies: air will be the minor term, because something is asked about it; heavy the major term, because this is the very thing that is asked about air; the pressure of bodies will be the middle term, because the other two are compared with this idea.

63 A Syllogism consists of three propositions, of which the first, which is composed of the major and the middle term, is called the major; the second, composed of the minor and the middle, the minor; the third, finally, composed of the minor and the major, is called the conclusion. Thus if I construct a Syllogism from the terms proposed a little earlier: what presses on lower bodies is heavy; air presses on lower bodies: therefore air is heavy, the first proposition will be the major, the second the minor, and the last is called the conclusion or consequent. In an Enthymeme the first is called the antecedent, the second the consequent.

64 A Dilemma is an argumentation from two questions, by either of which the respondent is caught, e.g. does he who sins remember hell, or not? If you grant it: then he is a fool; if you deny it: then he is a fool too, because he does not remember so great a punishment.

65 Induction is argumentation from singulars sufficiently enumerated to the universal, as if you say: gold can be melted; tin, lead and iron can be melted: therefore every metal can be melted. This argumentation will be bad and devoid of strength if it fails to examine even one part of those that are to be enumerated. Example, or parity, is argumentation from one thing to another similar thing in the same line. Demonstration is argumentation that consists of evident premises. Hence through demonstration a thing manifestly appears true to us. For that is truly and evidently known which is drawn out from clear and perspicuous principles. For the rest, we demonstrate either the effect from its cause, or the cause from its effect. The former demonstration is called a priori, the latter a posteriori.

66 Thus, e.g., if I demonstrate the roundness of the earth from its shadow in Lunar Eclipses, I demonstrate the cause from the effect, so

[p. 25] that this demonstration will be a posteriori. On the other hand, when I demonstrate the immortality of the mind from its spirituality, and this from thought, the demonstration will be a priori. The cognition that is acquired by means of demonstration is called science. Science, moreover, is defined: certain and evident cognition of a necessary thing, proceeding from demonstration.

67 It is called certain cognition, that is, firm and stable and altogether unshaken, and by this science differs from opinion, which is nothing but probable cognition of a thing. It is called evident cognition, namely clear and plainly perspicuous, and hence it is distinguished from faith, which is wholly concerned with obscure things. It is said to be of a necessary thing, so that it may thence be plain that, properly speaking, no science can be had of those things which can be otherwise than as they are known. It is said, lastly, to be proceeding from demonstration, so that it may be distinguished from understanding, namely from the cognition of first principles. For the notion of these does not depend on demonstration, since they are most evident from their own terms, e.g. the whole is greater than its part, etc. Just as one demonstration is a priori and another a posteriori, so a twofold science is distinguished: namely most perfect and less perfect.

The former is acquired through demonstration a priori, the latter through demonstration a posteriori.

## CHAPTER X

On the Form and Figure of the Syllogism.

he Form of a Syllogism is the disposition of the terms with a view to cor68

T          rectly inferring the conclusion: this form is twofold, namely mode and

figure. Mode is the disposition of the propositions with respect to affirmation or negation, universality or particularity; and since the middle can be disposed in the propositions in three ways, from this there results the threefold figure of the Syllogism, as is shown by these little verses:

The first first subjects the middle, then predicates it;

The second twice predicates, the third twice subjects it.

69 The first figure puts the middle in the major as subject, and the middle itself as predicate in the minor. The second figure puts the middle as predicate both in the major and in the minor. The third, finally, both in the major and in the minor, puts the middle

D [p. 26] as subject. Here are examples. First fig.: what thinks is spirit; the mind thinks: therefore the mind is spirit. Second fig.: body does not think; the mind thinks: therefore the mind is not body. Third fig.: whatever thinks is spirit; something that thinks is in man:

therefore some spirit is in man. All the modes, moreover, nineteen in number, are contained in these barbarous words:

Barbara, Celarem, Darii, Ferio, Baralipton,

Celantes, Dabitis, Fopesmo, Frisesomorum,

Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, Darapti,

Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison.

70 Here the Peripatetics would have it observed that all the words consist of three syllables, if you except Baralipton and Frisesomorum, to which, for the sake of the meter, as they themselves say, one or two syllables are added that do not pertain to the figure. Recall to memory that A denotes the universal affirmative, etc. Hence a syllogism in Barbara, e.g., consists of three universal affirmative propositions; in Celarem, of a negative major, an affirmative minor and a negative consequent, all universal. The first nine modes, contained in the first two verses, belong to the first figure, the next four to the second, and the rest to the third. Now we ought to treat of the reduction of the syllogism; but we, following the more circumspect Peripatetics, deliberately leave aside a treatment of this kind: for generally, as St. Augustine says, a man of wit sees sooner that a conclusion is not right than he grasps its precepts; a slow man does not see it, and much less what is prescribed concerning it.

## CHAPTER XI

A universal principle is handed down for recognizing whether a syllogism is legitimate or faulty, without any account at all being taken of the common rules.

his is that celebrated rule devised by the most illustrious Author of 71

T           the Art of Thinking: namely that, for the conclusion to be rightly in‐

ferred, it must be contained in one of the premises, and this very thing must be shown, or indicated, by the other, which is called the applicative, or indicative, just as the first is called the containing one.

[p. 27]

In affirmative syllogisms it makes no difference at all whether we call the major or the minor the containing or the applicative, since each in some way contains the conclusion, and each also mutually shows it to be contained in the other. For e.g. if I doubt whether an impious man is wretched, I shall argue thus: Whoever is a slave to his desires is wretched; but the impious man is a slave to his desires: therefore the impious man is wretched. Whichever of the premises you designate, it can be said to contain the conclusion, and this to be shown by the other. For the conclusion is contained in the major, because one who is a slave to his desires contains the impious man under itself; and it is shown by the minor, because one who is a slave to his desires comprehends in its idea the idea of the wretched.

72 Nevertheless, in affirmative syllogisms, since the major is almost always the more universal, it can for the most part be taken as the containing premise, and the minor as the applicative. In negative syllogisms, however, the negative premise is always the containing proposition, and the affirmative is the applicative proposition, because, since the consequent is negative, it is more reasonable that it be contained in the negative premise than in the affirmative, since a negation is included only in a negation. But let us apply the principle.

73 I doubt, e.g., whether this syllogism concludes rightly: The Gospel promises salvation to Christians; some impious men are Christians: therefore the Gospel promises salvation to some impious men. Having considered the premises, then, it is evident that the conclusion is by no means contained in the major proposition, although at first sight it seems to be comprehended in the minor. For the Gospel does not promise salvation to all Christians, but only to those who observe the commandments of Christ the Lord, which the impious do not do. Therefore the syllogism is illegitimate. By the same reasoning this one is null: every man is an animal; a horse is not a man: therefore a horse is not an animal. For the conclusion is not comprehended in the negative premise. On the contrary, these are excellent: They are wretched who are slaves to their desires; the avaricious are slaves to their desires: therefore the avaricious are wretched. No substance lacking parts can be destroyed by a created agent; the rational soul is a substance lacking parts: therefore the rational soul can be destroyed by no created agent. For the conclusion of each is contained in the major, as the minor proposition itself makes plain.

74 By the help of this principle, too, the fallacy of this syllogism can be detected with little trouble: he who says you are an animal says what is true; but he who says you are a goose says you are an animal: therefore he who says you are a goose says what is true. For it suffices to answer that neither of the premises contains the conclusion. For animal in the major is taken particularly, since it is the predicate of this proposition: you are an animal. Hence, too, may be sought the solution of the sophism that St. Augustine reports: you are not what I am; I am a man: therefore you are not a man: for each

D2 [p. 28] premise speaks of a thing singularly proper to me, and so it cannot contain the conclusion, which proceeds about a thing proper to you.

75 To this norm and easy rule submit every reasoning, and you will have no need of the laborious and altogether useless reduction of syllogisms, if you follow this law of arguing, which is common to all and placed almost before one’s eyes. For by the light of this principle the goodness of any argumentation whatever can easily be detected, so that the other laws can accordingly be deemed either more obscure, or less universal, or even useless; nay rather, they must be.

## CHAPTER XII

On the Fallacies of the Syllogism.

allacy of a Syllogism, which comes from many sources, is a fault both 76

F          to be recognized and to be avoided. First, then, a Syllogism deceives

by the equivocation of some name, e.g. a gallus [cock] is a bird; but a

Frenchman is a Gallus [Gaul]: therefore a Frenchman is a bird. Second, when there is a passage from genus to species, as Sempronius is an animal, but an ass is an animal: therefore Sempronius is an ass. The third fallacy is called ignoratio elenchi, namely when something other is attacked than what is in question, because either something is attributed to the adversary which he himself does not assert, or the state of the question is ignored. Here belongs the change of the middle, when, intending to prove, e.g., that God is to be loved because He is

Good, you abandon the middle of Goodness and take up Wisdom or Omnipotence.

The fourth is petitio principii, when that is supposed which ought to have been proved. To this sophism can be brought back those reasons by which the unknown is proved by the equally unknown, the uncertain by the equally uncertain, or by the more uncertain.

77 The sophism of petitio principii extends widely: for whoever, without any proof, sets down as if perspicuous what altogether needs proof asks that some principle be granted him which was to be proved. This happens either proximately or remotely. Proximately, as when one puts forward as a reason the conclusion to be proved, either in the same words or in synonymous ones, or by a circle.

Remotely, as when one brings forward a thing openly false, or mere words, or something of this kind [p. 29] to prove the thesis: for in such a case too he asks that the principle be granted him which he had to prove in order to accomplish what was proposed. When one of the premises, either plainly doubtful or plainly false, is adduced as a reason, this sophism too is called petitio principii. This can happen in very many ways, as we said above. Aristotle proves that the fixed stars twinkle because they are very far distant from us (l), and that they are very far distant because they twinkle (m). Behold a circle.

78 When they assign as a physical cause mere words that in reality signify nothing, we have said above that there is a petitio principii. Here is an example. Very many Philosophers, while they try to explain things wrapped up by nature herself, since they cannot accomplish this with firm and perspicuous arguments and are unwilling to confess their ignorance, have recourse to empty words and applaud themselves as though they had unlocked some such mystery. Hence horror of the vacuum, soporific virtue, and words of that kind, sonorous indeed and bombastic, but which have no meaning and do not make us more learned.

79 The fifth fallacy is non-cause as cause, e.g. Peter squandered his fortune on studies, and they did him no good: therefore time ought not to be spent on studies. To this sophism must be brought back that common fallacy of the human mind: after this: therefore because of this. The sixth is imperfect enumeration of the parts. Thus he reasons very badly who attributes to a whole College the sin of some of its members. The seventh is the fallacy of the accident, when one judges of the nature of a thing from what belongs to it by accident; thus all the evils that come from the errors of quacks are attributed to Medicine. The eighth is when one argues from what holds in some respect to what holds simply, e.g. an Ethiopian is white as to his teeth: therefore he is white.

80 The ninth is inept parity: namely when, because two things are similar in one or another predicate, we conclude that the one is very like the other. Authors of the same sophism are those who, in order to persuade someone that something is to be done, cunningly pass over its faults and extol its advantages to the skies; e.g. the Scholastic Philosophers, in order to persuade us that their Logic is to be preferred to the others, boastfully state that they dispute out of Aristotle’s Dialectic; that it is useful for learning Scholastic Theology; and finally that no one can dispute in the more abstruse disciplines without it. But they are silent about this: that such Dialectic is the art of caviling and of contending without any end; that it does not hand down the ways of searching out the true, whether the certain or the probable; that it contains nothing on the art

of

(l) On the Heavens, 2, ch. 8.

(m) Prior Analytics, 1, ch. 13. [p. 30] of criticism; and finally that it brings the human race no utility toward reason‐

ing rightly in the other disciplines: which ought not to have been passed over in silence.

81 The tenth fallacy is: when we weaken a true proposition by no other argument than by ridiculing its author. The Scholastics often sin in this when disputing with the Modern Philosophers. But this way of refuting is altogether weak. They must therefore be compelled to refute theses not with guffaws and witticisms, but with firm and perspicuous arguments. In the same way shall we deal with those who try to persuade us of something false by complaints, wailing and oaths, because they are guilty of the same sophism. Let what has been said suffice.

## BOOK II

On Truth.

f anyone uses the operations of the intellect rightly, he certainly uses 82

I       reason well, and it follows that, proceeding in this manner, he will find

the truth, of which we must now treat a little more accurately. Truth is either Metaphysical, or Moral, or Logical. Whatever has the essence befitting it is called metaphysically true. Every being, too, whether existing or possible, is called metaphysically true when it is in conformity with the idea that God has of it. Hence in this sense Peter is a true Peter, because he corresponds to the idea of God. This metaphysical truth is also called real. Moral truth is the agreement of words and of external signs with the thoughts of the mind. Hence one who speaks out what he thinks is said to speak the True; one who thinks one thing and says another, the False. We, however, are dealing with Logical truth, which is the agreement of our ideas with the object. Hence if, e.g., I conceive a tower, or something round, and these things truly are such, I am said to have attained the truth. For the ideas agree with the object. Conversely, the false is the disagreement of ideas with the object. Further, one truth is certain, another probable. Certain, when I am thoroughly persuaded that the thing is so.

Probable, when I am so persuaded that I fear lest it be false.

Chapter

[p. 31]

## CHAPTER I

On the Criterion of the True and the False.

here are, moreover, certain characters, or definite marks of assent, 83

T          which are likewise called Criteria of truth, by which the true is dis‐

tinguished from the false, and by looking upon which we find the truth we seek. It is asked, then, by what argument, in the end, we can be safe that the things we judge affirmatively are as we judge them to be, and that we are in no way deceived in them: in establishing which the Moderns disagree not a little.

84 Pierre Daniel Huet holds that the speech of God alone is what makes us certain that we do not err (n). This opinion is false; for if we can determine nothing with certainty by reason, how shall we become certain that God has said this to us? Not all are breathed upon by the Divine Spirit; and then men are very often deceived in judging. Therefore they cannot plainly establish whether they are made certain by God, or otherwise. I do not deny that the

Prophets, while they were inspired by the divine power, often needed no other argument by which to be convinced that God was speaking to them: but not all were Prophets; the greatest part of men, therefore, knew nothing at that time; so that today, since there are no Prophets, at least none whom the Church holds as such, all must necessarily be sunk in ignorance of all things. Whoever, then, defends this opinion casts us into the foulest Pyrrhonism.

85 Benedict Spinoza, a Jew by origin, whom the Pantheists and the more recent Fanatics follow, holds (o) that human reason is the criterion of the true for no other reason than that it is the very reason of God itself, because our mind is a particle of the Divine mind. These things are so monstrous that whoever would refute them would himself be going mad by reason. For the reason of

God is simple and infinite: therefore it cannot be divided: therefore wherever it is present, it is the same.

(n) Traité de la foiblesse de l’Esprit Humain.

(o) Theological-Political Treatise, ch. 1.

[p. 32]

Now if our reason is itself the reason of God, we shall be ignorant of nothing; for to infinite reason all things are open. Is anyone so mad as to flatter himself in this way, and to persuade himself that there is nothing he does not know? Spinozism (p), therefore, teems with the most inept ravings.

86 Nicolas Malebranche, Priest of the French Congregation of the Oratory, holds that our mind is essentially joined to God, and that we perceive all things in God’s idea and light, or that the light of God is the criterion of the true, because our mind sees all things in God (q). But if these things are true, I do not see what difference there is between the state of the blessed and that of wayfarers, in which the human mind, subject to so many errors, very often strays from the truth. I pass over other things, lest I be longer than the limits of Elements allow. But this I shall certainly not omit, that this substantial union of the mind with God cannot be understood except in the Spinozist system. For indeed, if God is the place of minds, as space is of bodies, they will be either parts of God, or modes, or God himself. More on this subject in the celebrated Genovesi (r).

Chapter

(p) Spinozism is the error of those who admit only a single substance endowed with infinite attributes, among which are numbered infinite thought and infinite extension: each of these has an eternal and infinite essence, while finite beings are imagined to arise from the necessary modification of the attributes of this substance, namely souls from the modification of infinite thought, and bodies from the modification of infinite extension. Spinoza does not distinguish God from the world; he makes God mutable, extended, and yet intelligent. As the basis and foundation of his impious hypothesis Spinoza assumes that there cannot be two substances of the same essence, because if they have the same essence, he says, they are one and the same substance. But there is no one who does not see at once that two substances cannot have the same essence by numerical identity (as they say), but can by identity either generic or specific. Nor is there any man endowed with common sense who, from the fact that Peter and Paul are men, and therefore have the same essence, or are alike by reason of humanity, would conclude that Peter and Paul are numerically one and the same man, or are a single individual. But of these things more opportunely in the Ethics.

(q) Recherche de la Vérité, bk. 1, ch. 2, §. 4.

(r) Disciplin. Metaphys. Elem., vol. 3, ch. 3.

[p. 33]

## CHAPTER II

On the Probable True, where also on Hermeneutic, Moral and

Physical Probability.

hat leaves some doubt in the mind is true only probably. The sole 87

W              foundation of probability is a hypothesis, that is, a proposition that we

assume as true for this reason, that the properties and effects of a thing are conveniently explained from it. E.g. if I assume as true that a subterranean inflammable matter, chiefly nitrous and sulphurous, is the cause of earthquakes, this hypothesis, until something more certain appears, cannot be held to be false: for from it all the phenomena can be explained both easily and plausibly. Or else I assume as a hypothesis the signification of the words, their position, and a connection in agreement with the aim of the author, or the authority of some witness. If the first, that probability is called Hermeneutic, or probable interpretation; if the second, Historical, which is specifically named faith.

88 The foundation, therefore, of Hermeneutic probability is of this kind: What agrees with the signification, position and connection of the words, and likewise with the

Author’s aim, is to be held probably as the Author’s meaning. The foundation of Historical probability is of this kind: What a trustworthy man testifies to be true is probably true.

89 What is handed down to us by men is, first, handed down either by those present, or contemporaries, or by those absent and later. 2. The witnesses are either several or one; and likewise 3. they either perceived the thing with their eyes, or heard it narrated by others; nay, and 4. they either give a reason for their knowledge, or not; and 5. they report a thing either possible in itself, or marvelous, or plainly impossible. Further, 6. they are either known or unknown; 7. they follow the zeal either of neither party or of one party only; 8. they are either prudent or foolish, honest or dishonest, and liars. From these divisions are easily understood the rules by which one can judge of the degrees of human faith. I. is: The more certain I am that the author did not wish to deceive me, the greater the faith I am bound to have in him. II. Whether anyone has wished to deceive me must often be judged from the very circumstances of the narration.

E                                              It

[p. 34]

90 It is therefore most certain, 1. that little faith is to be had in a single witness narrating a marvelous thing, even if he is otherwise not much suspected, especially when the matter is such that the witness could easily have been deceived by his imagination; 2. that the degree of probability is greater if several witnesses report a thing that, however marvelous, is yet not impossible, even if not in every respect in the same manner and with the same circumstances; 3. that what several trustworthy men report with the same circumstances is much more probable, and that this probability is increased not a little if the witnesses are eyewitnesses, if they are public persons, if they are sworn. Very many other rules of this probability can be seen in the celebrated Antonio Genovesi (s).

91 Moral probability is had when, from certain signs that men display, we either declare something hidden or predict something future. According to the things it predicts, this is called either Practical or Political. E.g. I see Titius with a sad face spurning lawful pleasures, given over to gain, in a worn and sordid garment, perpetually crying out that he is poor. Hence I probably infer that Titius is avaricious. This way of divining, then, which by reasoning from external signs investigates the propensities of the mind, is called moral Probability, or Practical. Sometimes, however, we foresee some future event from the counsels of men, and this divination is named by a word of its own, Political Probability. But these consequences are more or less probable, just as the force of judging and the experience of things are greater or less in those who conjecture; those who see far ahead judge much more truly and more probably.

92 Physical Probability is given when, from the observation of phenomena and of sensations, we think out some hypothesis that explains all the phenomena lucidly and skillfully. But if the hypothesis that I posit is such that from it I cannot prove that the thing is so, it is not a hypothesis but a fiction. E.g. when the Peripatetics say that the horror of the vacuum is the cause why a pump draws water, it is a mere fiction, because such words do not explain why water rises 32 feet and rises no further in a pump a thousand feet long.

(s) In the Elem. Art. Logico-Critic.

## CHAPTER III

Rules directing the human mind in believing doctrines that rest on

Divine as well as on human authority.

93

We are led by authority when, in passing judgment on things, we abide by the sayings of others. That authority which moves us to assent is either Divine or

Human. That we should be deceived by Divine authority is utterly impossible, as we shall say. But that we can be deceived by human authority escapes no one. It matters very greatly, therefore, that we instruct ourselves rightly in this respect. Here, then, are the rules that can be of use to us in believing doctrines.

94 Rule I. All those things are to be admitted with the firmest assent which rest on Divine authority. For it is more repugnant that God should be deceived, or deceive, than that those things should not be true which reason shows most evidently. In those things, therefore, which belong to Divine Faith it is most just, as the Apostle says, to bring into captivity the understanding unto the obedience of Christ, namely, so that we do not doubt even in the slightest of the truth of those things which are handed down to us to be believed on divine authority. Rule II. Those things are to be admitted with a firm and constant mind which are proposed to us by the Church to be believed with divine faith. For it cannot happen that the Church should be deceived in defining those things which pertain to faith, and lead us into error, since Christ our Lord said openly that it would never come about that the faith of Peter should fail, nor that the gates of hell should prevail against the Church.

95 Rule III. Great care must be taken that we hold that which has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. For that is of such a kind that it was handed down by word of mouth by Christ our Lord himself to the Apostles, and derived through them to us by constant tradition (t).

E2                                             Rule

(t) Divine Tradition is the doctrine of God, not written, but revealed by God to our forefathers

and communicated to their successors from ear to ear. This tradition is usually called Dominical, be‐

cause it has been derived from Christ our Lord to the Apostles, and by them through their successors down to us: of this kind is the tradition concerning the number of the Sacraments, and concerning the perpetual Virginity of the Blessed Mary. Another is Apostolic, which the Apostles received at the dictation of the Holy Spirit and communicated to the Church without writing, as the Council of

Trent teaches, Sess. 4.

[p. 36]

Rule IV. Not every opinion is to be deemed safe precisely because the Church has by no means proscribed it. For the Church does not openly condemn all errors, but only those that make a stir. For so long (says St. Augustine) is the sin or the error of anyone whatever tolerated, until it either finds an accuser or defends a depraved opinion with stubborn animosity. Rule V. That is to be held firmly as certain which, in matters of faith and morals, all the Holy Fathers teach. For since the Holy Fathers were sent by God to instruct the

Church, it could by no means happen that in those things which concern Religion all should have erred. I said all; for not every one of them was endowed with such infallibility that he could err in absolutely nothing, as St. Augustine expressly teaches.

96 Rule VI. In the natural disciplines and the human arts (such as, for example,

Philosophy) the authority of the Holy Fathers is of no greater weight than is the authority of those Philosophers whom the Holy Fathers themselves followed. Hence the sayings of the Holy Fathers are to be valued by us in this matter precisely as much as the reasons by which they are shown are worth. For, as the most illustrious Melchior

Cano excellently observes, the holy Authors were not so solicitous in scrutinizing the dogmas of Philosophy that they did not either bid farewell to the books of the Philosophers, so as to give themselves wholly to Divine Wisdom, or at times even greet them only from the threshold.

C H A P T E R I V.

On the chief causes or occasions of errors, and first, on the fallacies of the senses.

ome things, however, and that frequently, prevent us from attaining 97

Struth, which the Logician must have clearly understood, so that he may avoid them as far as he can, or, if he has not avoided them, may at least in some measure amend his errors. These are conveniently referred to three classes, those of the Senses, of the Will, and of the Mind, about which we shall explain a few things in order.

98 In the first place, our senses very often deceive us. Not that they themselves deceive, for they always present something that really exists, but because they furnish the occasion of our being deceived, by judging that the objects really [p. 37] are just as they appear to us. Thus, while we see light, colors and other objects, it is indeed true that we see them, even if we were suffering from frenzy. For all the delirious without doubt see what they see, and their error consists solely in the judgments by which they judge that what they see really exists outside themselves, by the very fact that they see it placed externally. But as we are about to treat of the fallacies of the senses, let us begin with sight.

99 We can scarcely ever judge with certainty that we grasp the true magnitude of things. For just as glass lenses, if they are segments of a larger or a smaller sphere, and hence more or less convex, then represent objects larger or smaller, so our eyes, if they are more or less convex, will do the same. If, therefore, the eyes of two men differ from each other (as they really do differ) either in the density of the humors, or in their figure, or in their position and situation, they will exhibit a different extension of a body, as glass lenses do: hence we cannot say for certain how large the object is that we behold.

100 Experience confirms this very thing: for spectacles, and likewise optical tubes arranged in one and the same way, do not suit the eyes of all men equally. We are also sometimes deceived when we determine bodies to be equal or unequal; for example, if on some given horizontal straight line another straight line, perpendicular and equal to it, is erected at its extremity, both appear equal to each other to the eyes; but if this perpendicular is drawn not at the extremity of the other but toward the middle, the more it approaches its midpoint, the greater it appears than the other, horizontal, line, as is plain in the adjoined figure.

101 Nor shall we determine with any certainty the figure of large bodies if they are a long distance away. For a square tower that is viewed from afar appears without angles. Also, the very smallest bodies that appear round, like a grain of sand, if we contemplate them with a microscope applied, have a great many surfaces and diverse figures. And insensible things that do not appear to the naked eye, if we explore them with a microscope, present themselves as very many and endowed with many figures: e.g., in water, in vinegar we behold almost infinite animalcules, which cannot be seen without the glass; of which the most sagacious investigators of Nature, Leeuwenhoek, Hartsoeker, Hooke, Joblot and others, supply further examples.

Men

[p. 38]

102 Men are also deceived when they think that colors are in the object body, which happens not only to the unlearned but also to the Peripatetics. For, to pass over Descartes and his followers Malebranche, Arnauld, Rohault, and other most illustrious men who philosophized in France after the middle of the past century, the great Isaac Newton, the light and ornament of England, seems to have hit the mark exactly when by the most certain experiments he proved that all colors are contained in light itself, whose rays, it is established, are endowed by their very nature with this or that color. Accordingly, assent is given neither to the Cartesians, who contend that colors are located in the varied texture and disposition of the surface of bodies, nor indeed to the Idealists, who hold that they are wholly in the organ of sight, as though they were mere illusions, and that nothing exists outside the mind. Although, therefore, we do not wish (for there is no time) to bring in here the Newtonian opinion on light and colors, set out as it deserves, we nevertheless acknowledge no other as more probable.

103 For no slight argument for the Newtonians is this, that when the light is changed the color is changed: for if spirit of wine with a very little water is poured on tow sprinkled with much salt, and this is set alight, the human face itself appears with a horrible look. He who has fixed his eyes on the orb of the Sun, or suffers from ophthalmia, sees objects covered and surrounded with many colors, and as it were with a kind of rainbow; but the objects are by no means girt with those colors in reality; for if it were so, the said colors would be seen by all, which is altogether false.

104 By an easy experiment of the illustrious Newton (u) this very thing is shown. If in a dark room you catch with a crystal prism the rays of light that come through a hole made in the window, these, while they pass through the crystal and the room, are not seen colored; but when they fall on a white paper set opposite, or are carried onto the opposite wall, they are so refracted, and so affect the eyes, that they excite in us sensations of these seven colors, namely violet, purple, blue, green, yellow, orange and red, and the wall appears painted with them, arranged in the order in which we have enumerated them. But the wall and the paper have no faculty of producing colors, nor of changing the nature of rays that were not colored. From this follows what we should determine about colors, if we approached the matter as it deserves, and not as though we were busy with something else.

105 Hearing likewise is a frequent cause of errors. For, first, we think that sound is a thing that is outside us and comes from the body

that

(u) Opticks, p. 103 & 153. [p. 39] that sounds; which, however, is false. For the sonorous body does nothing other than tremble very swiftly and in a certain manner, and this tremor drives the air to the tympanum of the ear and so moves it as to excite in the mind the sensation of sound. For no sound arises unless the particles of the bodies that are called sonorous take on a tremulous motion, which can be very easily proved by one or two experiments.

106 For if water is poured into a glass vessel and a finger, brought to the lip of the vessel, is drawn round the mouth of the vessel for some time, continually pressing and rubbing, a tremor and quivering is in this way excited in the walls of the vessel, which is at once communicated to the water it contains, and that tremor plainly appears to the eye. And as soon as the particles begin to tremble, the sensation of sound immediately arises; and when that tremor is extinguished, whether this happens of itself or by our doing, all sensation of sound is immediately extinguished.

107 Further, if in the air pump, the air having been exhausted, a little bell is struck (which can certainly be done), although the particles of that metal, struck by the little hammer, take on a tremulous motion, yet since that tremor cannot be communicated to the air (for there is no longer any air present), and so cannot reach all the way to our ears, no sensation of sound arises from it; but when the air is restored to the machine, the sense of sound is immediately excited. What we perceive and call sound, therefore, does not exist in external bodies; there is only the undulatory motion of the particles of which they are composed, and when this is given, sensations of sound are excited in our minds, provided, however, that that motion is communicated to the air and reaches all the way to our ears.

108 Smell and Taste deceive us in the same way, because they are the cause of our thinking, imprudently, that Odor and Savor are in the body we touch; whereas they are nothing other than sensations of the mind, which are excited in us by the insensible particles of the bodies that touch these two organs. This will be plain with little trouble if we consider that no sensation, pleasant or unpleasant, can in any way exist outside the mind.

109 Moreover, if odors and savors were things existing outside us, the same odorous body and the same food would affect each man in the same way. But it is otherwise; for civet, for example, or the scent of the lily, is pleasant to some, to others utterly intolerable. Nor are all delighted by the same food. In the sick, more wonderful phenomena very often occur. Who does not know that women suffering from obstructions devour earth, coals, lime and other things of that kind, which those same women, when they are well and freed from the illness, cannot see without nausea, nay, cannot even name?

Those

[p. 40]

110 Those who suffer from fever find bitter the things that the healthy hold sweet and agreeable. The same happens with odors. These things, moreover, teach clearly that odors and savors are not in the object bodies, but only the occasion of our sensing them: for these bodies, according to the diverse constitution of the organs, whether of two men or of the same man when he suffers from illness or from age, move and prick the fibers of the senses in diverse ways, so that the nerves, affected in diverse ways, excite other perceptions in the mind, which are themselves either odors or savors.

111 Touch, finally, is a most abundant source of errors. This is established by the plainest experiments, of which we shall adduce only a few. We judge without any doubt that the things we distinguish by touch are in external bodies, which is false; for neither does what we call heat exist in fire, nor what we call cold in ice; and this, besides the reason brought forward in §. 108, is proved by almost innumerable others. For if you plunge one hand, well warmed, and the other, very cold, into the same lukewarm water, the one that is cold will feel it hot, and on the contrary the one that is hot will feel it cold. We would not say so if the water were hot of itself: for both hands would feel a moderate heat, just as both hands feel that it is a body, that it is fluid, etc., because it is so.

112 Further, if someone in wintertime enters a well-closed room and says that the air enclosed there is hot, or lukewarm, while one who has just risen from bed, placed in that same room, asserts that that air is cold rather than lukewarm or hot: since the same body cannot in reality be at once hot and cold, it manifestly follows that we cannot argue that what we call heat and cold inheres in reality in a given body from the fact that that given body excites heat or cold in us.

113 We are deceived by touch in many other ways. For if, e.g., you place the middle finger of the hand over the index finger and hold a small globule in the middle between both fingers, unless you employ your eyes as witnesses, you will swear that two globules are being touched by you. From all of which it follows that our senses give us very much occasion for being deceived. But since God gave us the senses not for ornament, but that we might use them and by their help acquire knowledge, there must therefore be some Criterion by which we may distinguish true and false notions. The criterion, then, is this.

114 Those images must be held most certain which, all the circumstances having been accurately weighed, are always found the same by the same sense, or by the other senses; and this by one man, and much more by diverse men who have examined them diligently. For if not even in this case could the images be held true, God would perpetually delude us:

[p. 41] which is foreign to so great a Goodness. In this way, indeed, the fiction of the

Pyrrhonists is refuted by true Philosophers. For clarity’s sake we shall comprise this doctrine in three canons. I. Do not pronounce that the things the senses represent are true, or that things are not, because they do not fall under the senses, without first diligently weighing the matter and applying the opinion of experts. II. Beware of ever judging, by the help of your senses, of things as they are in themselves. III. Do not make experiments as some of the Ancients did, but use most diligently the most exact instruments that the Moderns have devised and perfected.

C H A P T E R V.

On the Affections of the Will that impede the attainment of truth. 115

We should have little to fear (says the illustrious Verney (u)) if the senses alone led us into errors: for since errors of this kind are conspicuous, the remedy would be at hand, namely, to pronounce cautiously about the things that are perceived by the senses, and to call them to examination again and again before we made a judgment. But there is another cause which, the more hidden it is, the more strongly calls a man back from truth and drives him to error. Of this kind are the affections of the mind. For when the mind perceives sensible things according as they are good or bad, there arises a certain motion of the mind, joined with a great commotion of the nervous fluid and of the blood, which is called an affection; and this is followed either by pleasure of mind or by pain.

116 It is wonderful to say how strongly and how swiftly these affections, if they are vehement, lead a man astray, as has been ascertained by experience.

First, they hinder the mind from examining accurately the things about which it ought to deliberate; from which it follows that it acquires obscure ideas and is deceived in judging. Next, they bring it about that we love some things, and shun others, as we ought not. For just like microscopes, they so enlarge and dilate the things that please and those that displease, that the mind, struck by such brilliance,

F                                        judges

(u) De Re Logica. [p. 42] judges to be good or bad what in reality is not. This can be proved by so many arguments that plenty makes me poor. I shall add a few, however; as for the rest, I advise each one to consult himself: for if he scrutinizes his own actions and weighs them as they deserve, he will find all too many examples.

117 The principal source of the affections, from which they all flow, is the immoderate love with which each one loves himself, which we call Philautia [self-love]: wherefore Philautia must be held to be the parent of the errors that arise from the Will. We love vehemently ourselves and everything that is ours, our sayings, deeds and thoughts. Nor do we think that anything so glorious can be declared of any man that we do not judge it ought to be said of ourselves with better right. This affection, like a kind of disease, sometimes pervades not only the half-learned but even the most learned.

118 Hence arises this too, that we pass judgment on things not as they are in reality, but according to the way in which they affect us. Thus what we think suits us we judge good, beautiful and just; what does not suit us, the contrary. Very many so extol their friends, kinsmen, teachers and countrymen that they think nothing holier, nothing more learned, nothing more heaped with every praise can even be conceived. But if they hear anyone noting their errors, they call down every evil upon him, and oppose him, as a man hateful to the gods above, pernicious to the commonwealth, and plotting new and nefarious crimes, so fiercely that nothing could go further.

119 This is seen more openly in those who have given their names to some sect. For who would tell such a Philosopher that his teacher has erred? Who would persuade him that he ought to bring his master’s opinions to the light of other doctors? Well known is that saying of Averroes, who, when he was interpreting Aristotle, did not hesitate to say this: The doctrine of Aristotle is the highest truth, since his intellect was the limit of the human intellect: wherefore it is well said of him that he was created and given to us by Divine providence, so that we might not be ignorant of what can be known. And in another place: None of those, he says, who have followed him up to this time, which is a period of one thousand five hundred years, has added anything; nor will you find in his words an error of any magnitude.

120 These things can be pardoned in a Heathen man, writing in so rude an age, and one who had not read good authors; but in Catholic men, and in this light of Letters, they are not to be borne. I have heard a Peripatetic say that the ancient Bishops, from the first century of the Church, held Aristotle as a kind of norm of disputing, even in matters of Faith, and did not depart a finger’s breadth from his opinions. Nor would I hesitate to affirm that very many even now persist in the same

[p. 43] heresy, though more covertly.

121 Hence arises this too, that those who are held by such opinions think nothing right except what flows from those sources. These they defend constantly and stubbornly; the rest they reject as false and harmful. They fear, namely, lest they incur the mark of inconstancy or of error, and lose by an ingenuous confession of error the praise they acquired with so much sweat. This philautia prevents men from tracking down the truth; and this happens much more in the old than in the young.

122 Hence the writings of those who hold the contrary opinion they either do not read at all, or read yawning; and if they examine them a little more attentively, they do so with this design, to refute their opinions. For how few are there, even of those who with great disdain censure the opinions of the Moderns, who, when they have turned over Descartes, Gassendi, Malebranche, Leibniz, Wolff and the other most acute Philosophers, do not rather condemn them on another’s judgment than call them back to their own circumspect examination?

123 Hence that zeal for dissenting, and a certain inexplicable desire of wrangling, which so drives some men that nothing is held so firm and so evident that they do not try to weaken and obscure it with their disputations. For these men, as if they had been born for discord, call everything to the balance of disputation; and if perchance arguments fail them on the matter proposed, they immediately ask whether they are making a conjoined or a separated kind of syllogism. There are Philosophers who, when about to hand down to youths the rudiments of some science, first teach them to contend with words and to chatter rather impudently, instead of handing down some precepts that would lead the boys into the very inner recesses of the science. Books are full of examples, which it would be easy to bring forward, were the matter not exceedingly well known.

124 Hence is born that intolerable pride by which men so arrogate to themselves the first place in letters that they either diminish the learning of others in other studies or, if they spare these, nevertheless prefer themselves to all in the faculty they profess. It is the way of men (says Cicero) that they do not wish the same man to excel in many things. (x) This way, moreover, has come down even to our own age. A jurist, for example, if he hears a Theologian disputing about Law, whether Public or Private, generally laughs at him. Jurisprudence, forsooth, is open only to him who is adorned with the insignia of a Doctor; all others

F2                                         it

(x) Cic., Brutus, ch. 21. [p. 44] it repels from itself. The Theologian, on the other hand, even if he praises the Jurisconsult, nevertheless thinks it a heinous crime if the latter touches on anything of the Sacred Science. As though the laws of the Caesars were not illustrated by the Sacred Letters and by Ethical discipline; or as though the statutes of the Sacred Canons were not aided by the constitutions of Princes. And so much in particular on philautia; and since the remaining affections are reduced to it, we shall append a few things about them.

125 Hope, and much more Desire, what do they not disturb in the breast of mortals! How they distract the mind, so that it does not attend to the things that are! Those who desire and hope feign dreams for themselves: these they love, these they adore, they see nothing besides. Hence they readily think that they have what they hope for; they lend their ears to flatterers, believe them, and are wonderfully deceived. Let some mountebank tell a man suffering from paralysis or dropsy that he has an exquisite remedy by which he would free such men from the disease within the course of a single day: though a thousand most weighty men should show that this cannot be done, the sick will think it true.

126 But Ambition, how vehemently it torments men! How it drives them headlong, without any shame, into many unseemly things that diminish the dignity of man! This affection spreads more widely than is commonly thought; and men take studious care to obscure it under one name or another, lest they be exposed to reproach and laughter.

127 There are those who say they seek honors so as to be a protection to their kinsmen and connections. These conceal their ambition under the title of piety. Others, a little more cunning, perpetually cry out that they will never allow themselves to be raised to honors, because they are altogether unworthy of them. These, namely, hope that by this art they can easily be advanced to some eminence. Here is ambition wrapped in the name of contempt of honors. Most of those who live in the courts of Kings cover it with the specious name of compliance. They, namely, perpetually praise the deeds and sayings of those from whom they hope for fortune; and, mindful of Terence’s saying, compliance begets friends, truth hatred, they command themselves to assent to everything and to hold everything as true. This habit corrupts judgment and blunts the edge of judging.

128 Most like this is Avarice: how far it has blinded the minds of men, how many wars it has stirred up in every age of the world, how many kingdoms it has made solitary and deserted, History shows clearly. Truly, those who are driven by such an affection can scarcely, or not even scarcely, hear the truth, much less comprehend it by reason and consider it attentively.

129 Fear also generates wonderful phenomena in the minds of men. Those who are seized by excessive fear scarcely ever understand things

[p. 45] as they are: they think they see what they do not see, and perpetually reason badly. Hence so many prodigies present themselves in the Histories of the Heathen, which flowed from this source, that peoples persuaded themselves that the immortal gods would exact the penalty for crime by a visible punishment. And once their minds had been stirred to religious awe, it was easy for them to think that whatever happened less ordinarily, whether an eclipse of the Moon or of the Sun, or an egg larger than usual, or a serpent in the house, and follies of that kind, that these, I say, were portents by which those Gods of theirs declared their anger and indignation.

130 But among our own people too, how many fables are born of fear! Those who fear assert that they themselves see apparitions of the night, specters of tombs, things horrible to tell. Whatever is heard by night is ghosts. If some old and ragged woman comes along, she, forsooth, displays a marvelous power of calling up demons at pleasure, of doing harm to whomever she will, and of killing a man with impunity: and six hundred most trifling things of this kind, which none but those seized with terror, or fools, will ever affirm.

131 How headlong Anger drives men, no one fails to perceive. It clouds the mind and blinds the very eyes, so that nothing so absurd can be said or thought that the angry man does not do in his very fury; so much so that, when master of himself, he is sometimes ashamed of having perpetrated such things. Hence the mind is so vehemently shaken that it can scarcely judge rightly of things: it thinks the things that stand in its way greater, and the rest much smaller, than they are; and therefore it always chooses the worse part. Wherefore, if we reckon up the account, we shall find that the greater calamities of mortals have proceeded from anger.

132 These things being briefly surveyed, it becomes manifest that those motions of the mind which disturb reason (for all of them disturb it) must be restrained, and that it is the Philosopher’s business to take care that we are not agitated by any affections, but have a serene mind, if we desire to judge rightly and wisely. For as a ship in mid-sea, driven by vehement and contrary winds, can neither hold its course nor make for port, so our mind, driven about by those affections as by a wind, will scarcely ever attain the truth toward which it tends; therefore commit this Canon to memory: Do not judge while you are occupied by some affection: and if you have judged, call the matter back again to examination; then at last pronounce, freely, and after the matter has been accurately weighed.
