## CHAPTER VI

On the fallacies of the Mind, which prevent us from finding the truth.

ut the weakness of our mind too (continues the cited Verney) will 133

B          more often be the cause of many errors, into which we very fre‐

quently slip, and which wonderfully retard the attainment of truth.

To avoid them it is necessary to know their causes thoroughly and to fix them deep in the mind, so that we may more easily avoid them when they occur. We refer them, not inconveniently, to three classes, our slowness, perverse method, and prejudices, which we shall explain in the same order.

134 The first and chief cause on account of which we are deceived in judging is the very nature of our mind, which both has its faculty of understanding confined within narrow limits, and understands the very things it understands so obscurely that it can scarcely be believed. We shall perceive this most plainly if we examine our cognitions more diligently.

135 For our mind, even though it dwells in the body, is nevertheless ignorant of the wholly wonderful fabric of the body, of the brain especially. Not that it is not at all suited to knowing it; for if another’s brain is set before it and its parts are visible, it knows them perfectly: but on this account only, because

God did not will that the soul should know corporeal things thoroughly except through the senses.

136 Next, it does not attain the nature of things, however common: for example, it cannot determine whether a body has infinite parts or not; what the nature is of the Sun, of the Moon, of the Stars, both of those that are called wandering and of those that are called fixed; finally, whether there are living creatures in the stars; and six hundred things of that kind. To pass over for the present the things that can be done by God, about which the School tells many most trifling tales, and which can by no means be understood, much less defined.

137 But this slowness and weakness cannot be wholly amended: we can apply one remedy, to beware studiously of defining those things for the investigation of which we are altogether unfit. Of these, moreover, there are two classes:

the one, of those things that surpass our intelligence, such as the nature of the divine properties; [p. 47] likewise all possible things, which can be neither determined nor explained by the reasonings of nature or by divine utterance. The other is of things that can indeed be understood, but we lack the necessary aids by which we might arrive at the knowledge of them: such are those we named a little before, and also the most ancient histories, and infinite things of this kind. And so much on the first cause.

138 The second cause is perverse method. This extends very widely, and from it arise very many errors and infinite evils. For in the first place there are those who, having entered upon a winding road set in darkness, do not arrive at the end they proposed to themselves, but frequently slip: nay, the further they advance along it, the more they swerve from the truth. Certain men of letters very often strike upon this rock.

139 There are men who, even if they are not versed in the Mathematical disciplines, nevertheless pass judgment quite confidently on the writings of the Modern Philosophers, and dare to work out a great many things in Physics. There are those who interpret the Sacred Bible without knowing Greek and Hebrew, without having any knowledge of Jewish and Profane history, who are plain strangers to the Critical art. There are those who expound the Roman laws who are tinged with no knowledge of Roman history, and have not tasted even with the tips of their lips the rudiments of Ethics and Politics. There are those who teach Pontifical law, who teach Sacred science, without ever having turned over the writings of the Fathers and examined the ancient discipline of the Church. Finally, to omit the rest, there are Physicians who persuade themselves that they will cure the infinite variety of diseases that afflict the human body without ever having seen a dissection of the human body. All these, because they are ignorant of what is necessary, will never be able to bring forth anything good.

140 Others, again, although they proceed rightly, nevertheless fall into the contrary vice. Namely, since they long to know everything and to be praised above the rest, they read quite different things at the same time; and though they desire to seem anything but unlearned, they are the most unlearned of all. For our mind, which scarcely grasps any one discipline perfectly, knows nothing thoroughly and deeply while it reads many things at once, and so acquires nothing but confused ideas, and for that reason is deceived in judging.

141 The third cause of errors is prejudices, or anticipated judgments that our mind makes about certain things: from which it comes about that we form our other judgments quite similar to them, and do not judge freely and deservedly about anything. For since men from their earliest age are accustomed to listen to others, who imprint on their minds the images of certain things,

[p. 48] they easily persuade themselves that what they hear is true, and attach such faith to such things that they can only with difficulty be turned to the contrary side. From this an infinite crop of errors springs up. And so the incredible multitude of prejudices that holds men is reduced to the prejudice of authority, if you take away a few that arise in adult men either from hatred or from love.

142 And first, the authority of parents is to children the norm of judging, and the cause of many errors. For parents imbue their children from the earliest age with foolish prejudices, which the nurses unceasingly confirm; and since tender minds are not strong in the use of reason and are not at all practiced in judging, they cannot persuade themselves that they have been deceived by their parents: and therefore they are deceived to a wonderful degree. Hence specters, and goblins, and ghosts, and the virtues of herbs and of medicines, and the miracles of mountebanks, and the other most trifling things that beat upon the ears of unhappy boys: so much so that, when they have become men, and are admonished by most learned men, they can scarcely at any time free themselves from those prejudices.

143 Next, nearly all parents treat their children softly and let them indulge their inclination, because they persuade themselves that if they did otherwise it would be to the harm and injury of their little ones. Hence boys are very often immersed in bodily pleasures, especially those of food and of venery, which both blunt the edge of the mind and weaken the memory, and so lead a man astray that he can scarcely ever think about and examine anything seriously and with meditation. For hold this for certain, young men: no more deadly plague befalls either body or mind than the pleasures of the body, which not only gradually undermine the fabric of man, but extinguish all the light of the mind. For laden tables carry off more men from our midst, frequent cups more, venery itself more, than plague, than war.

144 Parents are succeeded by Teachers, who frequently imbue little boys with marvelous opinions, and by their authority restrain them from learning other disciplines than those in which they themselves are versed.

145 The Peripatetic Doctor cries out that the disciplines of the Moderns are futile and weak; the Critical Art, Natural History, Geometry, Arithmetic, Mechanics and things like these he thinks to be boys’ trifles; and he hisses off men illustrious in these disciplines just as if they were madmen. On the other hand, he everywhere sounds forth Universals and Signs, and Syllogistics, and Topics, and the huge throng of despicable little questions that he entitles Physics and Metaphysics; and he contends that the limits of philosophical science are wholly defined by these. Nay, at times he strikes, as it were, terror into the minds of the boys,

[p. 49] lest they learn Mathematics or the Philosophy of the Moderns, or ever call back to a severe examination the things that he himself holds as settled and fixed.

146 The little boy, nourished on these admonitions, reverently kisses the pronouncements of his Teacher, and thinks that nothing more excellent can be conceived; he turns away from the splendid discoveries of others as though they were mere trifles, and shudders at the mere hearing of the name of the Systems of the Moderns: therefore he is ignorant of the sources of the disciplines, and can neither think nor utter anything worthy of learned ears. And so, when he has grown older, he too nourishes others with the same milk, and propagates ignorance with as much labor as would have been needed for him to be held most illustrious in the best disciplines.

147 This was the reason why the weightier disciplines lay in squalor for so many centuries: namely, because the teachers who were thought most learned strove with all their might to keep the boys from deserting the old Masters, or from thinking anything new that was not in them. For men of this kind grieved to be surpassed in learning by younger men, and ambitiously took care that this new doctrine and new way of teaching should not undermine the glory they themselves had won by so many labors. And so they confidently objected that very many heresies are stirred up in Theology even by the help of a better Philosophy; and by this argument, drawn from envy, false indeed but received with applause, they ruined the discoveries of others, nay, even their talent.

148 From this education, moreover, there arise all too many prejudices, which are usually taken from the circumstances of persons and of books. For who, they say, would not do, or think true, the things that are done by a man advanced in age? by one who has piety toward God? who displays wisdom and moderation of mind? who surpasses the rest in nobility, in riches, in dignity, in honors? who is distinguished from others by his kind of life, by his name, by his talent? who would think that such a man can err? On the other hand, who would persuade himself that anything excellent can be thought by a young man, or by a poor man, and a ragged one at that, known above others by no ornaments, by no insignia of dignity? by one who tells no stories readily at a banquet and a drinking-party? who shows something unsightly in his manner of life, his face, his gesture, and is therefore hissed off both by silly women and by effeminate busybodies?

149 These are the common prejudices of authority by which men are led in every part of life. Not that they say expressly: he is rich, or noble, or old: therefore he cannot err: for the fault of this consequence is at once placed before the eyes. But tacitly they feel and settle it so; and without thinking distinctly about

G [p. 50] these things, yet from a long habit of listening and of thinking imprudently, as if by a certain impulse of nature, they conform their actions to this rule.

150 Add to these those who measure the learning either of the author or of the possessor by the multitude, size, titles, rarity and price of books. Truly nothing occurs more frequently, not only among the unlearned but even among most of those who apply themselves to letters, than this prejudice.

151 For who would persuade some people that those copious volumes of Tostado, Bishop of Ávila, which expound Sacred Scripture, are in many respects to be ranked below, I do not say Calmet and other more copious writers, but even Tirinus and Menochius and the others who have written briefly? Who unskilled in History and Criticism would think that Salian’s Annals of the Old Testament, in six great volumes in folio (as they call it), are to be valued much less than Petau’s Rationarium or the brief commentaries of Sigonio and others on the Republic of the Hebrews? Which of the Casuists would persuade himself that the huge volumes of Leandro, Torrecilla and other Casuists that hand down Moral discipline ought to give place even to the single little book of Antoine On Moral Matters, to say nothing of others? Moreover, who that is ignorant of the newer Physics would think that Newton’s Principles of Natural Philosophy alone surpasses all the Libraries of the Scholastics in firmness, solidity and utility, if one weighs the sources and order of things? Let the same judgment hold for the rest, which very often lead men into errors.

152 Weigh the other circumstances of books, and with free judgment: you will plainly discover that not the pomp of a title that seems to promise something great, such as Theatre of Human Life, Thesaurus, Polyanthea, Encyclopedia, Library of Canon or Civil Law; not the rarity or price of books; not the other things of this sort, can give books either name or esteem. Yet from these prejudices nearly all the errors of the half-learned proceed. From these they would free themselves admirably, if they judged things by their own merit, not by the opinions of others.

153 Now when a man leaves the discipline of his teachers, he runs into the manners of those who live in popular fashion, who are so far from polishing his judgment that they rather generally confirm him in error. For since the errors we drank in with our first milk are cured only by the most accurate meditation, and there are few who weigh with free judgment their first ideas and the force of words, it so happens that the greater part of men persevere in the errors of childhood, and by their error and obstinacy confirm their fellow-countrymen in them. Hence fellow-countrymen generally have the same manners, gladly live on the same foods, and cherish the same opinions. And this not

[p. 51] only in a light matter, but also in the gravest affairs; and, what is more, in that affair of the greatest moment which concerns religion.

154 Ask the people what an Angel is: they will answer that it is a winged boy; ask what the Devil is: you will hear that it is a most hideous man, who bears the appearance of a satyr. Ask also what the Moon is, what the Sun: you will hear that it is an animal that resembles a man in its face, and things like these. Ask what God is: you will be sent off to the Theologians.

155 What? Even of those who are engaged in letters, very many embrace wonderfully absurd opinions. There are those who persuade themselves that, provided they confess their sins against God to the Priest and hear the words of absolution, they are truly freed from all guilt, giving no thought meanwhile to whether they grieve for the crimes they have committed and firmly resolve to live holily in the future. How frequent the number of these is, would that we had not ourselves experienced! Others defend other things no less harmful. So that I seem to myself to speak truly in saying that, of those who do not of set purpose devote themselves to the more solid Theology, there are few who have a true idea of religion and of the manner of worshipping God, and that everywhere there are very many who hold doggedly to one that is generally confused and erroneous.

156 Therefore, to meet these fallacies, the following Canons are to be established, according to the order of the errors, and what they prescribe is to be observed.

157 Canon I. Do not investigate the things that exceed the powers of the human mind: for you will lose your oil and your labor. Avoid the things that plainly cannot be understood. Do not investigate possible things. Canon II. Study with method and order: learn first the clearer and easier things, by which the things that follow may be elucidated. Do not learn many things at once, but meditate on each one separately and most keenly. Cut away useless and empty things; give your time to the more useful. Canon III. Beware of prejudged opinions, which you have acquired by the usage of the home, or of the School, or of the people. Call back each idea and each word to examination, and do not assent to them before you understand that the matter is so. Do not pronounce rashly on the opinions of others; and estimate things not by the sense of the crowd, but by that of the best.

## BOOK III

On the means of finding the truth, and of communicating it to others.

ince enough has now been said, as the plan of Elements allows, about 158

S      the operations of the human intellect and the very nature of truth,

and about the fallacies of the senses, of the will and of the mind which impede the attainment of truth, the next thing is that we should say a little more accurately how these operations of the intellect are to be used for investigating and communicating truth. We shall treat, therefore, first of the Method by which the truth is to be found, then of that by which a truth known to us is to be explained to others; to which we shall then append a few things on the method of Studying and of Disputing, and some on routing philosophical Pedantry.

## CHAPTER I

On the Logico-analytic Method, or method of invention.

hat manner and method of investigating hidden and desired truth 159

T          is called the Analytic Method, or method of invention, which can be de‐

fined: the art of disposing our thoughts so that, as far as the human condition allows, we may uncover the truth that is hidden from us. It is called Analytic, that is, of resolution, because, in order that what lies concealed in hiding may become open to us, every whole must be divided into its parts, every composite must be resolved into its principles, and every effect must be referred back to its cause.

160 The Peripatetic Philosophers scarcely, or not even scarcely, touched this most excellent, nay truly the most important, part of Philosophy, [p. 53] although it is the chief aim of this most excellent discipline, which takes upon itself the arduous charge of correcting and ruling the mind. We shall select whatever the Moderns have committed to writing on this subject, and shall explain it as briefly and as neatly as can be done.

161 Before we approach the work, however, it must be noted that the nature of this mind of ours is such that it cannot attain everything that is unknown to it. It must therefore be kept before our eyes that we are ignorant of the essences of things, and so ignorant of the essence of matter; and this being posited, there are insoluble questions which we cannot answer, such as those which depend on knowledge of essence, of which we are not speaking. Lest anyone, then, should perhaps incautiously waste his time in inquiring by the Analytic method into those things which, wrapped always in thick darkness, will lie hidden from men, we have thought it fitting to forewarn you to abstain from inquiring into them.

162 There are also useless questions, such as are nearly all those that are handled by the Peripatetics in endless quarrels, e.g. whether the copula is a term? Whether privation is a principle of the composite as already made? Whether matter desires corrupted forms? and others emptier still by far, which I should be ashamed to say I do not understand, if those who treat them understood them themselves: questions which either can never be settled, just as they are certainly still disputed on both sides by the Scholastics, or, if perhaps they could be settled perfectly, would nevertheless make us not a whit more learned; so that it is accordingly absurd to apply the laws of the Analytic method, or the force of the mind, or any part of precious time, to settling them.

163 We have, besides, questions that are soluble and not useless, which are conveniently divided into three classes; for in any question whatever, either, an attribute being given, it is asked to what subject it belongs? or, a subject being posited, it is inquired what determinate predicate belongs to it? or finally, a predicate and a subject being posited, it is asked whether the one belongs to the other. There are, therefore, three highest genera of all questions, nor can there be more. Of the first kind is, e.g., this question: what is the cause of earthquakes? For in this question, an attribute being given, namely the cause of the earthquake, it is asked what the subject is to which that attribute belongs? that is, what is that thing to which this attribute belongs, that it produces the earthquake? and so of the rest. Here, then, are the rules by which we must proceed in the investigation of the truth.

164 Rule I. Weigh whether you are so prepared in mind as to be fit for discovering that truth or for solving the question, lest you either wander about to no purpose, or blurt out inept and ridiculous things. Suppose, e.g., the matter in hand is Theological, Medical, Astronomical, things of which you are ignorant. Will you not be utterly ridiculous

[p. 54] who, ignorant of such faculties, come forth upon the stage to play the Theologian, the Physician, the Astronomer? To this may be applied that saying of Horace:

Take, you who write, a matter equal to your strength, and turn over long what your shoulders refuse to bear, what they can carry.

165 But if we have ideas of the thing in question, and are fit to solve the question, then follows Rule II. Weigh whether the question is simple or compound: and if it is compound, divide it accurately into all its simple questions, examined minutely, and inquire first into that one which can carry light before the others. E.g. It is asked, what is the use and the structure of the parts of the eye? Two questions are proposed: of these the second will be examined first of all; for unless it is known what the parts of the eye are, it cannot be explained what their uses are. Rule III. Explain the knot of the proposed question in the clearest words. For unless it is plainly established what is to be sought, the whole disputation will wander in uncertainty. Rule IV. Understand the question, and express it exactly and as simply as possible, that is, cutting away from it whatever does not at all bear upon it. Concerning which, if there are things in the proposed question that can be removed while the question remains intact, it belongs to prudence to cut them away.

166 Rule V. Let every genus be divided, as far as can be done, into its species, and let them all be separated and distributed into definite classes. Rule VI. Having established what is to be investigated, we must attentively observe what, in that very thing, becomes known to us. For our mind is equal to grasping unknown things only insofar as they participate in diverse ways in the nature of those things which were previously known to us. Rule VII. It is of the greatest importance (as Descartes excellently advises) to advance our thoughts in a fixed order, beginning, namely, with those things which are easier for us to know, and from these proceeding little by little, and as it were by steps, to the more difficult investigation. Rule VIII, and last. If you have searched long and have not found the truth, renew the examination. If you have tried again in vain, do not pronounce the thing either false or less than possible merely because you do not understand it, unless you are so utterly ridiculous as to think your own mind the measure of the true and the false.

## CHAPTER II

On the Logico-Synthetic Method, or the Method of Imparting

Doctrine.

ruth sought by the analytic method and found is demonstrated to 167

T          others by the synthetic method. Synthesis, therefore, is the method

of imparting doctrine, or of demonstrating the truth as conveniently as can be done. To demonstrate, moreover, is to reason so aptly for persuading that the person with whom we are disputing can in no way seriously and sincerely refuse his assent. But in order that the persuasion of others may be obtained beyond escape, these four laws must be observed.

168 Rule I. Use no word or expression that is, or can be, ambiguous or obscure, left undefined; but explain most lucidly the determinate sense and the precise signification in which you wish such words or expressions to be taken. Rule II. Do not, through carelessness, twist words or expressions once defined into another sense in the course of arguing.

Rule III. Draw no inference that is not connected by a necessary and immediate bond with the propositions from which you gather it. Rule IV, and last. Every proposition from which something is to be gathered or inferred by you must either be self-evident by simple intuition, or be deduced from other premises as a necessary consequence. These laws are not only necessary for constructing a demonstration, but they alone suffice, as the celebrated Soria excellently proves. (y)

## CHAPTER III

On the Method of Studying.

ethod of studying I call that by which our studies are to be directed, 169

M               so that from the reading of books we may thoroughly learn the

discipline we desire by our own efforts as well. Truly, I judge that it has come about only through lack of a right method

(y) Elem. of Logic. [p. 58] until one occurs both of whose premises are granted by the respondent. It is

characteristic of Pedagogues, whom in Spanish we call Pedantes, when they take it upon themselves to refute a thesis, not to prove the antithesis and to act in good faith, but to resort to stratagems: either to weaken things that are said in passing, and not deliberately and as one’s real opinion; or to drive the respondent off course with inept little questions, to mock him, or to weary the beginner with arguments utterly foreign to the matter in hand; or finally to thrust forward the same arguments again and again, as though the adversary had made no reply to them.

T H I N G S P RO P E R T O T H E R E S P O N D E N T.

176 The respondent should take up the syllogism proposed by the opponent, that is, repeat it, so that it may appear that he has grasped the opponent’s meaning. Let him repeat the premises a second time, noting at each one whether he grants it, or desires a further proof, or allows it to pass for the meantime until the other has been sufficiently proved, using, e.g., these formulas: I grant the major, I deny the minor, I deny the antecedent, let the major pass, etc. If he grants the premises in one respect and denies them in another, let him use a distinction and apply it to the argument; in which case it is the opponent’s part either to prove the premise under the limitation under which it is denied, or to attack the limitation as inept. When the President takes upon himself the part of the respondent, the same duties are his as are the respondent’s.

C H A P T E R V.

On Banishing Philosophical Pedantry.

his word Pedantry takes its origin from Pedagogues, who, because 177

T           they follow noble boys on foot, are called Pedanti in the Italian

tongue. These men, from long habit of commanding boys, affect such authority that even when speaking with other men and about other matters they display authority in their voice, their look, and their very gestures. And since they are educated in humane letters or in Philosophy only lightly, or not even lightly, they so imbue their minds with most inept opinions as utterly to deprave their judgment, [p. 59] and blunt the edge of their judging: nay (what is most to be lamented), they frequently instill the same vices even in those to whose education they devote their labor. From this is born that most rotten Pedantry, that is, a general ineptitude of judgment: which, like a plague of the liberal arts, creeps far and wide to the ruin of young men, and contaminates both humane letters and the weightier disciplines.

178 And hence it becomes manifest that a pedant is to the Moderns the same as an ineptus [inept man] was to the Latins. They called ineptus the man who was not apt for judging well about things. This ineptitude of judgment, however, is not confined within narrow regions, but extends far and wide. We nevertheless designate it by the single name of Philosophical Pedantry, because it flows from imprudence in judging, which is most directly opposed to the prudence of thinking rightly, that is, to Logic, whose chief use is in all the disciplines.

179 Hence those are deservedly condemned who swear by the words of a master, and make it a matter of conscience to depart even in the least from his opinions. This Pedantry darkened the old Pythagoreans, who attributed so much to their teacher that they always had in their mouths he himself said it; which for them stood in place of a Geometrical demonstration. The Arabs did this very thing with their Aristotle, and with Galen. Those who had received their doctrine from the Arabs practiced it from the twelfth century on with such zeal that they anxiously explored, not what was true, but what Aristotle had said; nay, they investigated not what Aristotle, a man not inept, had said, but what the Arabs, who had wrongly interpreted the Philosopher’s opinions, had foisted upon him. From this came those disputations which prevailed for so many centuries, and stood in men’s way, so that they attempted nothing distinguished in good studies. And unless, as the last century was drawing to its close, the Philosophers had thoroughly shaken off such a yoke, all the disciplines would still be lying in that barbarism and squalor.

180 Hence those labor under the same Pedantry who, when they apply their mind to some discipline, do not notice to what end the matter disputed pertains, and what fruit the human mind ought to gather from such disciplines. Of this kind are those who give themselves to the disciplines without any method, and take no thought for polishing the mind and forming the judgment. Of these the number is truly infinite. To the same class are referred those who apply themselves to one discipline with their whole heart without so much as touching those things from which it receives its light. Who would bear men who devote themselves to Natural philosophy without rightly grasping Geometry in their minds?

181 In the same number are placed those who dispute, with loud voice and straining of lungs, about things which they themselves, to say nothing of others, do not understand. This is frequently done by those who wrangle among themselves about quiddities,

H2 [p. 60] haecceities, formalities, the appetite of prime matter, and six hundred things of this kind. They understand, to be sure, the words, and sometimes the abstract ideas which they join to the words. But since no such things correspond to such ideas, they are disputing about nothing. Accordingly, though they pour out many words, they say nothing in truth, and therefore do not understand themselves, both because they say nothing and because they very often put different ideas under the same words.

182 Among the pedants are also reckoned those who confidently pass judgment on the writings of others without having the things that are necessary in order to judge aptly. For how rash it is to judge of the opinions of the Modern philosophers before having so much as greeted their tenets and the History of Letters from the threshold! Who would bear those who, imbued with no learning in true Theology, tinged with no knowledge of the Critical Art, repudiate with great haughtiness the opinions of certain authors as though they were repugnant to the Catholic faith, opinions which they, I will not say do not weigh, but do not even understand?

183 Deservedly, too, you would count among the Archpedants men of that stamp (to speak more merrily) whose heart’s concern it is to pronounce, before the benches of the women, on the right method of philosophizing and on the Newer Philosophy: forsooth, a great weight of authority must accrue day by day to the Peripatetic School from that very Decree of the Women’s Senate: as if it were not unbecoming for men, where there was need of counsel, labor, alacrity, and training in the best arts, to take refuge with chattering women and the ruder rabble. But enough of this.

184 To the Pedants are also added the Consequence-mongers: those, namely, who, while they refute the opinions of others, without overturning the foundations of the contrary opinion, take refuge in consequences, by which to bring the honor and good name of their adversaries into jeopardy; thinking that, if not by reasons, at least by threats and abuse, they will dislodge their adversaries from their ground and their cause. E.g. someone praises the philosophical investigation of Boyle, Leibniz, Newton, Leeuwenhoek, Clarke, Derham, and the other heretics who have set Philosophy in a good light. The consequence-monger infers: that he is a Heretic, or suspect of heresy; that he is not to be listened to; and that whatever learning flows from that source is to be hissed off the stage as pernicious.

185 Now this reasoning: He praises the philosophical investigation of Heretics: therefore he is a Heretic, is false. And so the other things that are drawn from it labor under the same vice. For not everything the Heretics have said is false, nor is everything Catholics have written true. Both have written things good and bad, which are to be weighed by the oracle of the Vatican: and if by Pontifical

[p. 61] laws they may exist and be read, they are surely censured rashly with arguments drawn from envy. By the same right we might argue in this way: he stubbornly defends the dogmas of Aristotle, adheres to the tenets of Galen, Avicenna, Averroes: therefore he is a Heathen, or a Mohammedan. Which, however, is a most inept kind of arguing.

186 Joined with the pedants, too, are those who think they will win the praise of the most polished Moderns in no other way than if, when about to write a Philosophy, they stitch together a patchwork of conflicting opinions: as if someone, e.g., about to write a Physics, after stubbornly defending the system of the Scholastics on substantial and accidental forms, nevertheless, in explaining certain phenomena, embraces the opinions of Gassendi, Descartes, Newton. He indeed is a pedant, and writes without any judgment.

187 Lastly, those are counted among the pedants who overwhelm the minds of boys with a multitude of precepts, and are wholly bent on weaving long disputations, without first examining whether they conduce to the end they set themselves. From this it comes about that the beginner, however well trained in those trifles and quibbles, if he is brought to some controversy that is not disputed in the school, does not know what he ought to decide.

188 Lest you should think, young men, that this has been said by me out of ill-will or for any other cause, I affirm to you for certain that in disputing and writing these things I am moved by no partisanship. I should certainly sin, and deservedly be laughed at, if I, who counsel beginners not to judge from prejudiced opinions, should myself pronounce on the opinions of others with a prejudice to be repented of. I do not wish to be judge in this cause: let those most learned men judge who have long and greatly tormented themselves in the Peripatetic philosophy; who, if they are honest men, must confess that this common Logic in which they are versed, and which they extol to the skies with praises and call a divine invention, that very Logic helps them not at all to dispute about matters that are not taught in the Schools.

189 And these are the chief kinds of pedantry, to which the rest are easily reduced. We pass over the others, lest our discourse run on without end. From what we have said it is sufficiently manifest that a preposterous, absurd, and inept manner of reasoning, and the want of true Philosophy, have been the cause of our falling into pedantry: that is, of our failing, in any discipline, properly to recognize its end and its aids, and to keep due measure. If we rightly recognized these, we should surely beware of the inepties that expose us to the mockery of the learned and the prudent; and this is the very thing that being a Philosopher in each matter means. The celebrated Verney, from whom we have excerpted these things, discourses of many others concerning pedantry. Consult him.

## SCHOLASTIC EXERCISES

## ON LOGIC

E X E RC I S E I .

Whether an idea, or the simple perception of a thing, can be false?

ogical truth, as was said above, is the agreement of our ideas with the 190

L        object, and this is also called the truth of cognition; whence, whatever

the idea may be, whether simple or complex, its truth consists solely in agreement with the thing perceived, apart from affirmation or negation. But the truth of judgment, which is called the truth of composition, lies in affirmation or negation. And so a judgment is deemed true when it says that that is which really is, or denies that that is which is not; but false if it affirms that that is which is not, or denies that that is which is. These things being posited,

191 I say I. A perception or idea, whether simple or complex, can be true.

Proof: a perception is called true when it agrees with its object; but a perception, whether simple or complex, can agree with its object: therefore. Proof of the minor: the perception of a mountain, which is simple, and the perception of a steep mountain, which is complex, can agree with their objects, or the things perceived, as all understand: therefore.

192 I say 2: a perception, whether simple or complex, can never, properly speaking, be called false. Proof: that perception would, properly speaking, have to be called false which disagreed with the object perceived; but a perception, whether simple or complex, cannot be said to disagree with its object; for if it represents a present thing as it is, e.g. gold when gold is present, then it agrees with its object, as no one denies. But if it does not represent the present object, but something else, e.g. if, when brass is present, [p. 63] it presents gold, it is indeed a true perception of gold, but by no means of brass, and so it is not a false perception of brass, but none, or rather it is no perception of brass at all: therefore a perception, whether simple or complex, cannot, properly speaking, be called false.

193 I say 3: a perception, whether simple or complex, can be called false materially, as they say, and by occasion of the subsequent judgment. Proof: for a perception or idea to be capable of being called false in this way, it is enough that it can be the matter and the occasion of a false judgment; but a perception, especially a complex one, can be the matter and the occasion of a subsequent false judgment: therefore. Proof of the minor: the perception of gold when brass is present can be the occasion for someone’s judging that to be gold which is only brass: therefore.

T H E A RG U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

194 Obj. 1, against I. A perception, whether simple or complex, affirms or denies nothing: therefore it cannot be true. Dist. the consequent: it cannot be true with the truth of composition, which belongs to judgment, I grant; with simple or complex truth, which is the truth of a cognition agreeing with the object perceived, I deny. Secondly: the same reason holds for a simple perception’s being unable to be false as for its being able to be true; but on our view it can be true: therefore also false. I deny the major of the argument: for a perception would be false only when it did not agree with the object represented and perceived, which certainly can never be said; nay, it is true precisely because it always agrees with the object represented; and if an idea does not agree with the object that was to be represented, it will not be false, but none, as we have said.

195 Obj. 2: an idea which does not represent the object as it is, is false in itself; but the idea of gold when brass is present does not represent the object as it is: therefore. Dist. the minor: it does not represent as it is the object which is present and which ought to have been represented, I grant; it does not represent the perceived object as it is, I deny; and I deny the consequent. You will say: a complex perception is a true judgment, for it is equivalent to a judgment; but a judgment can be false: therefore a complex perception can be too. I deny the major: for a perception, whether it be simple or complex, affirms or denies nothing, whence it cannot itself be a judgment, although it is said to be equivalent to a judgment. You will insist: a complex perception, e.g. of a golden mountain, or of a broken stick, attributes something to the mountain, namely that it is golden, and takes away from the stick its integrity; but a cognition which attributes something to some subject, or takes something away from it, is equivalent to a judgment, or is a true judgment: therefore.

Dist.

[p. 64]

## 196 Dist. the minor: a cognition which attributes something to some subject, or

takes something away from it, by affirmation or negation, is a true judgment, I grant; by a mere conception of the subject together with the attribute, without affirmation or negation, I deny. You will say: the perception of an unjust God is false: therefore some false perception can be given. I reply by denying the hypothesis, namely that there can be a notion of an unjust God; for either by the name of God is understood what must necessarily be understood, namely a supremely perfect being, or not? If the first, there is not, nor can there be, any perception of an unjust God, because there would be an evident contradiction; if the second, it is nothing to the purpose, since that idea is not false which attributes injustice to an imperfect being. We say the very same of those perceptions which are called chimerical: for either they are none, if they involve contradictories, or they are true, if no contradiction is found in them, because they agree with the things that are perceived, even though those things do not exist in the nature of things.

197 Obj., finally: an idea must express that by which it is excited; but the idea of gold which is excited in us when brass is present does not express brass: therefore it does not express what it ought to express: therefore it is false. Dist. the major: every idea, I deny; the greater part of them, I grant. For there are very many bodies different in nature, but quite similar as to certain sensible qualities. It is certain, moreover, that from similar motions made in the organs of the senses the same ideas are necessarily excited in the mind: therefore we cannot prevent dissimilar bodies from sometimes exciting similar ideas in us, nor, accordingly, some idea from sometimes presenting to the mind a thing altogether different from that by which it is excited.

E X E RC I S E I I .

Whether all ideas take their origin from the senses?

The opinions of the Philosophers are set forth and refuted, and our own view is established.

wo species of perceptions are distinguished. The first is pure intellection, by 198

T           which the mind knows something without the aid of a phantasm or of a

corporeal species, e.g. when it perceives itself, its thoughts and affections, say joy, sadness, etc. Where it must be observed that this [p. 65] perception is called consciousness, because it is conscious to itself of its own thoughts or affections, and in a certain way knows within itself that it is thinking. The other species of perception is called imagination, of which we have already spoken (§. 12.)

199 That all ideas are acquired by the mind is most certain; but how it acquires them is not sufficiently agreed among the Philosophers. Lucretius (z) thinks that from the objects themselves certain images fly off, which enter the senses and make similar motions in the brain, and that in this way the mind acquires its ideas. Which is altogether false: for according to him these idols are bodies, and since they would be continually flying off from the surfaces, these would at length be worn away and perish utterly. Moreover, abstract things, such as reasonings and volitions, etc., could not be understood, because no images come from them to the senses; but these things are repugnant to experience.

200 The Aristotelians admit no purely intellectual ideas, but believe that the mind acquires all the images of things from the bodily senses. Hence that most celebrated maxim among them (a): nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the sense. Gassendi defends the same opinion. Malebranche (b) thinks that the mind sees all things in God, to whom it is essentially joined, as in a mirror; which is false, for the mind does not see in God as in a mirror. For a mirror offers the same thing to all who look into it: yet not all men see all things. The unlearned do not see what the learned understand. (See what was said in §. 86.)

201 The Cartesians hold that our intellect is a merely passive power, which does not itself produce its ideas, but receives them from God. And they distinguish ideas of a threefold kind: innate, adventitious, and factitious. They call innate the ideas which were divinely impressed on our mind immediately from its birth, and which have their origin from the first cause alone, without the aid of the body or of any second cause whatsoever. They call adventitious those which are produced on the occasion of motions in the bodily organs. Such are the sensations of heat, sound, smell, etc. Factitious, finally, they call the ideas which are composed from those with which our mind has already been informed, as when someone, from the idea of a mountain and the idea of gold, makes up for himself a golden mountain.

202 About adventitious and factitious ideas there can be no doubt. But as regards innate ideas, the state of the question is not

I                            usually

(z) On the Nature of Things, bk. 4, beginning, and especially v. 703 ff.

(a) Aristotle, On the Soul, bk. 3, ch. 5 and 8.

(b) Recherche de la Verité, bk. 1, ch. 2. [p. 66] usually set out clearly enough, as the celebrated Jacquier excellently observes. For if by this name they understand ideas perpetually present to the mind, there can be no controversy. For who would say that there is some idea in us which we contemplate unceasingly? But if they mean ideas which are always at hand before all experience and all reasoning, no one surely remembers any idea of this kind which the mind thought of before all experience and all reasoning.

203 But if by innate ideas we understand those notions which are sometimes acquired without the occasion of external objects, and by an easy and ready use of reason, we say that ideas are to be admitted as innate in this sense only. And in truth nothing else can be signified by the term innate ideas, as he will confess who weighs this most weighty question, not from the heat of disputation or the ambiguity of a definition, but from the proper testimony of his own consciousness. These things explained, let the conclusion be against the Peripatetics, Gassendi, and Locke.

204 We have many purely intellectual ideas, some of which we acquire by an easy use of reason. Proof: in those things which pertain to the mind, no safer rule ought to be applied than the inmost testimony of consciousness: but by the testimony of consciousness we experience that we perceive many things by pure intellection without any bodily image: therefore we have many purely intellectual ideas. Proof of the minor: many ideas of things present themselves to our mind which are entirely separated from all matter and sensible quality, such as are the ideas of assent and dissent, of justice, of intelligence, of God: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: assent and dissent, justice, etc., and other objects of our ideas have no likeness to sensible things, are endowed with no sensible quality, and accordingly can be represented by no sensation or imagination.

205 The conclusion is confirmed: those ideas are purely intellectual whose objects are neither colored, nor savory, nor sonorous, nor affected by any sensible quality, as St. Augustine says (c): but there are many ideas whose objects are neither colored, etc., such as are the idea of being in general, the idea of God, etc.: therefore purely intellectual ideas are given.

## REPLIES TO THE OB JECTIONS

206 Obj. 1: if there is any purely intellectual idea which does not have its origin from the senses, it is above all the idea of being in general, the idea of God,

etc.:

(c) Bk. 10 of the Confessions, no. 17, otherwise ch. 10. [p. 67] etc.: but these ideas take their origin from the senses: therefore. I deny the minor: because being in general is neither colored, nor savory, nor endowed with any sensible quality. But you will prove the minor: the idea of being in general is formed by abstraction from singular and individual bodies; but singular bodies are perceived by the senses: therefore such an idea takes its origin from the senses. To the proof, I distinguish the major: it is formed by abstraction from corporeal and spiritual things, I grant; from corporeal things only, I deny the major and the consequent.

207 We call being in general that which can exist; and so, even if it were supposed that there are no bodies, we could form this idea of being from the inmost consciousness of the operations of our mind, and without any relation to body. Moreover, if this idea took its origin only from the senses, it would not comprehend in its extension absolutely all the genera of being, but only corporeal beings; which, however, is false. You will insist 1: Nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the sense; therefore all ideas, and accordingly the idea of being in general, depend on the senses. Dist. the antecedent: which was not first in the external or the internal sense, I grant; in the external sense only, I deny the antecedent, and the consequent.

208 We confess that there is a twofold origin of ideas: the external sense, by which we acquire the ideas of corporeal things, and the internal sense, by which, through the mind’s attention and reflection upon its own operations, we procure the ideas of spiritual things. You will insist 2: but nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the external sense only: therefore the distinction is false. Proof of the subsumption: that was first in the external sense which is not known by us except by comparison with corporeal things; but we do not know spiritual things except by comparison with corporeal things: therefore. Proof of the minor: God is a spiritual substance; but we have no idea of God except insofar as we represent Him to ourselves under the image of a Venerable Old Man: therefore.

209 I reply by denying the minor. It is true indeed that our mind cannot, without the utmost care and attention, entirely purge its ideas of every bodily taint, and that for this reason the ruder sort of men perceive nothing except with an image. But those images, e.g. of an Old Man and of a winged youth, are not themselves the ideas of God and of the Angels, but mere phantasms which accompany those ideas. For if we had no other idea of God than the idea of a Venerable Old Man, all the judgments that we form about God would have to appear to us entirely false, as being contrary to this idea; for we believe those judgments to be false which are contrary to the ideas of things that we have in our mind; and therefore we could not judge God to be incorporeal, invisible, since none of these can in any way agree with the idea of a Venerable Old Man.

I2                                       You

[p. 68]

210 You will insist 3: The Apostle writes in Rom. ch. 1: the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made: therefore God is not known by us except by comparison with corporeal things. Dist. the antecedent: insofar as from the consideration of corporeal and spiritual things we rightly conclude that the supreme Maker of all things exists, I grant; insofar as the idea of God is some phantasm formed by comparison with corporeal things, I deny. We must beware, therefore, lest, as St. Paul says in the same place, the glory of the incorruptible God be changed into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man.

211 You will insist 4: the idea of God is formed from the ideas of the perfections of all creatures, even corporeal ones: therefore the idea of God is formed by comparison with corporeal things. Dist. the antecedent: it is formed from the ideas of the perfections of creatures, even corporeal ones, taken eminently, I grant; taken formally, I deny, and the consequent. We do not include corporeal attributes in the idea of God formally, that is, as they are in bodies, but only eminently, that is, in a certain nobler and more sublime manner, without any imperfection, removing from God all the ideas of matter, of division, of color, and the rest, which, taken formally, necessarily include certain imperfections, and cannot belong to the supreme Being except eminently.

212 Obj. 2: if someone were born deprived of every sense, so that he neither saw nor heard, etc., he would surely have no ideas: therefore there are no purely intellectual ideas. I deny the antecedent: for in that hypothesis the mind would live; but the life of the mind consists in thinking, that is, in the perception of the intellect and the inclination of the will: therefore the mind would think. It would not, however, think of things remote from it, but of those which were present to it and by which it was moved. But nothing is more present to the mind than itself, as St. Augustine teaches: therefore it would know itself by a certain consciousness.

213 Obj. 3, against the second part of the conclusion: if there were any ideas acquired by an easy use of reason, such would be the ideas of God and of the morality of actions; but these are not: therefore. Proof of the minor: experience testifies that men have no idea of God and of the morality of actions unless they receive it from other men with whom they live: therefore the ideas of God and of the morality of actions are not such as to be acquired by an easy use of reason. Proof of the antecedent: from two examples which are reported by the Royal Academy of Paris,

it

(d) Bk. 14 of On the Trinity. [p. 69] it is plain that a man brought up among bears, and another who had been deaf

and dumb up to the twenty-fourth year of his age, had no idea of God and of the morality of actions before they conversed with other men and received that idea from them: therefore.

214 To the argument I reply by denying the minor, whose proof we shall explain. The examples adduced hold good only against those who think that those ideas are present to our minds before all attention. But since, according to our definition, innate ideas are not perceived without some use of reason, the cause to be assigned for so gross and almost incredible an ignorance is this:

that those men neglected the faculties of their mind and did not apply them to the investigation of the first truths.

E X E RC I S E I I I .

On the principal laws of sensations.

et the conclusion be: it is a law of sensations that as often as some 215

L          change is produced by a sensible object in a duly constituted sense

organ, so often there arises in the soul some particular sensation corresponding to this change. Proof: that sensation corresponds to the change which cannot be varied at our will; but the change made in a duly constituted sense organ cannot be varied at our will: therefore. Proof of the minor, from daily experience: if, e.g., the crash of a cannon strikes the ear, we necessarily perceive it, nor can we change that sensation into a gentler sound; if a stench fills the nostrils, we can in no way bring it about that in its place we perceive either a sweet odor or a less offensive stench: therefore.

216 From this general law of sensations four rules are gathered. I. If the change in the same organ is the same, the sensation in the soul must also be the same. II. If it happens that the same change is produced in the same sense organ by different sensible objects, the objects must appear the same. III. If the change in the sense organ is different, the sensation in the soul must also be different. IV. Hence if it happens that the same object produces a different change in the same organ, the object too must appear different.

From these flow the general principles for explaining vision, and the foundations of optical illusions.

The

[p. 70]

T H E A RG U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

217 Obj. 1: many changes are produced in a duly constituted sense organ without any sensation of the soul: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: when by day we gaze at the sky, the single stars send rays of light into the duly constituted eye, by which the image of the stars is delineated in the eye, and accordingly they produce changes in the sense organ; and yet the soul does not perceive the stars: therefore. Dist. the antecedent: many changes are produced without sensation that are insufficient, I grant; sufficient ones, I deny. To the proof, I grant the major and distinguish the minor: the soul does not perceive the stars by day, that is, the soul does not distinguish the weaker perceptions of the stars from the other, stronger ones, I grant; it has no obscure perceptions of the stars, I deny; and I deny the consequent.

218 Not every change made in the sense organ suffices for the soul to feel; but it is required that the change be transmitted all the way to the brain; and for this reason we said that the change must necessarily be made by a sensible object, that is, by an object which can produce a sufficient change in a duly constituted sense organ. But you will insist: the same sensation in the soul does not correspond to the same change made in the same sense organ: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the Sun and the Moon, when they hang over our zenith, appear smaller than when placed near the horizon; and yet in both places they produce the same change in the same eye: therefore.

219 I deny the antecedent, and to the proof I distinguish the minor: they produce the same change in the eye, joined with different other changes in each place, I grant; otherwise, I deny, and the consequent. We explain the phenomenon thus. The Moon and the Sun are usually seen larger on the horizon than at the meridian because on the horizon, together with their images, the intervening terrestrial bodies and the oblong vault of the sky are painted in the eye. This series of objects does not affect the eye when the Sun and Moon are seen at the top of the sky; and hence it is that if you look at the Sun and the Moon on the horizon through a narrow tube, they do not appear larger than at the top of the sky. When, therefore, we say that the same sensation in the soul corresponds to the same change made in the same organ, the proposition is to be understood of the changes each considered separately.

Exercise

[p. 71]

E X E RC I S E I V.

On the criterion of the true and the false.

e often observe that in many cases the agreement of the predi220

W               cate with the subject is known to us so clearly and plainly that it

is at once manifest and wrests our assent. By this supreme evidence we are persuaded that there has never been any sect of men that seriously doubted of all things. This being so, those seem not to understand sufficiently the state of the question who, in investigating the criterion of truth, place it in evidence, and demonstrate at length against the Sceptics that evidence exists. These, indeed, invent for themselves enemies to strike. We, however, shall explain this question by the following conclusion.

221 Conclusion: to distinguish the true from the false the rules of Logic suffice, and no other criterion of truth is needed. Proof of the 1st part: he discerns the true from the false who demonstrates that the predicate agrees with the subject; but the rules of Logic suffice for demonstrating this: therefore.

Proof of the minor: a demonstration consists of a chain of syllogisms whose premises are definitions, axioms, and propositions already demonstrated; but

Logic hands down the rules of definitions, establishes the distinction between axioms and demonstrable propositions, delineates the form of syllogisms, and shows, finally, the modes of joining syllogisms together, etc.: therefore. Proof of the 2nd part: if some other criterion of truth were needed besides the rules of

Logic, those rules would not suffice for discerning the true from the false; but we have demonstrated that they suffice: therefore.

222 Some place the criterion of truth in evidence itself. But that criterion of truth is not sufficiently determined: for clear perception, or evidence, must in any given case be applied through the rules of Logic. One must, namely, argue thus: whatever can be clearly and distinctly perceived is true; but this can be clearly and distinctly perceived: therefore this is true; and this is done through the rules of

Logic. Rules must therefore be handed down by whose help it may be judged that evidence, or truth, is present; and these are the rules of Logic. When it is said, therefore, that evidence is the criterion of the true, the matter stands just as if it were said that truth is the criterion of truth, which is to trifle.

Contrary

[p. 72]

C O N T R A R Y V I E W S A R E R E F U T E D.

223 Obj. 1: that is the criterion of truth which so separates the true from the false that we cannot refuse assent to the truth; but evidence does this, or, what is the same, the proposition whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived is true: therefore. I distinguish the minor: and that criterion is not sufficiently determined by itself, but through the rules of Logic, I grant; and it is so determined that there is no need of the rules of Logic, I deny; and the consequence. The solution remains explained. You will insist: that is not the criterion of truth which needs another criterion; but the rules of Logic need another criterion of truth, for evidence is needed to demonstrate the rules of Logic: therefore.

224 I distinguish the minor: evidence is needed, which must then be applied through the rules of Logic, I grant; evidence that does not need them, I deny. The whole difficulty vanishes if the state of the question is rightly understood. You will insist 2: the criterion of truth can be the principle it is impossible for the same thing at once to be and not to be: therefore, besides the rules of Logic, at least something else could be the criterion of truth. I distinguish the antecedent: and the proposition to be demonstrated must be reduced to that principle through the rules of Logic, I grant; otherwise, I deny. To this objection the reply is the same as to the preceding one.

225 You now have, excellent young men, the precepts and questions of Logic, which we put before you as the most useful; if you lay hold of them as befits your talent and your eagerness to learn, we are confident that you will have done work not to be regretted. These things are few, but for the character of your age many enough. If you want more, you will easily acquire it by reading the authors whom we have commended thus far.

## P R E FAC E 

fter Logic, not Physics, as the Peripatetics do, but Metaphysics 1

A         is what the Moderns teach, and rightly so; for since this discipline is

called first Philosophy, and in its first part is occupied with weighing the meaning of words and with unfolding the most generic principles, it must therefore enter into partnership and alliance with the faculty of discoursing. The name of Metaphysics, moreover, altogether unknown to the ancient

Philosophers, is said to have been first used by Alexander of Aphrodisias and

John Philoponus, interpreters of Aristotle. By this name, however, were entitled those writings of Aristotle which, once the Logical, Ethical and Physical works had first been put in order by Tyrannio the Grammarian and a certain

Andronicus of Rhodes,

L [p. 2] seemed unable to be referred to any definite class (a).

2 Now, however, by the name of Metaphysics there comes to the mind of Philosophers that discipline which pursues things placed on high, that is, things established above the nature of bodies, or spiritual things freed from all commerce with matter. Hence it is commonly and very well defined by all Philosophers: The faculty which considers all the general affections of being that are common to corporeal and incorporeal beings alike, and which also contemplates incorporeal substances and their affections, as they are perceptible to us by the light of reason alone. There are three principal parts of Metaphysics. The first of them is called Ontology, or Ontosophy, that is, the science of being, and so it treats of being taken in general, and weighs its affections as abstracted by the mind. The second so scrutinizes spiritual substances as to set before us their nature, existence and operations by the light of reason alone. And since there are chiefly two spiritual substances that can be known by us through the light of nature, namely God and the human mind, Pneumatology, or the Science of Spirits, has customarily been divided, quite fittingly, into two parts: that which treats of the human mind is called Psychology, or Pneumatology; that which discourses of God, with reason alone as guide, Natural Theology.

3 Accordingly we shall have three parts of Metaphysics, of which the first will comprise Ontology, the second Psychology, the last Natural Theology. The Peripatetic Philosophers handed down Metaphysics in so confused a manner that nothing more obscure can be conceived. We, however, excellent young men, shall give you a Metaphysics, not that old, long and intricate one, but a brief and very expeditious one, such as may sharpen the mind and pave the way for grasping the remaining disciplines.

Metaphysics

(a) The writings of Aristotle, which were left first to Theophrastus, then to Neleus, were hidden and buried under the earth by his heirs for some centuries. Then, when they were drawn out thoroughly corrupted by damp, they were sold to Apellicon of Teos, who unskillfully filled in the corrupted passages. When Athens had been subdued by L. Sulla, Apellicon’s library was carried to Rome by his order, where first Tyrannio, then Andronicus of Rhodes revised the works of Aristotle and put them in order. See what was said in the Hist. of Philos.
