[p. 23] if it were an intrinsic modification of matter, it would be matter itself modified; but thought neither is nor can be matter modified: therefore.

68 Proof of the minor: if it were so, thought would have the properties of matter; it would consequently be extended, divisible into parts, and figured; but this is most evidently repugnant: therefore. Proof of the minor: for who is so mad as to believe that an act of the intellect, e.g. assent or dissent, is spread out over a certain space of place, that it can be cut into two or four parts, and have a round, square, or triangular figure? Therefore thought does not have, nor can it have, the properties of matter: therefore the soul is the principle of operations that cannot belong to matter: therefore it is spiritual, and not matter.

69 But let us contemplate this matter a little more attentively with the most distinguished Valsecchi (z), and see whether we can persuade ourselves that matter can think. I think, and I consider my thought; I compose several notions, I separate them, I join them. Quicker than it can be said, I pass from heaven to earth, and turn over in my mind a great many most remote things. I weigh the nature, the properties, the relations of these things: I measure motions, spaces, times: I compare these things with those; from the open and clear I make my way by reasoning to the hidden and latent. Nor do I dwell only on the things that are subject to the senses, but I also turn over those that far surpass my senses. I know, and I discourse, about Being, about Order, about the Virtues, about Truth, about Reason, about God.

70 Of these and similar operations, which are called thoughts, I have consciousness, that is, an inner and most vivid sense, through which I know them; I know also that I, who think, and from whom these operations flow, cannot be a lump of stupid and inert flesh, but a self-moving substance, endowed with a power and efficacy of acting, and with that virtue of which matter is not capable.

71 Meanwhile I turn to this matter; I carefully carry out an analysis of it; and I find in it nothing other than extension, solidity, figure, rest, or motion. I cut it into a great many very fine parts. I give them every configuration I can, I impel them in every direction, with every degree of motion: but I never discern in them anything that is in the slightest degree like what I clearly know when I say to think; indeed nature itself draws me back from ascribing this attribute to them: and when I wish to assert that the finest dust and boiling blood can elicit those thoughts and reasonings, a greater force deters me than if I were saying that a circle is square; and when I hear that thought is hard or soft, triangular or pentagonal, this monstrous conjunction disturbs me more than either a goat-stag or a chimera.

72 To speak briefly, I know thought by an inner sense, I know extension clearly, and so far am I from perceiving the former in the latter, or vice versa,

that

(z) Dei fondamenti della Religione, & dei fonti dell’Empietà. [p. 24] that rather, comparing the one with the other, I see that there is such a discrepancy, diversity and distance between them that, however hard I strive, I cannot even imagine them joined to each other.

73 The same argument is set before our eyes by François Lamy, of the Order of St. Benedict (a). I shall give the whole passage, turned from French into Latin: “What, then, is the principle of these operations? (says the Monk just praised) Will it be the body, or a corporeal soul? Can it ever be conceived that a body, that is, a mass of flesh configured in this or that way, can elicit spiritual notions, perceive justice, wisdom, truth, and perceive and know itself?

74 “Who can seriously believe that a wind, a vapor, a smoke of animal spirits, which is diffused through my flesh and passes through my organs, can judge, that is, perceive the relations that exist between things? Is that thing, boiling and running about through my head, the cause why the animal spirits connect demonstrations with one another, that admirable order of inferences which is sometimes beheld in a single glance?

75 “Is it, finally, likely that this complex of corporeal organs and animal spirits can consider, discuss, foresee, weigh, will, desire, choose the good? That this being of clay is fit for solving questions and problems? And yet, if the matter is so, why, in solving questions that are somewhat more abstract and difficult, do we stop up the organs of the senses as far as we can, free ourselves from matter, impede its motions, and bring it about that through them it excites in us no impulse from that part which applies itself to the unravelling of the questions? Do we not evidently gather from this that that part is not corporeal?” Thus far he.

76 I say 2. Thought does not formally consist in this, that objects act on our organs, or in a certain motion of a most subtle and highly mobile substance, excited in our brain by the things with which we are occupied in thinking. Proof: if by this we understood that objects act on our organs, namely by moving that most subtle substance of the brain, the image of the objects would be impressed on us in no other way than this or that figure is impressed in wax: therefore, just as wax is not conscious of its figure, so we too could not be conscious of the things we know; but this is false to the point of evidence: therefore.

77 I say 3. Our mind is something altogether different from that most subtle and highly mobile substance which is elaborated in the brain from the purer blood. Proof 1: because, however subtle that substance be supposed, it is matter; but the soul cannot be matter, since it is the principle of operations that can in no way belong to matter,

as

(a) De la Connoissance de soi-même. [p. 25] as has been demonstrated: therefore. Proof 2: the soul cannot be placed in that liv‐

ing substance without thought itself being likewise placed formally in a certain motion of corpuscles that takes place in the brain; but we have demonstrated that thought differs by the whole breadth of heaven from every corporeal motion that takes place in the brain: therefore the rational soul is something altogether other than that living substance which is perfected in the brain from the purer blood.

78 I say 4: most absurd is the opinion of John Locke, who asserts that it is not impossible that matter should think, nay, that it can be brought about by the power of God that matter be endowed with the power of thinking. Proof: thought, or the power of perceiving, is intrinsically repugnant to matter, or body, as stands proved; but the power of God, however true it is that it is circumscribed by no limits, nevertheless cannot extend to impossible and contradictory things, since it cannot make the same thing at once be and not be: therefore Locke’s opinion is most absurd.

79 It must be noted here, however, that although the spirituality of the soul is most certainly established by Divine revelation, and we could prove it by the most splendid testimonies of the Holy Scriptures and of the Fathers, we abstain from them, because our business is with unbelieving and lost men who set Divine revelation at naught; therefore Philosophical demonstrations must be pressed against them, nor must we allow these weapons to be snatched from our hands, so that we may use them against the most bitter enemies of our Christian Religion. Lastly, I warn you that some Ecclesiastical Writers have at times called the human soul, the

Angels, God himself, a body, because, namely, as the most distinguished Jacquier remarks, since they could scarcely conceive an incorporeal substance, they called whatever existed a body in order to distinguish it from nothing, so that by the name of body they intended only to separate beings from nothing. But they clearly distinguished that body from matter, and therefore erred only by an abuse of the name. In

Leviticus, ch. 17, too, it is said that the soul of all flesh is in the blood. But this was said in such a way, says St. Augustine, as it was said: the rock was Christ; not, namely, because it was this, but because this was signified by it.

The arguments of the Materialists are answered. 80

Obj. 1. against the first: it is denied without any reason that thought belongs to matter, unless we know all the modifications of matter; but we do not know them all: therefore. I deny the major: for even if we do not know all the modes of matter, we nevertheless know for certain that contradictory modes cannot belong to matter. Now if matter thought, contradictory modes would belong to it, for thought excludes parts, extension, figure, division. But matter includes all these: therefore matter would have contradictory properties, if it could be endowed with the power of thinking.

O                                            81

[p. 26]

81 Inst. 1: although motion and rest are not something extended and divisible, they are nevertheless modifications of matter: therefore, although thought is not extended, divisible and figured, it can nevertheless be a modification of matter. I deny the consequence, and there is a disparity: because matter can have purely extrinsic modifications, such as motion and rest, which are neither extended nor divisible, because they are mere respects, mere relations that change nothing in the thing itself; but matter cannot have intrinsic modifications that are neither extended nor divisible, etc.: since, therefore, thought is an intrinsic modification of the thinking subject, it cannot belong to matter unless thought itself is divisible and extended, which is absolutely repugnant, as stands proved.

82 Inst. 2. When the body is injured the soul is injured: therefore the operations of the soul are modifications of matter. I distinguish the antecedent: it is injured, but in a different way, I grant; in the same way, I deny, and the consequence. For the body is injured insofar as the connection of its parts is either dissolved or violently disturbed, whereas the soul is injured insofar as, by the law of union, a grievous and troublesome sensation is excited in it. You will say: it cannot be conceived how what is spiritual is received in a body, which has extension and can be cut into several parts: therefore the soul is not spiritual, but of the same nature as the body in which it is received.

83 I deny the consequence, which does not follow. For is that which is open (says St. Augustine) to be denied because that which is hidden cannot be comprehended? Shall we, on that account, say that what we perceive to be so is not so, because we cannot find out why it is so? Assuredly the mind cannot comprehend how a material substance is able to think: therefore Materialism too, for this one reason, is a false hypothesis. But you will say: between body and spirit there is no proportion: therefore, if the soul is a spiritual substance, it could not be coupled to the body; but it is united to it: therefore it is not a spiritual substance.

84 I distinguish the antecedent: there is no proportion, that is, likeness in nature, I grant; there is no proportion, that is, the relation of a form to its subject, or of what perfects to what is perfectible, I deny, and the consequence. It is true that body and spirit are substances different in genus; and consequently that between body and spirit there is not that proportion which two beings of the same genus and order have to each other. But it is false that between body and spirit there cannot be that proportion which suffices for the body to be perfected by the spirit, and for a whole one by itself to arise from their union.

85 You will object 2: the condition of the soul and that of the body are one and the same: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the soul does not act in children, is vigorous in young men, is weakened in old men, undergoes the same affections as our body, and is changed in various ways: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: and all these things happen because of the close conjunction by which it is united to the body, I grant; from the nature of the soul itself insofar as it is a spiritual substance,

I

[p. 27]

I deny, and the consequence too. Just as no one ought to wonder if an artisan, although he has undergone no change as regards his knowledge, cannot accomplish his splendid works for want of instruments, so too there ought to be no room for wonder if, while the corporeal organs have not yet acquired their perfection, or have been impeded for whatever reason, the soul too, chiefly in those things in which it depends on those same organs, either cannot act at all or acts with great difficulty.

86 Hence, although the change takes place not in the soul but in the corporeal order, nevertheless the soul too, because of the union it has with the corporeal organs, seems to share in it. Besides, how many things are there that our soul sees, although the corporeal organs are badly affected? Can the soul not think about loftier things, placed above the senses, while the members of the body are suffering? Does it not mitigate and soothe its pain by the contemplation of these things, and fortify and defend itself against it? But it is no wonder if the Materialists contend that the soul perishes with the body; for unless they put on this false opinion, they can never quiet, at least in some part, the goads of conscience by which they are warned that eternal evils are prepared for them.

87 Obj. 3: against the second, with Helvétius in the impious work entitled in French L’Esprit. By physical sensibility, which is the faculty of receiving the various impressions caused by external objects, and by memory, which is the faculty of preserving the impressions that objects cause in us, all ideas and thoughts can be produced: nay, to speak more plainly, all thoughts are produced by physical sensibility alone: therefore all thought consists formally in this, that objects act on our organs: therefore there is no spiritual soul. Proof of the antecedent as to the first part: because when we remember some thing, our interior organs must then be in nearly the same state as when that thing acts sensibly on us. But this state of the organs must necessarily produce sensation: therefore to remember is the same as to sense.

88 Proof of the other part: when I judge of the size or color of an object set before me, it is evident that my judgment is a sensation, because it is referred to the various impressions that the objects have caused in my organs: whence I can equally say I judge and I sense. And likewise I can equally say that two objects, one white, the other black, produce different impressions in me: therefore to judge is the same as to sense. Thus, after his fashion, the pernicious Materialist talks nonsense. But nothing more inept or absurd than all this can be devised. And as regards the first:

89 Whence did Helvétius learn that our interior organs, when we remember something, must be in nearly the same state as when that thing acts sensibly on us? Surely, in recollecting the pleasures we have tasted, we do not always remember them with joy,

O2 [p. 28] but often also with sadness and grief, and then especially when we see that many evils have come to us from them. We would, however, always rejoice in the recollection of pleasure, if our interior organs were then disposed in nearly the same way as when we sensibly enjoy the pleasure. And what will happen when we remember at the same time many things that are contrary to one another, such as pain and pleasure? Besides: how many things are there by which we can in no way be sensibly affected, and yet we remember them? Do truth and falsity affect our senses? Does the turpitude or honorableness of actions affect touch, the eyes, the palate, or the nostrils?

90 And as regards the second, surely, if to judge is the same as to sense, it necessarily follows from this that while I judge of a taste, I sense the taste: therefore, for anyone to sense several tastes in succession at his pleasure, it will be enough for him to judge of them; for when two things are not distinguished from each other but are one and the same, what belongs to the one must belong to the other: therefore one who judges of colors, e.g., sees colors; one who judges of odors senses odors. Whom, then, would these things not move to laughter?

91 Although, then, we too grant that the diversity of the judgments formed about the things subject to our sense is referred to the diversity of impressions, yet that judgment is the same as the impression made on our senses is something we can in no way admit. For we are said to pass judgment when we affirm that something agrees or does not agree with another: wherefore the notion of that with which something agrees or does not agree, the notion of that which is said to agree or not to agree, and the faculty that compares both notions together and determines what agrees or does not agree with some being, must concur together in order to make a judgment; and this indeed cannot be had through the impression of the senses alone, since the impression of the senses is determinate and peculiar; those that affect vision cannot belong to the ear; through the impression made in the ears we cannot judge of the impression made on the palate: therefore, through the impression of the senses, one cannot be compared with another, nor can it be determined what agrees or does not agree with some being.

92 Obj. 4. against the 4th, with Locke: we deny that it can be brought about by the power of God that matter should think, because we cannot comprehend it; but this reason is altogether insufficient: therefore. 2: although the idea of a Musician is not included in the idea of a Physician, nevertheless these two things can be joined in a man: therefore, although the idea of thought is not included in the idea of matter, matter will be able to think. To the first I deny the causal proposition: for this is not the reason for our persuasion; we do not think so because we do not see how this can be done, but because we perceive by a most certain reason that it cannot be done. To the second I reply that to be a physician and a musician is not repugnant to the essence of man, but thought is repugnant to matter, because

[p. 29] matter must be extended, have parts, etc. But a thinking substance can have none of these things, as we have already demonstrated.

93 Obj. 5. In the idea of matter is contained the notion of an extended and solid substance, but not of vegetation: therefore, just as God can unite the power of vegetating to an extended and solid substance, so too can he unite the power of thinking. 2: Although we do not know in what way the power of vegetating can be present in plants, and that of sensing in brutes, nevertheless we do not deny that this can be done by God: therefore. To the first I deny the consequence, and the reason is that vegetation, as the Materialists themselves admit, can be accomplished through motion and the diverse disposition and configuration of the parts. But thought cannot belong to matter through motion and configuration, as we have already proved. To the second the reply is the same: for although we do not know those things, we nevertheless know at the same time this as well, that no contradiction follows if we admit them.

94 Obj. 6. If we say that God cannot bring it about that matter should think, because this appears impossible to us, it follows that the Omnipotence of God is confined by our ideas; but this is absurd: therefore. 2. We do not have a clear and distinct idea of substance, as we said in the Logic: therefore we cannot affirm that thought cannot belong to extension. To the first I deny the antecedent: because, just as nothing is taken away from the Divine power when it is said that the number two and the number three united together cannot constitute the number six, so too, since we have perceived that matter must be extended, divisible, etc., and that this is repugnant to thought, nothing is taken away from the Divine power if we affirm that thought cannot be attributed to matter. By this, moreover, we do not enclose the Divine Omnipotence within our ideas, but submit ourselves to that light of reason which God himself has given us, and which we would surely abuse if we affirmed that evidently incompatible ideas can be united together.

95 Most ineptly, therefore, does Voltaire (b) argue thus: God is Omnipotent: therefore to deny that he can give the power of thinking to matter is impious. But I reply: nay, to assert it is madness. The essences of things are not the object of the Divine Omnipotence, but their existence is. God can bring it about that a triangle exist or not exist; but he cannot bring it about that a triangle be round. Why so? Because this implies a contradiction, for in this case it would both be and not be a triangle. But between matter and thought, as Voltaire himself admits (c), there is a contradiction: God therefore cannot bring it about that matter should think. For the contradiction to be removed, the natures would have to be changed, so that matter would no longer be matter, or thought would no longer be thought: but then there would be no question. These things are known to anyone who has so much as greeted the first threshold of Metaphysics.

(b) Métaphysique, and Lett. XIII, Sur Mr. Locke.

(c) In the Elem. Phys. Newton.

[p. 30]

96 To the second I reply that it is true that we do not have a clear and distinct idea of substance, but we nevertheless know most certainly what necessarily belongs to corporeal substance and what is repugnant to incorporeal substance. You will say: God can create both a material and a spiritual substance devoid of all power of acting: therefore God can attribute an equal power of acting to them, so that a material substance may think. I reply that the things attributed by God to any substance must not be repugnant to one another; but it is repugnant that matter should be thinking.

97 Obj. finally: in the idea of Divine Justice Mercy is not conceived, and yet they are one undistinguished thing: therefore, although thought is not included in the idea of matter, it is not repugnant that matter can think. I deny the consequence. For the idea of Justice does not represent the thing as it is in itself, but insofar as it connotes an extrinsic object; and consequently it is enough that the object of Justice be different from the object of Mercy for the idea and concept of each to be distinguished. But through the idea of body I conceive an extended, divisible and figured substance, and I perceive none of these in the idea of thought; and therefore the different perception of body, or matter, and of thought implies a distinction between matter and thought, that is, not merely between objects, but between one substance and another. So the distinguished Berti.

## CHAPTER III

Whether our soul is immortal, or rather perishes together with the body at death?

he principal argument of the whole of Psychology is the one we un98

T          dertake to treat when we discuss the immortality of the rational soul,

as something of very great moment for rightly forming morals, and likewise for fostering the fear and worship of the Supreme Deity. In this argument we shall most obediently, as is fitting, respond to the most wise precept by which the Fifth Lateran Council (d) commands all Professors of

Philosophy to make this assertion of the immortality of the soul manifest with every effort, and to establish it, as far as they can, by natural reason.

99 And rightly so; for since those (as the most learned Cano excellently remarks

(e)) who deny the immortality of the soul believe neither in Christ the

(d) Held in the year 1513 under Julius II and Leo X. Sess. 8.

(e) Bk. XII, De Locis Theologicis, last ch. [p. 31] the Lord nor in the Gospel, and hold the faith of the Church and of the Saints as nothing, so it seems superfluous to draw arguments from the places that contain the authority of faith. In this dissertation, therefore, we must take our stand, as far as we can, not on Sacred authorities but on principles known by the light of nature, against Epicurus, Lucretius, and other most pernicious modern Philosophers, enemies of the truths of our most holy Religion, who strive with an utterly vain effort to show that the human soul is mortal and will perish together with the body. But before we approach the question, we must explain some things for the sake of clarity.

100 Absolute immortality, which can be called intrinsic, belongs to a living being that has in itself, and from its own nature, no principle of perishing. Relative immortality, which can be called extrinsic, belongs to a living being that cannot be destroyed or annihilated by another, extrinsic, being. It is certain that immortality both absolute and relative belongs to God alone; the rational soul, however, does not have relative immortality in every sense; for although it cannot be destroyed or annihilated by another created being, it can nevertheless absolutely be annihilated by God.

101 When, therefore, it is asked whether our soul is immortal, the question is not whether it can absolutely be annihilated by God; rather, it is asked only, first: whether the rational soul has in itself, and from its own nature, no principle of perishing? Second: whether there exists in the whole world no created extrinsic cause able to destroy the mind? Third: whether God wills never to annihilate it, or ever to change it so that it should lose the vital faculties we detect in it? This is the state of the question, which must indeed be carefully attended to. By faith, moreover, it is certain that the human mind will not perish with the body, but will endure, living, for eternity. Hence Christ the Lord (f) says: Fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul; and elsewhere (g): He that hateth his life in this world, keepeth it unto life eternal. But since, as we said above, the question must be settled by natural reasons:

102 I say 1. The rational soul cannot naturally perish by any kind of corruption, and hence it is immortal by its nature. The conclusion is proved. A spiritual substance can in no way perish or be corrupted naturally; but the rational soul is a spiritual substance, as stands proved in the preceding chapter: therefore. Proof of the major: a spiritual substance is a simple substance, or one consisting of no parts, as all admit; but a simple substance can in no way perish or be corrupted naturally: therefore. Proof of the minor: first, it cannot perish or be corrupted by division or dissolution, since it is devoid of parts and really indivisible. “For in the knowledge of the mind (as

(f) Matt. 10, v. 28.

(g) John 12, v. 25.

[p. 32]

Cicero elegantly puts it (h)), we cannot doubt, unless we are altogether leaden in physics, that there is nothing mixed in the mind, nothing concrete, nothing coupled, nothing joined together, nothing twofold. And since this is so, it certainly can be neither separated, nor divided, nor torn apart, nor pulled asunder: nor, therefore, can it perish. For perishing is, as it were, a departure, a separation and a disjunction of those parts which before perishing were held together by some bond.” Secondly, it can neither destroy nor annihilate itself, nor be destroyed by any created agent whatever. First, because nothing in the nature of things is contrary to its very self; Secondly: because no created agent can create the human mind: therefore it cannot annihilate it either: therefore the rational soul cannot perish naturally by any kind of corruption, and hence is immortal by its nature.

103 Our conclusion is also proved by moral arguments. First, from the most firm consent of all peoples and the constant opinion of all nations. For there was never any nation so barbarous that its mind was not imbued with the opinion of the immortality of the soul, which only he can be ignorant of who is an utter stranger to histories, and who knows nothing at all of the ceremonies, rites and laws of the Ancients. Secondly: because if there were to be no life for us after death, that desire for happiness which nature itself has impressed on us could never be fulfilled in us, and we would be of a worse condition than the other living things.

104 Thirdly: because it cannot be denied that over this universe there presides God, the Supreme Governor of all things, who repays crimes with just punishments and virtue with its due reward; which certainly could not be done if our mind perished together with the body, for here we see the innocent more often in want and oppressed, and the wicked abounding in delights; which indeed was expressed by Christ our Lord in the poor man Lazarus and the rich glutton (i): Remember that thou didst receive good things in thy lifetime, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted; and thou art tormented. From which it is to be inferred that the blindness of the Materialists is to be deplored, since from their most absurd opinion they can never hope for any profit. For if they perish entirely, as they madly imagine, no reward awaits them for this confidence of theirs; if the mind is immortal, as it certainly is, they will pay eternal penalties, because with such obstinacy, having cast off all religion, they have dared to resist manifest testimonies.

105 I say 2: The rational soul is in no way annihilated by God at death, but by His will survives the body after death, to live without end. Prob. 1: “For (as Leibniz (k), writing against Pufendorf, excellently says) it cannot be doubted

that

(h) Tusculan Disputations, bk. 1, ch. 28.

(i) Luke 16, v. 25.

(k) Letter to Gerh. Wolth., which is no. 16, vol. II of the Epistolae ad diversos. [p. 33] that the most wise and likewise most powerful Ruler of the Universe has appointed

rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked, and executes what He has appointed in the future life, since it is agreed that in this present one most things pass unpunished.” From which it is clearly inferred that it will never come to pass that souls are destroyed by God. Secondly: there is in us a natural inclination by which we desire always to be, and so to be that we may rest always happy, immutably, in our end: therefore to the future state of life there follows also the immortality of souls.

106 And in truth: “an intellectual creature (as the Angelic Teacher St. Thomas most wisely says (l)) does not reach its ultimate end except when its desire is naturally set at rest; but just as it desires happiness, so it naturally desires the perpetuity of happiness.” It is proved thirdly: it belongs to spiritual substances by their own nature to be incorruptible, as has been proved; therefore neither ought they to be destroyed by the ordinary power of God. The consequence is proved: “God (as St. Thomas says

(m)), who is the institutor of nature, does not withdraw from things what is proper to their natures”: therefore if spiritual substances have it from their own nature that they always exist, God must always conserve them: therefore our souls are immortal, even if they are considered with respect to their principle. So much against the

Libertines, who do not believe the word of God.

107 But we, who adhere so firmly to the Holy Scriptures that we are ready to shed our blood in their defense, constantly believe in the immortality of souls: for it is established by the most certain Oracle of God (n) that the dust, or body, shall return into its earth from whence it was, but the spirit shall return to God, who gave it; that the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and that it will never be that the torment of death shall touch them; that Christ our Lord (o) will say to the just on the day of judgment that they should come to Him, blessed of the Father, and receive the kingdom which He had prepared for them from the foundation of the world; but to the impious, on the contrary, that they should go, cursed, into everlasting fire, which the most just judge then likewise appointed for the devil and his Angels: to pass over other innumerable oracles of that kind, by which God makes us certain that our soul is to endure forever.

The arguments of the Libertines are answered. 108

The Libertines neglect and make light of the almost innumerable testimonies of

Sacred Scripture by which their impiety is most plainly refuted: they studiously seek out one or another which they can more easily abuse among the unskilled. They object, therefore,

P                                        first:

(l) III Contra Gentiles, ch. 51, no. 2.

(m) II Contra Gentiles, ch. 55, no. 17.

(n) Eccles. 12, v. 7. Wisd. 3, v. 1.

(o) Matt., ch. 25, v. 34 ff. [p. 34] first: that Ecclesiastes (p) writes that the death of man and of beasts is one. Reply: the death of men and of beasts is one as regards the bodily life common to all animals. Thus man has nothing more than the beast by reason of the body, since all things return to the same condition of earth from which they were made. The mind, therefore, does not return into the earth, since it was not produced from earth. Moreover, it can be answered that in all these places Solomon does not speak from his own opinion but from that of the impious; that is, he relates what the wicked hold in their minds, not what he himself thinks, as St. Gregory the Great (q) and the most learned Bishop Huet (r) excellently observe.

109 Obj. 2. In Wisdom, ch. 2, we read: after this, that is, after death, the spirit is poured abroad as soft air: therefore the rational soul vanishes when a man dies. Secondly: Ecclesiastes (s) says: “Who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam ascend upward, and if the spirit of the beasts descend downward?” Therefore the condition of man and of beast is equal, even as regards the spirit. To the first I reply that it speaks there from the opinion of the impious, as the beginning of the chapter declares: The wicked said, reasoning with themselves, but not right; and in v. 2 it adds: These things the wicked thought, and were deceived, nor esteemed the honor of holy souls, for God created man incorruptible. To the second I reply: those words are those of one reproving the impious, whose mind savors nothing but earthly things. For if we wish to measure all things by the senses: who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam, etc. Likewise, what is said in the Sixth Ecumenical Council, that the soul is immortal not by nature but by the grace of God, is to be understood in this sense, that the soul has immortality by God’s willing and conserving it, which conservation is from grace alone. Thus intrinsic immortality is natural to the rational soul; but extrinsic immortality is gratuitous.

110 Obj. 3, with Lucretius and the whole family of the ancient Epicureans: the rational soul is born with the body: therefore it must perish with the body, for everything that is generated is corrupted. I distinguish the antecedent: it is born with the body by generation, I deny the antecedent; by creation, I concede it. The body, therefore, perishes because it is destroyed by the mere dissolution of its parts: but the soul, as a simple substance, cannot perish without being reduced to its own nothing; and what cannot perish except by annihilation is immortal by its own nature. You will say: when the subject that is perfected by a form perishes, the form perishes; but the soul is the form perfecting the body: therefore when the body perishes the soul must perish. I distinguish the minor: it is the form of the body in such a way that it can exist and operate by its own nature without it, I concede; in such a way that it depends on it intrinsically, and therefore necessarily, both in existing and in operating, I deny; and the consequence.

111 Inst. The human mind is a part of man, and therefore an incomplete substance:

therefore

(p) Ch. 3, v. 19.

(q) Bk. 1 of the Dialogues, ch. 4.

(r) Demonstratio Evangelica, Prop. 4.

(s) Ch. 3, v. 21. [p. 35] therefore it depends intrinsically on the body, so that its essence is to be actually joined to the body. I distinguish the antecedent: it is an incomplete substance, that is, it is apt to inform a body and to constitute a man together with the body, I concede; that is, it is half a substance, which lacks something of the notion of substance, I deny; and the consequence. You will say: the human mind is not produced except dependently on the body: therefore it depends on it intrinsically. I distinguish the antecedent: except dependently on the body as on an occasion, I concede; as on a subject in which and through which it exists, I deny; and the consequence.

112 The roundness of wax, e.g., is produced dependently on the wax in which it is received; hence it depends on the wax in order to exist, and when the wax perishes the roundness perishes: but the soul is produced dependently on the body only as on an occasion, inasmuch, namely, as God determines to create the soul to be joined to the body; nor does He create it on account of the body alone, but on account of itself. Thus the soul depends no more on the body in order to exist than some wall depends on another, pre-existing wall, on the occasion of which it is built so as to make a house together with it. Inst.: the human mind depends on the body in order to operate: therefore also in order to exist. I distinguish the antecedent: it depends on it as on an occasion, that is, on account of the law of union between itself and the body, I concede; it depends on it as on the principle of its operations, I deny; and the consequence.

113 The body does not think, does not perceive, does not will, does not sense; it is not, therefore, the principle of the soul’s operations; but on account of the laws of the commerce that exists between those substances so unlike each other, the mind is determined to think on the occasion of the motions that take place in the body. Inst. The soul separated from the body cannot have any sensations: therefore it depends on the body in order to exist. I distinguish the antecedent: if by sensation you understand the perception of some impression made in the body, I concede; if you understand the interior affection of the soul, such as usually comes to it on the occasion of the body, I deny; and the consequence. The soul separated from the body can, if God wills, be immediately affected by the same perceptions by which it is affected by means of the body while it is united to it.

114 Obj. 4: the human mind is subject to innumerable changes, since it is capable of diverse operations: therefore it must naturally perish. I distinguish the antecedent: it is subject to accidental changes, while always retaining its whole essence, I concede; to substantial changes, I deny; and the consequence. Moreover, opposite modifications, such as love and hatred, volitions and nolitions, succeed one another in the same soul, but without any division or separation of parts in the subject, which does not happen in the modifications of the body: therefore diverse and opposite modifications, which can change and destroy matter, cannot do the same to a spiritual and simple substance such as the soul is.

115 Obj. 5. The soul is not immortal because it is a substance, since many substances perish; nor yet because it is spiritual, since grace and the habits of the soul itself are spiritual, and yet they perish:

P2 [p. 36] therefore it is maintained with no right to be immortal. I reply that the soul is immortal not precisely because it is a substance, but because it is such a substance, namely simple and thinking. For because it is a simple substance lacking parts, it cannot perish by the action of a created agent; because it is a thinking substance, it is of such a nature that it can operate, and hence also live, separated from the body. But the things that depend on the disposition of the subject, as spiritual accidents, e.g. habits, can be corrupted, because they are educed from a disposed subject and depend on it both in coming to be and in being conserved; whence, when the dispositions of the subject are removed, they perish: but the rational soul is not educed from the body, nor does it depend on it in coming to be and in being conserved. You will say: what has a beginning has an end; but the soul has a beginning: therefore also an end. I distinguish the antecedent: what has a beginning by generation, let it pass; by creation, I deny; and the consequence.

116 Obj. 6: The soul separated from the body would be in a violent state: therefore it cannot naturally exist separated from the body: therefore it must perish. Reply 1: granting the antecedent, I deny the consequence, which does not follow; for the souls of the damned, which are simple substances, even though they are in a violent state, do not on that account perish, but live forever for their pain. Reply 2: by denying the antecedent: since the propensity which the soul has toward the body does not so solicit it that it cannot most easily do without the presence of the body. And certainly the blessed souls, intimately joined with God, are by no means in a violent state, which would stand in the way of their happiness.

117 Obj. 7: we know by experience that there is the greatest similarity between men and brutes; but immortality does not belong to brutes: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: as regards the things that can affect the senses, I concede; as regards those through which we have proved the immortality of our soul, I deny. It is no wonder if brutes, as regards the things that can affect the senses, seem in some way to resemble men: for since they have an animal nature in common with us, they must be affected by the things that affect animal nature: yet the Materialists can never deny that in men alone there is such a capacity for learning that they can know both metaphysical and moral principles, or more sublime ones. It is always evident, therefore, that there is the greatest difference between men and brutes, whence the condition of both cannot be one and the same.

118 Moreover, many illustrious Theologians and Physicists (t) maintain

(t) The principal ones are: Calmet, Dictionnaire de la S. Bible, article Ame, French edition. Magalotti, Lettere Scientifiche, Lett. XI, & Lettere Familiari, Lett. XXIV. Antonio Genovesi, Disciplinarum Metaphysicarum Elementa, vol. 3, Dissertation on the soul of brutes. Giovanni Lami, Theologian to His Imperial Majesty, Novelle Letterarie for the year 1761. Alfonso Niccolai, Lezioni sopra la S. Scrittura, Lezz. XIII. Antonio Filippo Adami, Magazzino letterario di Livorno, vol. 5, and many others related by D. Boullier, Essai Philosophique sur l’ame des Bêtes. [p. 37] that the souls of brutes are an immaterial active principle, or spirit, that is, not a body of the same nature as all the bodies we know through the ministry of the senses. For they are persuaded that there has been created a certain kind of spiritual substance which is capable indeed of sensation and of simple perception, yet is not furnished with the other faculties in which the human mind is strong; which cannot be destroyed by the forces of nature, nor by any created cause, but is to be reduced to nothing only by Him who created it, when, the organic body being no longer fit for the functions of life, it shall have, as it were, discharged its office of sensing. These things indeed, as they deserve to be discussed at greater length, so would they call for a discourse and an explanation of their own.

119 But as for the matter at hand, I say that even if this System is admitted, no argument is deduced from it for overthrowing the immortality of the rational soul. For from the fact that in that System the soul of brutes is not endowed with the faculties with which the human soul is adorned, that is, from the fact that it cannot perceive abstract ideas but only sensations, it follows that in it there is neither liberty, nor merit, nor crime, nor the faculty of knowing the Supreme Good and of enjoying it, in which the happiness of the other life consists. Wherefore the arguments which persuade us that the human soul, separated from the body, is to endure forever do not support the soul of brutes, even if it were said to be spiritual. For this soul, when it has reached its end, which is to animate the body, will return to nothing by the act of Him who created it.

120 Obj. 8: The soul is affected by the same things equally with the body: therefore it is of the same nature as the body: therefore, just as the body dies, so too does the soul. Secondly: the body acts on the soul: therefore they are of the same nature, because nothing but a corporeal thing can be touched by a body. These are the principal arguments of Lucretius, by which he vainly tries to show that our mind perishes with the body. But lest I seem to take away from them all the force they have, let us hear the Most Eminent Cardinal Melchior de Polignac (u) proposing them and most learnedly refuting them.

Perhaps you will object that in us, by so close a bond,

Both mind and body are joined, that the two cannot

Be told apart; taught, namely, by our own experience

That nothing reaches our mind except through the senses:

And when sleep has lulled them, or a burning fever

Overturned them, the mind is troubled and strays wandering;

Often, too, stunned by a sudden disease, it falls prostrate.

························

(u) Anti-Lucretius, bk. V, from v. 712.

[p. 38]

Moreover, that men are seen bereft of reason,

Either from a hurt to the head, or born so from the mother,

So that all wisdom of mind fails them,

Because the settled order fails in the parts of the brain.

Nay, sunk even to the nature of a beast,

As when, through an unforeseen bite, along the channels of the blood

The foul madness of dogs has invaded a man, and in his inmost

Bowels, and in the midst of his heart, has fixed its venom;

How does the man differ from the dog? One fury carries both away,

And a hunger for biting, and the same insanity torments them.

But all these things, as the Most Eminent Author most wisely continues,

Show that the mind is joined together with the body.

Who would deny it? But that the nature of mind and of body

Is one, they do not signify. Thus anyone skilled

In the Aonian art of striking the sounding lyre

With nimble fingers, and of quickening the speaking strings,

And with the allurement of a sweet melody

Of soothing your ears, so depends on the lyre itself

That without it he can bring forth no songs at all.

For if, broken, it is silent, if it is impaired by some damage,

If the strings, stretched too tight or let too slack,

Have lost their tone, or if one or another is missing;

If dirt has filled the hollow and dulls the sound;

Behold, the lyre player remains idle, and, skilled in vain,

Sings either nothing or badly, and seems not to know how.

Will you then place the art of music in the lyre itself?

And will you on that account think that one thing

Are instrument and player? Such, further, is the bond

Of body and mind: except that the mind cannot lay aside

The body joined to it, nor take it up again at will.

But while life remains to us, it will always be joined

To the same instrument with which it was once joined.

All else is managed in a wholly similar way.

For just as certain things are proper to the lyre, which do not

[p. 39]

Concern the player, as the hollow, vaulted with thin boards

Through the joinings of its sides, whence in sounding

A light murmur arises, and the woven Echo answers;

Likewise the position and the measure of the strings, frequent

Or rare, swift or slow, in the same time,

Give back their quiverings, from which the sound comes out high

Or low. These the singer does not make; he uses them.

And he himself in turn holds many things within himself,

To possess which he needs no lyre at all:

Namely, the acquired faculty of making melody is in him,

And the whole theory of harmony: for by art he knows all things,

Both those that are consonant and those that are dissonant:

And nothing pleasing has come forth from the strings of the lyre

That does not flow from him, transmitted through his fingers.

And so the sweet melody is owed equally to both:

To the lyre, because it gives the sounds, whatever are stirred;

And to the player above all, because he knows how to draw them

Forth, and, as it were, to put a soul into the mute strings.

Not otherwise in us, the mass bound to it by a fixed compact

The mind moves, and the mass answers to its mover.

121 To the second I say: that nothing but a body can touch and be touched by contact of quantity; but it can by contact of power. The solution is St. Thomas’s. And let what has been said suffice.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N I I 

## On the Commerce between Mind

and Body.

## CHAPTER I

The more celebrated opinions of the Philosophers are set forth.

he commerce of the mind with the body is the name given to that won122

T          derful consent which certain operations of the mind have with certain

motions of the body, and in turn certain motions of the body with certain affections of the mind, by reason of which now the mind is, as it were, the interpreter of the body, now the body of the mind. There are two principal laws by which this mutual commerce of the mind with the body is maintained. The first: if things placed outside us make impressions on the sense organs, then the notion of those things is excited in the mind. The second: our mind so dominates the body that, if certain parts of the body itself are moved, they persevere in motion at its nod as long as it wills, and cease from motion as soon as it pleases it; both of which we are without doubt taught by manifest experience. Three systems have been devised to explain this commerce, namely the system of Influx, of

Occasional Causes, and of Pre-established Harmony.

123 The system of physical influx consists in a true and mutual efficiency, which is attributed to the soul with respect to the body and to the body with respect to the soul. The Peripatetics, namely, the defenders of this system, teach that these natures

(the soul, namely, and the body), most unlike as they are, are so bound to each other that the one truly and efficiently flows into the other; and yet that by this action nothing is transferred from the one into the other; but that, when motions are impressed on the sense and propagated by means of the nerves as far as the brain, the mind is determined to form the notions of things; and in turn, when a will to move some limb has arisen in the mind, the nerves are at once impelled, and voluntary motions follow in that limb.

114 Wherefore these Philosophers think that motions often begin in the human body which have no antecedent cause in the body itself, [p. 41] but are produced from the appetite of the mind and its faculty of moving; and likewise that motions in the limbs are often extinguished at the mind’s will, without any motion following in the corporeal nature.

125 The Cartesians, with Fr. Malebranche, defenders of the system of occasional causes, assert that the mind in no way acts on the body, but that on the occasion of the thoughts of the soul the body is moved by God, just as on the occasion of the motions of the body that same God modifies the mind. I wish to throw a ball: God extends my arm, applies my hand to the ball, closes my fingers so that I may grasp the ball, etc. In the same way, when external bodies act on the nerves, God is the immediate author of the perceptions that are to arise therefrom. While my hand is applied to the ball, I do not sense the ball, but God gives me the perception of the contact itself.

126 The air strikes the tympanum of the ear, I perceive a sound; but this sensation does not properly depend on the agitation of the air and on the motion of the nerve that follows from it, but God immediately impresses this perception on the mind. There you have the system of occasional causes, clearly and lucidly explained by the celebrated ’s Gravesande (x). Whence it appears that in this system the soul is deprived of the active force by which motion is produced in the body, and only through its volitions provides God with occasions of producing these motions: similarly the body, through its motions, provides God with the occasion of producing these ideas in the soul.

127 Leibniz put forward a new system, much illustrated by Wolff, which is commonly called pre-established harmony (y). In this system the soul is laid down to be of such a nature that by its own force (the words are Wolff’s (z)) “it produces all its perceptions and appetitions in a continuous series, independently of every external principle, and the presence of material ideas in the brain contributes absolutely nothing to producing them, so that the perceptions and appetitions in the soul would follow in the same way as now even if the body did not exist. Next, the organic body is laid down to be a machine so formed that by the force of mechanism, from the impressions of sensible things, motions arise corresponding to the volitions and appetitions of the soul, without any immediate extrinsic determination depending on the soul; and these would follow in the same way as now even if the soul did not exist.

Q                            128 “Wherefore

But afterwards he fought for it so seriously and so vehemently that he suggests to the reader the suspicion that he judged it so in earnest, and that at least, from the habit of reading and handling it, he embraced a cloud in place of Juno. 128 “Wherefore these two automata (Wolff continues), the one spiritual, the other material, are joined by this law, that the single motions which take place in the body by the efficiency of mechanism agree with the single perceptions, appetitions and aversions of the soul, following one another in exactly the same order in which the modifications of the soul succeed one another.

129 “That is, God pre-established the harmony inasmuch as He joined to the soul a body in which there can exist a series of motions agreeing with the perceptions and appetitions of the soul, and made such a connection of material things that those motions are brought into act through continuous impressions made from without on the sense organs.” Thus far Wolff. Conceive, then, a mind and a body which agree with each other in such a way that the motions of the latter correspond with the perceptions and determinations of the former, and you will have the whole System of pre-established harmony.

## CHAPTER II

The System of occasional causes, and that of pre-established harmony, is exploded.

say 1: The system of occasional causes cannot be maintained, because 130

I       it is entangled in the gravest difficulties. For, first: would absolutely all

the affections of the mind be effected by God, or only some? If all, there will be no liberty in us, nay, not even a soul; for whence shall we demonstrate that it exists? If some, why some? Why not all? Is more efficacy required to effect these than those? Why does the soul not distinguish those which it produces by its own force from those which God impresses on it? Why does it have the same and entirely similar sense of them all?

131 Secondly: if this system is admitted, all the motions of the mind and of the body will have to be held as miracles, since their effecting cause is in no way contained in the whole of nature. Nor would you exempt them from the class of prodigies because the soul and the body supply the occasion for effecting them; for the prayers of his Sisters also furnished the occasion for the recalling of Lazarus to life: is it on that account to be held less prodigious?

132 I say 2: The Leibnizian system has inexplicable knots, nor can it be defended by a Catholic Man. And first: if the human mind is determined by its nature to produce the notions of things successively, it produces them in itself necessarily, so that their production [p. 43] can in no way be hindered by us; and, this being posited, the mind is stripped of all liberty over its perceptions. In like manner, if the motions of the body are carried out by the force of mechanism alone, they are intrinsically necessary, and so follow in such a way that none of them can be hindered by us, just like the motions of the heart, which are not subject to the command of the mind. No action, therefore, will render a man worthy of being either commended or blamed on its account.

133 What of the fact that the system of pre-established harmony lays open a road to living dishonorably, since in it the care of the external senses contributes absolutely nothing to fostering honorable thoughts in the mind and repelling base ones? Moreover, it is plainly contrary to Sacred Scripture and to the Holy Fathers to say (as the Harmonists say) that the changes which take place in the sense organs from the impact of sensible things contribute absolutely nothing to exciting perceptions and appetitions in the soul, since Scripture and the Holy Fathers teach that it can be prevented that the human mind should know sensible things, and hence that it should be borne toward them by inordinate desire, if the external senses are so guarded that they can in no way be altered by the things themselves.

134 For, first: I made a covenant (says Job (a)) with my eyes, that I would not so much as think upon a virgin. Jeremiah says: death is come up through our windows. “For death (St. Gregory (b) explains) comes up through the windows and enters the house when concupiscence, coming through the senses of the body, enters the dwelling of the mind.” Secondly: Scripture (c) teaches that the face is to be turned away from a woman dressed up, and that one should by no means gaze about upon another’s beauty, because, namely, many have perished by the beauty of a woman, and hereby lust is enkindled as a fire; inasmuch, that is, as dishonorable thoughts follow in the soul upon the sight of an adorned woman, concupiscence is kindled by it, and base desires are excited.

135 Besides: the system of pre-established harmony cannot be admitted without our being compelled to reject mortifications of the flesh as altogether useless for subjecting it to the spirit; and all that the Catholic Church hands down concerning penance, both from Divine Scripture and from the Holy Fathers, will be laughable; for in this system our mind will have the same wicked desires when those mortifications are applied as it would have if the flesh were in no way afflicted by so many torments: in vain, therefore, would the Church cry out with the Apostle (d): “mortify your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence, and covetousness.” For none of those motions to which our body is already determined by its structure can be hindered by us, once the system of the Harmonists is admitted.
