It also favors Fatalism. For the Fatalists are those who subject all things that happen in the world, not even excepting human actions themselves, to an unimpedable necessity.

136 From what has been said thus far, it seems to me proved to the point of evidence that the Leibnizian system is to be altogether rejected. Nor can I pass over another difficulty common to both systems. For the Cartesian and the

Leibnizian hypotheses overturn all philosophical certainty about the existence of bodies. For in the hypothesis of occasional causes God, not the body, would produce the sensations in our soul: in Leibniz’s opinion the soul, by its own nature, would have the same sensations it now experiences even if no body existed. From these hypotheses, therefore, the way lies open to Idealism, by which the existence of all matter is denied as useless; and certainly many have fallen into this error, and also into another, more absurd one, which they call Egoism, raving, namely, that only one’s own existence is known with certainty.

## CHAPTER III

The opinion of the Peripatetics is embraced as the more probable, the opinions of the Moderns being rejected.

hose who glory in the name of Philosophers ought to be so inflamed 137

T          with the desire of seeking out the truth that, addicted to no Sect, fol‐

lowing not Aristotle, not Plato, not Leibniz or Newton, but the truth, they should swear by the words of no master. We, therefore, who profess the Eclectic Philosophy, setting aside all love of parties, neither attack the ancient Philosophers because they are Ancients, nor praise the Moderns because they are Moderns, but precisely because, according to the slenderness of our small talent, they seem to snatch the palm from the ancients in many things, as we have proved in several places, and shall show also in the Physics with great weight of reasons. But the love with which we embrace the Moderns does not so carry us away that we kiss their tenets without making any distinction; rather, we most willingly depart from their opinion when it seems to us contrary to the truth, as we make manifest in this most grave question, in which, rejecting the opinions of the Moderns, we embrace the opinion of the old Peripatetics. Let our conclusion, therefore, be:

138 The commerce of the mind with the body consists in that binding of the soul by virtue of which the soul is affected by the motions of the body, and in turn [p. 45] can effect motions in the body by a physical and true influx. Prob.: Although we cannot conceive how a spirit is so bound to a body that it can by no means leave it when it pleases, yet because we experience such a state of our soul, we must admit such a binding; but we also experience that the soul is affected with pain or pleasure by the motions of the body: therefore, although we do not attain the manner in which this happens, it will nevertheless be consonant with reason to admit it. And just as no one says that that binding is had through some idea or apprehension of the soul, but in truth through the real state of the soul itself, so those perceptions of bodily motions will have to have their foundation in the real motions themselves.

139 But that the soul also truly and physically moves the body seems sufficiently proved from this, that such a power is neither above the forces nor against the properties of a spirit; for to be active belongs to a spirit by its essence; and why should this activity be constrained within such narrow limits that it can never go forth outside the mind, when even bodies can act outside themselves? Moreover, if resistance or impenetrability were a condition sine qua non for acting, not even a spirit could move a spirit. And who will show clearly and certainly that the motions of the incorporeal mind cannot move the body itself? Certainly the substance of God, though incorporeal, can indeed impel a body whithersoever it pleases.

140 What, then, prevents God from having granted to our souls, which He destined to rule the body, this force too, that they can move the body itself, and that the acts of the will which are excited in the mind act on the body itself, not indeed by a corporeal but nevertheless by a physical influx, and hence produce a bodily motion consonant with the incorporeal act of the will? It must therefore be said that God can make a created power that moves the body, since we see in this no privilege or infinite perfection such that it would belong to God alone; and since both common sense urges it and the office the soul performs seems to demand it, we shall most fittingly say that such a force has been put into it by

God. Those, then, who on account of the dissimilarity of the natures remove from the mind the faculty of moving the body must also remove it from God; their discourse, therefore, is to be put down no longer by the Philosopher but by the Censor.

The arguments are answered. 141

Obj. 1: it is altogether impossible that a simple and unextended substance, such as the soul is, should act on an extended substance, such as the body is, as is self-evident: therefore physical influx is impossible. I deny the antecedent: for although we do not know how the simple mind acts on the body, yet that action is not on that account to be denied. The arguments of the

Cartesians and Leibnizians demonstrate [p. 46] that neither does the body act on the mind nor the mind on the body in the way that a body acts on another body; but they do not prove that one substance cannot act on another in any way, and that all influx is impossible. Although, therefore, we grant that the physical laws of motion are not observed in the commerce of soul and body, yet it by no means follows from this that intelligent and free beings have not received from God the force of producing some motions in bodies according to other laws suited to their nature.

142 You will say: The system of physical influx cannot be maintained unless it is granted that something is transfused from the mind into the body, and conversely, for that is what the very word influx means: but this is absurd: therefore. I deny the major of the argument: when we contend that the body acts on, or flows into, the mind, he must be of dull wit who understands the argument as he pleases; for by this we understand only that the force and nature of the mind are so affected and directed by the commotions of the brain that representations arise in it, but by no means that the ideas of external things pass, as it were, from the body into the mind. It is certain, therefore, that by the agitations of the brain no motion proper to bodies is communicated to the mind, but that the mind is determined to act in a manner suited to its own nature.

143 Obj. 2: The system of influx conflicts with the immortality of the soul: therefore it cannot be maintained. The antecedent is proved: for, this opinion being posited, the soul, once the body is dead, will be able to do nothing, since it will lack the aid necessary for acting. This argument has already been answered by us, but for the sake of explanation we say that, just as you would be ridiculous if, because when shut up in a prison you cannot look upon the sun without a window, you wished to conclude from this that you can see nothing when you have come out of the prison, so, although the mind, on account of its fellowship with the earthly body, cannot perceive without its help, you wrongly gather from this that, when it has flown away free, it cannot apprehend the surrounding bodies, as Cicero elegantly says (e).

144 You will say, with Bilfinger: if the influx of the body into the soul is admitted, the effect will be greater than its cause, which is quite absurd. For this Leibnizian contends that the entire and full effect corresponding to the forces of our body is the motions of the brain; the cause, therefore, is surpassed by the effect if the perceptions which are formed in the mind are attributed to those same motions of the brain. But these things cause no trouble. For we by no means assign to the body any effect other than motion; for we do not say that ideas are formed in the mind by the body, but by the mind itself, admonished, as it were, by the motion of the brain. Wherefore the full effect of the body is motion, but that of the soul is perception.

145 Obj. 3, with the Cartesians: the hypothesis of physical influx ought to be rejected as less probable if the system of occasional causes is both easier to understand and liable to no inconveniences;

but

(e) Tusculan Disputations, bk. 1, ch. 20. [p. 47] but so it is: therefore. The minor is proved: It is permitted, nay necessary, to have recourse to God if second causes do not suffice; and nothing else happens in the system of occasional causes; and in this hypothesis no miracle properly so called is admitted, since all things happen according to natural laws established by God, and hence suited to the order of nature. Nor is the existence of bodies rendered uncertain; for God, being supremely truthful, cannot will that we be deceived by perpetual illusions. Finally, the Cartesian hypothesis does not take active force away from the will, for the will itself, on the occasion of the bodily motions given, then acts, and freely elicits its operations: therefore the system of occasional causes is very easily understood and is liable to no inconveniences.

146 Let us reply to the several parts of the argument with the celebrated Jacquier. And first: in the explanation of natural effects one must at last have recourse to the first cause; but Philosophers ought not to do this if second causes are available, all of which indeed are referred to the first. Further, in the present question it is not necessary to take refuge immediately in the first cause, unless it is demonstrated that physical influx is impossible, which, as has already been proved, can be shown by no reason. Secondly: in the hypothesis of occasional causes the existence of bodies can indeed be shown from the infinite veracity of God and from revelation, but another kind of proof would be taken away, that which arises from our sensations, by which the Idealists, who make light of Revelation, ought certainly to be convinced.

147 Finally, in the same hypothesis that right and command which was granted to the soul over the body cannot be explained. For if the body itself were moved by the soul not as by an efficient but only as by an occasional cause, the motions of the body would be produced not by the soul but by God; and to this difficulty is added also the fact that, when an act of the will has been excited in the soul, a bodily motion consonant with it is seen to be excited in the body sometimes more easily, sometimes with more difficulty; which is best explained if that motion is traced back to the soul as its efficient cause, which can operate in the body now more languidly, now more vigorously.

148 But it can scarcely be conceived or explained if that motion is said to be produced by God, who joined body and soul by such a law that He alone, by His divine force, would produce in the body that motion which the soul desired to be produced in the body. Therefore the efficient cause of those acts must be not God, as the Cartesians will have it, but the human soul; or else let the Cartesians explain to us why, on the occasion of some volition being given, God would excite in the body now a similar, now a dissimilar bodily act; which they will certainly not be able to explain. But if they say that the bodily motion is truly produced by the soul, and that the soul, on the occasion of some bodily motion being given, truly and properly acts, then the whole dispute rests on a mere name; let them use the name of occasional cause, for all we care, but in reality they slip back into the hypothesis of physical influx.

[p. 48]

149 Obj., finally, with the Wolffians and the Leibnizians: that hypothesis is far more probable, and ought to be embraced, in which the difficulties common to the hypotheses of physical influx and of occasional causes vanish; but such is the hypothesis of pre-established harmony: therefore. The minor is proved: in this system, already explained, the human body produces its motions and the series of its acts independently of the soul, just as if it were joined to no body. Thus those two orders, of bodily motions and of thoughts, are carried on together and at the same time, not because the soul can flow into the body or the body into the soul. The first difficulty therefore vanishes, namely that of conceiving in what way the body acts on the soul and the soul on the body. Next, that pre-established harmony is between the bodily motions and the perceptions of the soul, but not between its appetitions. The second difficulty, therefore, concerning the liberty of the human will vanishes: therefore.

150 To the argument I reply that the hypothesis of pre-established harmony not only has difficulties in common with the system of occasional causes, but also far graver ones. And certainly it is undeservedly supposed that there will be in the human body a certain constant and invariable series of motions, depending solely on the texture of the parts and on the action of external bodies, since it is established by the testimony of experience that the motions of our body are wonderfully varied by extrinsic and sudden causes as well, so that the series of our motions arises not from some intrinsic and constant principle, but from altogether innumerable and arbitrary causes. Add, too, that the mind sometimes assents to those motions and affections which are excited in the body, but sometimes nevertheless resists and dissents from them, so that no constant and invariable series of similar motions, or harmony, can be feigned by which, while a certain motion is excited in the body, a similar and consonant one is produced in the soul.

151 Finally: The idea of perfect liberty requires that the human mind, which must be the master, author and cause of its acts, should exert them for no other reason than that it wills to exert them, and that by that command and liberty it can also follow the motions of the body or resist them, effect them or abstain from them. This most grave difficulty, therefore, always remains, that the motions of the body are necessary in the Leibnizian hypothesis, inasmuch as they cannot be other than those which exist. Nor is there any ground for the adversaries to say that this harmony was pre-established only between the bodily motions and the perceptions of the soul, but not between its appetitions. For Leibniz devised that hypothesis precisely because he believed that no dependence could be feigned between the soul and the body: and therefore he must admit a pre-established harmony no less between the volitions of the soul than between its perceptions.

152 Nor, finally, does the reply avail that the series of all motions was foreseen by God in accordance with the free determination of the will, and

ordered. [p. 49] ordered. For since the Leibnizians admit no action between the soul and the body,

God could in no way foresee and order a series of all motions agreeing with the free will. For if no dependence can intervene between the soul and the body, God could not foresee and order it; but if that dependence is not repugnant, then the hypothesis of pre-established harmony is useless. These things being so, it is readily apparent that the modern Metaphysicians have been no more fortunate than the Peripatetics in explaining the society of body and mind, but more audacious. It remains, therefore, that we most willingly confess that the laws of this secret covenant, established by the infinite power and wisdom of God, cannot be comprehended altogether clearly by our intellect.

## APPENDIX

On the Seat of the Mind.

he Scholastics think that our mind is diffused through the whole body, 153

T           not only by power and efficacy, but in reality itself. Among the followers

of Descartes, at least the earlier ones, it is said to reside in the pineal gland, which is a small part of the brain. But if the soul resides in all the members, why then are judgments carried out in the brain? For why would one judge that there are two globules, if one touches a single one with two fingers so placed that the nerves take up a position in which the outer ones become inner? [Log. §.

113.] Certainly no necessity for a diffusion of this kind appears. Indeed, how can it happen that some people think they feel pain in a hand long since cut off, and that, if a little water is poured over the brain, no sensation is had in the external organs?

154 But neither does the pineal gland seem to be established as a fit seat for the mind. Let us hear the Anatomists (f). “Frederik once saw this gland (the pineal) petrified, and found three stones in it. But more wonderful is what the most distinguished Charles Drelincourt long ago communicated to us, and what he had observed in a virgin of about 20 years, who, after she had been tormented for six months by a dreadful cephalaea (g), and at length blinded, and thereafter deprived of her senses, had met her death amid lamentations: in her, namely, the pineal gland was not only stony, but had even grown to the size of a hen’s egg, and by its bulk had compressed the thalami (h) of the optic nerves and finally the remaining nerves as well (i).”

R                                                 155

(f) Ruysch, in the Thes. Anat.

(g) Cephalaea is an inveterate pain of the head, yielding with difficulty, stubborn and persistent.

(h) The place from which the optic nerves issue Galen called the thalamus.

(i) See Bonet, Theatr. Anatom., vol. 2, p. 309.

[p. 50]

155 More recently M. de La Peyronie (k) has placed the seat of the soul in the corpus callosum (l). For he showed that when the other parts of the brain were injured and the corpus callosum alone was unharmed, the use of the senses and of reason remained whole in various persons; but when the corpus callosum was injured, sensations and the use of reason were taken away together. Notwithstanding these things, however, it seems to me that it must be asserted that the soul has its proper seat in the brain alone, although it cannot be settled with certainty in precisely which part of the brain it resides. For the soul must be said to reside in that part of the body alone which is the only one in which the soul operates immediately; but that the mind operates immediately on the brain alone is most plainly evident: for when the brain alone is impaired, the use of all the senses is lost; hence those seized by Apoplexy, as if struck by lightning, are deprived of all sense, so that they feel nothing. The affections of the body, too, which are not transmitted to the brain, remain wholly hidden from the mind, as happens in paralysis. (See Phys. §. 560 ff.)

156 The Peripatetics, however, at least from the thirteenth century of the Christian name, contend that the mind is in the whole body. They are moved by arguments such as these. First, because whatever part of the body we touch, the mind feels, which is a sign that it is there. Next, because it cannot be understood how the mind is the substantial form of the human body, as was defined at the Council of Vienne (m), that is, is that which governs the body, unless it occupies the whole body. But there is no need to bring reasons of this kind to the Lydian touchstone.

157 And as regards the first, I say with the distinguished Jacquier that the soul perceives an impression made on any part of the body because that impression is propagated to the brain by means of the nerves, which reach from any part of the body all the way to the brain; namely, from any part of the body nerves are stretched as far as the brain, so that when the extremity of a nerve which is, e.g., in the foot or in the hand is plucked, the other extremity, which is in the brain, is likewise plucked or moved, and by the force of this motion excited in the brain the soul is alerted, and feels pain if the impression made was vehement. This is moreover confirmed by many experiments. I. If some part of the body is bound very tightly, between the brain and another part of the body that is to be cut off or pricked, no pain, or almost none, is felt; because, namely, no motion, or almost none, reaches the extremity of the nerve which is in the brain. II. If someone, as sometimes happens, is deeply fixed on some thought, he very often does not perceive external objects, which nevertheless strike his external senses; because, namely, the nerves are then so stretched that they do not admit another motion by which the mind might be determined to perceive external objects.

(k) In the year 1741.

(l) The cortical substance of the brain is the name given to its outer substance, of an ashen color, as distinguished from the inner, whiter substance, which is called the medullary substance and the corpus callosum.

(m) Under Clement V, in the year 1311.

[p. 51]

158 But you will insist. Whatever part of the body is injured, the soul perceives the pain as existing in that very part of the body which is injured: therefore the mind is immediately present to every part of the body. I deny the consequence. For although the pain is perceived by the soul as existing in whatever part of the body is injured, the soul nevertheless does not perceive the pain in that very part of the body which is injured.

159 And indeed a blind man exploring external objects with a stick perceives their properties, e.g. fluidity or hardness, at the end of the stick, and as it were existing in a certain manner at the end of the stick. Yet no one would say that the blind man’s soul resides at the extremity of the stick. So too, although the soul perceives some sensation, e.g. of heat or of cold, as existing in the tip of the finger or in any other part of the body, it must not therefore be said that the soul acts upon the tip of the finger and immediately perceives in it the sensation by which it is affected; namely, the motion first communicated to the tip of the finger, then spread through the nerves to the brain, reaches the seat of the soul, where the sensation takes place, which the soul nevertheless naturally refers to the other extremity of the nerves, where the first impulse was made.

160 As regards the second objection, I say that the soul can be the true form of the body (as indeed it is), namely the principle from which human actions arise, although we deny that it is diffused through the whole body. That this may be set forth more clearly, let us hear a notable passage from the Angelic Master St. Thomas (n): Spirits (says the holy Doctor) can be bound to a body either by way of form, as the soul is bound to the human body to give it life; or else without this, that it be its form, as Necromancers by the power of demons bind spirits to images.

161 Let us note, moreover, that at the time when Clement V convened the Synod of Vienne there were those who taught that our souls make use of human bodies in no other way than demons make use of the bodies which they possess (o). These things show well enough what both the Ancient Theologians and the Fathers of Vienne meant when they taught that souls are substantial forms, namely that human minds do not possess human bodies, as demons sometimes do, but inform them, that is, give them life. There are therefore two questions to be distinguished here: the first, whether the soul informs the body, that is, gives it life, or not. The Synod of Vienne wills this to be dogma, and we too teach it. The other: if it informs it and renders it living, is it necessary that it be diffused through the whole body? This is a matter of Philosophy’s jurisdiction. Let what has been said suffice.

## S I N G L E D I S S E RTAT I O N 

By every kind of argument the Existence of the Supreme Deity is most invincibly demonstrated.

f God, being about to treat of him so far as concerns Metaphysics, we 162

O           shall weigh whether his existence can be shown by natural reason; for

time does not allow us to dwell on setting forth the attributes of the

Divine Essence; these, indeed, you will weigh more opportunely when you have applied your mind to the study of Sacred Theology.

163 He is called an Atheist (p) who denies the existence of the Supreme Deity. By the name of God is understood “a being from itself, and hence necessarily existing, full of reason and counsel, by whom the visible world and the things that are in it were founded and, having been made, are ruled.” This definition is a nominal one. Yet that all agree in it, no one, I think (as the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia says), can deny; for as Cicero has it (q): “God, who is understood by us, cannot be understood in any other way than as a certain mind, unfettered and free, separated from

(p) Whether there really are Atheists or not is a great question. Some learned men have thought

that no Atheists have existed, and Johann Christoph Wolf, in his book De Atheismi falso suspectis, and

others after him, contend that the ancient Philosophers in particular can in no way be called Atheists.

On the contrary, Johann Heinrich Poppius, after others, maintains that many of the Ancients were

Atheists, in De Atheismo Philosophorum Gentilium celebriorum; and so does Buddeus in De Spinozismo ante

Spinozam.

(q) Tusculan Disputations, bk. 1, ch. 27. [p. 53] from all mortal admixture, perceiving and moving all things, and itself endowed with everlasting motion.” These things laid down, we must inquire whether it is evident with physical evidence that God exists. We speak of physical evidence, namely of that which suffices to extort a constant and firm assent, not from a wanton man who doubts of everything, but from an ingenuous lover of truth. For it is not in my mind in this place to deal with those who so deny everything that they do not admit as true without doubting even the first principles of knowledge themselves, most evident though they are. It will be enough to pull up their sophisms and cavils.

164 I say, therefore: it is evident with physical evidence that God exists. Proof 1, from the perpetual and constant consent of all nations and peoples: for what nature universally confesses must necessarily be true. For it is impossible for nature universally to lie. Now that all races, all nations, however wild and barbarous, have perpetually agreed in this, that they admit some supreme Deity, is so plain that it could be denied only by one who is an utter stranger to History. “There is no race” (says Cicero (r)) “so untamed, nor so wild, that, even if it does not know what sort of God it ought to have, does not yet know that it ought to have one.”

165 “And surely, unless we had this known and grasped in our minds,” says the praised Cicero (s), “so stable an opinion would not have remained, nor would it have been confirmed by length of time, nor could it have grown old together with the centuries and ages of men. For we see that other opinions, feigned and empty, have wasted away with length of time. For who thinks that the hippocentaur existed, or the chimera? …… For time blots out the fictions of opinion, but confirms the judgments of nature.” But it is now permitted, to speak with the same Cicero (t) (and this will be the second proof), it is permitted, I say, “setting aside subtlety of disputation, to contemplate in a manner with our eyes the beauty of those things which we say were established by Divine Providence.”

166 “And first let the whole earth be beheld, set in the middle seat of the world, solid and globular, and on every side gathered into a globe by its own tendencies, clothed with flowers, grasses, trees, crops: the incredible multitude of all of which is distinguished by an insatiable variety. Add to this the cool perennial flowings of springs, the transparent waters of rivers, the greenest clothing of the banks, the hollow depths of caverns, the roughness of rocks, the heights of overhanging mountains, and the immensities of the plains. Add also the hidden veins of gold and silver. And what kinds of beasts, and how varied, whether tame or wild! What flights and songs of birds! What pasturings of cattle! What life of the creatures of the woods!

What

(r) Bk. 1 of On the Laws, ch. 8.

(s) Bk. 2 of On the Nature of the Gods.

(t) Bk. 2 of On the Nature of the Gods, ch. 39.

[p. 54]

167 “What shall I now say of the race of men, who, set up as it were as cultivators of the earth, suffer it neither to grow wild with the savagery of beasts nor to be laid waste by the roughness of thickets, and by whose works the fields, the islands and the shores shine, studded with houses and cities? If we could see these things with our eyes as we can with our minds, no one, gazing upon the whole earth, would doubt of the divine reason. And truly, how great is the beauty of the sea! What an aspect of the whole! What a multitude and variety of islands! What delights of coasts and shores! How many kinds, and how unlike, of creatures, partly submerged, partly floating and swimming, partly clinging to the rocks with their native shells! And the sea itself, so making for the land, sports upon the shores that the two natures seem fused into one.

168 “Next, the air bordering on the sea is divided by day and night, and it is now borne aloft, spread out and thinned, and now, condensed, is gathered into clouds, and, collecting moisture, enriches the earth with rains, and now, flowing this way and that, makes wind. It too produces the yearly variations of cold and heat, and it also sustains the flight of birds, and, drawn in by breathing, nourishes and sustains living creatures. There remains the last and, from our dwellings, the highest, the embrace of heaven, girding and confining all things: which is also called the ether, the outermost border and boundary of the world, in which the fiery forms trace out their ordered courses with the greatest wonder.

169 “Of these the Sun, by whose magnitude the earth is surpassed many times over, revolves around that very earth, and by rising and setting it makes day and night; and now approaching, now receding, it makes each year two returns from opposite extremes, in the interval of which it now as it were contracts the earth with a kind of sadness, now in turn gladdens it, so that it seems to be made joyful together with the sky. The Moon, moreover, which is, as the Mathematicians show, larger than half the earth, wanders through the same spaces as the Sun; but now coming together with the Sun, now parting from it, it both sends to the earth the light which it has received from the Sun and itself undergoes various changes of light; and sometimes, placed beneath the Sun and over against it, it darkens its rays and light; sometimes, falling itself into the shadow of the earth, when it is opposite the Sun, it suddenly fails, through the interposition and intervention of the earth; and through the same spaces those stars which we call wandering are borne around the earth, and in the same way they rise and set; and their motions are now quickened, now retarded, often they even stand still. Than which spectacle nothing can be more wonderful, nothing more beautiful.” Thus far the Prince of Roman eloquence.

170 Whoever, then, has seriously attended to these things and contemplated them with an attentive mind will, I do not doubt, at last come to confess with us that the excellent machine of the world, and the bodies that are in it, could by no means have come to be without reason and counsel. “Or when, by some contrivance,” (says the praised, most elegant Cicero)

we [p. 55] “(u) we see something being moved, as a sphere, as clocks, as very many other things, we do not doubt that those are works of reason; but when we see the onrush of the heaven moved with wonderful swiftness and turned round, most constantly bringing about the yearly alternations with the utmost safety and preservation of all things, do we doubt that these things are done not only by reason, but by a reason that is excellent and divine?”

171 It pleases me, therefore, to complete the argument thus in a few words. If there is something in the nature of things which the mind of man, which reason, which human force, which human power cannot bring about, that which brings it about is certainly better than man. But the heavenly things, and all those whose order is everlasting, cannot be brought about by man. That, therefore, by which they are brought about is better than man. And what would you call this rather than God? For if God does not exist, what can there be in the nature of things better than man? For in him alone is reason, than which nothing can be more excellent. But for a man to think that there is nothing in the world better than himself is the arrogance of a fool, not to say of a madman. Therefore there is something better than man. Therefore God exists.

172 Proof 3: from the structure of the human body, which is so wonderful and so astounding that by it, if it has been diligently considered and thoroughly examined, the existence of the supreme maker is plainly established against the Atheist to the point of evidence. Come, look around at the workmanship of the human body, and by its prompting learn thoroughly who is the founder of so beautiful an image, who the painter of the eyes, who turned the nostrils and the ears, who stretched the lips of the mouth, who drew taut the nerves and bound them, who watered the veins, who piled up the solid bones, who wove the flesh round with a thin skin, who parted the fingers and the joints, who laid out the foundation of the foot, who pierced the pores and opened the passages, who carved out the pipes of the lungs?

173 See how many works of Divine Art are displayed in a single matter, each of them beautiful and rightly measured, and also differing from one another in their proper functions. Who, then, fashioned each of them? Did not God himself alone contrive all these things by his own will? And when no one would dare assert that a statue and an image come to be without a sculptor and a painter, shall we think that the wonderful fabric of man came to stand without a founder? Finally, does not the human mind itself, with its powers and operations, show, and indeed to the point of evidence, that there exists a Supreme Deity by whom so sublime a substance was founded, placed in a body and ineffably coupled with it? Surely whoever does not perceive that the mind and intellect of man, his reason, counsel and prudence were perfected by divine care seems to me to be wholly lacking in these very things.

174 Proof 4. And I ask of the Atheists with Cicero (x) why, if they maintain that

(u) In the place cited.

(x) In the place cited, ch. 47. [p. 56] that all natural composites, and the most adorned and most beautiful world itself, not only could have come to be from atoms running together at random, but were in fact so made, why, I say, do they not also say that if innumerable forms of the one-and-twenty letters were thrown together somewhere, the Annals of Ennius could be produced from them, so that they could afterwards be read? That is certainly less laborious than a single paltry animalcule, not to say than the whole machine of the world itself. Why has not the Annals of Ennius, but even a single verse of Virgil, never been produced in this way? Moreover (as the same Cicero excellently argues (y)), if a concourse of atoms can make a world, why can it not make a portico, a temple, a house, a city, which are less laborious and indeed much easier? Surely the Atheists babble so rashly about the world that they seem to me never to have looked up at this wonderful adornment of the Heaven.

175 Add, with Lactantius (z): If all things arise from chance concurrences of atoms, why has it never happened by chance that those principles came together so as to make an animal of such a kind that it would hear with its nostrils rather, smell with its eyes, see with its ears? Moreover, the Atheists have their throats cut by the very reasoning they employ. They say that it is not repugnant that the world should be made from a chance concurrence of atoms, and that if it is not repugnant, there is no reason why it should not in fact have been made in this way. But against them this same argument is urged thus: It is not repugnant that there should exist a cause full of reason which determined the primordial atoms to that combination which is now found: therefore a cause of this kind in fact exists.

176 Proof 5. For the very contingency of things is, in the judgment of all, a most invincible argument that God exists. For hence it comes about that we are compelled, even against our will, to admit some Being from itself, and necessarily existing, from which the things that exist contingently have afterwards received their being. It is therefore certain that it is evidently repugnant that every being should be from another. For since outside the collection of all beings no being is found, the collection of all beings would be from nothing as from an efficient cause, if every being had from another that it should exist. Therefore there is some being not from another. But what is not from another, and is, is from itself, as is plain: therefore there necessarily is some being which exists from itself.

177 Likewise it is repugnant that the whole collection of beings should be contingent. For if the whole is contingent, the whole so exists that it could equally have not been; and if it could equally have not been, there is no reason why it was determined to existing rather than to not existing, unless perhaps one is pleased to say that that collection determined itself to existing, than which surely (as the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia says) nothing is more absurd, and nothing more worthy of laughter. There is, therefore, a necessary being,

and

(y) In the place cited, ch. 37.

(z) On the Workmanship of God, ch. 6. [p. 57] and indeed such that in it is contained the reason why contingent beings exist. There

are many other most invincible demonstrations of this most worthy argument, which you can see in the distinguished Tommaso Maria Cerboni (a).

The cavils of the Atheists are refuted.

bj. 1. The existence of God is an article of faith: for, as the Apostle has it 178

O            (b), he that cometh to God must believe that he is: therefore it cannot be

demonstrated by natural reason. I distinguish the antecedent: it is an article of faith in such a way, namely, that it can be known only through revelation, I deny; that is, it must be admitted through faith if it does not become known through reason, I grant; and I deny the consequence. Moreover, that there is no repugnance in the existence of God becoming known to us through means both natural and supernatural is so manifest that it needs no demonstration. Besides, since Divine Faith is an assent given to some proposition on account of Divine revelation as its motive, a man must be certain of the existence of God before he is moved to assent on the authority of God revealing. Hence the sense of the testimony praised above is this:

whoever cometh to God, that is, whoever wishes to embrace the true Religion, must be certain of the existence of God.

179 That it came about either through fear, or through ignorance of causes, or through the frauds of rulers and Legislators, or finally through education, that all men have agreed in some Religion, is falsely and rashly contended by Hobbes (c),

Spinoza (d), Bayle (e), Toland (f) and very many others.

180 They object, therefore, 1: men, because they are weak by their nature and anxious with the expectation of things to come, easily feign fearful things for themselves: therefore it is probable that it was induced by fear that they admitted some

Supreme Deity. I deny the consequence. For just as many incline naturally to fear, so also more incline to boldness: therefore fear cannot be the universal cause on account of which all agree unanimously in some thing. Next, the Atheists confess with

Hobbes (g) that men are lovers of liberty and of dominion by their very nature; but it is impossible that among all men the natural desire for dominion and liberty should be so overwhelmed by empty fear that

181 Obj. 3: men have it implanted by nature itself to investigate the causes of things; but if they have been unable to attain the true ones, they feign supposititious ones for themselves: hence they have falsely persuaded themselves that God exists, so that they might rejoice at having attained the first principle of all things: therefore ignorance and error were the cause why some God was admitted by men. I deny the antecedent and the consequence: for things established on account of ignorance rest on empty and light reasons, and therefore can easily be refuted: therefore it is impossible that all the most skilled men should agree in them. How absurd, then, it is, and how foreign to all reason, that all nations, and those far removed from one another and having no communication with one another, should have been able to agree in one and the same error and kind of fiction!

182 Obj. 4. Since Legislators understood that citizens would be kept in their duty much more easily if they believed that there exists some Supreme Deity by whom they could be punished when they did wrong, it came about by their cunning that Religion was introduced among the peoples and propagated: therefore the origin of Religion must be sought from the Legislators themselves. I deny the antecedent. For it has been found by experience that opinions which are disseminated by the craft of men do not last very long, especially if it comes about from them that no light burden is laid upon all. Therefore, since this consent has always endured, although on account of it men are subjected to more laws, it cannot have had its origin from the cunning of Legislators. Next, barbarous nations too, which were subject to no one, have always agreed in some Religion, and Religion itself had its origin together with the human race.

183 Obj. 5. It very often happens that we hold as most certain what is vain and empty in itself, now on account of prejudices, now also on account of the education and instruction which we had in childhood: therefore Religion too could have flowed from these two principles. I deny the antecedent. For what is altogether diverse cannot lead to agreement in one and the same thing; but education and instruction among the nations is, and always was, altogether diverse; and hence we see it has come about that their morals and customs are diverse: therefore. Next, the prejudices of education and instruction are driven out if the mind is seriously applied to attaining the truth; but although in every age there have not been lacking those who devoted their effort to the study of the sciences, there was nevertheless no one (if you except one or another raving man) who departed from this common consent: therefore.

184 You will say: there were Philosophers who thought that there are no Gods, as Cicero witnesses (h). Moreover, four physical sects of Atheists were distinguished by Cudworth

therefore

(h) On the Nature of the Gods. [p. 59] (i): therefore. Second: no one has ever seen God: therefore we believe the existence of the Supreme Deity from the instruction of our teachers and the education given by our parents. To the first I deny the consequence. For from the fact that some Philosophers have fought against this consent, it is rightly concluded that a greater force for persuading is in it; for from this it is established that this universal consent did not flow from ignorance, error, education or some prejudice, but proceeded from the inner voice of nature, from the reason itself which is inborn in each man, from the natural light itself, which on account of the follies of a few raving philosophers could never be obscured. To the second I distinguish the antecedent: no one has seen him in himself, I grant; in his works, I deny; and I deny the consequence. For who has ever seen the mind? Yet I acknowledge it from its works, because I think, etc.

185 Obj. 6. If the consent of nations is admitted as a firm argument for persuading, many absurdities follow: therefore. Proof of the antecedent. Polytheism was established by the consent of nations; for, if the Jews are excepted, all agreed in it. Second. Each nation, on account of the consent of its forefathers, ought to prefer its own Religion to the Religion of another. Third. No one can be ignorant that many errors were disseminated and various superstitions instituted by the consent of nations: therefore. I reply with a distinction: that in all these things the consent was certain and universal, I deny; that it was inconstant, uncertain and particular, I grant. The consent, therefore, from which we contend that a most firm argument for persuading of some thing is drawn must be such that it embraces firmly and constantly all men of all nations and of all times.

186 Obj. 7. It arises from prejudice that we say there is some order in the world; namely, says Spinoza, from the fact that men found within themselves and outside themselves many things useful to them, e.g. eyes for seeing, plants and foods for nourishment, the Sun for giving light, etc., it came about that they at once judged that all things had thus been prepared and disposed by some agent: therefore from the workmanship and order of the world it is not rightly proved that God exists. I deny the antecedent. For men do not labor under prejudice when they judge, e.g., that the organic parts of the eyes were prepared and disposed by a most wise maker, and did not grow together by some fatal necessity, any more than Spinoza himself (whose cavil this is) would labor under prejudice if, in considering either the structure of buildings or the construction of a clock, he were to suspect intelligent causes by which they were disposed with singular industry; but Spinoza would not labor under prejudice if he suspected that causes of this kind either exist or have existed; nay, he would be held a madman if he contended that all these things had been disposed by some fatal necessity; with how much better right, then, from the wonderful disposition of the whole world

S2                                        do

(i) Systema Intellectuale, ch. 3, §. 30. [p. 60] do we find, without prejudice, that there exists a supremely intelligent maker.

187 I think it will not be unpleasant for you if I set before you some arguments which Fr. Girolamo Maria Buzzi expounds in the Accurate Synopsis of the Theology of the distinguished Fr. Giovanni Lorenzo Berti, copied out in as many words; for even from this you will learn how clearly it embraces everything, how lucidly it sets things forth, and how useful a study of this kind will afterwards be to you in Theology (*).

188 Obj. 8. It is shown by several arguments that the world was not founded by God: therefore the existence of God is not proved from his Workmanship. The antecedent is proved: 1. For it cannot be conceived that God, being Eternal, made a mortal world, and that suddenly, when he had rested for so many ages before. What glory or joy did he gain from it, who could never lack glory or happiness? What instruments or ministers did he use? If he created light afterwards, how did he not lie in darkness before? Therefore God did not found the world. Second. God founded the world either for the Wise or for the foolish; but he founded it for neither, for the former are few, the latter wholly unworthy: therefore he founded it for none.

189 Third. There is no order in its parts, of which some are deserted, others suited only for beasts or for birds, as the air, the mountains, the seas, the marshes. The fields, moreover, put forth crops only with unremitting labor, and these are often ruined by hail or by flood: therefore it was not created by a most Wise God. Fourth. The most noxious wild beasts, pestilences, famines, diseases overthrow the Providence of God: therefore. Fifth. The wailing of infants, the nakedness of the body, and the innumerable calamities by which man is more wretched than any animalcule, prove sufficiently that the world was not built by God for his sake: therefore the world was not founded by God, and consequently the existence of the Supreme Deity is not well proved from the Workmanship of the world.

190 I reply: I deny the antecedent; and to the first proof I deny the antecedent as well, to which the Epicureans too must reply, who posit eternal matter although they attribute to the world a beginning and an end. Moreover, in eternity, where, as St. Augustine says (k), “there is no creature by whose changeable motions times are carried on, times can by no means exist,” and elsewhere (l): “If before Heaven and earth there was no time, why is it asked what thou wast doing then?” Nor did God need ministers or instruments, which betray the weakness of a craftsman; nor did he who always was the true light ever lie in darkness. To the 2nd I deny the minor. For God founded the universe first for his own sake, then for the sake of the wise. But that others are

wicked

(*) We use this Synopsis in the Salesian College for the study of Sacred Theology.

(k) Bk. XII of The City of God, ch. 15.

(l) Bk. XI of the Confessions, ch. 13. [p. 61] wicked is not from God, but from man, whom God placed in the hand of his own counsel, judging it better to do good with evils than to permit no evils to exist.

191 To the 3rd I deny the antecedent. For there is no part of the globe from which some advantage does not come to man. The mountains supply purer air, the woodlands pastures, the rocks metals and marbles. Rivers feed fish, water gardens, adorn and fortify cities. The sea contributes clouds and rains to the fertility of the fields, and carries goods across from the remotest shores. Heat and cold too are of use, for the latter makes the earth pregnant, the former ripens the crops: therefore, etc. To the 4th and 5th I deny the antecedent. For hardships, and death itself, are the wages of original sin. But since the Atheist mocks these things, I reply 2.: by these things men are led to contempt of earthly things and to praiseworthy industry; they are warned to live sparingly and not to hasten death upon themselves by excessive venery and wine. Of wild beasts, moreover, there is none which does not furnish us either help, or food, pleasure or remedy. To the last I deny the antecedent. For wisdom with weakness is better than even the greatest strength without reason. Thus far Fr. Buzzi.

192 Obj. 9. It is not certain that the visible world exists: therefore the existence of God too will be uncertain. Reply 1: I deny the antecedent. For there is more than one argument by which the existence of bodies is established against the Idealists. Reply 2: I deny the consequence. For the existence of the Supreme Deity is demonstrated also from the fact that a contingent being exists, namely the human mind itself, whose existence the Idealist cannot deny without holding that no one can have certainty even of his own existence; and how false this is, not to say more, there is no reason for me to show at length.

193 Obj. 10. From the fact that a contingent being exists, it cannot be gathered with certainty that a necessary being exists: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: a necessary being can exist without a contingent being existing: therefore, in turn, a contingent being can exist without a necessary being existing. I reply with the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia: I deny the antecedent; to its proof I let the antecedent pass and deny the consequence. The reason for the difference is evident. For since in a contingent being there is no sufficient reason why it should exist rather than not exist, a contingent being cannot exist unless there is also a necessary being in which its sufficient reason is contained. The case is the contrary when we speak of the necessary being. For this is such that it comprises the reason of its own existence.

194 You will say: the existence of a contingent being is not necessarily connected with the necessary being; otherwise the contingent being would exist necessarily: therefore a contingent being can exist without a necessary being existing. I distinguish the antecedent: that is, it is not of such a kind that a necessary being cannot be had without a contingent one being had, I grant; that is, a contingent being can exist without a necessary one existing, I deny; and I deny the consequence. It is true that the existence of a contingent being is not so connected with the necessary being that the necessary being could not exist unless there existed

[p. 62] a contingent being. For a contingent being is not produced necessarily. But it is false that the existence of a contingent being is not so connected with the necessary being that it is altogether repugnant that a contingent being be had without a necessary one being had. For since the necessary being holds the reason why the contingent exists, it is a contradiction that a contingent being should exist without a necessary one existing; just as the conflict is evident in this, that there should be an effect without a cause existing.

195 Obj. finally. It is evidently not repugnant that there be a process to infinity in efficient causes: therefore it is evidently not established that a cause must be admitted which is the first of all. Passing over the antecedent, I deny the consequence. For the existence of God has not been demonstrated by us from the fact that an infinite series of causes is repugnant. For whether it is repugnant or not, it is always true that a cause existing from itself must be admitted, since it cannot be that the whole collection of beings should be in such a way that it could equally have not been. That God, the Best and Greatest, exists is therefore beyond doubt. For (I shall conclude in the words of Cicero): “For if reason is on my side, if events, if peoples, if nations, if Greeks, if Barbarians, if our forefathers too, if, finally, this has always been so thought, if the greatest Philosophers, if the Poets, if the Wisest Men, who established Commonwealths, who founded cities: are we waiting until the beasts speak, and are we not content with the agreeing authority of men?” (m). And let what has been said of Natural Theology and of the whole of Metaphysics suffice.

Index

(m) On Divination, bk. 1, ch. 19.
