thics, or Moral Philosophy, has been instituted for directing

E          and perfecting morals, so that by love of virtue and flight from vices we

may attain true felicity and beatitude: there is no one who does not know this. Hence it is deservedly wont to be called the art of living well, the medicine of the mind, the investigator of virtue and the expeller of vices, the art of life, the mistress of morals. It can be defined, and very well: the knowledge of the good, or the science showing the way to arrive at the highest good and at the enjoyment of it. But since we feel that we are not only Philosophers but Catholics too, and glory in this wonderfully, I would deservedly incur the reproach of the Learned if I set the medicine of the mind before Youths not even to be tasted, as they say, with the tips of the lips.

T2                                              For

[p. 2]

For countless things would present themselves for us to say, if we had a mind to embrace everything that we see explained by the Ancients and the Moderns in setting out the science of Morals; we shall, however, select the principal and, as it were, the chief heads, so as to embrace the nobler precepts of morals in a briefer and clearer order. Since, moreover, no one can attain the highest good, namely God, and the enjoyment of Him, unless he observes his duties toward God, toward himself and toward others, unless he cultivates virtue and detests vices, the whole of Ethics can very well be reduced to two, as it were, supreme heads. First, therefore, we shall discourse on Duties; then we shall touch on a few things concerning virtue in general and its causes and signs. For the prescribed limits of the Elements do not allow us to draw out the discussion any further. Let there be, then,

## CHAPTER I

On the various duties of men toward God, toward themselves, toward others, and toward the Commonwealth. 1

“A     lthough there are many weighty and useful things in Philosophy, discussed ac‐

curately and copiously by Philosophers, those things which they have handed down and prescribed concerning duties seem to extend most widely. For no part of life, neither in public nor in private affairs, neither in the courts nor at home, neither if you transact anything with yourself nor if you contract with another, can be free of duty; and in discharging it lies all that is honorable in life, and in neglecting it all that is base,” says the most eloquent consular Philosopher M. T. Cicero (a). And rightly indeed: for since man is not without law, he must pursue certain duties in order to answer best to his end.

2 Duties of this kind are derived both from reason and from Revelation. For in the present providence of things the light of reason is dim and weak, and therefore, lest it err, it needs the protection of another light. Now the duties which man must perform by reason and Revelation either regard God, and are those of Religion; or are referred to man inasmuch as he is his own guardian; or regard man inasmuch as he is related to others, and are called those of Society; or inasmuch as he is related to the Commonwealth, and are named the duties of the Citizen.

3 As regards God, it is certain first of all that not only with an internal and spiritual, but also with an external and sensible worship of Religion

(a) On Duties, bk. 1, ch. 1.

[p. 3]

He must be adored. By the name of Religion we understand the worship of love, of obedience and of service, to be rendered to Him to whom it is due. And hence the true Religion, which is the Catholic one, excludes all impiety and superstition. I call impiety both the neglect and the contempt of Religion, each of which directly conflicts with the light of reason; superstition, on the other hand, is either a worship arising from erroneous opinions about God, or one shown to a thing to which it is not due, or one shown indeed to God, but in ways and rites not consonant with His perfections. Hence Atheism, and Pantheism, and Polytheism, and the Mahometan superstition, and Jewish obstinacy, and every sect whatever proscribed by the Catholic Church, are excluded.

4 And from this it follows that there is the highest obligation to embrace the Catholic Religion, inasmuch as it alone is the true revealed Religion. For in it are found the signs of credibility, of which the chief are: the holiness and unity of its doctrine; then also the probity of life of its principal, and above all of its first, preachers and propagators; the signs that testify that God is speaking, such as miracles and prophecies fulfilled in deed; the testimony of the Martyrs; the continual succession of the Interpreters of Religion and of the Judges of controversies. Such a Religion, in no way overcome by the wicked assaults of the most abandoned men, has stood immovable and constant from the beginning of things down to these times in which we live: it is therefore the work of God Himself.

5 Yet who would have brought his mind to believe this, most accomplished Young Men, had not the thing itself demonstrated it, to the very great disgrace of our times? A crowd of men has arisen who have resolved, not to call back the ancient superstitions, but, by disseminating the impiety that is the opposite of superstition, to eliminate Religion from the face of the earth after so many centuries, and to thrust God Himself, its author, down from Heaven. Among the more notable leaders of this design are counted Hobbes, Spinoza, Toland, Bayle. These are followed, like a hired band, by Collins, Woolston, the Marquis d’Argens, Voltaire, Rousseau, Helvétius, and very many others, who, not daring for shame to put their names to their pestilential little books of Letters, Specimens, Treatises, Thoughts, Examinations, Ephemerides (b), and to many

other

(b) Here are the titles of the little books. La Philosophie du Bon Sens (commonly the Marquis d’Argens). Epitres Persanes (commonly M. de Montesquieu). Lettres sur la Religion essentielle à l’homme. Pensés Philosophiques. Les Oracles de la Raison. Examen de la Religion. Code de la Nature, ou le veritable esprit de ses loix. Le Christianisme aussi ancien que le monde. Les Mœurs. Tolerance des Religions. Epitres Turces. Epitres Chinoises, Epitres Cabalistes. Epitres Peruvienes. L’Esprit. Dictionnaire Philosophique. Dictionnaire Raisonné des Sciences, des Arts, & des Metiers, ou Dictionnaire Encyclopédique. At [p. 4] other works of this stamp, with which Europe teems, have come down into the battle line.

6 For my part I would not dare to decide (I use the words of the most distinguished Valsecchi) which feeling ought rather to be aroused in a wise man beholding this crowd, whether that of indignation, or of contempt, or rather of pity. Ah, wretched men! Do you think you have so much strength that you judge yourselves able, by bringing out a few little pages, to refute the consensus of so many centuries, to convict the whole human race of error, to stifle the voice of nature, and to wage war on the Supreme Deity? Will that Religion which neither idolatry, then dominant, nor the cruelty of Tyrants equipped with the arms of the whole Roman empire, nor the acumen of so many Philosophers practiced in all the arts of disputation could overwhelm, be subdued by avarice, pleasure, the manners and bearing of a world corrupted by every desire and made effeminate? Fables.

7 Nay rather, Religion itself, victorious over all obstacles, triumphant over hearts and minds, has multiplied its victories by its contests, and has found its adversaries, after the battle, to be its keenest champions. Shall that Religion, I say, be laid low and utterly destroyed by some infamous satire, a collection of libertine little tales, a selection of a few ambiguous words and puerile sophisms? If this is not the height of audacity, nay, a signal madness, I do not know what ever could be. And in truth it is enough to read even in passing the little writings of these Masters for the marks of light-minded and raving men to be recognized at once. Do not, I beg you, think that in them you can find

some Neufchatel 1751. 17 vols. in fol. (It cannot be denied that Physics, Mathematics, in a word the Sciences and Arts, are set forth excellently in this work, since what is handed down about them regards Religion and morals neither directly nor indirectly. But the things that belong to Religion, that regard the authority of the Prince, and finally that pertain to good morals, are ruined, debased, derided. With all these removed, the Work, revised anew and expurgated, is now coming out at Lucca and at Livorno in Tuscany, to the applause of the learned and to the very great good and profit of the whole Republic of Letters.) Rousseau, L’Emille, ou traité d’Education. Voltaire in his various little works. With most valid reasons these Libertines, and many others besides, have been censured by most distinguished men: Tommaso Maria Cerboni O.P., in the work entitled De Theologia Naturali, & Revelata; Anton. Valsecchi O.P., in the work entitled Dei Fondamenti della Religione, e de i fonti dell’Empietà; P. Muniglia O.P., Dissertazzione contro i Fatalisti; the author of the work entitled La Pretessa Filosofia degli moderni increduli; Abbé Nonnotte, in the work entitled Les Erreurs de Voltaire; Abbé Gauchat, in the work entitled Lettres Critiques, ou analyse & refutation des ecrits modernes contre la Religion; and others. [p. 5] some well-deduced system, in which the first things answer to the last, the middle ones both to the last and to the first, and all cohere aptly with one another, by which war might be waged both on Religion and on God, the Best and Greatest.

8 Nothing is heard but confused declamations and voices, as they were heard in the land of Sennaar among the builders of the huge tower, who did not even understand one another’s speech. Each one spews out unspeakable and false things, but so various, so contrary, that not only do they not mean the same thing, but these destroy those.

9 The Atheist denies that God exists; the Deist (c) says that He exists, but does not care for human affairs. The Naturalist fights against both, and defends with all his might both Providence and God. But this man, since he will recognize nothing in God except what he himself can grasp with so dull a wit, offers himself to be pierced by the weapons both of the Atheist and of the Deist. Helvétius gives man a soul of the same kind as horses and wolves have, and strips it of all freedom. Rousseau makes it free and spiritual: but the primeval, original condition of man, in his opinion, differs in nothing from the origin of wolves and horses.

10 These assert that the whole man perishes when life perishes; others think that he will be immortal. Among the latter, however, some hold that in the other life he is to be punished with no torments; others will have it that there will be those torments which the law necessarily prescribes; others laugh at these laws, these penalties, as the pure and simple fictions of Poets and of Kings. If you listen to these, the world has been from eternity; if to those, it had a beginning: from God, as some hold; from chance and the fortuitous concourse of eternal and wandering atoms, as others do.

11 What, however, is no less true than astonishing is this: that each of them rages against himself in a restless war, and very often pierces himself with his own weapons. How many things there are in the works of Hobbes of which some overturn others, only those are ignorant who have not read them. The whole Ethics of Spinoza rests on a definition which can be understood in two ways, of which the one, which is true, overturns the other; and this other, once overturned, destroys geometrically the whole book, which depends on the definition from beginning to end (d). The herd of Libertines

religiously

(c) A Deist, or Theist, is the name given to one who indeed grants that God exists, but professes no Religion, no worship. The Deists disdainfully decry all Religion and divine Revelation as mere fables, and prattle that it is enough if God is adored in the simplicity of nature and of the heart.

(d) The definition on which Spinoza’s system rests is the definition of substance conceived in these words: By substance I understand that which is in itself and is conceived through itself: that is, that whose concept does not need the concept of another thing from which it must be formed (Ethics, Pt. 1, Def. 3). Now these words, that which is in itself, can have a twofold meaning. I. That which is in itself, that is, which is from itself, excluding a cause that produces it. II. That which is in itself, [p. 6] religiously imitates its illustrious leaders in this point: having learned lying from them, it has also learned this, to reject what it has approved and always to contradict itself.

12 Besides this, you will find in little books of this sort a whole Polyanthea, or a rude and undigested collection of declamations and of erudition. They dispute in them about Jurisprudence, about Politics, about Astronomy, about Commerce, about Ethics, about War; Dialectic alone, or the Art of Thinking, is wholly lacking. They fly from Athens to Sparta, from Jerusalem

to that is, which is through itself, excluding a subject that sustains it. Modes, e.g. motion, shape, etc., do not exist from themselves, because they need a cause by which they are produced; but neither do they exist through themselves, for they require a subject in which to inhere, e.g. a ball. But the most perfect Being exists through itself and from itself. For it does not need a subject by which to be sustained, nor can it even have a cause by which it is produced. A horse exists through itself, since it inheres in no subject; but it does not exist from itself, since it has had a cause by which it was produced. Spinoza used the ambiguous expression exists in itself, and will have it proper to substance to exist from itself, excluding a cause that produces it; but this is what everyone denies, and what that circumcised philosopher nowhere proved in his book. Let us pass to the other parts of the definition and, with the torch of the distinction just given going before us, uncover his fraud. By substance I understand that which is in itself, and he adds, and is conceived through itself. If Spinoza believes that the concept of substance is so absolute that it implies no relation to a subject that sustains it, as motion implies one to the movable, he thinks truly, but this helps Pantheism not at all. What then does he mean? This, namely: that the concept of substance is so absolute that it removes from itself every relation to a cause that produces it; but this is altogether false, and this he will never prove. The same must be said of the other words that follow, which the impious Apella adds to explain the definition of substance just given, that is, substance is that whose concept does not need the concept of another thing from which it must be formed. For if he means that the concept of substance must exclude from itself a relation to another substance to which it is referred, as an effect to a cause, we deny it, nor will he ever prove it. The crafty Hebrew, however, understood this; for from this one false principle he derived his whole Pantheistic system, and he wished to include in that definition, as its foundation, that which was the head of the whole controversy: namely, that it is of the essence of substance that it exist from itself, excluding any cause whatever, and that there can never be conceived in a substance a relation of effect to another substance as to the cause that procreates it. [p. 7] to Rome, from the age of Augustus to the age of Louis. A passage is made from the Caribs of the Antilles to the Hottentots of Africa; from these to the northern Greenlanders; thence to the wild men of other remote regions. Hence the laws of regions of the world so unlike one another are now examined, now their customs are compared with one another, now their turpitudes are recounted, now irreligion is celebrated with applause. Chinese antiquities carry greater weight with them than sacred Genesis. Diodorus, Strabo and Tacitus are cited as more expert in Jewish antiquities than Moses himself. Horace, Petronius, Manilius, Lucretius, Poppius are brought forward as incomparable teachers of wisdom.

13 Yet all this is mostly done without the passages of the authors being examined; for the most part they bring in those passages unfaithfully, and always without the art of Criticism; for it is enough that they be pronounced in a fearless, censorious voice, which alone, as they suppose, can give weight to fables and lies.

14 Libertine youths stand fixed in their gaze as they read such a heap of erudition, such a variety of matters, such confidence in deciding. They admire Philosophers of this kind as oracles of wisdom. Religion, whose foundations and whose system they have never meditated, wavers in their minds. These teachers, for their part, think that they have in fact achieved what they intended, and by their rapid and turbulent loquacity have really shown that the Catholic Religion is a fiction, the Gospel a jest, its Martyrs madmen, that the Holy Fathers know nothing at all, and that all true Catholics are a herd of fools, useless, nay pernicious to Society and to the Commonwealth.

15 But if in so great a farrago of useless and absurd things certain sophisms are mixed in which attack natural and revealed Religion, this nevertheless is most certain: that these have been resolved, not once but very often, by our Doctors, and especially by the Angelic Master St. Thomas Aquinas, nay, so to speak, reduced to ashes and blown away.

16 You will now understand that it was not without grave cause that I said at the beginning that no other feelings than those of indignation, contempt and pity can be aroused in a prudent man whenever he looks upon these Writers, who trust that with such puerile arts they can overturn Religion: that Religion, I say, whose divine origin, the truth of its dogmas, the holiness of its precepts, and the eminent virtue and force of the protection by which it is defended, have brought it about that through the course of so many centuries, after so many vicissitudes, it has been neither conquered by the sword, nor shaken by writings, nor overcome by superstition and impiety: in a word, that it has beaten back all the assaults of men and of demons.

17 In so great a cesspool, then, of most pestilential books, by which (as Pope Clement XIII of happy memory most wisely says (e)) men

V                                            corrupt

(e) Letter in the form of a Brief, given to Fr. Anton. Valsecchi on 21 March, in the year 1767. [p. 8] corrupt and reprobate concerning the Faith, with a most impudent license joined with impunity, try to pour most absurd and impious opinions into the minds of the unlearned, I have thought it altogether necessary to warn you that, should books of this kind (which God forbid) perhaps at some time fall into your hands, you abstain altogether from reading them, lest they cheat you by philosophy, and vain deceit; according to the tradition of men, and not according to Christ, as St. Paul says (f). But let our discourse return to the point from which it set out.

18 As regards God, since He is most excellent and rightly and deservedly claims for Himself the supreme right and the supreme authority over all things, everyone understands that He is to be honored with as great a homage and veneration as is owed to the Best Founder and the most Loving Preserver of things. There are many things by which we testify our homage toward others, and indeed love is the chief proof of our homage. For by it it comes about that we cultivate in a wonderful way, with zeal and devotion, those whom we judge worthy of our benevolence. There can therefore be no doubt that God, the Best and Greatest, who by right of dominion is to be worshipped by us, is to be loved above all else and cherished supremely. Nor indeed is there only one reason by which we are driven to do this. For God is that highest good which, if it were seen with the eyes, would arouse (as Plato says of Wisdom) wondrous loves of itself. For whatever is good for us in this life we understand to proceed from Him alone, and we are to receive eternal beatitude in the other life from the enjoyment of Him.

19 Hence we are taught by Sacred Scripture that God is to be loved with the whole heart, with the whole soul, and with all one’s strength (g), so that, if our heart, kindled as it were by a perpetual and restless flame, could be consumed as a victim of love, that love would scarcely, nay not even scarcely, be equal to repaying in some measure the love of a most loving Father. With all the powers of the mind, therefore, we must strive to love God above all things; and since God is charity, and is a fire, and came to cast fire on the earth, and wills nothing else but that it be kindled (h), we ought to ask Him Himself with tears and outpoured prayers that the ardor of divine charity may be kindled more vehemently in our hearts, consume all our affections, and at last make us a victim acceptable and pleasing to God.

20 We venerate the Supreme Deity, however, not with love alone but also with fear. And since, as the Schools say, the fear of God is twofold, namely filial and servile, it is best to employ both in worshipping Him. The first is born of love for Him and cannot be separated from this sweet bond. The other arises from punishment and cannot be disjoined from servitude. To this love, moreover, and to fear, a most certain faith must also be added. For who would not trust Him whom he knows for certain can neither be deceived nor deceive? God is indeed

supreme

(f) To the Colossians, ch. 2, v. 8.

(g) Matthew, ch. 22, v. 37.

(h) Luke 12, v. 29. [p. 9] supreme reason itself, goodness itself, and truth itself. Concerning His promises and words, therefore, once it is established that He has spoken and promised, no one may doubt. From faith there necessarily follows Hope, by which we ought to expect both the reward appointed for virtue and also those helps which, since they assist the weakness of our powers, are therefore altogether necessary for attaining it.

21 That filial love, therefore, by which we love God as a Father, ought to rouse us to hope with certainty from Him for all the goods that will profit us; and therefore we ought to ask and entreat of Him help, and aid in adversity, as the Redeemer Himself very often invites us to pray and to ask: Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. By divine counsel, however, He admonishes us to ask in the name of Christ Himself: If you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you.

22 But not even from the invocation of God and from prayer can we abstain, whether Rousseau will or no. For this is the first part of our duty, in which we certainly cannot fail without bringing on ourselves the greatest inconveniences and losses. For since we are afflicted by so many and such great evils, it is granted to us to be refreshed in them only by the power and wisdom of the Supreme Deity. Immortal thanks, too, are not only to be felt toward God, but also to be rendered to Him. For who, heaped with innumerable benefits, would think himself exempt from performing this duty? And if, endowed with the single benefit of creation and conservation alone, we would owe God very much, what must we judge of that condition of life in which far more has been imparted to us?

23 But these are the internal duties of Religion. Concerning the external ones, the following seem to us to be laid down, as it were in summary. God is to be adored not only with an internal and spiritual, but also with an external and sensible worship of Religion, as we said above. And indeed there is nothing in us that is not the gift of God, and therefore subject to Him in every respect. Therefore the external members of the body too must serve Him. To this argument another is added, and that a very weighty one, taken from the very condition of our nature. For if the acknowledgment of the Deity is the necessary bond of natural Society and of the civil state, the worship of that same Deity will also be supremely commended to both conditions of men. But it is certain that neither Society nor this Civil form can subsist without sensible operation; wherefore, in order to establish it, an external and sensible worship must also be added. From the law of rendering external worship other duties follow. The first is that we speak of God and of Divine things only in the most honorable way. The second, that by all external signs we manifest our internal duties for the example of others. The third, that we also explain the knowledge of Divine things to others, so that in turn one may profit another. Finally, that we promote the glory of God with all piety and zeal.

24 But let us treat fully of the duties which are to be

Y2 [p. 10] cultivated by man toward himself. The things that pertain to this kind of duties are contained in the custody and cultivation both of the mind and of the body. But although we are bound to both, the perfecting of the mind must nevertheless be greater and more careful, by as much as the mind itself is more excellent and nobler than the body. Now the care of the mind is perfected by the amendment of the intellect and of the will. Whatever, therefore, seems to regard this amendment must be performed by a Christian man above all, with all zeal and diligence. And since the vices of the intellect are more easily removed by the study of the disciplines, as the errors of the will are more safely amended by the exercise of the virtues, we shall have to take refuge in both. Nothing, however, among the aids just mentioned, can be offered or devised that is more apt for procuring the cultivation of the mind than an attentive and vigilant moderation of our affections.

25 The principal affections are Love, Hatred, Desire, Joy, Hope, Sadness, Distrust, Boldness, Despair, Pleasure, Ambition, Avarice, Anger, Shame, Weariness, Envy, Derision, Jealousy, immoderate Love of self, Emulation, by which we see human minds enticed, moved or excited, so that from them all the virtues or vices arise as from most abundant springs. [See what was said in the Logic, bk. 2, ch. 5.] Hence in every kind of life we have this precept: that we correct the motions of the mind that do not obey reason. As for the body, since no one is Lord of his own life, whatever Voltaire may blurt out, neither can anyone exercise an absolute dominion over it. And indeed such custody of the body must be kept as is required in order neither to destroy it nor to impair it. All of which, however, is to be understood and performed always without prejudice to the business of Religion.

26 There have not been lacking those who thought that, in order to avoid grave harm, and above all to escape an ignominy more shameful than death itself, it was lawful for them to inflict death on themselves. But it is certain that this in no way agrees either with the prescriptions of the law of nature or with Christian laws. For there is no necessity of nature why we should claim for ourselves, against the will of its very master, that dominion too which is proper to God alone, and to Princes, who act in God’s stead on earth. Add that those are injurious to Providence and distrust the Divine Goodness too much who, in the extreme straits of affairs, complain that they have been deserted by the most loving Father of lights; not to speak of the virtue of Fortitude, which certainly shines out in adversity the more, the more bravely evils are endured.

27 The remaining duties to be observed by man toward man are these. That the human race is generated for mutual Society, whatever Rousseau, still living and the talk of men, may think to the contrary, is ascertained among all. For what would organs fit for speaking profit, or to what use would affections for helping others serve, unless we were destined by nature itself, namely by God, the most wise author of nature, to enter as it were into one great Society? We are therefore joined by a mutual bond of friendship

[p. 11] and benevolence. And just as all that is honorable lies in observing it, so all deformity and baseness lies in breaking and violating it.

28 From this friendship, moreover, two kinds of duties are derived. The first, that we offend no one by word or deed; the second, that we help our fellows with beneficence as far as we can. And indeed the injury of others, which is forbidden by that natural law, what you would not have done to you, do not do to another, can extend very widely. For since there are goods of the mind, of the body and of fortune, we can be harmful to others in three ways.

29 Thus the chief part of what is honorable is to impel no one to commit evil, either by depraved opinions or by examples. For impressionable minds are undermined equally by words and by deeds, and those who sin in this are reproved with the greatest justice for the sum, not of one crime only, but of many, nay of manifold, nay plainly of innumerable ones.

30 Hence much greater care must be applied by Parents, Guardians, Curators, Pedagogues, Masters of the liberal arts, or whoever at length they may be on whom the education of youth chiefly falls, that in instructing the young they keep to that method of discipline which is exactly conformed to the norm of probity. In discharging this duty, moreover, there is no one who does not see that the nature and condition of the children must be followed.

31 As for those things that are referred to the goods of fortune, I explain much in few words thus. Whatever things are placed in the possession of others, and procured from outside for their preservation and advancement, cannot be violated except with a transgression of the law of nature. For although no things are private by nature, they nevertheless become so by ancient occupation, victory, war, compact, condition, lot.

32 That excellent name, therefore, which has fallen to each man through the exercise of the virtues, can be injured by another neither privately nor publicly. In this matter, if we falsely charge the words or deeds of others as crimes, we are both guilty of calumny and sin against justice. If, on the other hand, we make manifest to another what is a vice and a sin in someone else, which is indeed true but hidden, we are already acting against mutual benevolence. But nothing is more shameful, nothing fouler in the Society of men, than inconstancy in words and compacts. For since the chief foundation of Justice is Faith, once this virtue is removed, Justice too, and together with it sociability, must collapse. Wherefore, if the faith given to anyone must not be violated, by the same reasoning every license of deceiving another by a lie has also been taken away. This indeed we understand of every kind of lie, so that whether it is done to the detriment of another, or you lie for the advantage of yourself and of others, you will be judged a violator of both rights, namely the perfect and the imperfect. Concerning beneficence and liberality, I think that all the duties derived from this head are contained in that principle: whatever you would have done to you by others, do also to others. Thus the omission of these is to be referred not to injustice, but to inhumanity

[p. 12] and baseness. In conferring benefits many cautions must be applied, and first of all we must see to it, with Tully, that the kindness not harm the very persons to whom it will seem to be done kindly, nor others; next, that the kindness not be greater than one’s means; then, that to each be given according to his worth. But I judge it necessary to say something about the duty of man toward the Commonwealth.

33 It will therefore be the duty of a prudent and honorable Citizen to embrace his Country and the Prince himself with sincere love; humbly to obey his rule, his laws and his ministers; to win over the minds of all by eminent charity, munificence, sweetness of manners, justice, and all the virtues; to outshine others in talent, skill, the liberal arts, good faith, prudence, care of the household, solicitous education of children, piety and religion; to shrink from public honors and dignities for which he knows himself to be unequal, but to administer those he has merited, and those offered of their own accord, sedulously, diligently and faithfully; finally, to provide diligently, by counsel, strength and resources, in prosperity and adversity, for the common welfare, liberty or safety of the Citizens and of the Prince; and, where the debt of the office laid upon him or a grave calamity shall have demanded it, steadfastly to pour out honors, fortunes, children, and life itself in a sweet and becoming death.

These and other such principles do not savor of laxism, nor are they drawn from the putrid springs of Laxism.

## CHAPTER II

On Virtue in general, and its causes and signs.

34

“T      he whole sum of Philosophy,” says Tully (i), “is referred to living happily, and

men, seeking this one thing, have devoted themselves to this study.” All acknowledge that virtue is necessary for living well and happily; and on that account I have undertaken to treat the things that pertain to virtue in general, and its efficient causes, the more gladly as the matter is one that concerns our nature the more.

35 Virtue, moreover, is (says the most distinguished Genovesi (k)) whatever perfects nature and renders it more apt for attaining its end; as, on the contrary, vice is what makes it more hindered with respect to its end, or draws it away from it. But since the affections of human nature are certain more vehement impulses by which we are driven toward our end, the whole nature of virtue and its function are placed chiefly in this, that

(i) On Ends, 2.

(k) Dissert. on Virtue, which we give here with a few changes. [p. 13] that it temper them, modify them, and direct them to the highest good of our nature.

36 Now the ends of our nature regard either the present life only, or the future one as well. The virtues that perfect men for the happiness of the future life and direct them toward it are called Theological virtues, about which it is for Theologians to discourse; those, on the other hand, that train the same man for holily cultivating and preserving society, and produce the tranquillity and security of society, are called Civil virtues; and finally whatever virtues perfect man for the tranquillity of a private or solitary life are named Monastic and Ethical virtues.

37 But here a grave and ancient question arises for us: can virtue be acquired? For there are those who think that virtue comes wholly from nature, and not also from art, discipline and exercise. For our nature, they say, is necessarily driven by the temperaments, so that we can neither root them out nor change them. There are some who, endowed with a sanguine temperament, are carried away as if against their will into jests, buffoonery, love affairs and the other pleasures of the body; whoever would curb them must change their whole nature. Others are endowed with a melancholic temperament, so that on that account they are perpetually restless, least of all satisfied with themselves, turbid, grim, savage. He who would make them tame must overturn the fibers, the vessels, the fluids, the whole structure of the human body, and the constitution of nature. Some are by nature timid and pusillanimous, others irascible; some soft and inert; others avaricious; others by nature ambitious; some sly and fraudulent. When we wish to compose these to virtue, we must begin from the first Elements of nature. Add that the constitutions of human nature, so diverse according to climate, if they are not wholly born of it, yet depend on it very greatly. Thus these men think they conclude that virtue, unless it be from nature, can in no way be acquired, or else is a dissimulation of nature.

38 They are mistaken, however, and they feign to be untamable those things in human nature of which none is not patient of the rein. For in the first place, the temperaments have more force for receiving than for acting morally. They move nature by reason, sense and imagination, more easily indeed and more promptly, or more slowly and with more difficulty, than if they were absent; they do not always elude the command of reason. And just as softness or hardness in wax is an ease or a difficulty in receiving letters, not the force that carves them, in the same way the temperaments bring it about that we are stirred more promptly and easily, or with more difficulty and more slowly, by certain images of things, but not that we are perpetually impelled against our will. Next, let them have the force of acting physically: they certainly cannot have the force of acting by moral necessity; for they do not necessarily drag freedom to moral malice, even though they often entice it not lightly.

39 Wherefore, if we strive to amend reason, to purge the imagination, if we measure exactly the goodness or malice of things, if we discern the true relations of things to our nature and our ends,

[p. 14] we shall indeed be able to be stirred by them somewhat more vehemently toward vices, or to be held back somewhat from conceiving virtue, but in no way to be driven to the former, or drawn back from the latter, against our will. Nor can there be any greater argument that those things can become instruments of virtue than what experience teaches: that very many have so subjected them to themselves and to reason that, while they felt themselves either more vehemently agitated or hindered by a great force, they meanwhile either curbed them or drove them on with goads. I say that there is no one, however depraved, who, if he would be candid, would confess that he is carried to vices against his will; no one so very wicked that he cannot be bent to what is honorable and to virtue. Hence Horace said very elegantly and admirably (l) that

The envious man, the wrathful, the sluggard, the drunkard, the lover,

No one is so savage that he cannot grow gentle,

If only he lend a patient ear to cultivation.

40 I would not indeed deny that climates have some influence on temperaments and manners; but that they act necessarily, that I affirm to be false. M. de Montesquieu (m) strives to prove that the diversity of climate has more power over us than moral diversity, nay that the latter has almost no power over us, and that the opinion of metempsychosis is proportioned to the climate of the Indians in the same way as the Religion they profess is proportioned to the Spaniards. Elsewhere (n) he affirms that it appears of itself, if we wish to speak in human fashion, that limits have been prescribed by the diversity of climate both to the Christian Religion and to the Mahometan. In this Work climate performs the same office as motion in this universe of things, and it is the cause of the things that are done by us. Since such is the foundation of this Work, what must the things be that are deduced from it?

41 But that no necessity can be brought upon the will by the diversity of climates, as I said above, has been found by experience. For how diverse are the climates in which either one and the same Religion is kept, or now one Religion, now another; or in which the true one has suddenly come into esteem, the ancient and ancestral one being cast aside, or the contrary? Do not men in one and the same climate, in London for example, most constantly profess Religions altogether different from one another? And what of the fact that we do not find the same manners in the same nation at different times? Unless someone wishes to say that the manners and pursuits of the Greeks and Romans who once were are the same now; that the same peoples who once ran wild in barbarism or savagery are now humane and virtuous; or, on the contrary, that those are savage who were humane, or soft who were brave, or unjust who once held most tenaciously to right, or impious who were pious. And let what has been said suffice.

But

(l) Epistles 1, Ep. 1. See also Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4, ch. 37.

(m) L’Esprit des Loix, bk. 24, ch. 24.

(n) Ch. 25.

[p. 15]

42 But since the virtues are not born with us, as is evident, it will rightly be asked at this point: what are the efficient causes of the moral virtues? And there seem to be five in all: God, talent or temperament, education, exercise, precepts. And in the first place, the first source of true and perfect virtue can only be the first cause of all things: for from Him our essence and nature are, by the same they are both preserved and perfected, and they are led to their ends most powerfully and most wisely. Moreover, no one but God can know most accurately the ends of rational natures, the means to the ends, the proportion of the means to the end, and the powers necessary for this. God alone, therefore, can be the first giver of true and perfect virtue.

43 Talent, or nature and temperament, contributes chiefly two things to moral virtue. First, the faculty or aptitude for receiving virtue, for otherwise we should never attain virtue. Second, the impulse and inclination toward virtue, which is a certain perfection of that natural aptitude. The third and fourth causes of virtue are education and exercise; for by education and exercise our nature is at length bent toward virtuous habits, as tender plants are brought to bear fruit by continued cultivation. He who said that the civil man is nothing other than a heap of habits contracted by education and exercise pronounced a word worthy of a philosopher. The man of Nature, namely, differs as much from the Civil man as an animal, so to speak, from a man.

44 But the precepts of doctrine, which are the fifth cause of virtue, contribute very greatly to education and exercise. For if those precepts are attentively received and very often gone over again, so that they are turned into sap and blood, they acquire such force for refashioning nature that they seem to be a second nature. But of these let us now discourse more accurately. The precepts to be observed by one who wishes to rouse and exercise himself to virtue are of two kinds, some general, others special. Of these we treated in the preceding chapter. The general ones we shall set forth here.

45 The first precept is that we implore with assiduous prayers the divine help by which we may receive strength for cultivating virtue. For God is also the first efficient cause of virtue, and in the divine Scriptures the fear of God is called the beginning of Wisdom. The second precept is that the signal beauty of virtue and its most abundant fruits be kept continually before our eyes. Socrates used to say that if honorableness and virtue showed their face without a veil, they would kindle incredible flames of love in us. Among the fruits of virtue, moreover, the chief are: I. Tranquillity of mind, which proceeds from virtue alone. II. True praise and glory, which can be expected not from vices but from virtue alone, even in this depravity of morals in which nearly all of us live. III. True utility, since vices can feign utility, but cannot furnish the true kind. IV. True nobility; for nobility

X [p. 16] was first born of virtue, and is placed essentially in virtue, so that those who glory in ancestral nobility, while themselves wholly void of virtue, are to be called sons of nobles rather than nobles. V. Finally, virtue brings with it this great benefit, that it wrings love even from barbarians; hence that admirable saying of Tully: virtue is loved even in an enemy.

46 The third precept is that you set before yourself, to be pursued in virtue, not only middling things or things easier to do, but that you always aspire to its highest summit, and to the virtue that is called heroic; for unless you do this, you will scarcely cling to its lowest part. The fourth precept is that we perpetually paint all the vices to the mind in vivid colors, and accustom ourselves to shudder at them. For it can scarcely be told how much force the horror of vices contributes to establishing virtue. The fifth precept is that we weigh to which vice we are more prone, whether because of temperament, or of education, or of the manners of the age, so that we may draw ourselves farther away from it. And to this above all the man who loves virtue must give his effort. Elegantly Horace (o):

……………………… Finally, shake out

Yourself, whether nature, or else bad habit, has at some time

Sown in you any vices; for in neglected fields

Springs up the fern that must be burned.

47 The sixth precept is derived from the preceding one. Namely, since there are certain vices proper to the ages of life, as intemperance and rashness in adolescents and youths, ambition in men of mature age, avarice and querulousness in the old, these must above all be restrained and avoided, lest, once they invade us, they throw our whole moral life into confusion. The seventh precept is that you flee idleness worse than a dog and a snake: for it is, as it were, the sink of all the vices, and so the especial enemy of virtue. Wherefore the man who loves virtue must apply himself to labor. And since labors are twofold, of the mind and of the body, the labors of the body are indeed to be undertaken according to each one’s condition; but the mind is never, or rarely, to be removed from serious occupations. Men devoted to the study of letters will themselves do something worth the effort if they learn some honorable art, worthy of the freeborn, and exercise themselves in it in their spare hours. We know from their Lives that excellent philosophers of the last age practiced with pleasure either sculpture, or painting, or the art of optical glasses, or of clocks. Among the labors of the mind, moreover, are the studies of letters; those who seriously give themselves to these have no time to spend on vices. It is reported that Newton, when asked whether he had ever given his attention to love affairs, answered that no time had been left him from his philosophical meditations in which to think about that matter.

The

(o) Satires, bk. 1, Sat. 3, from v. 34.

[p. 17]

48 The eighth precept is that we not only read most attentively the histories of men illustrious in virtue, but also choose honorable, virtuous and sincere friends, and converse with them most familiarly. For indeed, both from reading the lives of illustrious men and from the conversation of virtuous men something continually passes over into the mind, by which we are gradually shaped to virtue. Besides, with virtuous friends we cannot fail to be virtuous, and to be perpetually bent toward virtue: for all men, however shameless, fear the reproof and the judgments of grave and honorable men. Excellently Seneca (p): The greater part of sins is taken away, if a witness stands by those about to sin.

49 The ninth precept is that, if a witness grave in holiness of morals, and one who inspires shame and reverence, is not always present, at least some perfect image of him should perpetually hover before the mind: for it draws the mind very greatly away from vice and impels it toward virtue. But in moral matters this is above all of the greatest moment: to reflect carefully within oneself that we are, and act, in the presence of God, and that the eye of God is an avenger; for all things are full of God. The tenth precept is that we flee all occasions of vices, and most vehemently resist their beginnings: because, namely, it is always easier for a man still whole to resist a vice that is only creeping in than for a man already seized and weakened by vice: for his strength gradually decreases, and the vice grows in the same proportion. And while this is to be applied in all vices, it is so especially in those to which we are by nature more inclined. Alexander of Macedon (as Plutarch relates), having once visited the daughters of Darius, King of the Persians, in the flower of their age and most beautiful in form, refused to visit them a second time, because he feared for himself on their account: They are, he said, torments of the eyes.

50 The eleventh precept is that what Hippocrates wisely pronounced concerning the health of the body, consider nothing small, nothing to be despised, we should refer with better right to the mind; for very often a small spark neglected has stirred up a great conflagration. The twelfth precept is that we institute daily and carefully an examination of our deeds, words, or thoughts. Seneca testifies that he was accustomed to rule his whole life by this precept, and never to take sleep until, as a severe censor of himself, he had weighed all his words, deeds and thoughts, forgiving others much, himself nothing. There is in the golden poem which is attributed to Pythagoras a remarkable passage on this matter, which it is worth the effort to hold in undying memory. In Latin it runs thus:

When first you wake from sleep, as you leave your bed,

Arrange in your mind what must be dispatched in the coming day.

When black night, coming on, takes from things their color,

Do not admit sleep through your sweet eyes

X2                                        Before

(p) Letter 11, to Lucilius.

[p. 18]

Before you have thrice gone over each act of the day now past.

Have I done wrong? What have I done in due time? What not?

Why was honor lacking to this deed, or reason to that?

51 The last precept, finally, is that we think of ourselves most modestly, and consider not so much how far we have advanced as how far we still have to advance. For nothing so obstructs progress in virtue as arrogance and a great opinion of ourselves: since no one will strive to arrive where he thinks he has already arrived. Therefore what Plato said of the intellectual virtues, many would have arrived at knowledge, had they not thought they had already arrived, you can say with greater right of moral virtue. For this reason we must beware lest we be captivated by praises and, growing proud, turn aside from the right path of virtue. Many other precepts could be handed down; but if those which we have set out above are turned into nature by practice itself, they suffice for governing early Adolescence (for whose benefit we undertake this labor). But this must now be explained: by what arguments can we know whether we have advanced in virtue or not? Here are the principal ones.

52 The first argument is the love of virtue itself. He, namely, may know that he has advanced in virtue who loves virtue intensely. And he will recognize that he loves virtue if he impatiently seeks an occasion of exercising it; if he is held by a great desire for it; if he is delighted by the conversation of virtuous men; if he shudders at the presence of vicious ones: in a word, it is discerned that we love virtue by the same signs by which it is known that we love any other thing whatever. The second sign is if one perseveres constantly in virtue in the face of the mockery of others, and is not greatly disturbed in mind. And to obtain this it is necessary not only to grow hardened in virtue, but also to weigh carefully that the greater part of men is corrupted by vices; and that therefore the virtuous man must needs displease many, be often exposed to envy, be torn by calumnies. Let him reflect within himself beforehand that these things will come, so that he is the less disturbed when they happen.

53 Indeed, from this a third argument of progress in virtue can be drawn: for to displease the wicked is a great argument of goodness. Thus that Philosopher of whom Laertius speaks, when it had been reported to him that he was being publicly praised, said: wretch that I am, what great evil have I committed? The fourth sign is if we listen with a glad mind to rebukes and reprehensions. The reason for this is that virtue makes the mind not insolent, fierce, savage, contemptuous of others, but gentle and most easy to deal with. Therefore where meekness is lacking, as may be seen in worthless fellows, it is a manifest argument that one has made either no progress, or very little, in virtue. Elegantly Plutarch: full ears of grain bend down, empty ones stand upright.

54 Now the fifth sign that we have advanced in virtue is if, in the face of the difficulties [p. 19] which virtue offers in prospect, we do not yield timidly, but go against them boldly. To kindle this ardor, the fruits of virtue must be perpetually considered. The sixth sign is if adversities are borne with an even mind. For indeed, he who is so disturbed by even the smallest evils that he is miserable has not advanced even a finger’s breadth. And this is what the Stoics taught, that distress does not befall the Wise man. Excellently Cicero (q): “He who is brave,” he says, “must likewise be great of soul; he who is great of soul, unconquered; he who is unconquered must look down upon human affairs and judge them to be placed beneath him: but no one can look down upon those things on account of which he can be affected by distress. From which it follows that the brave man is never affected by distress. But all wise men are brave; distress therefore does not befall the wise man.”

55 The seventh sign is if the virtuous man despises enticements to vice: for if he is easily moved from his purpose, he has made either no progress or little. For vicious men are above all wont to adorn their vices with the most beautiful appearances, so that they may seem less vicious, and to take away from others the horror of vice: to make it respectable by custom, to excuse it by the weakness of human nature; to traduce and deride the virtues as the figments either of weak minds or of enthusiasts; to call those wise who have learned to deceive others cunningly for the sake of private advantage, and those fools who do not know how. If you by no means allow yourself to be taken in by them, know that you have advanced in virtue.

56 I set down as the eighth sign of progress in virtue if those devoted to letters take up most eagerly, out of all studies, those that are useful to themselves and to society, and bid farewell to the rest, or greet them in passing. For who is so mad as to affirm that the interminable questions which are disputed in the Schools with such contention of minds, and which smell of the old oil of the Arabs, will be useful to himself or to Society? The last sign by which one can know that he has taken a great step in virtue I hold to be this: if, namely, he feels himself so peaceful in mind, and is so secure in Divine Providence, content with virtue, that he does not anxiously and over-solicitously ask what will be tomorrow, nor is much disturbed by care for the time to come. You therefore, if you are wise, forbear to ask what will be tomorrow. Do you cultivate virtue? For the rest, be tranquil.

57 And let these things suffice for the present: they are few, but for the scope of Elements they will already seem too many to most. It seemed good to us to devote this effort to a most beautiful discipline, neglected hitherto by I know not what fate in the Schools of our America, not without the greatest loss to Youth and detriment to Philosophy. These things are more useful than to fight sharply over the Being of Reason, over the Connection of God with the possibility or impossibility of possibles, and over six hundred other things.

Short

(q) Tusculan Disputations 3, ch. 27.
