## P R E FAC E 

ince it is acknowledged among the true cultivators of the best

S       arts that without a knowledge of Geometry scarcely, or not even

scarcely, can anything good ever be brought into Physics; and that access indeed does not lie open to the other disciplines which will bear upon an investigation of Nature worthy of a Philosopher, except to those more than moderately learned in Geometry:

Y                                       I

[p. 2]

I had long since resolved, and had promised you, excellent Young Men, that I would not speak on physical matters before I had handed down to you Geometrical Institutions, very brief indeed, such as the narrowness of the time required. By good fortune I had brought away with me from Italy a little Book, small indeed in bulk, but one which I should believe would be sufficient for our purpose, and of benefit to you above all for cultivating and advancing physical matters rightly and in order. For whoever will wish to treat seriously of corporeal nature, let him, in short, learn Geometry thoroughly above all things, as diligently as he can: otherwise he will be pursuing not Physics, nor Philosophy, but the smoke and shadow of Philosophy. But those who think themselves Physicists, worthy of so great a name, because all day long they exhaust their brains on long hundreds of syllogisms in a row, as though they wished to entangle the Nature of things, and the Supreme Maker of Nature, in their own fabrications and foolish questions, to their utmost disgrace and sloth: let them see whether it would not have been better for them to have kept away from things abstruse and clouded over with much darkness. For it is shameful, and wholly unworthy of a Philosopher, to wish to discourse about what you do not know; more shameful to prefer to obey custom rather than to embrace the truth that lies in the open sun; and most shameful of all to envy bitterly others, whose minds are not so perverse, and who preside over the apprenticeship of Young Men and over their right instruction. But be that as it may, here is the Author’s Preface, to be placed at once before your eyes. For thus he writes.

## Elements

[p. 3]

## ELEMENTS

O F G E O M E T RY

O F G R E AT E R U S E . G    eometry has a slight Name, but a most ample Office. Its Elements, namely the

principles of demonstrations, were collected by Euclid of Alexandria, about the Year 280 before Christ, a Man greater than all praise, so that by them access might be opened to the whole of Mathematics and to the other natural disciplines. Most young men, however, deterred by their difficulty, having scarcely greeted Mathematical studies from the threshold, and lacking either in wit or in constancy, turn their backs and cut themselves off from all hope of obtaining the fruits of a more solid science; not only because they are left destitute of the first and simplest demonstrations of natural things, but because nothing so sharpens the edge of the mind, and prepares it for perceiving the other disciplines more easily and more rightly (for which use chiefly Plato said Geometry was to be learned), as Geometrical exercise, which opens the surest way of investigating truth.

For this reason we set forth the Geometrical Elements, especially those which will be of very great use to Natural Philosophy (which others have furnished excellently in other ways), in a briefer, and perhaps also a clearer, method. And in the first book we set forth the figures which are contained by straight lines; in the second, curvilinear figures; in the third, the proportions of figures; with great hope indeed of being of help (which is the aim of our Institution), since experience has taught that these principles have helped young men much.

Y2                                         Book

[p. 4]

## BOOK I

On Rectilinear Figures.

In the Elements of Geometry, some things are Principles, which consist solely in the explanation of names; others, deduced from them and pertaining to practice, are called Problems; others, ordered to the knowledge of Truth, are named Theorems. First, then, this Book will give the Principles; second, Problems concerning Rectilinear figures; third, the more select Theorems.

## CHAPTER I

Principles.

Principles are either definitions, or Common notions, which either concern the consideration of truth, and are called Axioms, or concern the carrying out of a Work, and are usually named Postulates. We propose each of them here, with explanations added to some, where there is need: so that by these, too, they may be rendered clearer to learners, and the Theorems may afterwards be demonstrated more briefly.

§. I.

Definitions.

In these we depart somewhat from the common Method, so as to begin from the things better known.

I. A Body is that which has a threefold dimension, namely Length, Breadth and Depth.

II. The Extremity of a Body is the surface, in which Length and Breadth alone are considered.

III. The Extremity of a Surface is the line, in which Length alone is considered.

IV. The Extremity of a Line is the Point, in which neither Length, nor Breadth, nor Depth is considered.

And hence a Point is usually defined as that in which there is no Part.

V. A Line is conceived to come about from the flowing of a point; a Surface from the motion of a line in breadth; from the motion of a surface according to depth a Body is generated.

[p. 5]

VI. A straight Line is the Shortest from one point to another.

Hence straight Lines which are bounded by the same points are equal, and wholly coincide with each other. And curved lines, or lines bent in any manner whatever, have a greater length than a Straight one, if they are bounded by the same Points.

VII. A plane surface is one to which a Straight line can be fitted in every direction; and it is the shortest from one line to another.

VIII. An Angle in a surface is the mutual Inclination of Two lines beyond one common point.

IX. An Angle is called Rectilinear which is composed of straight lines; Curvilinear, which of curved ones; Mixed, which of one curved and the other straight.

X. An Angle is Right when a Straight line, which is called Perpendicular, is inclined equally on either side upon another Straight line.

XI. An obtuse Angle is greater than a Right one.

XII. An Acute Angle is less than a Right one.

But since learners find very great difficulty in the knowledge of Angles,

Note 1, that when only two lines meet at one point, the Angle can be designated by one letter. But since it often happens that several lines are united at the same point, to avoid equivocation the Angle is usually designated by three letters, of which the Middle one indicates the Angle; the first and third letters, taken in whatever order, designate the lines containing the Angle. As in Figure I of the Theorems, Plate II, the Angle DAB is Right, because the Perpendicular line BA is inclined equally on either side, by a Quadrant of a Circle, upon the line DE: and so the Measure of the right Angle DAB is the Quadrant DB of a Circle, whether larger or smaller. The Angle DAG is Obtuse, whose Measure is the Arc DG, greater than a Quadrant. The Angle DAF is Acute, whose Measure is the Arc DF, less than a Quadrant.

Note 2, that since every Circle is divided by Mathematicians into 360 parts, which they call degrees, a right Angle is usually called an Angle of 90 degrees (which is the fourth part of a Circle); an obtuse Angle, greater than 90 degrees; an acute Angle, less than 90 degrees. Hence right Angles are all equal to one another; and so, when several Angles are equal to one or to several right angles alike, they will also be equal to one another.

Note 3, that lines make a greater or a lesser Angle, not when they are longer or shorter, but when, with the same length of each, they recede more or less from each other. Hence if two lines AD, AL (in the same Figure) are each equal to the two AE, AN, and their extreme Points D and L are as far apart from each other as E and N, the Angles DAL and EAN will be equal. And conversely, if the Angles are equal, the extreme points will be equally distant. On the other hand, when D and M stand farther apart from each other

[p. 6] than E and N, the Right Angle DAM will be greater than the Acute Angle EAN.

XIII. Parallel lines are those which stand apart from each other by an equal space everywhere, and, however far they are produced, never meet so as to make an Angle.

As in Figure II of the Theorems, Plate II, are the Lines CD, AB, between which the same Perpendicular CA, DB falls. And if any other line cuts them, as the line GP, the Parallel lines are inclined equally toward it on either side: for if they were inclined more toward the middle secant on one side or the other, e.g. toward I, M, they would approach each other more on that side, and so would not be Parallel. Hence the Two Angles L and N together are equal to the Two Angles I and M together: because the Inclinations are equal on either side.

XIV. A Figure is a Quantity which is contained under one or several bounds.

That is, one which is enclosed either by one curved Line, as the Circle; or by one curved and the other straight, as the Semicircle; or by several straight ones, as the Triangle.

XV. A Circle is a plane Figure, comprehended by the circuit of one Line, which is called the Circumference, or Periphery: to which all straight lines drawn from one middle Point are equal.

XVI. And this middle Point of the Circle is called the Center.

XVII. A Diameter is a Line drawn from one point of the circumference to another, passing through the center, and cutting the Circle into two equal parts.

XVIII. Rectilinear Figures are those which are contained by straight lines: Trilateral, which by three; Quadrilateral, which by four; Multilateral, which by more.

XIX. A Triangle, considered according to its Sides, is Equilateral, which has three equal sides; as in Fig. V, Plate II, AHI.

XX. Isosceles, or Equal-legged, which has only two equal sides; as in the same Figure, ABC.

XXI. Scalene, which has three unequal sides; as in the same Figure, BAL.

XXII. A Triangle, considered according to its Angles, is Right-angled, or Orthogonal, which has one Right Angle; as in Fig. III, Plate III, ACB.

XXIII. Obtuse-angled, or Amblygonal, which has one Obtuse Angle; as in the same Fig., AEB.

XXIV. Acute-angled, or Oxygonal, all of whose Angles are Acute; as in the same Fig., ADB.

XXV. A Square is that whose sides are all equal, and its Angles right; Fig. VI, Plate I.

XXVI. A Rhombus, whose sides are all equal, but its Angles not right; Fig. VII, Plate I.

XXVII. A Rectangle longer on one side, whose Angles are right, [p. 7] but only the two opposite sides equal: Fig. VIII, Plate I.

## XXVIII. A Rhomboid, of which only the two opposite sides are equal, and the

Angles not right; Fig. IX, Plate I.

XXIX. And these four Quadrilateral Figures are called by a common name

Parallelograms, because they have the two opposite sides parallel.

## XXX. But the other, irregular, quadrilateral Figures, which have neither the two

opposite sides nor the opposite Angles equal, are called Trapezia; as in Fig. XII, Plate I,

## LHMI

§. II.

Postulates.

I.

From any Point to any point a Straight Line can be drawn.

II. A straight Line can be continued in a straight line as far as you wish.

III. From any center at any interval a Circle can be described.

IV. Any line can be divided into Equal or Unequal parts.

V. To any Straight line another can be placed, Equal or Unequal, Perpendicular or

Parallel.

## §. III

Axioms.

I.

Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other.

And things which have a common measure are equal.

And what is greater or less than one of equals is also greater or less than the other of the equals.

II. If to equals you add equals, or something common, or take them away from them, the things that remain are equal.

III. If to equals you add unequals, or take them away from them, the things that remain are unequal.

IV. Things which are double, triple, or half of the same thing, or of equals, are equal to each other.

And whenever two things are equally exceeded by the same thing, or equally exceed it, they are equal.

V. Things which mutually coincide with each other are equal.

VI. The Whole is greater than its Part.

And it is equal to all its parts taken together. And the Part which is equal to all the other parts taken together is the Half of the whole.

## VII

[p. 8]

VII. Two straight Lines do not enclose a space.

That is, to enclose a space on all sides, at least three straight Lines are required.

VIII. Two straight Lines do not have a common segment, or Part.

That is, two straight lines which make an angle cannot be continued into one straight line unless they are bent.

## CHAPTER II

Problems.

Problems are Propositions which teach how to do some Work concerning Lines,

Angles, or Figures. The principal ones, pertaining to rectilinear Figures, are proposed here, and their demonstrations are only indicated, except for the first: both because these are easily deduced from the Principles laid down, or from the Theorems to be demonstrated; and because Problems are not Principles for showing the other truths, but can be supposed as Hypotheses. This Method seems better suited to Learners, so that they may not be thrown into confusion at the beginning, but, once the Theorems have been demonstrated, may exercise themselves in finding the demonstrations of the Problems.

Problem I. (Plate I. Fig. 1.)

To make an Equilateral Triangle.

Let the Compass be opened to the interval of the given line AB; then from each end of the line, with the Compass unchanged, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at C; finally from the Point C let the lines CA and CB be drawn, which will constitute the Equilateral Triangle ABC.

For the demonstration, let the circles ACF and BCE be completed.

Demonstration. The line AC is equal to the line AB, because they are drawn from the center to the circumference of the same Circle: from definition XV. But the line BC is also equal to the same line AB, by the same definition: therefore the lines CA and CB are equal to each other: from Axiom 1; and so the Triangle ABC, consisting of three equal lines, is Equilateral.

To make an Isosceles Triangle, let the compass be opened once to a greater or a lesser interval than the given line; and then let arcs be made, as above. But if, while the arcs are being made, the interval of the compass is changed each time, a Scalene Triangle will be made.

Problem

[p. 9]

## Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

To bisect a line.

From the ends A and B of the given line let two arcs be made with the same opening of the compass, cutting each other at C; and two others below the same line, cutting each other at D. The line CD will bisect the line AB. It is demonstrated from Theor. IV of this book, pt. 1, if from C and D lines are drawn to the ends A and B.

## Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

To bisect an angle.

From the vertex of the angle A, at any interval you please, let equal sides be cut off on either side at B and C; then from the points of section B and C, with the same opening of the compass, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. The line DA will bisect the angle. Dem. from the same Theor. IV, with lines drawn from B and C to D.

Problem IV. (Fig. 4.)

To draw a parallel line.

Let a line parallel to FG be drawn, passing through the point D. First, let one foot of the compass be placed at D, the other at any point of the line FG, as at A. Second, from A, with the opening of the compass unchanged, let the same line be cut at B. Third, from the points B and D, with the same spread of the compass, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at C. The line DC will be parallel to the line FG. From Theor. VI, Cor. 2.

Otherwise. From any point, such as the middle point E, let an arc DF be made, and another, GH, on the other side; then let the arc GH be cut equal to the arc DF. The line DH will be the parallel sought.

Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

To draw a perpendicular line.

If from a given point F outside a line a Perpendicular is to be drawn to the line BG:

placing one foot of the compass at F, let the line be cut on either side, extended further (if need be), at B and G; then from B and G let two Arcs be made, with the same opening of the compass, cutting

Z [p. 10] each other at H. The line FH will be the Perpendicular sought. From Theor. IV, pt. 2.

It must be noted, however, that a Perpendicular cannot be drawn from any point whatever to any point whatever of a line; but it is sometimes necessary to produce the given line further, so that a Perpendicular can be drawn to it from the given point.

If a Perpendicular is to be drawn at a given point C within the line BG, whether that point is the end of the line or not: from the point C let an arc of nearly a semicircle be made, at any interval you please, and, with the compass unchanged, let there be cut off first the arc GE, then the arc ED; then also, with the compass unchanged, from the points D and E let two arcs be made, cutting each other at F. The line FC, when drawn, will be the Perpendicular sought. From the same Theor.

Problem VI. (Fig. 6.)

To make a Square.

Let a perpendicular CA, equal to the line AB, be drawn at its end: then, with the same interval of the given line, from C and B let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Square will be had. From Theor. VI, Cor. 2.

Problem VII. (Fig. 7.)

To make a Rhombus.

At the end of the given line AB let another, CA, equal to it be drawn, at any

Angle that is not right: then from the extremities C and B, with the same interval of the given line, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Rhombus will be had. From the same Theor.

Problem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

To make an oblong Rectangle.

At the end of AB let a perpendicular greater or less than it be drawn: then from the end C let an arc be made with the interval of the line AB, and from the end B let an arc be made with the interval of the line CA, intersecting the former arc at D: finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and a Rectangle longer on one side will be had. From the same Theor.

Problem

[p. 11]

## Problem IX. (Fig. 9.)

To make a Rhomboid.

At the end of the line AB let an unequal line CA be drawn, at an angle that is not right: then from the end C, with the interval of the line AB, let an arc be made; and from the end B, with the interval of the line CA, let another be made, intersecting the former at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Rhomboid will be had. From the same Theor.

## Problem X. (Fig. 10.)

To make a Triangle equal to another.

Let a line DE be taken equal to the line AB: then, with the interval of the line

AC, let an arc be made from the end D; similarly, with the interval of the line BC, let an arc be made from the end E, which intersects the former at F. The Triangle DEF will be equal to the triangle ABC. It is evident from the construction itself.

In like manner a Triangle is made from three lines not joined, A, B, C; provided that the two taken together which constitute an angle are greater than the one Straight line: by def. VI.

Problem XI. (Fig. 11.)

To make an Angle equal to another.

From the given Angle A, at any interval, let an arc BC be made: then from the end D of the line DE, where the equal Angle is to be placed, with the same interval of the compass, let an arc be made which cuts the given line at F: then let the arc FG be cut off equal to the arc BC. The line drawn from D through G will constitute at D an angle equal to the angle A. From the def. of an Angle, note 1.

Problem XII. (Fig. 12.)

To make a Rectangle, or another Parallelogram, equal to a given Triangle.

Let a Parallel CD be placed to the Base AK of the given Triangle: then let the

Base be divided in two at E, and upon a line equal to half the Base let a Rectangle, or any Parallelogram FDBG, be made, within the parallel CD: and the Parallelogram BD will be equal to the given triangle ACK. From Theor. VIII.

Z2                                       Hence

[p. 12]

Hence it is evident how a Parallelogram may be made equal to any Trapezium whatever. For let the Trapezium be divided into two Triangles by drawing a line to the opposite Angles HI, to which let Parallels be drawn through the vertices L and M: then, HI having been bisected at N, between the same Parallels, upon a base BG equal to the half HN, let the Parallelogram FBDG be made: which will be equal to the Trapezium LM, inasmuch as it is equal to the two Triangles HLI and HMI, which compose the Trapezium. From the same Theor.

## CHAPTER III

Theorems.

A      Theorem is a Proposition demonstrating some property of quantity. Its prin‐

cipal parts are three: the Proposition itself, which proposes the truth to be shown; the Preparation, which arranges the lines sometimes necessary for the demonstration; the Demonstration, which concludes the proposed truth from the Principles laid down, or from Theorems.

Twelve Theorems selected from the 1st and 2nd books of Euclid are proposed in this chapter, with Corollaries, or inferences, added, which follow easily from the Theorems: some of these are contained in the propositions of Euclid, others lie outside Euclid; the order of that Author has been varied somewhat, so as to keep, if it please Heaven, a clearer method. For, beginning from Angles and Lines, we come to the properties of Triangles, and from these to demonstrating Quadrilateral figures.

But lest the Number of the more notable Propositions of Euclid, as it is commonly used by Mathematicians, should lie hidden, we shall place it at the foot of the page. The Principles, however, from which the Demonstrations descend, we shall not always indicate, because they are so clear that they may be supposed present to the mind.

Theorem I. (Plate II. Fig. 1.) A straight line falling upon another straight line, as GA upon DE, makes the angles on both sides together equal to two Right angles. (a)

Preparation. A Circle having been made from the center A at any interval, let a Perpendicular BC be drawn to the line DE.

(a) Euclid, bk. 1, prop. 13.

[p. 13]

Demonstration. The two Angles DAG and GAE together have the same Measure as the two Right angles DAB and BAE, namely two quadrants of a Circle, according to the def. of an Angle, note 1. Therefore the two Angles DAG and GAE together are equal to two Right angles: from Axiom 1.

Corollary I. If two lines are not placed in a straight line, as DA, AG, they comprehend on one side an arc less than a semicircle, on the other an arc greater, as is evident; whence only a straight line, as DE, upon which another straight line falls, comprehends Angles equal to two right angles. (a)

II. If two lines cut each other, the vertically opposite Angles, as DAF and EAI, are equal. For the arc DBE is a semicircle; likewise the arc FGI is a semicircle, inasmuch as they are cut off by diameters: therefore if the common arc FE is taken away from each, there remains the arc DF equal to the arc EI, and the Angle DAF equal to the Angle EAI. (b)

III. If several straight lines are united upon the same straight line at the same point, they make all the angles equal to two right angles. And if two straight lines, or more, cut each other, they make all the angles about the same point equal to four right angles: for they are all comprehended by two semicircles. (c)

Theorem II. (Fig. 2.) If a straight line cuts two Parallel straight lines, then I. the two Internal Angles L and N together will be equal to two right Angles. II. The Alternate Angles I and N will be equal to each other. III. The Exterior Angle H will also be equal to the Angle N, the Interior opposite toward the same side. (d)

Dem. I. The four Angles I and L, M and N together are equal to four right Angles: from the preceding Theor.; but the two internal Angles L and N together are equal to the two internal ones together on the other side, I and M: according to defin. 13, Parall. Therefore the two internal Angles L and N together on one side are equal to two Right angles, just as the two internal ones on the other side, I and M.

Dem. II. The two Angles L and N together are equal to two Right angles: from what has just been demonstrated; but the two Angles I and L together are also equal to two Right angles: from Theor. I; therefore, the common Angle L being taken away, there remains the Angle I equal to the alternate Angle N.

Dem. III. The two Angles L and N together are equal to two right angles: but the two Angles L and H together are also equal to two Right angles: from Theor. I; therefore, the common Angle L being taken away, there remains the Angle

the

(a) Prop. 14.

(b) Prop. 15.

(c) Cor. of prop. 15.

(d) Prop. 29. [p. 14] the exterior H, equal to the Angle N, interior and opposite toward the same side.

Cor. The Converse of this Theorem is easily demonstrated; namely, that if a Line cutting two other lines makes the two internal angles on the same side equal to two right angles, those two lines will be Parallel: For they will be equally inclined to the middle secant, and to each other. Likewise if it makes the alternate angles, or the internal and the external, equal (a).

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.) In any Triangle I. the three Angles together are equal to two Right angles. II. The exterior Angle G is equal to the two interior opposite ones together, A and B. (b)

Preparation. Let a Line DE be drawn Parallel to the Base BC through the vertex A.

Dem. I. The Angle B is equal to the alternate angle D, from the preceding Theor., and the Angle C is equal to the angle E, likewise alternate: but the Angles D, E and A together are equal to two right angles, from Theor. I; therefore if to the Angles B and C the Angle A is also added, the three angles B, C and A together are equal to two Right angles.

Dem. II. The Angles B and A together with C are equal to two Right angles: but the two Angles C and G, the exterior, together are also equal to two right angles; therefore, the common Angle C being taken away, there remains the exterior Angle G equal to the two interior opposite Angles A and B together.

Cor. I. When two Angles of any Triangle are known, the third at once becomes known, as the remainder up to two right angles.

II. If two Triangles have two Angles equal, they will also have the third, the remainder up to two right angles, equal.

III. From the same point to the same straight line only one Perpendicular can be drawn; because a Triangle cannot have two right Angles.

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.) Two Triangles are wholly equal, I. If they have two sides equal, each to each, and the angle comprehended by them equal. II. If they have three sides likewise equal. III. If they have two equal angles, and the side comprehended by them

equal.

(a) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 28, 27.

(b) Prop. 32. [p. 15] equal. IV. If they have a side opposite one of the two equal angles equal (a).

Dem. I. If the side AB is equal to the side DE, and the side AC equal to the side DF, and the Angle A equal to the angle D: the Side DE, superposed on the side AB, will coincide with it, and the side DF with the side AC, and the points E, F with the points B, C: therefore both the Bases and the remaining Angles at the Base will coincide, and will be equal in each triangle: from definition VI of the straight line.

Dem. II. If the distance BC is equal to the distance EF, and the remaining sides containing the Angles A and D are equal, each to each, the angle A will be equal to the angle D: from the definit. of Angle, no. 3; therefore the whole triangle DEF will be equal to the triangle ABC: from pt. I of this.

Dem. III. If the line EF is equal to the line BC, then, superposed on it, it will coincide with it; and if the angle E is equal to the angle ABC, the side DE will also coincide with the side AB (for if the side DE fell inside, as at H, the angle E would be smaller; if outside, as at G, the angle E would be greater than the angle ABC, contrary to the hypothesis); and if the angle F is equal to the angle ACB, by the same reasoning the side DF will coincide with the side AC; therefore the triangles ABC, EDF will be wholly equal.

Dem. IV. If the line EF is equal to the line BC, and the angle E equal to the angle ABC, and the angle A equal to the angle D: the angle F will also be equal to the angle ACB: from Theor. III; therefore the triangles ABC and DEF will be wholly equal: from the third part of this.

Cor. Hence it is plain that the nearer to the Base the lines produced from the extremities of the same Base are joined, the greater they make the Angle H than the Angle A, and the Angle A than the Angle G: because, since the angles at the Base HBC and HCB are smaller than the angles ABC and ACB, the third, H, above the Base, the remainder up to two right angles, must be greater than the Angle A. From Theor. III. (b)

Theorem V. (Fig. 5.) An Isosceles Triangle, as ABC, has the angles above the Base, B and C, equal to each other. (c)

Prep. Let the Base be understood to be bisected at L, and let AL be drawn.

Dem. In the Triangles ABL and ACL, the line BL is equal to the line LC: from the construction. The side AB is equal to the side AC: from the supposition. The side AL is common: therefore the Triangle ABL is wholly equal

to

(a) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 4, 8, 26.

(b) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 21.

(c) Prop. 5. [p. 16] to the Triangle ACL, and the angles B and C, opposite the common side, are equal. From the preceding Theor.

Cor. I. The Angles D and E below the Base are also equal; for the two angles B and D together are equal to two right angles, and no less the angles C and E: from Theor. I; therefore, when the equal angles B and C are taken away, the angles D and E remain equal.

II. If the angles B and C are equal, the sides AB and AC will also be equal; for when CL is placed upon the equal LB, the angles and the extreme points B and C will coincide; the Point A is common to both sides AB and AC; therefore the lines AC, AB will be equal: from defin. VI of the straight line. (a)

III. If the Triangle AHI is equilateral, each of its three angles will be equal; and conversely, if the three angles are equal, the three sides opposite the equal angles will also be equal.

IV. If the line AL bisects the Base, it will also bisect the angle A: and if it bisects the angle A, it will also bisect the Base of the Isosceles triangle ABC, and perpendicularly: for two Triangles ABL and ACL come out wholly equal, from Theor. IV; and the angles at L, being equal on either side, are right.

Cor. V. In Triangles the greater angle is opposite the greater side, and conversely. For let the Triangle HAI be equilateral and equiangular: if, e.g., the Side HI grows to C, the angle A also grows, and the angle C diminishes (from Theorem III), which is opposite the smaller side AH: and if the angle A grows, the Side HI also grows to C, or B. (b)

VI. The Perpendicular AL is the shortest of all the lines that can be drawn from the same point A to the line BC: for the other lines, being opposite the Right angle L, which is greater, are greater; and the farther they recede from the perpendicular, the greater they are, because they are opposite more obtuse angles.

Hence the Perpendicular Line measures all distances; because of all the straight lines that can be drawn from one point to the same line it is the shortest, and therefore the one and certain Measure.

Theorem VI. (Fig. 6.)

The Diameter divides a Parallelogram into two equal Triangles. (c)

Dem. The Triangles ABC and BDC have the side BC common, and the Angle ABC equal to the alternate angle BCD, and also the angle

(a) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 6.

(b) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 18, 19.

(c) Prop. 34.

Cor. I. Hence it follows that in a Parallelogram the opposite angles are equal: for since the alternate angles about the diameter are equal, from what has just been demonstrated, the other two opposite angles will also be equal, from Theor. III.

II. In a Quadrilateral Figure, if the lines opposite each other on either side are equal, they will also be Parallel; and if two opposite lines are equal and Parallel, the other two will also be equal and Parallel; for when the Diameter is drawn, two equal Triangles will be formed, from Theor. IV. (a)

III. The complements AE, ED about the Diameter have an equal surface. For the Triangles ABC and BCD are equal, from the preceding Theor.; therefore if from them we subtract the Triangle HBE, equal to the Triangle EBI, and also the Triangle FEC, for the same reason equal to the Triangle ECG, the complements that remain, AE and ED, are equal. (b)

Theorem VII. (Fig. 7.)

Parallelograms constituted on the same Base and between the same Parallels are equal. (c)

Dem. Since AG and GF are Parallelograms constituted on the same Base CG, the sides opposite it, AE and FB, will be equal, from the preceding Theor.; adding the common line EF, the sides AF and EB will be equal; and the side CF is equal to the side GB, and the exterior angle AEC equal to the interior opposite angle ABC, from Theor. II; therefore the Triangles AFC and EBG are equal: therefore, taking away the common Triangle ELF, there remains the Trapezium AECL, equal to the trapezium LGFB: therefore, adding the common Triangle LCG, the Parallelogram AG becomes equal to the Parallelogram GF.

Cor. I. Parallelograms AG and ED constituted on equal Bases and between the same Parallels are also equal to each other; for both are equal to the same Parallelogram FG. (d)

II. But since the distance between the Parallels AB, CD is measured by the perpendicular AC, from Theor. V, last cor., the Surfaces of Parallelograms are generated by drawing the base into the perpendicular, according to Def. V; so that if the side AC is, e.g., 9 palms, and GC 4, the surface made by the motion of the line CG along the line AC, and the Parallelogram AG, or GF equal to it, will be 36 palms.

III. Hence if Parallelograms on the same or an equal Base are equal, it is manifest that they also have the same perpendicular altitude, or are between the same Parallels.

## Theorem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

A Triangle constituted on the same Base and between the same Parallels is half of the

Parallelogram. (a)

Dem. The Triangle BCG is half of the Parallelogram FG, from Theor. VI; but the Parallelogram FG is equal to the Parallelogram AG, from the preceding; therefore the Triangle BCG is also half of the Parallelogram AG, constituted on the same Base CG and between the same Parallels.

Cor. I. It is plain that the Triangle BHD also, constituted on an equal base and between the same Parallels, is half of the Parallelogram AG, since it is half of the equal Parallelogram FD.

II. It is also manifest that Triangles which are on the same or equal bases and between the same Parallels are equal to each other, since they are halves of equal Parallelograms (b).

III. But since half of the Parallelogram AG is made by drawing half the base into the Perpendicular AC, the surface of the Triangle, which is equal to half the Parallelogram, from Theorem VI, is likewise known by drawing half the base into the same Perpendicular altitude; whence if the base of the Triangle BCG is 4 palms, and the Perpendicular altitude BD, or AC, 9 palms, the whole Surface of the Triangle BCG will be 18 palms.

IV. Equal triangles, therefore, on the same or an equal base, have an equal perpendicular altitude, or are between the same Parallels (c).

Theorem IX. (Fig. 9.) In a right-angled Triangle the Square of the side AC, subtending the right angle B, is equal to

the two Squares together of the sides AB, BC, which contain the right angle (d).

Prep. Eight equal Triangles having been constructed, which are marked by the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, let there be understood the Square HO upon the line HI, equal to the line AB; the Square DM of the side BC; and the Square AE of the side AC.

(a) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 41.

(b) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 37, 38.

(c) Prop. 39, 40.

(d) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 47, very celebrated.

Likewise the Square AE is composed of the same Square LO and four equal Triangles 5, 3, 7, 8; therefore the Square AE is equal to the two Squares HO and BM together, since they consist of equal parts.

Cor. In a Square, since the Diameter is opposite a right angle, the Square of the Diameter will be equal to the two squares of the equal sides, and consequently double one Square.

Theorem X. (Fig. 10.) If the straight line AB is cut anyhow at F, the whole Square of the line AB will be equal to the two Squares of the parts together, and the two Rectangles which are made from the same parts

(a).

Prep. Let the Perpendicular FI be drawn Parallel to the line AC; let AH be cut equal to AF, and let the Perpendicular HE be drawn Parallel to the line AB: from which all the lines in the square AD will be at right angles, and the opposite ones will be equal, from Theor. VI, cor. 1 & 2.

Dem. The Square AG upon the part AF, the Square GD upon GE, equal to the line FB, and the two Rectangles CG and GB from the parts of the line AB, are all the parts of the whole Square AD: therefore they are equal to it.

Cor. I. If the straight line AB is cut anyhow at F, with the same construction, the Rectangle AI, one side of which is equal to the whole line AB, the other to the part AF, and the Rectangle FD, one side of which is equal to the whole AB, the other to the other part FB, are together equal to the whole Square AD, of which they are the parts (b).

II. If the same line is cut anyhow at F, the Square AG from its part AF, and the Rectangle FE from the two parts FB and AF, or the equal FG, are likewise equal to the whole Rectangle EA from the whole line AB and its segment AF, since those two are all the parts of the Rectangle AE (c).

contains, besides the Squares of the two sides CB, BA, two rectangles which

Theorem XII. (Fig. 12.) In any Triangle whatever, the Squares of the sides AB, BC exceed the Square of the side AC, opposite the Acute angle ABC, by two Rectangles of the whole side CB and its segment DB,

IX. But, by the same, the Square of the side CA is equal only to the Squares GC, DO: therefore the Squares of the sides CB, BA exceed the Square of the side CA by the double Rectangle HG and the double Square GI, which together are equal to the two Rectangles EI from the whole side CB and its segment BD, from Theor. Cor. Hence it becomes manifest that in Triangles, if the Squares of the sides are greater than the Square of the Base, the angle opposite it will be Acute; if they are less, Obtuse; if they are equal, Right.

The four Theorems just demonstrated are very well explained by numbers, which you have in Clavius and others. Of these, however, the last two, although very useful for practical Geometry, are nevertheless not necessary for the following Propositions, after which they can be gone over again, if they seem rather difficult to anyone. In the Demonstrations that follow, moreover, when the Book is not indicated, the one under discussion is understood.

## BOOK II

On Curvilinear Figures.

Among the figures that are contained by a curved line, the first place in

Geometry is held by the Circle, which alone is completed by one sure sweep of the Compass. Aristotle, in ch. 2 of the Mechanical Questions, considers three especially wonderful properties of it. The first is that the circle is made from a line that is moving and at rest: for while the whole line is carried round to make the circle, its end rests in the point of the center.

The second is that the single points of the line, although continuous, are moved with unequal velocity while the line is carried round: for the point that is farther removed from the center runs through a greater space.

The third is that the Periphery that surrounds the circle consists in a certain manner of contraries, and of extremes without a middle: namely of the concave and the convex; between which the Straight is a middle, just as the Equal is between the great and the small. For just as a line, in order to become small from great, must first become equal, so, in order to become convex from concave, it must first become straight. And this is the more wonderful in that these contraries are found in a line having no breadth, such as the Periphery of the Circle.

Of the Circle, then, Euclid treats in the third and fourth books of the Elements; and here we, having laid down the principles, shall deliver both the Problems that pertain to Circles and to Figures to be inscribed in the circle, and the more useful Theorems for investigating their properties.

Chapter

[p. 22]

## CHAPTER I

Principles.

No other Axioms and Postulates are employed in this Book than those which we delivered in the first book. There remain only some Definitions to be explained, of which:

I. Circles are equal whose Diameters are equal.

II. A straight line is said to touch a circle which, when produced further, does not cut the circle.

III. The angle that is made by a tangent line and the circumference is called the Angle of contingence.

IV. In a Circle, lines are equally distant from the center when the Perpendiculars drawn from the center to them are equal.

V. Segments of a Circle are the parts of the Circle that are cut off by some straight line.

VI. An angle is said to be in the Segment of the circle by which the lines constituting the angle at the circumference are surrounded.

As in Figure I, Theorems, Pl. III: a Semicircle surrounds the Angle BAC; the greater part of the Circle the Angle BAG; the lesser part of the Circle the Angle BAE.

VII. An angle is said to stand upon the Segment that is opposite the angle and closes it.

As in the same Figure, a semicircle closes the Angle BAC; the greater part of the Circle the Angle BAE; the lesser part of the Circle the Angle BAG.

VIII. The angle of a Segment is that which is mixed of a straight line and a part of the Circumference within the circle. But if the straight line is a Diameter, it is called the angle of the semicircle.

As in the same Figure, the angle composed of the diameter CB and the circumference BA.

IX. A Sector of a Circle is the Portion of the Circle comprehended by two semidiameters.

X. A Figure is said to be inscribed in a circle when the vertices of all its Angles are in the circumference. As, in the same place, the Triangle BAC.

Chapter

[p. 23]

## CHAPTER II

Problems.

Problem I. (Pl. III. Fig. 1.)

To find the Center of a given arc, and to complete the Circle.

Let ABC be the given portion of a circle, whose Center must be found and the

Circle completed. From two points taken at pleasure, A and B, with an equal radius, let two arcs be made outside and inside the circle, cutting each other at O and E. Likewise from the points B and C, taken at pleasure, let two arcs be made cutting each other at F and G. Then through the points of the sections let the lines OE and FG be drawn, which will bisect the arcs and will meet each other at H, where the Center of the circle to be completed is. Dem. from Theor. III, Cor. 1, with the lines AB, BC drawn.

In the same way a Circle is made that passes through three points A, B, C which are not placed in a straight line.

Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

To draw a Tangent.

First, if a Tangent is to be drawn to a given Point in the Circumference, as A: let the semidiameter AD be drawn, at whose extremity A let a perpendicular be raised in this way. With the interval of the Semidiameter AD let the circle be cut from A at B, and through B let the indefinite line DF be drawn, which from B, with the same interval of the semidiameter, is to be cut at F. When FA is joined, the perpendicular will be Tangent to the circle. From Theor. I & V.

Second, if from a Point F outside the circle a straight line Tangent to the circle is to be drawn: let the line FD be drawn to the center of the Circle, and let it be bisected, as at B; then from B, with the interval of the half, namely FB, let the Periphery be cut at A. (Having made, for the demonstration, the semicircle FAD.) The line FA will be Tangent to the circle. From the same.

Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

To construct a Right-angled, Obtuse-angled, and Acute-angled Triangle in a Circle.

Let any Diameter AB whatever be drawn in the Circle: if upon the Diameter a

Triangle is made whose vertex C touches at any point [p. 24] the Circumference, BCA will be Right-angled: if the vertex D falls outside the Circumference, BDA will be Acute-angled: if it falls inside the Circle, as at E, BEA will be an Obtuse-angled Triangle. From Theor. I of this book, & Cor. of Theor. IV, Bk. I.

## Problem IV. (Fig. 4.)

To inscribe in a circle a Triangle Equiangular to another given one.

## L   et there be given any Triangle PHO, to which an Equiangular one is to be in‐

scribed in the circle DBE. Let any tangent AC be drawn: then let the Angle ABD be made equal to the angle O, and the angle CBE equal to the angle P: then let DE be drawn. The angle D will be equal to the angle P, and the angle E equal to the angle O, from Theor. VI of this book; and the Triangle BDE equiangular to the Triangle PHO.

But if a straight line DE is given, upon which a segment of a circle is to be described that contains the given angle H: let the angle D be made equal to the angle P, and the angle E equal to the angle O, and let DB, EB be produced until they intersect; then through the three points D, B, E let a Circle be drawn, according to Probl. I. The segment DBE will be the one that was sought, in which the angle B will be equal to the angle H, from Theor. III, bk. I.

Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

To inscribe a Square, a Hexagon, a Trigon in a Circle.

First. A Square is inscribed in a circle if two Diameters AB, CD are drawn at right angles; for the lines drawn through their extreme points will constitute the Square ACBD, from Theor. I & IV, cor. 2.

An Octagon, moreover, is inscribed in a circle if each arc subtending a side of the Square is bisected: for the lines drawn through the eight points of the circumference will constitute a regular Octagon, that is, one all of whose sides and Angles are equal.

Second. A Hexagon is inscribed in a circle if the semidiameter is carried round six times in the circle; for the lines drawn through those points of the circumference will constitute the Hexagon AEMBNG, from Theor. III, cor. 2. A Dodecagon is inscribed in a circle if the arcs of the Hexagon, as AE, are bisected.

Third, if through three points of the Hexagon, omitting the intermediate one, lines are drawn, they will constitute an equilateral Trigon in the circle, as AMN, from Theor. V, cor. 2.

Half the side of the Trigon gives the side of the Heptagon in the same circle, not Geometrically and perfectly, but very nearly.

Problem

[p. 25]

## Problem VI. (Fig. 6.)

To inscribe a Pentagon in a Circle.

A      Pentagon is inscribed in a circle when two diameters AB, CD have been drawn

at right angles: then let the semidiameter EB be bisected at F: let the interval FC be transferred from F to G: and CG will be the side of the Pentagon, from Theor. XI, bk. III. The side of the Decagon, moreover, will be the line GE, from Theor. X, bk. III. But if the arcs of the Decagon are bisected, one will have the side of the Icosagon, or regular Figure of twenty sides.

If in a circle in which a Pentagon is inscribed a regular Trigon is also inscribed, in such a way that a vertex of the Trigon coincides with some vertex of the Pentagon, the least distance between an angle of the Pentagon and one of the Trigon will be the side of the Quindecagon.

All Figures, moreover, are circumscribed about Circles if the Figure sought is first inscribed in the Circle; and then through the vertices of the angles of that same Figure, inscribed in the Circle, Tangents are drawn, which will constitute a similar Figure about the circle.

These and all other Figures can also be inscribed in a Circle when a Quadrant of the Circle has been divided into 90 degrees. For let as many degrees be taken in the Quadrant as belong to the Figure sought; if the circle is divided according to them, there will be given the arcs which the sides of that Figure subtend and which its Angles at the Center comprehend.

But in order to know how many degrees belong to each Figure, let the 360 degrees of the circle be divided by the number of the sides of the Figure to be constructed; and the Quotient will give the degrees sought. E.g., 120 degrees of the circle belong to the Trigon, because 360 divided by 3 gives 120.

Similar Figures can also be constructed without a circle upon a given line, by finding the angle that two sides of the Figure to be constructed comprehend; which is usually called the Angle at the Circumference.

This, moreover, is found by subtracting the angle at the center from 180 degrees of the circle. E.g., if the angle of the Trigon at the circumference is sought: since its angle at the center has been found to be of 120 degrees, when these are subtracted from 180, there remain 60 degrees for the angle of the Trigon at the circumference, which, that is, the sides of that Figure comprehend: as may be seen in the adjoining Little Table.

## CHAPTER III

Theorems.

Here we shall consider first the lines and angles within the circle; then the lines touching the circle; some having been put off to the third book, on Proportions, where they will be shown more clearly.

Theorem I. (Pl. III. Fig. I. Theor.)

The Angle in a Semicircle is Right. (a)

Prep. For the demonstration, let the semidiameter AD be drawn.

Dem. The angle CAD is equal to the angle ACD; and the angle ABD is equal to the angle DAB, since they are opposite equal semidiameters, from Theor. V of the first book. Therefore the whole angle BAC is equal to the two B and C together; therefore it is half of two right angles, or is Right, from Theor. III, bk. 1, & Axiom VI.

Cor. When the line AE is drawn, it is plain that the angle BAE, having for its base an arc greater than a semicircle, is Obtuse; and the angle GAB, standing upon an arc less than a semicircle, is Acute.

(a) Eucl. bk. III, prop. 31.

[p. 27]

Theorem II. (Fig. 2.) The Angle at the Center, as BDC, is Double the angle at the Circumference BAC, if they stand

upon the same arc. (a)

Prep. For the demonstration, let the Diameter AE be drawn.

Dem. The angles DAB and DBA are equal, as being opposite equal semidiameters, from Theor. V, bk. I; therefore the exterior angle BDE is double the angle DAB, from Theor. III, bk. I. Likewise the angles DAC and DCA are equal, as being opposite equal semidiameters too: therefore the exterior angle CDE is also double the angle CAD: therefore the whole angle BDC at the center is double the whole angle A at the circumference.

Cor. I. Angles at the circumference, as G, A, F, if they have for base the same portion of the circle, are equal to each other: for the angle BDC at the center, as exterior, is double each of them, from Theor. III, bk. I. (b)

II. The angle at the circumference has for its measure half the arc upon which it stands, since it is half the angle at the center, whose Measure is the whole arc upon which it stands. From the def. of angle, note 1, bk. 1.

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.) If a Diameter in a Circle bisects another straight line, it will be Perpendicular to it; and if it is

Perpendicular, it will bisect it. (c)

Prep. For the demonstration, let the semidiameters FB, FC be drawn.

Dem. The Triangle FBC is Isosceles: therefore if the line FA bisects the line BC, it is perpendicular to it: if it is perpendicular, it bisects it. From Theor. V, bk. 1, cor. 4.

Cor. I. If a perpendicular bisects some line in a circle, the center is in the middle of the perpendicular; for it is easily demonstrated that only from that point are all the lines to the circumference equal. (d)

II. If BC is the side of a Hexagon, it will be equal to the semidiameter; for since the arc BC in the Hexagon is the sixth part of the circle, the angle BFC will be of 60 degrees: and on account of the Isosceles Triangle, the two equal angles B and C will each also be of 60 degrees, half of the degrees

Bb 2                                           120

(a) Eucl. bk. III, prop. 20.

(b) Eucl. bk. III, prop. 21.

(c) Prop. 3.

(d) Eucl. bk. III, cor. prop. 1.

[p. 28]

120 that remain up to two right angles: therefore the single sides of the triangle FBC will be equal, as being opposite equal angles. From Theor. V, bk. I, cor. II. (a)

III. If the Chord BC is bisected by the diameter ED, the arc BC will also be bisected at D by the same diameter: for when the point C is laid upon B, the whole semicircle ECD will coincide with the semicircle EBD, and the arc CD with the arc BD; and so they will be equal.

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.)

In a Circle, equal lines are equally distant from the Center. (b)

Prep. From the center let the Perpendiculars AB and AC be drawn: then let AD, AE be joined.

Dem. Since the lines AD, AE are equal, their Squares will be equal. Again, the Square of the line DA, on account of the right angle at B, is equal to the two Squares together of the lines DB, BA, from Theor. IX, bk. I; and the Square of the line AE is equal to the squares of the lines EC, CA: but the lines DB and EC are equal, from the preceding; and so their squares are equal too; therefore, when the equals are taken away, the squares of the perpendicular lines AB, AC also remain equal; and so the perpendiculars themselves are equal: therefore DF and EG are equally distant from the center. From Def. IV of this book.

Cor. I. Lines that are equally distant from the center are equal to each other: which is plain from the same demonstration.

II. If chords, or lines DF, EG, subtending an arc, are equal, the arcs will also be equal; and conversely: because if they are laid upon each other, they coincide. (c)

III. Hence the greatest of the lines in a circle is the Diameter; and lines that recede farther from the Diameter are less, because they subtend a lesser arc. (d)

IV. Whatever has been demonstrated of the same Circle is true also of equal Circles, which, when laid upon each other, coincide entirely.

Theorem V. (Fig. 5.) If a line is placed Perpendicular to the extremity of a Diameter, it will Touch the circle in one

point. (e)

Dem. The Semidiameter AD, perpendicular to the line BC, is the shortest

(a) Bk. IV, prop. 15.

(b) Eucl. bk. III, prop. 14.

(c) Eucl. bk. III, pr. 28, 29.

(d) Pr. 15.

(e) Pr. 16. [p. 29] of all the lines from the center to the same line; therefore the line AC, and any other drawn to the line BC, is greater than the semidiameter AD: and consequently every other line to the line BC falls beyond the circle, because it is greater than the semidiameter: therefore the line BC touches the circle in one point D.

Cor. I. No straight line can be drawn through the point D between the Circumference and the Tangent: for the perpendicular from the center A, which can be drawn to any line drawn through the point D, according to Problem V, bk. 1, must be shorter than the semidiameter AD, which is not perpendicular to the line DE, from Theor. V, bk. 1, last cor.; and so the line DE, and any other that is drawn through the point D below the tangent, does not fall outside, but inside the Circle.

II. Hence, they say, no acute rectilinear angle can be made less than the angle of contact, and none greater than the angle of the semicircle; because through the point of contact D no straight line can be drawn between the Tangent and the Circumference that would constitute an acute angle with the line of contact or with the semidiameter.

III. From the center no line is perpendicular to the tangent except the one that is drawn to the point of contact; for only the semidiameter AD is the shortest of all those that can be drawn from the center A to the tangent BC. (a)

Theorem VI. (Fig. 6.) The Angle that is made by a line tangent to the circle and any secant, as ABC, is equal to the an‐

gle BDC at the circumference, which has for its base the same secant BC. (b)

Prep. For the demonstration, let the Diameter BE be drawn.

Dem. The angle ABE, a right angle [from the preceding], is equal to the angle BDE, as being in a semicircle: but the angles CBE and CDE are equal, as standing upon the same arc CE, from Theor. II, Cor. 1; therefore, when these are taken away, the remaining angles ABC and BDC are equal.

Likewise it is demonstrated that the angle FBD is equal to the angle BCD, which has for its base the same secant and the arc BD. These angles are said by Euclid to be in the alternate segment of the circle.

Cor. In any quadrilateral Figure inscribed in a circle, the two opposite angles, even if they are not right, are nevertheless equal to two right angles: for when the tangent is drawn to the point of the angle B, and the secant BE, the two angles ABE and FBE, from Theor. I, bk. 1, are equal to two right angles; but the angle ABE is equal to the whole angle D, from what has just been demonstrated: likewise the angle FBE is equal to the whole angle C: therefore the two angles C and D are equal to two right angles (c)
