## BOOK III

On Proportional Figures.

## CHAPTER I

Principles.

Under the Name of Principles we comprehend the Definitions which belong to

Euclid’s books 5 and 6; certain Axioms; and the Arguments about Proportions, which need explanation rather than demonstration.

§. I.

Definitions.

A    I. part is a lesser magnitude that measures a greater.

Part is divided into Aliquot and Aliquant. An aliquot part is so called which, repeated a number of times, exactly equals its whole: as 4 is exactly contained in 8, 12, 16, etc. An aliquant part is so called which, repeated a number of times, does not exactly equal its whole, but either exceeds it or falls short of it: as 4 in 6, 7, 9, etc. Only the aliquot part, which measures and exactly equals the whole, is defined here; both because its chief use is in demonstrating proportions, and because an aliquant part is not properly called a part, but parts of the whole; for the number 4, e.g., is called two thirds of the number 6.

II. A multiple magnitude is one that a lesser measures.

That is, a magnitude is called multiple when compared with its aliquot part, which it contains exactly several times; as 6 contains 2.

III. Ratio, or (as others prefer) Proportion, is the Mode in which one quantity contains another of the same kind, or is contained by it.

Those things, moreover, are said to be of the same kind which, when multiplied, can exceed each other: hence between God and the Creature, the Finite and the Infinite, there is no proportion, because they cannot exceed each other: likewise between the angle of contingence and a rectilinear one; because the angle of contingence, however much increased, does not exceed a rectilinear angle.

[p. 31]

Proportion is divided, 1, into rational and irrational. That is called rational which can be expressed by numbers: as double, triple proportion, etc. That is called irrational which cannot be expressed by numbers: such is the proportion of the diameter to the side of the square; for by no number can it be expressed by how many parts the Diameter exceeds the side of the square (whoever does not know this, says Plato, is to be counted not among men but among the brutes). And quantities that have a rational proportion to each other are called Commensurable; those that have an irrational one are called Incommensurable.

Proportion is divided, 2, into the Proportion of Equality, which obtains between equal things, and of inequality, which obtains between unequal things: of these, when the greater contains the lesser exactly, it is called multiple proportion, as in definition 2. When it contains the lesser and, besides, some aliquot part of it, it is called superparticular proportion, as 6 to 4. When it is greater by some aliquant part, it is called superpartient proportion: as 8 to 5. But if the lesser is referred to the greater, the particle sub is prefixed: as 2 to 4 is subduple proportion.

IV. Proportionality, which is also usually called Proportion and Analogy, is the Comparison and Similitude of Ratios, or Proportions.

It is divided first into Arithmetical and Geometrical. Arithmetical proportion is the Equality of the excesses among several quantities: as 1, 2, 3, 4, which numbers all exceed one another by unity; or 1, 3, 5, etc., which exceed one another equally by two.

Geometrical proportion is the similitude of the excesses among several terms that contain one another in the same way: as 1, 2, 4, 8, etc., which likewise exceed one another in double ratio; or 1, 3, 9, 27, etc., which are in triple ratio.

There is, besides, Harmonic Proportion, which does not pertain to the present matter.

Proportion, or proportionality, is divided secondly into discrete and continuous. It is discrete when there is some interruption between the terms: as if you say, 8 is to 4 as 6 to 3; there is an interruption in the middle terms, because 4 is not to 6 as 8 to 4.

Proportion is called continuous when there is no interruption: as if you say, 1 to 2, as 2 to 4, as 4 to 8, as 8 to 16, etc.; for in these terms the earlier are referred to the later in the same way, with no interruption made. This continuous proportion is also usually called a progression: and if it goes from the lesser to the greater, it is called an increasing progression; but if from the greater to the less, a decreasing progression.

V. Four terms are said to be in the same Proportion when the first contains the second, or is contained by the second, as many times as the third contains the fourth, or is contained by the fourth; and terms of this kind are called Proportionals.

Of these, moreover, the first, which is referred to another, is called the antecedent; the later, to which the first is referred, is called the consequent: and the two antecedents

and [p. 32] are called homologous to each other, just as the two consequents are to each other: e.g., if it is said, as 4 to 2, so 6 to 3: 4 and 6 are called antecedents and homologous to each other; 2 and 3 are also called consequents homologous to each other.

VI. Proportion, moreover, or Proportionality, consists in at least three terms;

Because proportionality is the comparison of two relations, each of which requires two terms. For if the Proportion is continuous, three terms suffice, because the second is repeated: e.g., as 8 is to 4, so 4 to 2. But if the Proportion is discrete, four terms are required: e.g., as 8 is to 4, so 6 to 3.

VII. Compound Proportion is that which is produced by the multiplication of proportions.

As duodecuple Proportion is that which is produced from sextuple and duple proportion, because twice six make 12.

Hence the Proportion of the extremes is said to be compounded of the proportion of the Means: as if there are 20, 10, 2, the Proportion of 20 to 2 is decuple, compounded of the duple proportion of 20 to 10 and the quintuple of 10 to 2.

VIII. But when Magnitudes are continuously proportional, as 27, 9, 3, 1, the First is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second, and the triplicate to the fourth, and so on.

Double and duplicate ratio are very different; for Proportion is double or triple when one quantity contains another twice or three times. But Proportion is duplicate or triplicate when between several magnitudes there intervene two or three continued proportions. Thus, because between 27, 9, 3 there intervene two triple proportions, 27 is therefore said to have to 3 the duplicate proportion of that which it has to 9. And because between 27, 9, 3, 1 there intervene three similar proportions, 27 is therefore said to have to 1 the triplicate proportion of that which it has to 9.

IX. Similar Figures are those that have their angles equal, each to each, and the sides about the equal angles proportional.

In these, moreover, the sides opposite equal angles are called homologous: [as in Figure 6, Theor., Pl. V] the side GE homologous to the side NL, and the side ED homologous to the side LH.

X. Reciprocal Figures are those that have their sides mutually antecedent and consequent.

That is, mutually double and half; triple and subtriple, etc., as in Figure 1, Theorems, Pl. V, are the Rectangles X and Y: for the Rectangle Y has the side GA double the side AD of the rectangle X, and reciprocally the other side AF half the side AB of the same rectangle X.

[p. 33]

§. II.

Axioms.

In place of Axioms I put most of the Propositions of Euclid’s bk. 5, of which

Geminus, the illustrious Mathematician, seems to have spoken in Proclus, bk. 3, ch. 1, where he says: Others have devised demonstrations even of indemonstrable things: they have tried to prove things that are known to all by less known Means.

I. If two quantities are equal to each other, they will have the same proportion to one third thing, or to equal things: as 8 and 8 contain 4 twice in the same way. (a)

II. If two things have the same proportion to the same third thing, or to equal things, they will be equal to each other. As, if the number 4 is contained twice by two numbers, these will be equal to each other, namely 8 and 8. (b)

III. Of unequal quantities, the one that is greater has a greater proportion to the lesser, or contains the lesser more times.

As the number 8 contains the number 4 more times than the number 6 does. And that which contains the same quantity more times is greater: and that which is contained more times is less. (c)

IV. Proportions that are equal, the same, similar to the same one (they signify the same thing by different names) are equal, the same, similar to each other. (d)

V. If single magnitudes have the same proportion to single magnitudes, all together will also have the same proportion to all together.

That is, twice the double will also be double to twice the half; three times the double to three times the half, etc.

Hence all the antecedents together are to all the consequents as the single antecedents to the single consequents: as, if 4 has to 2 the same proportion as 6 to 3, namely double: 4 and 6 together will also have a double proportion to 2 and 3 together. (e)

VI. Similar parts, that is, those that are contained equally, are to each other as the wholes containing them. That is, as 2 to 3, so twice 2 to twice 3; three times 2 to three times 3.

Hence if similar parts are added to or taken from similar wholes, what remains is similar. (f)

VII. If, as the whole to the whole, so the part taken away to the part taken away, the whole will also be to the whole as the remainder to the remainder. (g)

Cc                                        As

(a) Eucl. bk. V, prop. 7.

(b) Prop. 9.

(c) Eucl. bk. V, prop. 8 & 10.

(d) 11.

(e) 12.

(f) 15.

(g) Eucl. bk. V, Prop. 19.

[p. 34]

As, if from three times 4 and three times 2, in double proportion, you take away once 4 and 2, in double proportion, there remain twice 4 and twice 2, that is, 8 and 4, also in double proportion.

VIII. If equals are added to equal proportions, the wholes will be equal.

As, if to the two numbers 4 and 4, in double proportion to 2, there is added to each 6, which number is in triple proportion to the same 2, there will be 10 and 10 in equal, quintuple proportion to 2.

Hence, since multiplication is multiple addition, if equal proportions are multiplied by equals, the wholes will be equal: as, if two double proportions are each multiplied by a triple proportion, both will be sextuple.

## §. III

Arguments about Proportions.

Mathematicians, and also all Philosophers, use six modes of arguing for inferring proportions, the truth of which is readily plain either of itself or from the Principles laid down.

I. Inverse, or converse, Ratio is the Change of the antecedent into the consequent, and of the consequent into the antecedent: e.g., as the antecedent 9 to the consequent 3, so the antecedent 6 to the consequent 2; therefore, by converting, as 3 to 9, so 2 to 6.

It is plain of itself: because if the antecedents contain the consequents equally, the consequents are also equally contained by the antecedents.

II. Alternate, or permuted, Ratio is the comparison of antecedent with antecedent and of consequent with consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2: therefore, by alternating, or by permuting, or conversely, as 9 to 6, so 3 to 2. (a)

It is plain from Axiom VI: because similar parts are to each other as the wholes, and the wholes as the similar parts.

In alternate proportion, however, the four terms must be of the same kind; for if the first two are of a different kind from the second two, the argument by alternation is not valid: because between things of a different kind there is no proportion. From definition III.

III. Compound, or conjoined, Ratio is the Comparison of the antecedent and the consequent, as of one thing, to the consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2: therefore, by composition, as 9 and 3 (that is, 12) to 3, so 6 and 2 (that is, 8) to 2. (b)

It is plain from Axiom VI: because when similar parts are added, similar

(a) Eucl. bk. V, prop. 16.

(b) Eucl. bk. V, prop. 18. [p. 35] wholes also result. And proportional terms are those whose excesses are similar parts.

IV. Division of ratio is the comparison of the excess of the antecedent over the consequent to the consequent itself: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2; therefore, by division, as 6 (the number by which 9 exceeds 3) to 3, so 4 (the number by which 6 exceeds 2) to 2. (a)

This is plain from Axiom VI: because when similar parts are taken away, what remains is similar.

V. Ratio reversed, or conversion of ratio, is the comparison of the antecedent to the difference of the terms, as to a consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2; therefore, by conversion, as 9 to 6 (which is the difference between 9 and 3), so 6 to 4, which is the difference between 6 and 2. (b)

This is plain from the same Axiom.

VI. Equal ratio is the inference to equal proportions of the extremes from equal intermediate proportions: as if there are set down

On the one side 27, 9, 3;

On the other 18, 6, 2.

The argument runs thus: as 27 to 9 on the one side, so 18 to 6 on the other; and as 9 to 3 on the one side, so 6 to 2 on the other: therefore, from equality, as 27 to 3, so 18 to 2. (c)

And this indeed is called an ordered ratio, because the proportion of the first with the second, and of the second with the third, is compared in order on each side. But if this order is not kept, it is called a disturbed ratio: as if there are set down (d)

On the one side 12, 6, 2;

On the other 24, 8, 4.

The argument runs thus: as 12 to 6 on the one side, so 8 to 4 on the other; and as 6 to 2 on the one side, so 24 to 8 on the other: therefore, from equality in disturbed order, as 12 to 2, so 24 to 4. It is called a disturbed ratio because on the one side the proportion of the first with the second is compared, on the other that of the second with the third.

Each argument is plain from the definition itself and from Axiom 8, because in both cases the proportion of the extremes arises from equal intermediate proportions, whether these are taken in order or in disturbed order.

“Since, however, what has been said about proportions by the celebrated Author is apt to cause difficulty to young men, I have therefore thought it opportune to set these things forth and explain them again, perhaps more clearly.

If one quantity is referred to another, e.g., a number to a number, and attention is paid to the manner in which the former contains the other, or is contained in the other, that relation of the one to the other is called a Geometric Ratio; the number which is referred is called the antecedent, and the number to which it is referred is called the consequent of the ratio. But if the antecedent is divided

Cc 2                                      by

(a) Prop. 17.

(b) Cor. prop. 19.

(c) Eucl. bk. V, prop. 22.

(d) Prop. 23. [p. 36] by the consequent, the quotient is called the exponent of the ratio. Now the Quotient, or Quotient number, is that which denotes how many times some number is contained in another. Thus in the ratio 8 to 2 the number 8 is the antecedent, 2 the consequent, and the quotient 4 is the exponent of the ratio; and 4 is the quotient because 2 is contained four times in 8.

If the antecedent equals the consequent, the ratio is one of equality, as 4 to 4.

If the first quantity contains the second twice, the first is said to be to the second in double ratio; if three times, in triple ratio, etc.; and the one that is contained is said to be in subdouble, subtriple ratio, etc. Thus, e.g., a line of 8 feet is to another of 4 feet in double ratio, and the line of 4 feet to the line of 8 feet in subdouble ratio.

The equality or likeness of ratios is called Proportion, and it is expressed in this way: 8 : 4 :: 6 : 3, or 8 : 4 = 6 : 3; that is, 8 is to 4 as 6 is to 3, or, e.g., a line of 8 feet is to a line of 4 feet as a line of 6 feet is to a line of 3 feet. These four terms, or numbers, are proportional, and this proportion is called Geometric because it is an equality of ratios. The following, however, is Arithmetic: 4 is to 3 as 2 to 1, because the excess of the first antecedent with respect to the first consequent is the same as that of the second antecedent with respect to the second consequent.

Two ratios, then, are equal to each other when the antecedent of the first contains its consequent as many times as the antecedent of the second contains its own, or when the antecedent of the first is contained in its consequent as many times as the antecedent of the second is contained in its own. Thus the ratio 12 to 6 is equal to the ratio 48 to 24, and the ratio 3 to 6 is equal to the ratio 50 to 100. Two equal ratios, then, make up a Geometric proportion.

Two quantities are said to be in direct ratio when the first and third terms of a Geometric proportion belong to one quantity, and the second and fourth terms of the same proportion relate to another. Let us suppose, e.g., that Peter has 100 of wisdom and 100 of study, but that Paul has only 50 of Wisdom and 50 of study. Peter and Paul will have Wisdom in the direct ratio of their study: I shall say, therefore, that the Wisdom of Peter is to the knowledge of Paul as the study of Peter is to the study of Paul. In this proportion the first and third terms belong to Peter, while the second and fourth relate to Paul, as is evident. This ratio is therefore called direct.

Two quantities are in inverse, or reciprocal, ratio when the first and fourth terms of a Geometric proportion belong to one quantity, while the second and third relate to another. If Peter, e.g., has 100 of knowledge and 50 of study, and Paul has 50 of knowledge and 100 of labor, the knowledge of Peter and the knowledge of Paul will be in inverse, or reciprocal, ratio. I shall say, therefore, that the knowledge of Peter is to the knowledge of Paul as the labor of Paul is to the labor of Peter. The first and fourth

[p. 37] terms of this proportion belong to Peter, the second and third relate to Paul, as is self-evident.

The ratio which arises from the multiplication of several ratios with one another is called a compound Ratio. Thus, if there are the ratios 8 to 4 and 3 to 5, and you multiply the antec. 8 by the antec. 3, and the conseq. 4 by the conseq. 5, the ratio of the product 24 from the antecedents to the product 20 from the consequents is said to be compounded of the ratios 8 to 4 and 3 to 5.

If there are several quantities, of which the first has the same ratio to the second as the second to the third, and the third to the fourth, then the first is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Likewise it is said to have to the fourth the triplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Thus if, e.g., there are four lines, of which the first is of 16 feet, the second of 8 feet, the third of 4 ft. and the fourth of 2 ft., and you ask the ratio of the first to the second, I shall say that it is double, or as 2 to 1. But if you ask the ratio of the first, of 16 ft., to the third, of 4 ft., I shall say that it is twice double, because it is compounded of the ratio of the first line, of 16 ft., to the second, 8, which is double, and of the ratio of the second, namely 8, to the third, 4, which again is double; whence the ratio of the first to the third is the duplicate of the ratio of the first to the second, or is twice double, or in a word quadruple. And the ratio of the first to the fourth, or 16 to 2, is the triplicate of the ratio of the first to the second. And so it must be compounded of the double ratio, which is that of the first to the second, and of the quadruple ratio, which is that of the same first to the third; and thus it is twice quadruple, or, in a word, octuple.”

## CHAPTER II

Problems. H    ere, besides the Problems selected from Book VI of Euclid, we add those

which teach a very useful way of enlarging or diminishing Figures in any Proportion whatever.

Problem I. (Plate IV. Fig. 1.)

To divide a line in a given Proportion.

Let the line AB be divided into five parts, just as the line AC is divided. Let them be joined so as to make any angle whatever at A, and let CB be drawn. Then through the points at which the line AC has been cut let DE, FG, etc. be made parallel to CB, cutting the line AB. These divisions

[p. 38] will divide the line AB in the same proportion as the line AC is divided. From Theor. II of this book.

Any line, however, such as AB, is divided more easily if it is to be divided into equal parts. For let an indefinite line AC be joined to it at any angle whatever, and at the other end, at an equal angle, the line BI (which by Theor. II, bk. I will be parallel to the line AC, because of the equal alternate angles); then from A toward C, and from B toward I, with any opening of the compass, let as many equal parts be cut off as you wish. The lines DL, FM, and the others drawn through the opposite points of section, will also divide the line AB into the equal parts sought. From the same.

Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

To find a mean proportional.

Let there be two lines AB, BC, between which a mean proportional is to be found.

Let them be joined into one line ABC; then, with the interval of half of AC, as from the point E, let a semicircle be made; then at the point B, which joins the two lines, let a perpendicular BD be erected, produced as far as the circumference; this will be the mean proportional sought. And the square on the line BD will be equal to the rectangle of the lines AB and BC. From Theor. IV and I of this book, cor. II.

Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

Given two straight lines, to find a third continued proportional.

Let there be two lines BD and DA, for which a third continued proportional is to be found. Let them be placed at the right angle D, and joined by the straight line BA; then let AC be drawn perpendicular to the line BA, and let BD be produced until it meets the line AC at C. The line DC will be the third proportional sought; and the rectangle made of the lines BD, DC will be equal to the square on the line DA: from Theor. I, cor. 2.

Similarly, by placing the second and third at a right angle, a fourth continued proportional is found, etc.

Problem IV. (Fig. 4.)

To find a fourth proportional, even one not continued.

Let there be three lines AB, BC, AD, for which a fourth proportional, even one not continued, is to be found. Let the first two, AB,

[p. 39]

BC, be set out in one straight line, and let the third, AD, make any angle whatever with the first, AB; then let DB be drawn, and through C let CE be placed parallel to it, meeting the straight line AD, produced, at E. DE will be the fourth proportional. From Theor. II of this book.

## Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

To divide a line in extreme and mean ratio.

Let the line AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio, that is, by finding in the same line the mean and the extreme proportionals. At A let a perpendicular AC be placed, equal to half of the whole AB; then let CB be drawn, and from it let CD be cut off, equal to the line CA; and let the remainder DB be transferred from A to E; and the line AB will be cut proportionally at E, so that the greater part AE is a mean proportional between the whole AB and its smaller part EB. Moreover, the square on the line AE will be equal to the rectangle of the whole AB and its smaller part EB. Because of its outstanding uses this was called by the ancients the Divine proportion. From Theor. VIII of this book, cor. I.

## Problem VI. (Fig. 6.)

To make a Rectilinear figure similar and proportional to another.

Let the Rectilinear figure ABCD be divided into Triangles by drawing a line to the opposite angles A, B; then let a Triangle EGF be made having angles equal to the Triangle ACB, according to Probl. XI, bk. I; and similarly let a Triangle EHF be made having angles equal to the Triangle ADB. And the whole Rectilinear figure EGFH will be similar and proportional to the Rectilinear figure ACBD. From def. IX and Theor. III.

Problem VII. (Fig. 7.)

To add, or to multiply, similar figures.

Let there be given three figures, circular or rectilinear, whose diameters or homologous sides are AB, BC, DE. Let AB, BC be set at a right angle and produced indefinitely, and let AC be drawn; then let AC be transferred to BF, and DE to BG. The line FG will be the diameter, or homologous side, of a figure similar and equal to the three together upon the lines AB, BC, DE. If the lines AB, BC are taken as equal, the figure upon AC will be double the similar figure upon AB or BC; and when AC is transferred to BF, the figure upon FC (which is here understood to be drawn) will be triple; and when FC is transferred to BH, the figure upon HC (were it drawn) will similarly be quadruple the figure upon AB; and so on to infinity. From Theor. VI, cor. 3.

Problem

[p. 40]

## Problem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

To subtract a similar figure from another, or to diminish it, or to enlarge it in any proportion whatever.

Let there be two similar figures, rectilinear or circular, whose diameters or homologous sides are AB, CB. Upon the greater line BC let a semicircle be made, within which let another line be fitted equal to the line AB; then let the straight line AC be drawn, which will be the side of the figure sought: the figure by which the similar figure upon BC exceeds the figure described upon AB. From the same Theor.

Hence it is plain how any figure whatever is to be diminished to a given proportion: e.g., let a third part be taken away from the figure described upon BC. Having made the semicircle, let BC be divided into three parts, and then at the intersection of one third, DC, let a perpendicular DA be erected; finally let AC be drawn. The figure upon AC will be the third part of the similar figure upon BC, and the figure upon BA two thirds of the same. From the same.

It is plain also how figures are enlarged in any proportion whatever. For let a figure be constructed one and a half times a similar figure described upon BD. Let half of the line, DC, be added to it; and when a semicircle has been described upon the whole BC, and the perpendicular AD erected, let AB be drawn in the semicircle; the figure described upon it will be one and a half times the similar figure described upon the line BD. From the same.

Problem IX. (Fig. 9.)

To make equal parallelograms upon a given line.

Let there be a parallelogram AC, to which an equal one is to be constructed upon the given line CH. Let CH be placed in a straight line with the line DC, and let the parallelogram CI be completed. Then let the diameter ICE be drawn indefinitely. Let AD be produced until it meets the diameter; through the point of meeting E let EG be made parallel and equal to the line DH. And the parallelogram CG, constructed upon the given line CH, will be equal to the given parallelogram AC. From Theor. VI, bk. I, cor. 3.

Problem X. (Fig. 10.)

To convert any Figure whatever into an equal Rectangle.

We taught in bk. I, last Prob., how to convert a Trapezium into a Rectangle, or into any parallelogram whatever. How to convert any rectilinear figure whatever into a rectangle, or another parallelogram,

[p. 41] we teach here more conveniently. Let there be, then, any rectilinear figure BAC whatever, to which an equal rectangle is to be constructed. First, by drawing lines to the vertices of the angles, resolve the whole rectilinear figure into Triangles, which will always be two fewer than the sides of the figure. Then upon any given straight line make a rectangle DG equal to the triangle B; and, DN being produced indefinitely, upon the straight line FG let a rectangle FI be made equal to the triangle A; and upon the straight line HI a rectangle HM equal to the triangle C. The whole rectangle DM will be equal to the rectilinear figure BAC: From Theor. VIII, bk. I.

## Problem XI. (Fig. 11.)

To know the Proportion of dissimilar figures.

## L  et there be two dissimilar figures A and B, whose mutual proportion is to be

known. Let them be reduced, according to the preceding Problem, to two Rectangles equal to them, C and D, of the same height. Then the proportion of the base GF to the base FH will be the same as that of the figure A to the figure B. From Theor. I of this book.

## Problem XII. (Fig. 12.)

To make a figure equal to one and similar to another.

Let a figure be made equal to the Polygon A which shall nevertheless be similar to the Polygon B. Upon DC of the Polygon B, to which a similar figure is to be constructed, let a rectangle CE be made equal to the same Polygon B; again, upon DE let a rectangle DG be made equal to the Polygon A, to which an equal figure is to be constructed. Then between CD and DF let a Mean Proportional, such as IL, be found according to Prob. II, upon which let a figure H be made similar to the figure B; it will be equal to the figure A. From Theor. VI, cor. 4.

## CHAPTER III

Theorems.

welve Theorems are comprised in this chapter, selected chiefly from the

T          sixth book of Euclid, in which are demonstrated first the Proportions of

Rectilinear Figures, then of Lines and of Figures in the circle, and also of the circles themselves,

Dd [p. 42] some things that bear on this having been brought in from Euclid’s books 3, 11 and 13.

Theorem I. (Plate V. Fig. 1.) Parallelograms and Triangles that have the same Height, or that are between the same Parallels,

are to each other as their Bases. (a)

Dem. If the base BA of the Parallelogram X is twice or three times equal to the base AF of the Parallelogram Z, the Parallelogram X will be twice or three times equal, that is, double or triple, of the Parallelogram Z, and so on to infinity, since Parallelograms of equal bases between the same Parallels are equal, from bk. I, Theor. VII: therefore Parallelograms of the same height are to each other as their bases.

Similarly the triangle X, half of the parallelogram X, will be double or triple the triangle Z, according to their bases.

Cor. I. If the base BA is double or triple the base AF, and the base GA is likewise double or triple the base AD, the whole rectangles X and Y, or their halves, the triangles, will be reciprocal and equal, because they are likewise double or triple the same rectangle, or of the half, the triangle Z, from what has just been demonstrated. And this is likewise plain of other Parallelograms. (b)

II. Hence it is plain that if four lines are proportional, as GA, AD, AB, AF, the Rectangle Y, which is made of the extremes GA, AF, will be equal to the Rectangle X, which is made of the means AD, AB. (c)

III. And if three lines are continued proportionals, that is, if the two means are equal to each other, as AD, AB, the Square X of the mean will be equal to the rectangle Y, which is made of the extreme lines AC, AF. (d)

IV. Rectangles of proportional bases and heights, as O and Z, are in the duplicate ratio of their sides: for if the base GA is double the base AD, and similarly the base BA is double the base AF, the rectangle O will be double the rectangle X or Y; but the rectangle X or Y is double the rectangle Z; therefore the rectangle O will be quadruple the rectangle Z.

Similarly, if the same bases are triple, the rectangle X or Y will be triple the rectangle Z, and the rectangle O will be ninefold of the same; and so on successively, always in duplicate ratio.

V. Hence the triangles O and Z, halves of rectangles, which have proportional bases and heights, also have the duplicate ratio of the bases and heights.

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 1.

(b) Eucl. bk. VI, Prop. 14, 15.

(c) Prop. 16.

(d) Prop. 17.

[p. 43]

VI. And if the base BA is double the base AF, and the base GA triple the base AD, the rectangle O will have to the rectangle Z the ratio produced, or compounded, of the triple and the double of the same sides: that is, the rectangle O will be sextuple the rectangle Z, because it is triple the rectangle X or Y, which is double the rectangle Z. These things are demonstrated in like manner of all similar Parallelograms. (a)

## Theorem II. (Fig. 2.)

If a Parallel is placed to a side of any Triangle, it will cut the two remaining sides proportionally.

(b)

Prep. For the demonstration, let ED, BC be drawn.

Dem. The Triangles EDB and BCE are equal, since they are on the same base BE and between the same Parallel DC; therefore, by Axiom II of this book, they have the same proportion to the Triangle ABE. But the Triangles ABE, BDE have the same vertex E, and therefore the same height. Similarly the Triangles AEB and CEB have the same vertex B: therefore the base BD has the same proportion to the base BA as the base CE to the base EA. From the preceding.

Cor. I. Therefore, by alternation, as BD to CE, so BA to EA.

II. Therefore, by composition, as DA to AB, so CA to EA.

III. And if the line BE cuts the sides of the Triangle proportionally, it will be Parallel to the remaining side: for similarly the two Triangles EDB and EBC will be equal to each other, since they have the same proportion to the Triangle ABE as their bases, from the preceding Theor.; therefore, since they have the same base BE, they will be between the same Parallels BE, DC, from Theor. VI, bk. I, last cor.

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.)

Equiangular Triangles have their sides about the equal angles Proportional. (c)

Prep. Let the line GH be drawn, so that the side DG is equal to the side AB, and the side DH is equal to the side AC.

Dd 2                                           Dem.

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 23.

(b) Prop. 2.

(c) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 4.

[p. 44]

Dem. If the angle A of the Triangle ABC is placed upon the angle D, the base BC will fall upon GH (for the angles and sides are supposed equal); but the angles B and C are supposed equal to the angles E and F: therefore, by Theor. II, bk. I, in the cor., the line BC, or GH, will be Parallel to the base EF: therefore, by the preceding Theor., as the side DE to the side AB, so the side DF to the side AC.

But if the angle B is placed upon the angle E, the base AC will also become parallel to the line DF: therefore, as DE to EF, so AB to BC. The same will be shown if the angle C is placed upon the angle F.

Cor. I. A Parallel drawn to one side of a triangle, as GH to EF, cuts off a smaller triangle wholly proportional to the larger.

II. If the angles A and D are equal, and the sides about those angles proportional, the two triangles ABC and DEF will be wholly equiangular; for GH will be parallel to the side EF, by cor. 3 of the preceding Theor., and the triangle DGH will be as the triangle ABC. (a)

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.) In a Right-angled Triangle the Perpendicular drawn from the right angle to the base divides the

whole Triangle into two triangles similar to the whole and to each other. (b)

Dem. I. The whole triangle ABC and its part, the Triangle ADC, have two right angles, CAB and CDA, by supposition, and therefore equal; but the angle C is common to both; therefore the remaining angle CAD is equal to the angle B, by Theor. III, bk. I; therefore, by the preceding Theor., these two equiangular triangles have the sides about the equal angles proportional.

Cor. I. Therefore the line AC is a mean proportional between the whole base BC and its segment DC. For as in the whole triangle is CB to CA, so in the triangle ADC is the same CA to CD.

Dem. II. The whole triangle BAC and its other part ABD have right angles BAC and BDA, by supposition; but the angle B is common to both; therefore the remaining angle BAD is equal to the angle C: and so they are wholly similar.

Cor. II. Therefore AB is a mean proportional between the whole base BC and its other segment BD. For as in the whole triangle is BC to BA, so in the triangle BDA is the same BA to BD.

Dem. III. The two triangles ABD and ACD both have right angles at D; but the angle BAD is equal to the angle C, and the angle CAD equal to the angle B, from what has just been demonstrated; therefore these two triangles are wholly similar.

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 6.

(b) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 8.

[p. 45]

Cor. III. Therefore AD is a mean proportional between the two segments of the base, BD and DC. For as BD to DA, so in the other triangle is AD to DC.

## Theorem V. (Fig. 5.)

Any similar Triangles whatever have the duplicate proportion of their homologous sides. (a)

Prep. From the equal angles let Perpendiculars AG, DH be drawn to the bases.

Dem. Since the angle B is equal to the angle E, by supposition, and the angles at G and H are right, by construction, the triangle ABG will be equiangular and proportional to the Triangle DEH, by Theor. III; therefore the right-angled triangle ABG will be to the right-angled triangle DEH in the duplicate ratio of the sides. By Theor. I, cor. 5.

The same is demonstrated, similarly, of the triangles ACG and DFH: therefore the whole triangle ABC is to the similar triangle DEF in the duplicate ratio of the sides.

## Theorem VI. (Fig. 6.)

Similar Polygons are divided into as many similar and proportional Triangles. (b)

Prep. Let lines be drawn from angles to angles, dividing the Polygons A and B into Triangles.

Dem. The angle E is equal to the angle L, and the sides about them are proportional, by the definition of a similar figure: therefore the Triangle GED is similar and proportional to the Triangle NLH. By Theor. III, cor. 2. By the same reasoning the Triangle GFC is equiangular and proportional to the triangle NMI: therefore, since from the whole angles G, D, C, which by supposition are equal to the angles N, H, I, equal angles have been taken away on either side, the triangles A and B that remain are also equiangular and proportional.

Cor. I. The whole Polygon A has to the Polygon B the duplicate ratio of the sides, since it is composed of as many proportional triangles, which have the duplicate proportion of the sides. From the preceding Theor.

II. Therefore all similar Polygons are to each other as the Squares and the other proportional

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 19.

(b) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 20. [p. 46] rectangles proportional, which likewise have the duplicate proportion of the sides. By Theor. I, cor. 4.

III. Therefore, just as in a right-angled triangle the square of the base is equal to the two squares of the sides containing the right angle, so any similar figures whatever described upon the base of a right-angled triangle will be equal to the two figures together similarly described upon the sides containing the right angle, since they are likewise in the duplicate ratio of the sides. (a)

IV. If there are three continued proportional lines, as DC, HI, OP, then as the first is to the third, so is the rectilinear figure A, described upon the first, to the similar rectilinear figure B, described upon the second: namely, in the same duplicate proportion.

Theorem VII. (Fig. 7.)

If two lines cut each other in a circle, the Rectangle of the parts of the one is equal to the

Rectangle of the parts of the other. (b)

Prep. For the demonstration, let BC, ED be drawn.

Dem. The Triangles EAD and BAC are equiangular: for the vertical angles at A are equal in both. The angles C and D are equal, since they stand on the same arc EB, by Theor. II, bk. 2; and the remaining angle is equal to the remaining angle: therefore, by Theor. III, they have the sides about the equal angles proportional: namely, AD is to AE as AC to AB: therefore, by Theor. I, cor. 2, the rectangle of the extremes AD, AB is equal to the rectangle of the means AE, AC.

Theorem VIII. (Fig. 8.) If, of two straight lines drawn from the same point C, one cuts the circle and the other touches it,

the Square of the tangent CB will be equal to the Rectangle of the whole secant CA and of its part outside the circle, CD. (c)

Prep. From the center let a Perpendicular EB be drawn, and let AB, DB be joined.

Dem. The Triangles ACB and DCB are equiangular; for they have the angle C in common, and the angle CBD equal to the angle A in the alternate segment of the circle, by Theor. VI, bk. 2: therefore, as AC to CB in the whole triangle, so is the same CB to CD in the smaller triangle

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 31.

(b) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 35.

(c) Eucl. bk. III, prop. 36.

[p. 47]

CBD: therefore, by Theor. I, cor. 3, the square of the mean CB is equal to the rectangle of the first and the last, CA and CD.

Cor. I. If the diameter of the circle is equal to the tangent BC, AC will be cut at D in extreme and mean ratio; for the square of the line AD, which is equal to the line BC by supposition, will be equal to the rectangle of the lines AC and DC, from what has just been demonstrated. (a)

II. And if from the line BC, equal to the diameter of the circle, CF is cut off equal to the line CD, the line CB will also be divided in extreme and mean ratio at F, according to Probl. V. For from what has been demonstrated, as the whole AC to the whole CB, so the part AD to the part CF, equal to the line CD: therefore, by Axiom VII, so also will the remainder DC (or its equal CF) be to the remainder FB.

Theorem IX. (Fig. 9.) The Square of the side of the Trigon inscribed in a circle is triple the Square of the semidiameter,

or of the side of the Hexagon. (b)

Dem. The Square of the Diameter is quadruple the square of the semidiameter, or of the side of the hexagon, since squares are in the duplicate ratio of their sides. It is also equal to the squares of the sides AM, MB, because the angle M in the semicircle is right: therefore, when the one square of the side MB is taken away, there remains the square AM, triple.

Cor. Since, moreover, the square ACBD inscribed in the circle is double the square of the semidiameter, because of the right angle at the center E, the square of the side of the trigon will be to the square inscribed in the same circle as 3 to 2, or sesquialteral.

Theorem X. (Fig. 10.) If the side of the Decagon, AB, and of the Hexagon, AE, or of the semidiameter, of the same circle, are put together into one line, EB, the whole line BE will be cut at A in extreme and mean

ratio. (c)

Prep. Let CA be drawn; and the three lines CB, CA, AE will be equal, by supposition; and the triangles EAC, BCA isosceles.

Dem. Since the arc DA is quadruple, by supposition, of the arc BA of the Decagon, the fifth part of the semicircle; and the measure of the angle B at the circumference is half of the whole arc DA on which it stands, by Theor. II,

bk.

(a) Prop. 30.

(b) Eucl. bk. XIII, prop. 13.

(c) Eucl. bk. XIII, prop. 9. [p. 48] bk. 2, cor. 2, the angle B, or the angle GAB equal to it, will be double the angle BCA, whose measure is the fifth part of the semicircle; but the same external angle CAB is double the angle E; therefore the angles E and BCA are equal; the Triangles ECB and BCA have, moreover, the angle B in common; therefore they are equiangular and proportional: therefore, as in the whole triangle ECB is EB to BC, so is the same BC to AB in the smaller triangle ACB; but AE was made equal to CB; therefore, as the whole EB to the greater segment EA, so is the same EA to the smaller segment AB.

Cor. It is plain that the triangle ECB is also isosceles, and that its angles at the base are double the angle at the vertex: if this triangle is constructed in a circle and the angles at the base are bisected, the whole circle will be divided into five equal parts, for inscribing a Pentagon.

Theorem XI. (Fig. 11.) The Square of the side of the Pentagon, AC, is equal to the two Squares together of the side AB

of the Decagon and of the side FC of the Hexagon. (a)

Prep. Let the arc AC of the Pentagon, of 72 degrees, be bisected at B; whence the arcs AB, BC of the Decagon will each be of 36 degrees. Then let a perpendicular FD be drawn which bisects the line and the arc AB at D; whence the arcs AD, BD will each be of 18 degrees, and the whole arc CD of 54 degrees.

Dem. Since the whole angle F of the Pentagon is of 72 degrees, and the equal angles FCA, FAC are each of half of 108 degrees, the remainder to two right angles, they will each be of 54 degrees, as is also the angle EFC, whose arc DC is of 54 degrees: therefore, since the two Triangles AFC and EFC have the angles EFC and CAF equal, and also the angle C in common, they will be equiangular and proportional: therefore, as in the larger triangle is CA to CF, so in the smaller, CEF, is the same CF to CE; therefore the Rectangle made of the extremes CA, CE is equal to the Square made of the mean CF, the semidiameter, or side of the Hexagon. By Theor. I, cor. 3.

Again, since DF is perpendicular to AB, which it bisects, the sides AE, EB will be equal, by Theor. IV, bk. 1, and the angle ABE equal to the angle EAB, to which the angle BCA is also equal, because of the isosceles triangle ABC: therefore the two triangles ABC and AEB are also equiangular and proportional: therefore, as the whole AC to AB, so the same AB to AE: therefore the rectangle made of the extremes AC, AE is equal to the square of the side AB of the Decagon.

(a) Eucl. bk. XIII, prop. 10.

[p. 49]

But the two rectangles made of the whole AC and of each of its parts are equal to the square of the whole AC: by Theor. X, bk. I, cor. 1; therefore the square of the side AC of the Pentagon is equal to the squares of the sides AF of the Hexagon and AB of the Decagon.

Cor. From which it follows that, if the side of the Hexagon, or semidiameter, and the side of the Decagon are placed at a right angle, the line subtending the right angle will be the side of the Pentagon to be inscribed in the same circle.

Theorem XII. (Fig. 12.)

Angles and sectors in the same or in equal circles are to one another as the arcs on which they stand. (a)

Dem. If the arc CG is equal to the arc GD, the angle CBG will be equal to the angle GBD: from the definition of an angle, bk. 1; therefore the whole sector CBG, superposed, will coincide with the sector GBD, and will be equal to it. Likewise, if the arc CG is double the arc CP, the angle and the sector CBG will be double the sector CBP, and CBM triple the same, and CBD quadruple: therefore angles and sectors always have the same ratio as the arcs of the same or of equal circles.

Cor. I. Angles at the circumference in the same or in equal circles also have the same ratio as the arcs on which they stand, because they are halves of the angles at the center. From Theor. II, bk. II, and Axiom V of this book.

II. Circumferences, Chords and Arcs are to one another as the radii. For let the arcs CD, FE be similar, e.g. a sixth part of a circle: since the angle B is common, and the sides CB, DB are equal, as are also FB, EB, the triangles FBE, CBD will be similar: by Theor. III, cor. 2; therefore the chord CD will be to the chord FE as the radius CB to the radius FB; and, dividing the arcs equally at G and H, CG will be to FH as CB to FB; and, continuing the bisection, CP will be to FR as CB to FB: but to equal arcs correspond equal chords, by Theor. IV, bk. 2; therefore the arcs also have the same ratio as the radii; and all of them together, that is, the circumferences, are to one another as the radii.

III. Similar figures inscribed in a circle have to one another the duplicate ratio of the radii. For let FE, CD be homologous sides in similar figures inscribed in a circle: these have the duplicate ratio of the sides FE to CD; therefore, since FE is to CD as the radius FB to the radius BC, by the preceding Cor., the single Triangles, and the whole figures inscribed in the circle, will have the duplicate ratio of the radii FB, CB. (b)

Ee                                             IV.

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 33.

(b) Eucl. bk. XII, prop. 1.

[p. 50]

IV. Circles also have the duplicate proportion of the radii; for the Triangles BCD and CFE have the duplicate proportion of the radii CB and FB, by the preceding Cor. Let the arcs be bisected at G and H. The similar Triangles inscribed, CBG and FBH, will also have the duplicate [proportion] of the radii. Likewise, the bisection being made again at P and R, M and N, all the similar triangles inscribed in the circle will have the duplicate proportion of the radii: by the preceding Cor. But the circles are equal to the whole sum of the triangles that can be inscribed in them (for if any space were left over in the circle, another triangle could be inscribed by bisecting the arc; and so the sum of all the triangles would not be understood to have been inscribed, contrary to the hypothesis); therefore circles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their radii. Hence whatever was said in the Corollaries of Theor. VI on similar rectilinear figures must also be applied to circles. (a)

Moreover, just as Surfaces, which consist of a twofold dimension, namely breadth and length, have, if they are similar, the duplicate proportion of the Diameters, or of the homologous sides, so similar bodies, such as two whole spheres, have the triplicate proportion of the same, since they are made of a threefold dimension, namely breadth, length and depth. For example, if the Diameter of the earth is quadruple the Diameter of the Moon, the surface of the Earth will be four times quadruple, that is, sixteen times the surface of the Moon; and the whole terraqueous body will be four times sixteen, that is, sixty-four times, greater than the body of the Moon. Likewise, since the diameter of Venus appears as the tenth part of the diameter of the Sun, its apparent circle will be the hundredth part of the whole circle of the Sun; and so, when Venus comes between us and the Sun, it will appear like a spot on the Sun. And whoever knows these things has the most open access to all the natural disciplines.
