51 Nor does it matter that the attractive force of the mountain is not sensible in comparison with the other force, that of the earth; for, granting that it is held insensible when compared with that, is it nevertheless to be reckoned such if it is regarded relative to a body hanging in the air from the summit, and hence not far from a part of the terraqueous globe; if it is regarded as conspiring jointly with the earth in the same downward motion? Then: if the earth impedes every other attraction, how can it happen that, in the presence of these forces, the surging sea is attracted by the

Moon? when yet the waters are both nearer to the earth, and also compose it as a part of the terraqueous globe, and the mass of this globe exceeds that of the Moon.

But let what has been said suffice for you to have tasted the Newtonian system of attraction, as they say, with the tips of your lips. For it was not my intention (which would be impossible) to weigh it in its entirety in a few little pages: it is indeed a mystery impenetrable to those who are not initiated in the higher mathematics. The system of Newton is defended rightly and deservedly by very many most illustrious and most weighty philosophers, whom you ought to consult if you are lovers of good

Philosophy.

## CHAPTER VIII

The elementary, or sensible, physical systems, and the chemical system.

52

There were some of the Ancients, called Elementarians, who said that one element only was the first principle of natural things. Of these Thales of Miletus held water, or the moist, to be the principle of things (j); Xenophanes, earth (k); Anaximenes, air

(l); Heraclitus, fire (m). Others laid down two elements. Among the Moderns, Eller,

Fellow of the Berlin Academy, holds water as the passive principle, from which air and earth come to be, and fire as the active (n). The principal system of the

Elementarians was founded by Empedocles. He took as prime matter the four common elements, namely earth, water, air, and

(j) In Plutarch, On the Opinions of the Philosophers, bk. 1, ch. 3.

(k) Sextus Empiricus, Against the Physicists, bk. 1, sect. 360.

(l) Plutarch, bk. 1, ch. 3.

(m) Plutarch, loc. cit.

(n) Dissertation on the Elements. [p. 27] and fire, but as their form, their combination [o]. Others held otherwise: for nothing (as Cicero says) can be thought up so absurd that it has not been said by some one of the philosophers.

53 Chymia, which by the Moderns is also called Chemia, that is, the art of resolving bodies, is said to have been invented by Hermes, and is therefore also called Hermetic. It was greatly illustrated, not only with a view to preparing medicines but also to explaining the principles of natural things, by Theophrastus Paracelsus, called the Father of the Chemists. The chemists, then, are the Spagyrists, or Empirics, who are occupied with the analysis of bodies and seek nothing else by their art and operations than to unfold the principles joined and bound together in mixed bodies and, once unfolded, to subject them to the senses themselves. The object of this art is every sensible body, and it is divided into three classes, or kingdoms, or families, as they themselves speak, namely the animal, the vegetable and the mineral. And what they draw out of these, chiefly by the help of fire and through menstrua, or dissolvents, those are for them the principles of bodies, according to their axiom: that anything is constituted of those parts into which it is resolved. Their principles are numbered five, namely Mercury, Sulphur, Salt, Water and Earth. The first three are called active, the last two passive.

54 Mercury, or spirit, is a subtle, penetrating and volatile liquor, which usually comes out of bodies first when fire is applied; on which, according to its greater or lesser dose, the growth and corruption of bodies depend; and from which the motions of all mixed bodies immediately proceed. Hence it is plain that the mercury of the chemists is a substance far different from quicksilver, which is otherwise also called mercury. Sulphur they call a certain fat, oily substance, through which mixed bodies that abound in it are able to catch flame. Salt is a savory substance [because it is the origin of savors], which can be diluted by water and liquefied by fire. It is divided into fixed and volatile, acid and alkali: the former does not fly off in the fire, though it is dissolved and melted; the latter flies off and is dissipated by heat. It is called acid because, placed on the tongue, it affects and twitches it with a certain sense of sharpness known to all. Alkali is that which is of a looser texture and of a taste as it were burning, and broken up by many passages; whence, if it is mixed with an acid, it produces a great ebullition. Therefore every body is called alkaline which cannot be mixed with an acid without exciting a great effervescence.

55 Water, which is also called phlegm by the chemists, is a fluid substance, extremely moist, odorless, insipid. Earth, lastly, the damned earth, which is also called caput mortuum, is not much the concern of the chemists, who almost neglect it; it is a dry, fixed, insipid, solid and powdery substance, which remains after the said liquors and the fixed salts have been extracted. These are the five elements of the chemists, which

are

(o) Diogenes Laertius, bk. 8, sect. 76. [p. 28] are admitted by them as the principles of bodies. Here I note in passing that the op‐

erations of the chemists are by no means to be neglected, nor indeed to be held of no account. For it must be confessed, as Du Hamel says [p], that Physics has taken great increases from the labors and experiments of the chemists. Hence many arts very useful for life have flowed. What is to be determined about the system of the

Elementarians and of the chemists we shall see later.

## CHAPTER IX

Our doctrine on the internal principles of bodies is set forth. 56

I   say, first: The physical nature of matter seems to consist in this, that it is a substance impenetrably extended, consisting of primordial parts that are most minute, and these homogeneous as regards substance, but unequal and diverse as regards bulk, figure, motion and like affections. Proof, by parts. The physical nature of the matter of natural bodies is placed in that by which it has the capacity, as first subject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite, and which it is known to have both by reason and, so far as is permitted, by the experience of the senses; but by this very fact, that matter is a substance impenetrably extended, it has, and is understood to have, whatever is required for it to be able, as first subject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite: therefore. The minor is plain:

for, this being established, it is capable of motion and rest, of varied disposition, composition, texture, and other affections of this kind; from which results, as will be plain hereafter, the substantial form with which it constitutes the natural composite.

57 The second part of the proposition is evident: for since matter in the composition of bodies is understood to be something first, as belongs to the notion of a first principle, it is therefore rightly asserted to consist of primordial particles. That these particles are most minute the stupendous divisibility of bodies, to be weighed hereafter, demonstrates to evidence; but now, in confirmation of this matter, we shall employ only two experiments.

58 The most illustrious Boyle observes [q] that one grain [*] of copper, dissolved in spirit

[p] Tract. 1, General Physics, Diss. 3, ch. 5.

[q] De mira subtilitate effluviorum, ch. 3.

[*] An ounce contains 480 grains. [p. 29] spirit of sal ammoniac, imbued so great a quantity of water with a blue color, and that a conspicuous and saturated one, that it contained 256806 parts equal to that little grain. The most learned Fr. Francesco Lana testifies [r] that as much gum lac as would suffice to fill a walnut shell tinges with an intense color such a quantity of water as is enough to imbue a thousand paper leaves on both sides with the same color. Since, then, on any one leaf a thousand millions of colored points can conveniently be marked, there will be on all those leaves 1,000,000,000,000 visible colored points, distinct from one another. These things certainly prove that the parts of matter are most minute. Next, that these smallest parts are unequal in their magnitude, and diverse in figure and motion, is manifest from this, that this inequality and diversity of the most minute parts must be asserted in order that the sensible qualities and operations of any natural body may be rightly and conveniently explained.

59 These most minute parts of bodies, finally, can certainly be homogeneous, and not diverse as regards substance, since it is by no means required that they be substantially diverse in order that from their union bodies may emerge whose sensible qualities are diverse from one another, and whose operations are quite dissimilar. For composites can be made from those primordial parts of matter whose sensible qualities and operations are quite diverse from one another, although the parts themselves differ not at all from one another as regards substance: for since they are of unequal magnitude and diverse figure, they can be artfully disposed among themselves in diverse ways; finally, some of them can be moved in diverse directions within the whole that they constitute, and others be at rest in it, which quite suffices for bodies endowed with dissimilar qualities to be capable of being composed of them: therefore those parts can certainly be homogeneous.

60 I say, second: The essential, or substantial, form of natural bodies devoid of life, if it is regarded physically, is nothing different from that disposition, congruence and proportion of the particles of which the bodies themselves are composed intrinsically and as to their essence. Proof: given a certain disposition, proportion, etc., of the parts of matter, and everything else taken away, a corporeal being, or a substantial composite specifically distinct from others, is understood perfectly well: but by substantial form nothing else is understood than that ground by which this composite is actually such, specifically different from others, and by reason of which it has these special effects and properties: therefore. The major is proved by the example of a plant: given precisely a certain disposition, organization, etc., in the particles of matter, an excellent account is had of how the nutritive sap is sucked up, distributed, etc., and why such a vegetating body is a plant and not a stone, etc., without there ever being need to recur to anything else in order to explain these phenomena, these attributes of the plant: therefore.

(r) Magisterium naturae et artis, vol. 1, tract. 1, ch. 1, Obs. 3.

[p. 30]

61 The same reasoning holds in the remaining bodies. For if (as Du Hamel rightly says (s)) we wish to designate the form and species of gold, we shall adduce its properties: that it is the most ductile of all, that it is not dissolved in aqua fortis as silver is, etc. And a skilled goldsmith, when he has seen those qualities come together in some body, will not doubt that it is true gold, nor will he be anxious whether there is in it some absolute form of gold. For were that form withdrawn, so long as those endowments remained, it would be pure gold: and the same is the reasoning for all bodies; therefore the essential, or substantial, form of bodies devoid of life is nothing different from a certain aggregate of sensible qualities, which arises from a certain disposition, motion and other affections of the parts of matter. To these is added that, from a substance extended, impenetrable, mobile, divisible, yet everywhere like itself and uniform, things most dissimilar can spring up if it is variously configured, determined, modified.

62 For just as from the varied drawing of little lines, dissimilar only in situation, posture and figure, all the letters of the alphabet come forth, which, variously placed, make innumerable words, and can be permuted in such a way that, having made the calculation, the excellent geometer Tacquet (t) does not hesitate to affirm that a thousand millions of writers could not in a thousand millions of years write out all the permutations of the 24 letters of the alphabet, even if each of them finished 40 pages daily: so too the homogeneous parts of matter, disposed in diverse mode, figure and situation, and connected and combined in diverse order, produce that incomprehensible variety of things which the Infinite Creator has displayed in reality, and which so many most acute men who have lived since the founding of the world have not been able to attain even in thought.

63 To these arguments greater strength accrues from the analogy that exists between the mode of operating of nature and that of art; for the works of both, however great the difference that separates them, yet agree wonderfully in this, that in both the ground by virtue of which they are composites in a certain class of corporeal things, and both are and come to be, falls back on certain modifications, coordinations, motions and textures of the parts of matter, and consists in the complex of qualities and affections of this kind. Now, from the axioms established above, our system of the physical nature of matter and of form must be confirmed.

64 That system is to be preferred which is simpler and explains the properties of a natural body from fewer principles (Axiom II). Likewise, that which unfolds more of the things pertaining to Physics, and expresses the reasons of the phenomena not merely by general notions, but sets forth the nature and affections of bodies specifically and to the capacity of the mind (Axiom III & IV). In which, finally, nothing is asserted or assumed that it would never be possible sufficiently to comprehend in thought or to explain

(s) General Physics, tract. 1, Diss. 1, ch. 2, Concl. 2.

(t) In Verdries, General Physics, Tract. 1, §. 3.

[p. 31]

(Axiom V). And such is our system, inasmuch as it excludes the multiplicity of so many semi-substances and, when nature is considered, lays down a homogeneous matter: in which (as will be plain in the course of the Physics) the nature and affections of bodies and the causes of effects are rendered in a way accommodated to our understanding, and by distinct notions; which, finally, repudiates abstruse mysteries never to be explained, as everyone will understand from the discussion of the systems: therefore it is necessary that our system should prevail in Physics.

65 From what has been said you will infer I. That in our opinion form is not an absolute entity, but something modal and relative: for that texture, proportion, combination, etc., of the parts of matter, in which form consists, are mere modes. You will infer II: that if this name substance is taken for a being existing by itself, the essential form of natural composites devoid of life (for we are speaking only of these) is not entitatively a substance, as is self-evident. You will infer III, that the said form, properly speaking, is neither produced, nor made, nor generated, as the Angelic Doctor excellently says in very many places; for everything that is made, says St. Thomas (u), is always a composite, but form is not a composite. We are by no means speaking of the rational soul, which is truly and properly the form of man, and is created by God alone.

66 Material form, therefore, or essential form, is not produced, nor made, nor generated, but the composite is: for since the said form is nothing else than that disposition, proportion, texture, etc., and these are nothing else than something modal, form cannot be made except improperly, inasmuch, namely, as it is so denominated from the production of the composite; for when the parts of matter are joined, variously disposed, etc., which is for the composite to be composed or generated, there are necessarily in them those presences, dispositions, etc., which we call form; form, therefore, is not made otherwise than insofar as the composite is made or generated, which can best be set out in an artifact. You will infer IV. that for form to be contained in the potency of matter is nothing else than that the parts of matter can be variously disposed and conformed. You have an analogy in a statue, which, before it is made from wood, is contained in that wood in potency, inasmuch, namely, as the wood can be formed into a statue.

67 You will infer V. That matter and form are really distinguished, not indeed entitatively, since form is not an entity but something modal, as we have said, nor by the major real distinction, but by the minor real distinction, or modal distinction. When the idea of one thing positively and completely excludes the idea of another thing, then we say that they are distinguished by a major real distinction; thus body and soul are distinguished. The minor, or modal, real distinction is that which is found between a thing and the mode of the thing itself, as the distinction of body from figure, which has already been stated in the Ontology too. But everything that does not subsist by itself

E                                            is

(u) Metaphysics, bk. 7, lect. 7 & 8; pt. 1, q. 65, art. 4, in the body of the article; and in other places. [p. 32] is not properly a being, but a mode of a being, since to subsist by itself belongs no less to

a substance, or thing, or being, than to inhere belongs to an accident, or mode of a being.

## CHAPTER X

By inescapable arguments drawn from Tosca (x), substantial forms that are absolute entities, as they are commonly defended by the Peripatetics, are struck from the roll of Philosophy.

68

I    say, first: substantial forms of bodies devoid of life, such as are absolute entities,

entitatively distinct from matter, and incomplete substances in the Peripatetic sense, are of no use in Physics, and can be of no help for explaining the causes of natural things, and accordingly ought to be banished far from Philosophy. Proof.

For what experiment will be assigned that has ever been explained by their help?

What have they contributed to understanding the impressions of the air, or the actions of earth, sea or fire? What phenomenon of nature has ever been set forth by the help of these same forms? Turn over, for all I care, the authors who have toiled at uncovering the hidden secrets of nature, and you will find none who has called in the help of the said forms to accomplish it: therefore.

69 I say, second: the said substantial forms by no means agree with the principles of natural Philosophy, especially the Aristotelian. Proof 1. Every entity existing in the nature of things, and which is outside God, is produced; but such substantial forms, if they were given, would exist outside God in the nature of things: therefore they would be produced; but they are not produced: therefore they do not exist. The subsumed minor is proved, 1. because this is the express doctrine of

Aristotle and of the Angelic Teacher. For the first, in bk. 7 of the Metaphysics, ch. 8, text 26 & 27, proves at sufficient length that the form is in no way made, but only the composite, and concludes the proof of this matter thus: it is manifest, therefore, that neither the species is made, nor whatever the form ought to be called; which afterwards, in ch. 12 of the same book, text 32, he extends to accidental forms as well.

Moreover, in

(x) Philos., vol. 3, bk. 1, tract. 3, prop. 35. [p. 33] in bk. 1 of the Physics, text 64, he says: It is manifest from what has been said that everything that is made is always composite. The Angelic Doctor defends this very point in the places cited [§. 65]. Indeed, this very thing is shown most clearly also by the testimony of Cicero, who, since he knew Greek to a marvel, and understood Aristotle and Plato and the others, whom he had read attentively, much better than even all the common Peripatetics gathered into one, says in more than one place that the Peripatetics and the Academics differ in names but agree in substance; and since it is clearer than daylight that the Academics in no way admitted such substantial forms, we must say that Aristotle, in expounding physical things, never took refuge in such forms.

70 Proof 2. Whatever is produced outside God is produced either by creation or by generation; but substantial forms are produced neither by creation nor by generation: therefore. The minor is proved as to its second part: if forms were generated, they would be made out of something existing in them; but this can be nothing else than matter: therefore they would be made out of matter existing in the forms themselves: therefore the forms themselves would coalesce out of matter and form. I will frame the same argument about the form of the form, and so on to infinity: therefore, to avoid an inconvenience of this kind, it must necessarily be said that form is neither generated nor made, and consequently is not an absolute entity, as the Peripatetics contend.

71 They reply: the form is truly not made when the composite whose form it is is generated, but is educed from the potency of matter, and therefore is not created. But against this: for to be educed from the potency of matter does not befit a form that is entitatively a substance: therefore either that form is not entitatively a substance, or it is created when the composite is produced. The antecedent is proved: that a form is educed from the potency of matter is nothing other than that it is so made that it is necessary, at least in the natural order, that a subject exist in which it is produced and conserved: therefore a form which is educed from the potency of a subject necessarily depends on it in becoming, in being, and in being conserved, which is the same as saying that the form inheres in the subject; but to inhere in a subject befits only a physical accident, because a physical accident inheres in a subject and depends on it, at least by the forces of nature, in becoming, in being, and in being conserved: therefore, taking substance as it is taken by the Peripatetics, namely for a being existing by itself, a form that is a substance in this sense cannot be educed from the potency of matter. For to exist by itself and to inhere in a subject are wholly opposed modes of existing, as is evident.

72 Proof 3. Every substantial entity really distinct from others can properly be made and generated; but form, according to Aristotle and St. Thomas, cannot properly be made and generated [§§ 65 & 69]: therefore it is not a substantial entity, but only a mode modally distinct from matter. Proof 4. If the said entitative forms were given, they would be annihilated in the destruction of the composite; but they are not annihilated: therefore. The major is proved: an entity which ceases to be according to its whole being is annihilated,

E2 [p. 34] but the said forms, in the destruction of the composite, cease to be according to their whole being: therefore.

73 They reply that the said forms are not annihilated although the composite is destroyed, because their subject remains. For annihilation is the ceasing of a thing with no subject remaining; destruction, on the contrary, is that in which the subject always remains, as is clear from the definitions. But against this: for these very definitions are arbitrary, and by no means consonant with common notions. For who, unless he clings tooth and nail to Peripatetic prejudices, would not grasp that a thing goes into nothing when it no longer exists in the nature of things? And what does it matter that the subject (namely a wholly different thing) remains, so that we should use the word not of annihilation but of destruction? as though there were in reality some difference whether we speak in this way or otherwise. We shall therefore be offering mere words, and Philosophy will not be advanced a nail’s breadth by these circumlocutions and logomachies.

## T H E A R G U M E N T S O F T H E P E R I PAT E T I C S A R E A N S W E R E D

74

Obj. 1, against 1. It implies a contradiction that the parts of matter should be homogeneous, or of the same nature, and should differ from one another as to figure, bulk, etc.: therefore either they do not differ from one another, or they are not of the same nature. I deny the antecedent: for although the parts of matter do not differ as to substance, since all are homogeneous, they differ nevertheless in their artful dispositions, and no repugnance is found in this: for all admit that very many molecules, or parts, of gold, certainly of the same nature, can by art differ in affections of this kind, while some are made cubical, others spherical, etc.

75 Obj. 2. If the parts of matter differ from one another as to bulk, figure, etc., then matter is not indifferent to receiving all forms: therefore it will not be a determinable principle. The antecedent is evident: for one body, e.g. air, by the very fact that it has dissimilar properties, must also comprise particles, by which it is constituted, different from those of fire. Reply: by the very fact that the most minute parts are apt for a most diverse combination among themselves and demand none in preference to another, it is sufficiently understood that matter is indifferent. The four and twenty letters we use differ in figure and magnitude; yet who would deny that of themselves they are indifferent to being gathered into definite words, or to being bound by no laws, to being constrained into verses by the laws of meter, or to composing a more freely flowing speech? We by no means contend that it belongs to the notion of matter that the very same parts which are in one composite should, with no change at all supervening, constitute any other.

76 Obj. 3. It belongs to matter to be the first subject of all natural changes, and of bodies of incredible variety and discrepant [p. 35] from one another; but matter, which is everywhere of the same kind and not of diverse nature, cannot accomplish this: therefore. I deny the minor. For all variety must be derived from the varied disposition, combination, etc., of matter, that is, from form. Thus from the juices of the earth, by the mere percolation of their parts transmitted through the fibrils of a tree, bark, flowers and fruits are born. From foods likewise chyle, blood, bones and flesh, which differ greatly from one another, are formed by the mere transposition of parts, a new order, etc. Accordingly the variety of bodies coheres most aptly with a matter homogeneous as to substance.

77 You will insist. If the parts of matter are supposed homogeneous, from their addition and conjunction there would not result some new essence, but a certain homogeneous integral whole, which would not be of a different nature from one part of it; just as, when we add water to water, we do not make another essence, but extensively increase the same essence of water that is found in any drop; but this is against experience: therefore. It is confirmed: if a musician joined two voices like each other in all respects, he would by no means make a diapason; for this it is necessary that they be of diverse nature, the lower, namely, double of the higher: therefore the same must be said in our case.

78 To 1, I deny the consequence: for in order that a composite specifically different from others may be produced, it suffices that the parts of matter be of diverse nature, not indeed substantial, but only modal; that is, it suffices that they be diversely figured, diversely extended, etc.; which is very different in the addition of water to water: for what is added is of altogether the same nature as the other, namely of the same figure, of the same state, namely of fluidity; and from the addition no new combination is made, no new texture, and consequently no new form and essence, but only the same water becomes more extended.

79 The confirmation of the argument, however, rather confirms our opinion; for the voices that compose a diapason do not differ essentially, but only accidentally, namely in quantity and motion: for the lower is greater and moves more slowly, the higher shorter and quicker; for the diapason, or octave, consists in this alone, namely that the lower voice moves twice as sluggishly as the higher, so that the latter performs two vibrations in the time in which the lower completes only one. Just as, therefore, the species of this consonance, the diapason, coalesces from the combination of voices diverse only in motion and magnitude, so from particles of matter diverse in magnitude, figure, etc., all the species of things can arise.

80 Obj. 4. If we say that matter is a substance consisting of parts diverse in bulk, figure, etc., it is not the essence of matter that is explained by us, but body itself: therefore. The antecedent is proved: it is the nature of matter that it is not complete; but the particles of which matter consists are complete: therefore. I distinguish the minor: they are complete in the character of matter, I grant; in the character of a natural composite, or sensible body, I deny. By us only the essence of matter physically considered is set forth:

[p. 36] in the character of matter it is something complete; but in the character of sensible body it is not completed except by the form, which arises from a certain complex, order and proportion of the parts.

A RG U M E N T S AG A I N S T T H E S E C O N D C O N C LU S I O N .

81

Obj. 1, the principal argument of the Peripatetics. In the Sacrament of the Altar the accidents of bread and wine remain, but the substantial form of bread and wine does not remain: therefore the substantial form is something besides a certain aggregate of accidents. I distinguish the major: the accidents remain, taken in the

Peripatetic sense, for accidental forms, or absolute qualities inhering in a subject, I deny the major; in the Theological and Dogmatic sense, taken for species, which in an ineffable and plainly miraculous way deceive us, I grant the major. And, having roundly granted the minor, I distinguish the consequent: the substantial form is something besides a certain aggregate of Peripatetic accidents, I let the consequent pass; besides the aggregate of accidents such as are so called by the Moderns, that is, besides the texture and combination of the molecules of corporeal matter, I subdistinguish:

where such a texture and combination is really given, I deny; where it is not really given, but nevertheless so appears to the senses as if it were truly given, I grant.

82 The matter comes back to this, that we understand the accidents of bread and wine in the Most Holy Sacrament of the Altar not to be true corporeal qualities, abstracted from the body of the bread and wine and left without a subject connaturally proper to them, but mere appearances (if I may so speak), or species of bread and wine, under which the most true Body and the most true Blood of Christ the Lord lie hidden. We, therefore, taught by the Orthodox faith, deny that the substance of bread and wine lies beneath them after the consecration; but, taught by Philosophy, we shall deny that those things which appear are true accidents.

83 It is, therefore, a Dogma of the Catholic Faith that in the Venerable

Sacrament of the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ the Lord exist truly, really and substantially. So it was expressly defined in the Council of the Lateran (y), in that of Constance (z), in that of Florence (a) and in that of Trent (b), against Berengar,

Calvin and other impious Innovators, who dogmatize no less falsely than wickedly that Christ the Lord is contained in the Eucharist only in sign, or figure, or virtue. It is also a Catholic Dogma that by virtue of the Consecration there takes place a real conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the blood, of Christ the Lord; which altogether wonderful and singular conversion the Catholic Church transubstantiation most

(y) Under Innocent III, ch. 1.

(z) Sess. 8.

(a) In the Decree of Union.

(b) Sess. 13, ch. 1, & Can. 1. [p. 37] most aptly calls. This transubstantiation, moreover, as the celebrated Theologian Honoré Tournely (c) excellently says, has no example in nature, because it is singular; nor can it be comprehended by human reason, because it is wonderful; it lies wholly hidden in the mysteries.

84 It is also altogether most certain that the most Sacred body of Christ the Lord (and the same must be said of his blood) is in the Eucharist Sacramentally, namely in such a manner as, although we can scarcely express it in words (as the Council of Trent wisely admonishes), we must nevertheless most steadfastly believe to be possible to God (d). That mode of existing, indeed, has no example in created things, and is full of miracles, and is therefore deservedly called Sacramental, that is, a mode which belongs to the Sacrament alone. Let these things that have been said suffice for the Peripatetics to see that the most Sacred Dogmas of our Religion are kept safe and sound by us.

85 But since they leave no stone unturned to brand the opinion of the Modern Philosophers on non-substantial forms as heretical, and to persuade the unlearned that the Catholic Dogma of Transubstantiation is overthrown once the opinion of the Moderns is posited, it is worth the trouble to add some things, so that they may see that they have no right whatever to think us guilty of violating the faith. In the first place, then, I should have to count very many Catholic Philosophers who most steadfastly defend the opinion on forms in the very words in which it has been set forth and proved by us, without their Works ever having been proscribed by the Church; nay, they have been approved with the highest praise by great Theologians. Let it suffice to name some. Klaus, Macko, Regnault, Paulian, Scherffer, Lanis, Corsini, Hamel, Purchot utterly explode the substantial forms of the Peripatetics. From the family of the Minims, Maignan, Saguens and Jacquier; from the illustrious family of the Minors, the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia, who suffices for a thousand; from the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, the celebrated Tomás Vicente Tosca, and very many others from the French Oratory.

86 What of the fact that this doctrine is publicly defended throughout all Europe, and at Rome especially, in the Universities and Colleges, before the Roman Pontiff himself? Let us now hear the illustrious Melchior Cano. I think (says the celebrated man) that the testimony even of many Scholastic Theologians, if other learned men contend against them, is of no more weight for producing belief than their reasoning; that is to say, that in a Scholastic disputation a Theologian ought not to be overwhelmed by the authority of the greater number, but that if he has a few Men with him, provided they are weighty ones, he can surely stand against very many (e). Among the Theologians, moreover, there are not a few who expressly teach that the opinion of the Moderns on non-substantial form agrees perfectly with what the Church holds concerning the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist, and that it can therefore, without harm

to

So the most Eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church Pierre d’Ailly (g). So the most learned Prelate Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (h). So the celebrated Lodovico Antonio Muratori (i). So Father Vanrroy (j). So the most renowned light of the Augustinian Order, Lorenzo Berti (k). So the celebrated Noël Alexandre (l).

87 But it is better to hear the most learned Theologian of the illustrious family of the Preachers, Hyacinthe Serry [m]: “Why should I relate other things” (says the celebrated man)? “Are the systems of the recent School to be subjected to the rash censures of certain Theologians? Most philosophers now, following Descartes, place the essence of physical body in the extension of quantity, and hold that substance itself is in no way distinguished from quantity; and the Church, as I know for certain, permits them to philosophize thus. Why then do you brand them with censures? And those whom the common Mother cherishes as sons, do you curse as heathens and publicans, because they seem to you perhaps to shake the faith of the most holy Eucharist? Your study and zeal for the House of God I praise highly and commend: but I would have it be according to knowledge. You will be by far a better Theologian if you reconcile the system permitted by the Church with the faith of the Eucharist.

88 “This will perhaps be done not unfittingly if you say that the conversion of the substance of bread which is wont to take place in the Sacrament of the Eucharist has been defined by the Church, but that the mode of the change has not been so defined; and that the Mystery stands just as well if, the substance being changed together with the quantity, only the external sensations produced in our senses remain (as Descartes thinks), as if, the substance alone being changed, the true quantity remains with the other accidents, as the Peripatetics judge. And that for this reason the Fathers of Trent used the word species for what remains when the substance has been taken away, when they could have named them accidents: namely, so that by the word species they might signify simply those sensations which both Cartesians and Peripatetics profess to be produced in our senses alike, whether the quantity, being undistinguished from the substance, perishes, or, being distinct, does not perish. If you do not say this, but charge the Cartesians with violating the faith until the Church passes sentence against them,

you

What do the Peripatetics say to this? Let them see to it themselves.

89 “For it is not enough” (says the celebrated Cano) “for passing sentence of heresy to have touched upon the heresy itself by suspicion; but a certain comprehension is needed, so that we may judge of errors without error” (n). “Let the Peripatetics therefore cease” [I use the words of the celebrated Muratori] “to leave no stone unturned whereby they may defame the Modern Authors of new opinions, though these have nothing at odds with our Holy Religion, and tear their books to pieces, proscribe them, and present them to the Supreme Tribunals of the Church to be pierced through” (o).

90 Further, it must not be passed over in silence that that opinion too is held by many Peripatetics to be heretical which denies that quantity is really distinguished from corporeal substance. This censure, then: is it true or false? If true: then the Most Eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church Pierre d’Ailly, Auriol, Ockham, Biel, Melchior Cano, who deny that real distinction of quantity (p), are heretics, which surely no sensible person will say of such great Men: then likewise all those Scholastics are heretics, especially of the School of the Scotists, who think the quantity of bodies is to be placed not in their entitative extension but in their impenetrability, chiefly for this reason, that extension is not an absolute accident really distinct from corporeal substance, but substance itself is of itself entitatively extended, that is, with every accident excluded.

91 Then the Subtle Doctor himself is a heretic, who (q) steadfastly maintains (as the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia says) [r] that continuous permanent quantity consists in extension, that is, in the order of the parts in the whole, as Father Hiquaeus, the Commentator of Scotus, says. But if that censure is false (as in truth it is): then that one too must by the same right be held entirely false which the very same men pronounce on the opinion that denies absolute accidents. For what the Church understood by the name of species, or what at length their physical nature may be, has nowhere been handed down by her, just as it has nowhere been defined by her either that quantity too is comprehended under the name of species.

92 Nor let the Peripatetics say that the Council of Constance (s) defined against Wycliffe and John Hus that there are accidental forms in the Eucharist. For that is false: for, as the celebrated Verney says [t], it is established from the Historians that Wycliffe never said that there are no accidents in the Eucharist, but that under the accidents is the substance of bread, and not Christ.
