This error, then, the Council condemned; it did not say that the existence of accidents in the Peripatetic sense is a Dogma.

93 It is therefore established by Faith that under the species of bread and wine which present themselves in the Eucharist there is contained, not the nature and substance of bread and wine, but the true Body of Christ the Lord. But that the aforesaid species are absolute accidents, as the Peripatetics contend, the Church has nowhere defined: nor has any question of this kind ever been raised in the Church; nay rather (u), I nowhere read that the existence of the species in the Eucharist was doubted, which no one but a blind man or a madman could have denied. And so much on the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist. Let us dissolve the other arguments of the Peripatetics.

94 Obj. 2. If a natural composite devoid of life were composed essentially of particles of matter differing among themselves only in mechanical affections, it would not be one per se but one per accidens, as consisting by no means of an act per se and a potency per se: but this is false, just as it is also manifestly false that there is no difference whatever between natural and artificial composites: therefore. Dist. maj.: it would not be one per se, if by this name is understood a whole made of a double semi-substance, I grant; if a whole is understood which is primarily and per se intended by operating nature, I deny the maj.; and in the same way dist. the min.; I deny the conseq. In the opinion of the Moderns, which is also ours, the natural composite is one per se, and is more than sufficiently distinguished from the artificial one.

95 For it is one, because it is undivided in itself and divided from everything else. It is one per se, because the particles which constitute it are united together by the diverse intention of operating nature: whereas in an artificial composite the parts which constitute the artificial whole are coupled together by the direct intention of the artificer. It also consists of an act per se and a potency per se. For the mechanical affections are in matter by the direct intention of nature, and by the same intention they determine the matter itself to constitute a composite one in species. Nor do I think that anything else can be understood by the name of potency and act per se without a manifest begging of the question, as I shall say below.

96 Inst.: every natural composite is one substantial whole: therefore its essential form must be entitatively a substance; for otherwise it would in no way be distinguished from an accidental composite. Dist. antec.: it is one substantial whole, that is, intended per se by nature, I grant; in another sense, gratuitously devised by the Peripatetics, let it pass; and I deny the conseq. I call a substantial whole, then, that which, whatever at length the essence of the component parts may be, is regarded by operating nature primarily and per se when it acts; an accidental whole, on the other hand, that which either is not regarded by nature, as an effect by its cause, but only by art; or is regarded by it not primarily, but secondarily

only

(u) So the above-praised Verney, De Re Metaphysica. Rome, printed by Generoso Salomoni. [p. 41] only, and as it were for the sake of another thing directly willed by it. Thus a house, e.g., since it is made only by art, is an accidental whole. For the rest, these and other instances of the kind which fill the writings of the Scholastics rest on principles which are neither known from the terms themselves nor demonstrated from others, but which, first devised according to arbitrary hypotheses, were soon believed rather than known, when they had been entered on the authority of others in the register of axioms.

97 For what, I ask, do those words mean: One per se, a whole per se, a substantial whole? What do these mean: act per se and potency per se, or a whole being composed of act per se and potency per se? For if by the name of one per se, etc. a composite is understood which arises from a double semi-substance, what is in question is assumed as if certain, or the same is shown by the same, as they say. For to say a natural composite is one per se is just the same as to say a natural composite arises intrinsically from a double substance, or the form of any natural composite is entitatively a substance. But if by the name of one per se is meant that which is regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, it is plain that nothing can legitimately be inferred from this which would in the least favor establishing the existence of the forms of the Scholastics.

98 Obj. 3: one natural composite is distinguished substantially from another: but to be distinguished substantially is the same as to be distinguished by an entity which is a substance: therefore its essential form is entitatively a substance. Dist. maj.: it is distinguished substantially, that is, essentially, or in respect of something pertaining intrinsically to their essence, I grant; that is, by an entity which is a substance, I deny; and the conseq. For substance can be taken in two ways: first, for the essence of a thing; second, for an entity which does not need a subject in order to exist. Taken in the first way, those things are distinguished substantially which differ among themselves by something pertaining intrinsically to their essence. Taken in the second way, those things differ substantially which are discriminated among themselves by an entity that is a substance. That natural composites differ essentially is certainly true; that their difference arises from the form, all admit; but that they are distinguished substantially, namely by a form which is entitatively a substance, this must be proved by the Peripatetics, not assumed without hesitation as though it were most certain. For in this lies the question, as is plain.

99 Inst.: things that differ by a form which is entitatively an accident differ accidentally: therefore, for natural composites to differ substantially, they must differ by a form which is entitatively a substance. Dist. antec.: things that differ by a form, etc., differ accidentally, if that form does not pertain to the essence of the things compared with one another, I grant; if it pertains to their essence, I deny; and the conseq. For no one is unaware that a white thing, e.g., differs no less essentially by whiteness from everything that is not white than a man

F2 [p. 42] is distinguished essentially by rationality from that which is not a man. And the reason is that whiteness pertains intrinsically to the essence of a white thing no less than rationality does to the essence of man. Artificial dispositions, therefore, although considered in themselves they are accidents, nevertheless, because they essentially constitute a natural composite, bring it about that the composite itself is distinguished essentially, or substantially, from any other.

100 They urge: a natural composite is essentially a substance: therefore its form cannot be an accident; for it cannot happen that a substance be composed of an accident. Dist. antec.: it is essentially a substance by reason of the matter, I grant; by reason of the form, if it lacks life, I deny; and the conseq. A natural composite devoid of life, then, is not a substance except in the way in which man is called a corporeal substance; namely, just as man is not a corporeal substance except by reason of matter, and by no means by reason of form, so a natural composite which lacks life is a substance not by reason of form but only by reason of matter; and just as it is not repugnant that man should consist intrinsically of body and spirit, so it implies no contradiction that a natural composite should be essentially composed of substance and accident as of parts.

101 Obj. 4. If a form which is entitatively a substance is taken away, there is no longer any substantial generation: for matter is not generated: therefore a form which is entitatively a substance must necessarily be admitted. Dist. antec.: there is no longer any substantial generation, if by this name is understood the production of a composite whose form is a substance, I grant; if by this name is meant a composite which is regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, I deny the antec. and the conseq. For just as a natural composite can be regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, and so be one per se and a substantial whole, although its essential form is not entitatively a substance, so this very thing does not prevent its production from being rightly called substantial generation. But if this does not please the Scholastics, let them prove that substantial generation occurs in nature in the sense in which they themselves take it: for otherwise they hold as certain what is in question.

102 “To show,” says a most renowned man (x), treating of this matter, “that this argument is a mere begging of the question, we need only lay bare the equivocation that lies hidden in the word generation. For if by generation we understand the natural production of a new whole in nature, such as is the production of a chick from an egg, then rightly and deservedly it must be said that in this sense there is generation; but from this it could not be inferred that substantial forms also exist, since the disposition of the parts effected by nature is able to produce these new wholes and these new natural beings. But if by the word generation

is

(x) The author of the Art of Thinking, pt. 3, ch. 19. [p. 43] is understood, as is commonly done, the production of a new substance which had never existed before, namely of a substantial form, the very thing will be supposed which is in question, since it is clearer than daylight that one who denies substantial forms cannot grant that nature produces such things. Nay, so far is anyone from being driven by this argument to admit substantial forms, that he ought even to draw from it a wholly opposite conclusion, in this manner: if there were substantial forms, nature could produce anew substances which did not exist before; but nature does not produce such things anew; for such a production would be a kind of creation: therefore there are no substantial forms.” Thus far the praised Author.

103 Obj. 5. There is in every natural composite, not even excepting those which lack life, an active principle of diverse operations; but this principle cannot be anything but a substantial form, as it is taken by the Scholastics: therefore we must admit a form of this kind in every composite. Reply by denying the min.: for the active principle, if any exists in natural composites which lack life, is nothing but the subtler portion of those corpuscles of which the composite itself essentially coalesces: for there is no purely corporeal operation in nature which is not wholly accomplished through the motion of the subtlest corpuscles.

104 They say: it is evident that there is in each natural composite a force by which they recover their congenital qualities. For it is plain that heated water recovers its former coldness as if of its own accord: therefore some substantial principle, wholly different from the artificial dispositions of matter, must be admitted in them. Reply by denying the antec.: for it is manifest that the parts of a tree’s bark, if they have been somewhat scorched by a torch brought near, no longer recover their power of attracting moisture; that an egg violently shaken becomes wholly unfit for incubation; that an apple bruised in some part gradually rots. Nor does the example of heated water prove anything. For, as we shall say in its place, the recovery of coldness arises from without. But if it sometimes happens that some composite recovers lost qualities, we judge that this is to be derived solely from the living substance which is in it.

105 Obj. 6. Prime matter is not a physical and substantial act, because it is pure potency; but this act is the form: therefore prime matter is entitatively not the form: therefore the substantial form is entitatively distinguished from matter. Granting the whole argument, I deny the last conseq.; for although prime matter in itself is entitatively not form, yet from this it by no means follows that the form is entitatively distinguished from matter; for since the form is not an entity but a mode, it is only modally distinguished from matter.

106 Obj. 7. If form were nothing entitative, but only modal, creatures would produce nothing anew, and there would be no created agent,

[p. 44] but this must not be said: therefore. Proof of the conseq.: for a created agent does not produce matter anew, since it presupposes it; nor the form, which is neither generated nor produced: therefore it produces nothing. I reply that created agents produce neither matter nor form, but only the composite: for creatures, as St. Bonaventure excellently says (z), only bring it about that what was in one mode comes to be in another mode.

107 Obj. 8. Each natural being devoid of life has its own peculiar operations; e.g., in fire is found a particular operation of heating, and so of the rest; but operations of this kind cannot arise from matter, which of itself is inert and has no operative force, and is the same in species in all natural composites: therefore they proceed from the special form of each: therefore this is something entitatively distinct from matter. Dist. min.: the aforesaid operations cannot arise from matter considered in itself, I grant; from matter as modified, I deny; and the conseq.

108 Obj. finally: once our opinion is posited, there is no difference between alteration and generation; but there is one, for in alteration only qualities are produced, in generation a substantial form must be produced: therefore the substantial form is a semi-substance distinct from matter, as the Peripatetics maintain, following the opinion of the Arabs, against the doctrine of Aristotle. Reply: I deny the maj.: for in alteration the same sensible body remains which was there before, since only a few accidents perish from it and a few newly arrive, as when water from hot becomes cold, or when wax from yellow becomes white, or from soft hard. But in generation either all the accidents perish, or, if some remain, they are not enough for the sensible body to be called the same: e.g., when wax has been dissolved into smoke, it cannot be called the same body, although perhaps certain accidents which were before in the wax, e.g. the odor, remain in the smoke, because these few accidents are not enough to constitute wax.

109 Inst. If the matter stands so, generation and alteration are not distinguished except according to more and less; but more and less do not change the species, as the common axiom of the Schools has it: whereas diverse forms constitute diverse species: therefore the substantial form of a body devoid of life is not an artificial disposition of the parts. Dist. min.: more and less do not change the species where only a few accidents perish, I grant; where all or nearly all perish, I deny. But when a new form is given, nearly all the accidents which were in the former subject are destroyed, and new ones succeed, as when from wood comes fire, from wax smoke, etc. Hence a new species then results; for smoke is of a different species from wax, and fire from wood; for those things are judged to differ among themselves in species in which there appears so great a diversity

that

(z) On 2, Dist. 18, art. 4, q. 1. [p. 45] that what has been proved essentially of the one need not belong to the other. Let

these things that have been said suffice.

## CHAPTER XI

On the Secondary, or Sensible, Principles.

efore we propose our opinion, it is useful to affirm that three of the com110

B          mon elements, fire, water and earth, seem nothing different from as many

principles of the Chemists, namely mercury, phlegm and caput mortuum. And as regards mercury, Willis (a), Sennert (b), Boerhaave (c), Lémery (d) and many others assert that the mercury of the Chemists is that principle which is elemental fire, or a certain most subtle substance, wholly different from air, and from flame and common fire; but that water is not discriminated from phlegm, nor earth from caput mortuum, the Authors praised above show, with others. This laid down, let the conclusion be:

111 The sensible principles of bodies, besides the four common Elements, are rightly held to be also the twin principles of the Chemists, salt and sulphur. Proof:

from the fact that the said principles can be drawn out of individual bodies by means of resolution; which indeed, as regards vegetables and animals, no one will call into controversy who has observed the manifold operations of the Chemists and the diverse condition of the parts dissolved by them. An obvious experience in the burning of green wood declares this very thing: for the spirituous and most agile particles, released as it were from their bonds, are roused into flame and, torn away from the rest, fly off entirely; the sulphurous, or oily, ones feed the flame, and are gradually raised up, concreting into the part of soot; the saline ones partly go off into smoke, sharply stinging the eyes, partly settle in the ashes; the watery ones burst forth at the very beginning like the tiniest buds, to be dispersed into vapor; earth, finally, remains as survivor once the salts have been drawn out.

112 This very thing can be demonstrated of the mineral kingdom by the example of iron. The celebrated Boerhaave (e), speaking of iron dissolved in Rhenish wine, says: this is the highest remedy known to me so far in the art and

(a) De Fermentatione, ch. 2.

(b) Works, ch. 11.

(c) Elementa Chemiae, vol. 1.

(d) In the Chemistry.

(e) Elementa Chemiae, vol. 2, p. 445. [p. 46] and in nature for restoring the haematopoietic force (namely the force of converting chyle

into blood) to the human body, whenever this arises solely from the weakness of over-lax solids, and from a not very light, watery, cold and inert character of the humors. He adds that the medicinal power of metals is demonstrated chiefly by this experiment: for by no virtue of anything vegetable or animal, by no rule of diet, will anyone bring about in the said case what is accomplished by this Mars.

113 These things surely indicate that there reside in iron certain peculiar endowments, an active and at the same time subtle substance, to which the Chemists give the name of spiritus rector, and which we, consistently with what was said above, think to be the elemental fluid of fire, bound up in a certain ratio, quantity and texture with the other principles constituting iron: at least the same solution shows that such a principle is present in this metal; and hence we deduce by legitimate reasoning that water likewise is comprised in it, as being what all kinds of salts give off in evaporation. Sulphur is perceived from the odor of iron growing hot under pounding: finally, both its very hardness and the vitriol contained in iron, which is itself made up of earthy molecules, show that it is compacted of earth.

114 Finally, it will easily be shown convincingly that air is a sensible principle of bodies, if it be ascertained that those things belong to air which are required for the character of an element of mixed bodies. For in almost every analysis of composites, among the rest, aerial particles betray themselves: there is scarcely any humor, says

Boerhaave, with whose parts air does not mingle itself, scarcely any solid from which it cannot be drawn out by some art; these things being established, we deduce that the sensible principles of corporeal things are rightly held to be mercury, which we do not distinguish from fire, or the most subtle fluid; then air, salt, sulphur, water and earth.

The arguments are answered.

115

Obj. 1. The Elements of the Chemists are not found in mixed bodies in the form in which they themselves set them out to us: therefore they ought not to be sensible principles of bodies. The antecedent is proved: for fire by its action brings it about that the parts of a body show themselves after the resolution in another form and state than they were in the mixture; and therefore they must be considered as new substances, as it were, produced by fire: therefore. Reply by denying the antec. of the proof: for, as we shall say in its place, the whole nature of heat consists in a swift, disturbed and expansive motion impressed on corpuscles; and nothing else is effected but, first, an expansion, then a disturbed agitation of the parts in the body, when it conceives heat. Moreover it is evident that by means of the disturbed and expansive motion of the corpuscles which enter the pores of a natural composite no new substance can be entitatively produced, but only that the texture is loosened and the bond dissolved by which the component particles of the composite itself are held united together; and therefore the destruction of a natural composite, [p. 47] which is effected per se by the action of fire, or heat, consists not in the production of some new substance, but only in the dissolution of the bond by which the component parts are tied together.

116 I said that fire, or heat, effects nothing else per se, when it destroys a natural composite, than to dissolve the component parts. For I do not deny that it happens not rarely that some new substance, which had not been in the composite, is produced by the action of heat. But this is entirely per accidens; for a new substance comes to be if the heat is more vehement than the dissolution of the parts requires. For the particles, agitated beyond measure by too great a heat, are so mingled together, those of diverse kinds, that new concretions emerge from it, and hence new substances seem to be produced; but this does not prevent the aforesaid substances from being found in mixed bodies; for from bodies of the same species salt, sulphur and mercury, likewise of the same character, are perpetually extracted, which would surely not happen with such constancy if those substances were produced entitatively by heat; for what is effected by chance happens rarely.

117 Obj. 2. If salt, sulphur and mercury are secondary principles of the composite, the principles will be plainly innumerable, namely as many as there are species of those same things; but this is absurd: therefore. Maj. proved: for, to make mention of salt alone, there will be nearly as many salts differing from one another as there are composite bodies; for salt extracted from ash wood is caustic, that is, it corrodes by burning the flesh to which it is applied; extracted from other woods, it is not so: therefore. Dist. maj.: the principles from which the essential difference of the things themselves is taken will be plainly innumerable, I grant the maj.; those by which they are specifically distinguished, I deny the maj.; and dist. the min.: it is absurd to constitute as many principles by which things differ as there are species of the things themselves, I deny; to constitute as many genera of all the principles as there are genera of composites, I grant the min.; and I deny the conseq.

118 But from this argument nothing is gathered which does not utterly overturn the Scholastic hypothesis of principles. For the Scholastics posit as many genera of essential forms, or formal principles, as there are composites that differ from one another in species.

119 Obj. 3. Iron too must be admitted among the secondary principles: therefore. Proof of the antec.: for in the ashes of very many plants granules are found which go to the magnet and are fused by means of a burning mirror, no otherwise than iron filings, which at length flow together into metallic spherules, as the most renowned Geoffroy attests (f): therefore. The argument proves only that the component parts are bound to one another by so tight a bond that, even when divided into the most minute parts, they retain and preserve the integral nature of iron; but it does not prove that iron must be admitted among the secondary principles of bodies; for, as is attested by

G                                           the

(f) Histoire de l’Académie Royale, 1704, p. 37. [p. 48] the great Boerhaave, iron coalesces out of the very principles which are established by us, so that this metal has its place not among the principles or elements, but among mixed bodies.

120 And what forbids us to say, rather, that in the very act of combustion the fatty, saline, vitriolic-acid and earthy parts, which are the elements of iron, fused into one and joined together, coalesced into true iron? So that, consequently, the extraction of iron from ashes and clay is a true making of it. An argument for this may perhaps be what the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris (g) record: namely, that those composites which burn less readily and give off smoke more copiously, such as herbs and the harder woods, yield iron in their ashes in greater quantity than those which flare up suddenly and give off a more brightly shining flame.

121 Nor perhaps is the origin to be sought elsewhere of the granules of iron which, drawn out of a calcined human calculus by the most renowned Lister, were exhibited to the Royal Society of London (h). So that for this reason the most renowned Boerhaave opportunely came down to this opinion: If any metal, he says, is changeable, if any destructible, it will certainly be this one (i). Yet it will not be permitted to affirm the same of the elements established by us, concerning every resolution universally. For no one is unaware that it is wholly preposterous to draw a general consequence from singular cases, in which circumstances sometimes intervene.

122 Obj. 4. It is established by experience that sulphur especially, and mercury, are resolved into earth and water, as the most renowned men Du Hamel (j) and Du Clos attest: therefore sulphur and mercury are not of that condition of which they must necessarily be in order to be rightly and deservedly held for principles of things. Passing over the antec., I deny the conseq. For since those are laid down as secondary principles of a natural composite, their composition from others does not prevent them from being legitimately held for principles of this kind. However the matter may stand, then, concerning the composition of salt, sulphur and mercury, our assertion will be safe by this alone: that any natural mixture whatever, when it is corrupted by the action of heat, is resolved into earth, water, salt, etc., by their mere separation.

123 Obj. 5. Our opinion being posited, it follows that any particle whatever of a mixture is mixed of salt, sulphur, etc., and so to infinity; but this is repugnant: therefore. Reply: if the talk is of absolutely any particle that is in the mixture, it is true that each of them does not consist of all those things from which the mixture itself essentially arises. But to will that there is no particle in the mixture which is not mixed is just the same as begging the question. For to ask whether a natural mixture is so composed of earth, water,

salt

(g) Mémoires de l’Académie, 1705, p. 363.

(h) Journal des Sçavans, 1719, p. 378.

(i) Elementa Chemiae, vol. 2, p. 447.

(j) Vol. 4, Philosophia, ch. 20, no. 9. [p. 49] salt, etc., that the particles of those substances are formally in it, what else is it but to ask whether any natural mixture whatever is of such a nature that there are in it some particles which are not mixed?

124 Moreover, the argument must also be answered by the Scholastics. For if there can be no part in a mixture which is not mixed, there could also be no essential part in a composite which is not essentially composite: therefore matter and form must necessarily be composed essentially of other principles, which likewise must be essentially composed of others, and so on, so that it would be true, namely, that there is no part of a composite which is not composite; but this is absurd: therefore it is absurd also that there is absolutely no part in a mixture which is not mixed. Finally, note: not all the sensible principles are found in every composite, nor always in equal quantity, since experience teaches us that some bodies abound in salt, e.g., but contain less oil and mercury; in others earth holds the chief place; of others the greatest part is sulphur.

125 Obj. 6. Only the four common elements should be laid down as principles of natural body: therefore the Chemical ones are superfluous. Proof of the antec.: there must be as many elements as there are first and principal qualities; but these are four, namely heat, cold, moisture, dryness: therefore. I distinguish the maj. of the proof: if from those qualities alone all the affections, forces and phenomena occurring in composites can be derived, I grant; if they cannot be so, as in truth they cannot, I deny; and the conseq. For, as Sennert (k) argues excellently, an alteration and injury arising from manifest qualities cannot kill a man as suddenly as poisons do. Moreover, poisons in the least quantity can lie hidden unharmed in the body, and at length after a long time put forth their forces.

126 Thus a tiny quantity of the saliva of a rabid dog can remain unharmed in the body and protect itself against the action of our heat, and at length, after not only six but even many more months, induces most grievous changes in our body. And what we have said of poisons can be said of very many other things, whose forces are far greater and nobler than that they could be referred to the first qualities. Who will conveniently reduce the actions of the magnet to the first qualities? Who, again, will derive the manifold colors, odors, flavors, etc. from the said four qualities? These four elements alone, then, endowed with as many qualities, do not settle the matter.

127 Nor does it avail to say that from the mixture of several things it mostly comes about that forces emerge which were not at all present in the miscibles before the mixture; for we grant indeed (says the praised Sennert) that there is more in the composite than in any simple taken separately. Meanwhile it does not follow that there is more in the composite

G2                                      than

(k) In Klaus, vol. 1, Phys., p. 150. [p. 50] than in all the simples which enter into the composition. If several colors are

mixed, there arises indeed a color other than all the simples taken separately, but still only a color; never, however, from colors mixed in whatever way, will there come an odor, or a flavor, or another quality of a different species. So the temperament made of the four first qualities is indeed something other than the simple qualities taken separately, yet no other quality of another species arises from it; and however the first qualities are mixed, never will a color, or any other quality differing in species, come from them.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N I I I 

On the properties of bodies.

he principles of bodies having been established and their nature set 128

T         forth, those affections now come to be weighed which are derived

most proximately from the nature of body; and they are magnitude, figure, situation, divisibility, and above all motion: for a substance by its nature impenetrable acquires a certain mode of extension, or magnitude, and is divisible into parts; it likewise obtains some figure, and a position among other extended substances; and finally it is understood to be endowed with an aptitude for motion and rest. Moreover, it must be in place and time, of which

Physicists are also wont to treat. We shall give the more useful things.

## CHAPTER I

O N T H E M A G N I T U D E O F B O D Y.

It is shown in what the magnitude of body formally consists.

think it certain that the magnitude of a body formally consists in that 129

I      by which one body, if compared with another, is said to be equal or un‐

equal to it; just as by the name of quality is meant that by reason [p. 51] of which one thing is called similar or dissimilar to another. This established:

## 130 I say, first, against many Scholastics: the magnitude of body does not

consist formally in its impenetrability. Proof: it is plainly established that any two bodies agree in impenetrability in such a way that, if they are considered in respect of it, one can in no way be discerned from the other: therefore either the magnitude of body is not formally placed in impenetrability, or any two bodies whatever are equal to each other; but this manifestly opposes the truth: therefore the magnitude of body by no means consists in its impenetrability.

131 I say, secondly: the magnitude of body is nothing different from the entitative extension of the body itself. Proof: the magnitude of body is formally that in respect of which one body, if compared with another, is said to be equal or unequal to it; but it is by entitative extension that one body is said to be equal or unequal to another: therefore the magnitude of body is nothing different from its entitative extension. The maj. is evident: for two bodies a palm in length are judged equal for this reason, that the extension of both is the same; whereas bodies of which one is a palm and the other two palms in length are called unequal, because the extension of both is not the same, but the one is exceeded by the other in respect of it. Confirmation of the concl. It is agreed among all that rarefaction is motion toward greater, and condensation motion toward lesser quantity; but rarefaction is motion toward greater extension, and condensation toward lesser: therefore.

132 They reply: the magnitude of body consists indeed in extension, but in solid, or impenetrable, extension. But against this: because, when impenetrability is prescinded and extension alone is posited, the foundation of equality and inequality is had: therefore impenetrability in no way pertains to the formal notion of magnitude; just as, for altogether the same cause, it is certain that the hardness of a body does not concern magnitude. Surely hardness does not pertain to the formal notion of magnitude for this reason, that two bodies can be unequal and at the same time equally hard: therefore neither does impenetrability concern magnitude in any way, since two bodies can be unequal and at the same time equally impenetrable.

## CHAPTER II

On the Figure and Situation of bodies.

he extension of any body is limited by terms, or surfaces, which en133

T         close the matter proper to the body. That order and position which

the surfaces bounding the volume of the body have among themselves [p. 52] is called figure, by which a body is said to be spherical, cubical, etc. The exterior conformation of a body, then, is called figure, which namely does not pertain intrinsically to the nature of the thing, and can be common to altogether diverse bodies; but the figure of the parts themselves, constituting a body definite in its kind, which in wax, e.g., must doubtless be other than in iron, is called configuration. Situation is a certain posture, order, combination, texture, or artificial disposition of the molecules themselves in the whole which is intrinsically constituted of them.

134 The surfaces of bodies can be varied in altogether manifold ways. This prodigious variety of figures, moreover, is confirmed by innumerable experiments of the Physicists, of which we shall select the more useful. Keep some drops of the best vinegar on a fragment of glass for some hours, so that they partly evaporate; then look at them through a microscope: you will observe innumerable salts, nearly all pointed. If you keep vinegar in some vessel exposed to the air for some weeks, and more quickly in summertime, you will see with the microscope innumerable, as it were, most tiny eels running about hither and thither. From these, however, it is plain that the sharp taste of vinegar draws its origin not from the eels, as some have thought, but from diverse salts.

135 Put a drop of pure water on glass, and in it dissolve thoroughly a little common salt reduced to powder; after all the water has evaporated of its own accord, observe the drop with the microscope: you will see the salt reduced into crystals of cubical figure. If you dissolve sugar in the same way, you will observe crystals of nearly round figure. Richard Mead, in his Mechanical Account of Poisons, placed upon glass a very small part of the venomous juice which is emitted from the tooth of a viper when it bites, and in a short space of time it was changed into most slender and extremely sharp crystals, which were so rigid that they remained for a month without any change. From the figure and hardness of this poison, then, is to be derived its untamable nature, which sometimes scarcely yields to remedies opportunely applied. If a portion of crushed pepper is kept for some days in a vessel full of water, innumerable animalcules of diverse kind and diverse figure are observed with the microscope.

136 Insects figured in other ways are detected in stagnant water into which bits of cut hay, of chaff and of various plants have been thrown: certain animalcules are seen like globules, others longer and turning themselves round in a circle; in some, feet are distinguished; some are seen ringed like worms; and, in a pleasant spectacle, the greater are often observed to pursue the lesser so as to devour them.

137 If you collect the parts emitted spontaneously, or drawn out of bodies by art with the help of fire, you will notice that they are of the same nature, and produce the same effects, as the bodies themselves. Thus the vapor of water, collected, gives water; the vapors of sulphur and of camphor restore sulphur and camphor anew. But these things would not happen if the parts of bodies did not

[p. 53] have, and when released did not preserve, the same figure. The parts of water and of other vapors can be observed if bodies evaporate in a small room closed on all sides, into which only a ray of the sun passes to illuminate the vapors. In this way it became known that the parts of water are perfectly round. Many other things worth noting are found in the writings of Leeuwenhoek, Robert Boyle, Martin Lister, Erasmus Bartholin and John Freind, which Authors you will be able to consult when you have the means and the leisure.

138 Since, then, any part whatever of matter, or of body, has its peculiar figure, necessarily, while the parts of some body are actually separated, its surface must be increased. For when the parts are disjoined, and each is contained by its own surface, because it has figure, those internal surfaces of the body by which the parts touched one another become visible, and, together with the old surface under which the whole body was contained, compose the entire surface of the body cut into parts. When, therefore, a body is divided into several parts, its surface is increased while the same mass, or solidity, remains. Wherefore, since the same matter remains and the surface of the body is increased by the continued separation of the parts, the surface will acquire a greater ratio to the matter of the body.

139 From this, moreover, are explained several phenomena which are very often observed when some fluid, such as air, fire or water, acts upon bodies. The action of fluids follows the ratio of the surface of the body; for the greater the surface of the body, the greater the quantity of fluid that acts upon the body. Hence it is excellently explained why a wind which cannot lift a cubic foot of marble carries up in a moment of time several cubic feet of sand to a remarkable height, namely a weight a hundred times greater than the first. For a cubic foot of sand is the same as a cubic foot of marble cut into as many parts as there are grains of sand; but the wind can exert a greater force on marble in powder than on a cubic foot of the same; it will therefore lift a cubic foot of sand, nay several feet of sand, and will not be able to raise a whole foot of marble.

140 In the same way is explained the very great medicinal force of quicksilver, or mercury, for driving out stubborn diseases. A drop of mercury is easily resolved into innumerable most tiny globules, as will be plain if you throw upon it the rays of the sun collected by a concave mirror or a crystal lens. Wherefore its surface will quickly be increased to a wonderful degree within the body, and, this being increased, the mercury will more easily be driven by the fluids of the body into the vessels, and with the force acquired will expel the morbid matter from them; or it will easily open for itself an entrance into the smaller vessels, and so will at least deplete them, whence the circulation of the fluids will become more unimpeded, by which the body recovers from long-lasting diseases. Mercury, then, does not operate by its own weight, as most think, but by its divisibility.

141 From the figure and situation of bodies many phenomena can be explained [p. 54] and these no less useful than pleasant to know, of which we shall set forth only some, so that from those which are now to be set forth by us very much light may come to what we shall afterwards say on Statics and Hydrostatics. All bodies, then, are seen to have a certain gravity; hence it comes about that stones, e.g., descend until they are held up by meeting other bodies. They begin to be held up, moreover, when their center of gravity is prevented from descending. The center of gravity, moreover, is the point placed in any heavy body by which, if the body is suspended, all its parts will keep whatever situation you have given them, and so will be in equilibrium. E.g., if a staff or an iron rod is suspended by a thread at its middle part, and each part of it is in equilibrium, that point from which it will be suspended will be its center of gravity, since its parts on either side will be of equal weight.

142 But if that rod is not everywhere homogeneous, that is, of the same nature, suppose if in one part it is of iron and in the other of wood, its center of gravity will not be in the middle of its extension, but will recede from it toward that part of the matter which is denser. Wherefore the center of gravity and the center of magnitude, or of extension, do not always coincide in the same point, but only when the matter of the heavy body is homogeneous: e.g., in an iron globe the center of extension, or its middle point, which is equally distant from the individual points of the surface, can also be conceived as the center of gravity, since the matter in the iron globe is everywhere homogeneous.

143 Now, when a heavy body tends downward, namely to the center of the earth, which they therefore call the center of heavy things, since all heavy things strive toward it, its motion, or descent, is directed along a certain line on which the center of gravity always stands; and for this reason it is called the line of direction, and is defined: the straight line which is understood to be stretched from the center of gravity to the center of heavy things. Now the Axioms are these. First: A heavy body resting on another remains at rest, if the body on which it lies prevents its center of gravity from being moved downward. For since the whole gravity of the body is as it were collected in one point, it cannot happen that the body moves downward if its center of gravity cannot move downward.

144 Second: a heavy body resting on another slips, if its center of gravity is not supported by that on which the body itself rests. For if the center of gravity is not supported, nothing prevents the center itself from tending downward, as the law of nature requires, and consequently the whole body from moving downward. A heavy body, then, can never fall unless its center of gravity falls. But that center cannot fall as long as the body is so placed on a horizontal plane that the line of direction is conceived to pass within its base. Third axiom: The center of gravity of any heavy body cannot ascend except violently; for it is against the law of nature that a heavy body should tend upward as it were of its own accord.

Let

[p. 55]

145 Let a heavy solid A rest on the horizontal plane D E (Fig. I) by its plane surface m n x, and let its line of direction a b fall within its base m n x. I say that it can then in no way happen that the body A slips downward. For it is evident that the center of gravity a is supported by the plane D E on which the body A rests; but a body cannot fall if its center of gravity cannot move downward [§. 43]: therefore the body A will not fall down. But let there be another body H G (Fig. II) whose line of direction Cd falls outside the base F G; it is understood that it will at once fall toward the side e, because, while the whole body is carried with a circular motion about F, its center of gravity C is continually descending: therefore it must needs fall [§. 144]. Moreover, the center of gravity C is not supported by the plane D E, since the line of direction Cd runs outside the base F G: therefore it is necessary that the body H G should tumble down [§. 144].

146 Hence the reason appears why some leaning towers do not fall, such as those of Bologna and Pisa, observed by me while I was traveling through Italy in the year 1767. The Bologna tower is square, 130 feet high (1). The Pisa tower is round, 138 feet high. The plumb line of the Bologna tower stands off from the base by an interval of 9 feet, while the plumb line of the tower of Pisa runs outside the base over a space of 15 feet. Yet they remain firm and stable, because the line of direction of each is within the base, and therefore neither can tumble down. Hence it also follows that slender bodies, such as a needle, for example, can by no means stand upon their point, for its base is too narrow; whence any inclination, however slight, any impulse of the air, however small, suffices for its line of direction to run outside the base.

147 Hence it is also gathered why a bucket A (Fig. III) full of water, suspended from a rod B C laid on a table, does not fall, provided another rod G D is set upright below the handle and against the end C of the first rod, perpendicular to the bottom of the bucket. For since both rods together with the bucket make one and the same body, the bucket cannot fall without the end B of the rod B C being raised, describing, namely,

But it cannot be raised without the center of gravity i, which is in the bucket, describing at the same time the arc i M, which it cannot describe without ascending upward against the tendency of heavy bodies (Axiom 3, §. 144): therefore the bucket will not be able to fall, but will necessarily hang motionless from the rod.

That foot, namely, contains 12 inches, the inch 12 lines, the line 10 particles, or points, and so the whole Paris foot will contain 1440 particles.

148 By means of the motion of the center of gravity it is also explained how it can happen that a body, while ascending, continually descends, which at first sight seems a Paradox. Let a triangle A B C (Fig. IV) be constructed of three pieces of wood, whose base C B is equal to the axes of two cones joined together by their bases G F. Under the base C B let two supports C D, B E be placed, shorter than the radius of the base of the cones G F. If those two cones are set upon the extremity A, they will seem to ascend into C B, where the elevation is greatest; yet the center of gravity will descend.

149 That this may be understood more plainly, consider the plane A B b (Fig. V) in which the center of gravity a of the two cones is found. This center is raised above the horizon by as much as the line a b, which is equal to p F. If the cone advanced upon F D, the center of gravity a would describe the line a p parallel to the horizon F D. But the cone in the IV. figure moves along the two planes B A, A C in such a way that its vertex x x is in B C, or in C (Fig. V): therefore in the motion of the cone the center of gravity a describes a C, that is, it continually descends, so that when it arrives at C, its center of gravity will have descended by as much as is marked by p C; but the motion of bodies is determined by the motion of their center of gravity: therefore if the center of the cones descends, as has been demonstrated, the cone must ascend. It is necessary, then, that the double cone should ascend along the two planes of the IV. figure.

150 The knowledge of the center of gravity and of the line of direction is suited to explaining many other things. A man, for example, who sits in such a way that his legs make a right angle with his thighs, and his thighs too are at a right angle with his trunk, will not be able to rise unless he first inclines his shoulders or draws his foot back, so that the line of direction may fall within the base of the feet. If a man stands touching a wall with his shoulders and heels, and resting on the ground only with the tips of his feet, he will not be able to bend himself unless he puts a foot forward; otherwise, when he bends, he must needs fall, because the line of direction then falls outside the base.

151 But it is enough to have touched on these things lightly: for if it were my intention to report all the things that are derived from the figure and situation of the parts, almost all the phenomena both of nature and of art would have to be heaped together here: for nearly all qualities arise from the figure and situation of the parts.

Chapter

[p. 57]

## CHAPTER III

On the divisibility of bodies.

hat divisibility is an affection proper to all bodies, as it is beyond 152

T           doubt, so it ought by no means to come into question here; the

Physicists consider only this: how far does that divisibility extend? This contemplation is indeed of the highest moment in Physics, and for that reason the modern Physicists have instituted very many experiments and have illustrated this subject in published writings. But can matter, body, or the physical continuum be divided to infinity, or must one at last come to a stop at indivisible parts? It is a controversy which, as Fr. Regnault says (m), has from the very rise of Philosophy tormented famous and most elegant wits without fruit. We shall approach the matter with this design: that, having set forth the state of the controversy, we may candidly expound what can seem certain in it.

153 That, then, is called a continuum which results from parts so joined that their extremities are one, that is, belong to altogether the same substance, as are the parts of wood, which compose the same single substance of the wood.

That, however, is called contiguous whose extreme parts are together, as when hands, or two bodies, touch each other. The parts of some composite are also said to be placed in succession, or placed side by side, when particles of another body, e.g. of air, lie between them, as are the grains in a heap of wheat. Those parts are called aliquot which, repeated some number of times, exactly equal the whole. Thus the foot is an aliquot part of the fathom, because, repeated six times, it exactly equals the fathom.

154 Those parts are called aliquant which, repeated any number of times, never exactly equal the whole, but either exceed it or fall short of it: thus a part four feet long is an aliquant part of the fathom, because if it is taken twice it exceeds the fathom, while taken once it does not yet equal it. Proportional parts are those which decrease in continued proportion; thus the fathom can be divided into two halves, and either of these into two others, and so on. The

Peripatetics and very many Cartesians judge the parts of the physical continuum to be divisible to infinity. Those who follow Epicurus and Gassendi defend the contrary opinion.

155 The defenders of the first opinion argue thus. Everything extended is divisible into parts; but every body, however thin, is always

H2                                   extended:

(m) Entret. Physiques. Entret. I. [p. 58] extended: therefore every body is always, and to infinity, divisible. The Epicureans reply by distinguishing the major: everything extended taken mathematically, they grant; taken physically, they deny. That is said to be extended mathematically which is considered only by reason of its dimensions, without regard to the condition and nature of the extended subject; that, however, is called extended physically which is considered as a certain physical substance endowed with a definite nature and condition. Whatever is extended can be divided mathematically and by the mind, but not always in reality itself and physically, since there can be a certain simple substance not composed of parts, namely the atom, which is the first subject of which all sensible bodies consist, and the last into which they are resolved. Thus far the Epicureans and Gassendists.

156 These, moreover, argue thus against the Peripatetics: If matter were divisible to infinity, a tiny body, such as a grain of wheat, would contain within itself infinite parts in act, for a body is conceived as divisible only into those parts which it contains; but this is manifestly contradictory: therefore matter, or the continuum, is not divisible to infinity. The Peripatetics reply by distinguishing the major: if matter were divisible according to aliquot parts, a tiny body would have, etc., they grant; if it is divisible only into proportional parts, each of which includes infinitely many others within itself, they deny. You have the state of the question.

157 But all these things (as Purchot and Klaus very well observe) (n) are of such a kind that, if only the reasons, and not the replies, are weighed, they seem on both sides to carry the force of demonstrations. So that it may therefore be permitted to pronounce this one thing: it is uncertain whether corporeal magnitude can always be divided, or whether all its division at last terminates in indivisible parts; which we assert all the more fittingly as we know the more certainly that for the advancement of Physics it is altogether the same whether the parts of the continuum are posited as indivisible or as divisible to infinity; for, for the principles of natural body and for explaining the phenomena in general, it suffices to show that any bodies whatever can be split into parts so minute that reason itself is astonished, which is to be proved by us as clearly as possible in the following proposition.

158 I say, therefore: bodies are actually divided, and can be divided, into utterly minute parts in an altogether stupendous manner. First, indeed, the diffusion of odor furnishes an argument of the extreme subtlety to which an odoriferous substance can attain. Beyond what we have said (§. 58), let an example be the calculation which Fr. Lana Terzi (o) carries out of the smoky exhalations that issue from a tiny grain of incense and occupy every point of a small room. The said Father therefore, supposing a room 20 feet long, as many wide, and rising to a height of 15 feet, affirms, having made the calculation, that the particles

of

(n) Pt. 2, General Physics, no. 128.

(o) Magist. Nat. & Art., Tract. 1, bk. 1, ch. 1, Obs. 4. [p. 59] of smoke actually contained in the room will be 75,000,000,000,000, all of which, though previously shut up in one tiny grain of incense, are nevertheless still so many that they can affect a man’s sense of smell.

159 Fill the vial A (Fig. VI) with a bent neck, which is called an Aeolipile, with rose water or any other fragrant water; put a fire under it, or the case B, in which there is spirit of wine with a lighted wick; the water will soon evaporate through the slender neck, and the odor will be diffused through the whole room, however large. After two or three minutes remove the vial from the fire and stop it up: the diminution of the water will scarcely be sensible, so that a very small quantity of it has been dispersed through the whole air of the room. Now, by a calculation made by the learned Fr. Giovanni della Torre (p), a man most perspicacious in searching out the secrets of nature, it has been ascertained that that very small portion of water which evaporated in the space of three minutes is resolved into 3,583,180,800 particles sensible to the nostrils, which truly surpasses all comprehension.

160 The odors of the fragrant fields of the island of Ceylon are carried toward approaching ships even at a distance of ten leagues. A tiny particle of musk so imbues other larger bodies — clothes, gloves, books — with its odor that they keep the odor for a very long time, and yet continually never cease to give off odoriferous parts. Many similar things are related by Boyle, Keill, ’s Gravesande, and other Physicists. Since, then, with so many odorous particles perpetually flowing off, no sensible loss of substance can be observed in many cases, these effluvia will have to be incredibly subtle.

161 Secondly, it is shown from tinctures. The said Boyle relates that he found by experience that if a grain of copper, dissolved and mixed with spirit of wine, is poured into a lamp whose wick, made of plume alum, is not consumed, a flame tinged with a blue color is produced for a whole half hour; and so new particles of copper continually succeed one another and produce the same color in the flame: so that we cannot sufficiently wonder by what means that particle of copper could have been cut up so minutely as to supply always new color, that is, always new particles.

162 Thirdly, the same is proved from the ductility of gold; for, as the most celebrated Physicist Réaumur (q) testifies, a cubic ounce of gold is beaten out by the gold-beaters into more than five hundred times a hundred thousand square leaves of the utmost thinness; but, what altogether surpasses every power of the imagination, if one of these leaves is wrapped round a silver cylinder and covers its whole surface, and the cylinder is then drawn gradually through several successively narrower holes until it is reduced to the thickness of a very fine thread, or of a hair, the surface of this very long thread will nevertheless appear gilded everywhere, which

certainly

(p) Elem. Physic., vol. 1, no. 135.

(q) Memoires de l’Academ., 1713. [p. 60] certainly cannot happen, as is shown when the calculation is made, unless a single grain of gold is extended to about two leagues.

163 Fourthly, an abyss of minuteness in matter is demonstrated from microscopic observations. Fr. Lana Terzi (r) relates that he observed a very white animalcule which had been invisible to even the most perspicacious eyes, and which, placed under a microscope magnifying twenty-seven million times, appeared equal to a grain of wheat: with a very swift motion it scarcely covered the length of a grain of wheat in twelve seconds of time. What, then, must be the wondrous subtlety of the steps, of the feet, of the eyes, of the pupil, of the blood, of the animal spirits in an animalcule of this kind! The same must be said of those very fine animalcules which are seen in cheese with the help of a microscope. How tiny, moreover, is the pupil of those animalcules, through which nevertheless far finer rays of light pass? How tiny are those parts which can be called animal spirits? If we consider these things, we must needs confess that something greater, and more than our faculty of imagining can present to us, lies hidden in the smallest things.

164 That most skillful investigator of Nature, Leeuwenhoek, observed in water kept for some days, with the help of an exquisite microscope, very small animalcules, thousands of which do not exceed the size of a globule of common sand. Now since any animalcule whatever is an organic body, let us weigh for a little how delicate and subtle must be the parts necessary to constitute it and to preserve its vital action. It is not easily conceived how in so narrow a little space there can be comprised the heart, which is the fount of life, the muscles necessary for motion, the glands, the stomach and intestines, and innumerable other members without which an animal cannot exist. Moreover, since each of the members mentioned is also an organic body, they cannot lack other parts necessary for their actions. They will therefore consist of fibers, little membranes, tunics, veins, arteries, nerves, and similar little canals, whose minuteness far surpasses the powers of the imagination. But almost infinitely smaller than these must be the parts of the fluid which runs through the little canals, namely the blood, the lymph and the animal spirits. What prodigies in the meanest animalcule, and what proofs of the Divine Omnipotence!

165 Nor do the works of nature alone manifestly demonstrate the admirable subtlety of matter: the most celebrated works of art also prove the same, and must with full justice fill us with admiration. The distinguished Derham (s), Fr. Klaus (t) and Sigaud de la Fond (u) relate that Oswald Nerlinger fashioned out of a peppercorn a cup in which were set twelve hundred little ivory cups, each of which was furnished with a stand

(t) Phys. Gener., pt. 2, no. 127.

(u) Leçons de Physique, vol. 1, p. 64. [p. 61] and adorned with a gilded rim, so much space being still left over that four hundred
