L AW S O F T H E P R E S S U R E O F F L U I D S .

414

Law I. Fluids comprised in vessels press them in the ratio of the height by which they stand above a horizontal plane, and of the breadth of the base which is opposed to their descent: their pressure is therefore to be estimated according to the compound ratio of the height and the base.

415 Firstly, a fluid contained in a uniform vessel A B C D (Fig. LI.) set up perpendicularly is urged along the direction perpendicular to the horizon, or to the bottom of the vessel: and not only the parts nearest the bottom, but the sum of all, which results from the breadth of the base B D and the height a B, exerts its force (by §. 412.). Therefore it is necessary that the pressure on the bottom be estimated from the whole mass, that is, from the height multiplied into the base.

416 Secondly: but if the fluid is comprised in a vessel M E N O inclined to the horizon (Fig. cit.), although the mass is greater, yet, since the parts of the fluid rest as it were upon the inclined plane a N, they therefore exert part of their gravity against the side, or length, of the plane. That force alone, therefore, acts on the bottom E N which is equal to the height a b, account being taken of the base. This is clearly set before the mind by dividing the mass of the fluid into columns, lines parallel to the perpendicular a b being drawn.

417 Thirdly: in a divergent vessel (Fig. LII.) the base c d is pressed no otherwise than if the fluid contained in it were in the cylinder e c d f: for it is clear that the columns m m, l l, etc. rest upon the walls of the vessel itself as on supports, and that only those rest upon the base which hang perpendicularly over it.

But these are defined by the height e c = f d and the diameter e f = c d. The bottom of a divergent vessel is therefore pressed just as if the fluid were committed to a cylinder of equal height and base.

418 Fourthly: it remains, finally, to be shown that in a convergent vessel the bottom K H (Fig. LIII.) is urged by the fluid itself no less than if the vessel kept everywhere an even breadth K Q T H. I wish to establish this principal head of

Hydrostatics by the very elegant reasoning of the illustrious Varignon (l): let the perpendiculars B M and C O be let fall to the bottom from the upper margins (B and C), opposite each other along the diameter; then let the portion K M of the base be divided into parts equal to, or smaller than, half the line M O, and in such a number as is always equal to the sum of the terms of a double progression beginning from unity, e.g. into 3, into 7, into 15, into 31, into 63, etc. Namely, let K

M be divided, if you please, into K U, U L, L M; and, M N and O N having been taken equal to each of these parts, let K Q, L R, A N, T H be drawn parallel and equal to B M or C O.

S                                    These

(l) Memoires de l’Academ. 1692, p. 16, Holland ed.

[p. 136]

419 These things being set up, the column of fluid B N will exert a balancing action upon the fulcrum M against the column E M, which is confined by the margin E D of the base: it will exert it (I say) just as the weight Z would do upon the balance E X, if its hypomochlion were at Y and the extremity E of its arm were held back by the margin of the tube K E D. Since, therefore, in this way the load sustained by the fulcrum Y would be double the weight Z (for the arms of the lever E X are equal, or depart little from equality), the support would accordingly sustain both the weight and, at the same time, a resistance equal to it; therefore it is necessary that the point M, or the portion L N of the bottom itself, be pressed by double the column B N; or the part L N will be urged just as if R N were an entire column of fluid and hung over the bottom.

420 Wherefore, if A N L E D is regarded as a column of this kind, it will be found similarly that, while the fluid balances itself upon the support L against the portion K E L of the fluid, held back by the margin K E of the vessel standing in its way, the part K N of the bottom must be pressed by the fluid A N K D B no otherwise than by the equal column Q N. In like manner the fluid A N, H, F C will press the part N H of the bottom just as if an equal column N T stood upon it. Wherefore the whole mass of the fluid B D K H F C will press the whole bottom K H with precisely that quantity of forces with which it would be weighed down by the fluid Q K H T, of equal height and of a breadth everywhere equal to the base K H. And this foundation of the pressure of fluids is confirmed, among other things, by an experiment in which several equally high tubes are set up and the bottom of each is pierced with an equal opening, to be closed with equal stoppers; for the outcome will make plain that the same force must be applied to sustain the stoppers of each, whatever figure or position these vessels may have.

L AW I I . F L U I D S P R E S S I N E V E R Y D I R E C T I O N .

421 That fluids strive downward, as do other heavy bodies, no one doubts. But that they also strive against the sides can very easily be traced back to, and explained from, the very pressure which is produced along the direction of gravity, and from the aptness of their parts for motion, their figure, minuteness and disconnection. For let a mass of fluid be understood to be divided into columns composed of most minute spherules touching one another in a very few planes. (Fig. LIV.) Since the parts of the column 3a yield most promptly to any pressure, and are very easily set in motion while they are pressed in a perpendicular direction, they would by no means keep this place and position of theirs unless they were held back by the molecules of the columns ab and 4c, and on every side. The smallest spherules are therefore pressed along their sides and points of contact: which must be concluded of all the columns.

422 Finally, from the pressure by which they are urged by the force of gravity, it follows that fluids also press from below upward, namely when, others pressing downward, they are raised up, almost as in a balance the heavier solid lifts the other by its descent. Many indications establish this law, phenomena

[p. 137] that occur daily. From a vessel inclined to the horizon the liquid would not flow out if, like firm bodies, it exerted its force only on the underlying plane; a ship gaping at the side takes in water at that place, and the more quickly, the higher the water surrounding the vessel stands above the hole: a cask pierced in any part whatever affords an exit to the liquid.

423 By a single trial one may explore the pressure of fluids in every direction. For if several holes are made in a vessel, one looking perpendicularly down toward the horizon, another vertical to it, another let into the side, and a stopper of cork is fitted to each opening under the condition that it fit the hole exactly, yet can be removed by a rather light impression; then, the liquid being let in, it will be observed that the cork is pushed out by the water reaching the height of the opening, whether it was inserted in the bottom hole, the lateral one, or the one stretched out toward the top. L AW I I I . H O M O G E N E O U S F L U I D S A R R A N G E T H E M S E LV E S

AT A L E V E L , O R A L O N G T H E S A M E H O R I Z O N TA L L I N E .

424 Namely, all the parts of a fluid sustain one another mutually in equilibrium, not only along perpendicular lines but also along oblique ones. And as to the first there is no doubt, namely that fluids balance themselves along perpendicular lines; for one of the columns into which the fluid is thought to be divided cannot descend unless the neighboring and contiguous ones ascend: just as a weight in one pan cannot be depressed without the other in the other pan being raised at that very same time. In homogeneous fluids, certainly, it is evident that the momenta of the columns of the fluid are equal; for the striving of the parts toward descent, and their velocity, is equal in all, and so also is the mass, being of the same kind among them; the force for motion is therefore held to be equal in each.

425 Next, since (by Law II.) the pressure of fluids extends in every direction, the perpendicular columns are balanced by the oblique ones. Wherefore equilibrium will be obtained among all the parts of a homogeneous fluid; nor will one portion of it rise higher above the horizontal line than another. This indeed is not contrary to experience, by which it is known that a liquid rises a little at the lips of the vessel; or that, if the space in which the fluid is comprised is extended more widely, those parts which stretch from the extremes toward the middle go off into a convex surface; for the first proceeds from the very proportion of the liquid and of the sides of the vessel, and so from adhesion; the second depends entirely on the law of equilibrium, since, while fluids adapt themselves to the surface of the earth, it is necessary that, though in a smaller space they keep a straight line so far as the senses go, yet in a larger one they bend their surface evenly outward with respect to the center.

426 Law IV. Homogeneous fluids in communicating tubes (whatever position these may hold, and by whatever perimeter they may be defined) are balanced when suspended to the same height.

427 In the first place, if the tubes are endowed with an equal perimeter and are erected perpendicularly, the matter is ascertained. Next, if they are supposed to be inclined to the horizon,

S2 [p. 138] the reason of the equilibrium shines out no less (from Law I.). If, finally, the perimeters of the tubes are unequal, it is derived from the principles of Statics that the fluids will be in equilibrium if it holds that the ratio of the mass in the one is reciprocal to the ratio of the velocity in the other. But this ratio of mass and velocity is had in a fluid contained in tubes of this kind. For let the tube a b (Fig. LV.) be supposed to exceed the other, C d, a hundred times in breadth: it cannot happen that the fluid in the former is depressed toward e by the height of one inch without a motion taking place in the narrower one to the height of a hundred digits.

428 As, therefore, the mass of the fluid comprised in the wider tube is to the mass in the narrower, so reciprocally is the velocity in the latter to the velocity in the former: the momenta are therefore equal on both sides; and hence the equilibrium of the fluid in both. Now, that in homogeneous fluids this comes about when they obtain the same height is clear: for since the pressure is in the compound ratio of height and base (from Law I.), if the vertical section e f is regarded as a common base, and the horizontal line m n is drawn through it, and the perpendiculars m a, n d are erected, the pressure toward the base will be, on the one part, = e f m a, on the other = e f n d. But since the momenta of the fluid are equal (from what has been said), and the specific gravity (by hypothesis) is the same, and therefore in the mutual comparison of the pressure no account need be taken of it as though it were different, it follows that the pressure in each leg toward e f, tending in opposite directions, is equal, that is: e f m a = e f n d; and, division by e f being made, m a = n d will hold, or the heights are equal, and hence m n and a d intercept equal perpendiculars. But m n (by construction) is a horizontal line. Therefore a d, or the twin surface of the fluid in each tube, is settled at a level.

429 Law V. Heterogeneous fluids in communicating tubes of any figure and perimeter whatever, and inclined to the horizon in any manner whatever, persist in equilibrium when their heights are reciprocally as their specific gravities.

430 For let fluids be so arranged in the tubes that the height a E (Fig. LVI.) is to the height b F as, reciprocally, the specific gravity of the fluid G is to the gravity of the fluid g: I assert that they will rest in equilibrium. For since account must here be taken of the diverse gravity, contrary to what holds in homogeneous fluids, the momenta of each, and the pressure toward the common section B D, must be compared with each other in such a way that the difference of gravity is brought into consideration: although, where they are regarded separately and without comparison, the pressure of fluids (by Law I.) is estimated only from height and base; therefore equality of momenta will be obtained, and the equilibrium will stand, when the ratio of the distances from the center of motion is the same as that which is reciprocally the ratio of the gravities (by Princip. Stat. III.)

431 But the common section, or base, is understood as the center of motion; and the heights themselves are the distances from it; since

[p. 139] indeed (by the Law cited) the pressure and balancing of fluids, when they are regarded in themselves, must depend upon these and be derived from them. Heterogeneous fluids will therefore compose an equilibrium if their heights are reciprocally as their specific gravities.

432 Law VI. Fluids in actual flow, when they pass from a wider space into a narrower one, accelerate their motion in the very passage.

433 Let a fluid be supposed to flow out of a vessel under this condition, that the breadth of the space, e.g. of a cylinder, is ten times greater than the opening, which is called the lumen of the tube, from which the fluid bursts out: I say that the fluid will burst out at the opening with a velocity ten times greater than that with which it moved in the wider space. For let the fluid comprised in the cylinder be driven by any force whatever toward the narrower part, in such a way that in the interval of one moment it must traverse an inch of space. It is clear that a tenfold mass of fluid, relative to the diameter of the orifice, cannot be moved forward in this way without a portion of the fluid, equaling in height the space of a digit and ten times greater than the breadth of the orifice, being at the same time driven out thence through the narrower part. But a quantity of fluid one inch high, and containing the opening ten times in breadth, cannot pass through a space ten times smaller in the given interval of time unless its velocity grows tenfold; it is therefore necessary that the ten parts which the length or height of the digit comprises correspond in order to as many parts into which the breadth of the hole is divided, or be applied to them in the same moment of time. This cannot be done without an increase of the velocity to tenfold: since, as regards the velocity of motion, it is altogether the same whether a body = 1/10 of the space runs through, in a given time, a space ten times the body, or a corporeal mass ten times greater than the extension of the space is carried in the same time through a space = 1/10 part of the body.

434 Next, the same thing rests also on this ground, that when a fluid passes from a wider space into a narrower, the lateral parts strike against the narrowed walls of the opening and so meet with a hindrance to their own outflow; but, the fluid continually urging them and pouring itself more freely through the larger space, they are squeezed into the narrower path; and in this way it comes about that the parts of the flowing liquid that are to flow straight and freely through the orifice make a greater impetus and, having found an easy exit, at once leap out: for which reason it is necessary that the velocity of the motion receive an increase.

On

[p. 140]

O N T H E R AT I O O F T H E E Q U I L I B R I U M O F F L U I D S W I T H

I M M E RS E D S O L I D S .

435

Having just considered the pressure of fluids among themselves, there remains to be explained the ratio of their equilibrium with immersed solids. On this subject, after Archimedes (m), Galileo, Stevin, Mersenne, Boyle, Varignon, Mariotte,

Newton and very many others have treated: we shall weigh the matter summarily, embracing the doctrine in a few laws; before we connect these in order, it is necessary to contemplate a little what is, as it were, the nature of the immersion and balancing of solid bodies in fluids. Namely, a heavy solid cannot be immersed in a heavy fluid unless a volume of the fluid equal to the solid itself, which is received by the immersion, is moved from its station.

436 Except, however, if the body is spongy: for then the fluid in great part enters the pores of the solid; or unless, being immersed, it is easily dissolved; for in that case the particles torn from the solid will insinuate themselves into the pores of the fluid.

Wherefore, in order that immersion actually follow, the solid must by its weight overcome the resistance of the mass of fluid to be excluded from its place: whence it comes about that precisely so great a part of the solid body is to be received within the fluid as is the volume, or mass, which the solid can move from its place by its own weight; and that the immersion proceeds until that same volume is equal in weight to the immersed body. These things will be clearly understood if the fluid is divided in the mind into equal parts, or columns, and the solid body is thought to correspond to, and rest upon, one of them. This being understood, there follow, for a threefold condition, as many laws.

L AW S O F T H E B A L A N C I N G M O T I O N O F S O L I D S

I M M E RS E D I N F LU I D S .

437

Law I. If a solid body is of the same specific gravity as the fluid in which it is immersed, it will remain unmoved anywhere within the surface of the fluid, and in the place in which it has been set.

438 Since the solid and the fluid have the same gravity under equal dimensions, the solid behaves in altogether the same way as that volume of the fluid whose place it occupies. But this volume of the fluid, before the immersion, had kept its equilibrium with the other parts of the fluid, unmoved in its place. Therefore the immersed solid also rests in equilibrium with them. This will be clearly perceived if the fluid is conceived to be divided into columns equal to that on which the solid rests, and the volume of fluid expelled from its place is supposed to be torn away from the rest of its mass, the immersed solid being substituted there.

(m) The two books commonly called De insidentibus humido, illustrated with commentaries by

Federico Commandino.

[p. 141]

439 Law II. If a solid body is specifically lighter than the fluid in which it is immersed, it is sunk in it with only some part of itself.

440 For the fluid (by hypothesis) is specifically heavier than the solid. Therefore the fluid, taken under a smaller volume, will equal the solid itself in weight, so that this volume of the fluid equals only one part of the solid. But the immersion of the solid body reaches only so far, until the volume of fluid expelled is of as great a weight as the immersed body (by §. 435.); therefore a solid specifically lighter than the fluid is sunk into it with only some part of itself.

441 Law III. If a solid body is specifically heavier than the fluid, it is wholly immersed in it and seeks its bottom.

442 The solid is immersed until the volume of fluid thrust out of its place is equal to it in weight (by §. 435.). Therefore, if the expelled volume contains less weight than the solid body, the latter will be wholly immersed. But that volume of fluid is of less weight; for the solid body is supposed to be specifically heavier: the fluid therefore comprises less weight in a volume equal to it. The solid will therefore be wholly immersed. Further, once it is immersed by this law, since at any distance whatever from the bottom it holds that the column of fluid which is placed under the solid has a greater weight, and is able to press with a greater striving than the others, that column will not establish equilibrium with these: hence it will come about that the solid body nowhere stands unmoved, but hurls itself to the bottom of the vessel. Hence

C O R O L L A R Y. 443

Since the immersed solid excludes a volume of the fluid from its place, and this had been sustained in its position by the other parts of the same fluid, it is necessary that, where the solid succeeds into the place of the excluded volume, as much weight is sustained in the solid itself by those same parts of the fluid as the portion of the fluid moved from its position contains; and hence that the solid is, as it were, deprived of as much of its weight as is the volume of fluid that was excluded from its place when the immersion was made. This diminished weight of the solid is wont to be called respective, comparative, or apparent gravity; while the other, which belongs to the body in a space altogether void, is rightly called true and absolute.

444 Hence, since this gravity proceeds solely from the difference which exists between the specific gravity of each, that is, from the difference of densities, the respective gravity of the same immersed solid is therefore the same whether the immersed body is level with the surface of the fluid or is driven more deeply, the density of the fluid being supposed everywhere equal. Further, that which departs from the absolute gravity, or the loss of weight which the same solid suffers in different fluids, has the same ratio as the specific gravities of the fluids. But the losses which different solids undergo in the same fluid are to one another as the volumes themselves of the solids.

[p. 142]

PHYSICS,

PA RT I I I .

E L E C T R O L O G Y, or

O N E L E C T R I C V I RT U E .

here is perhaps nothing which in this age of ours has brought 445

T            greater honor and increase to the study of Natural science, or has

more keenly roused the wits of Philosophers, than the electric force, so that it seems shameful for those who inquire into the secrets of

Nature either to have entirely neglected this most beautiful part of Philosophy, as the Ancients did, or to have barely touched it lightly, as very many of the

Moderns too have done, for I know not what reason. Wherefore, so as not to pass over anything that pertains to this matter, with the most illustrious

Philosophers of all Europe, and especially the illustrious Paulian (n), carrying the torch before me, I have resolved to hand down this question, truly most useful and most pleasant, first of all in our America, by a more accurate method and with the greatest clarity I can.

446 In treating, then, this question of the causes of electric virtue, about which there has been dispute, with the greatest contention of minds, among the

Modern Physicists for nearly sixty years, we have chosen the following method.

I. We shall set down beforehand some definitions, which are rightly called the first notions of Electricity. II. We shall report the electric experiments which must necessarily be explained in any physical hypothesis. III. We shall hand down the various opinions of the more celebrated Physicists concerning electric matter, and shall point out their blemishes. IV. We shall disclose the opinion of the illustrious Paulian, which is ours too, and in it we shall attempt to explain the phenomena already reported. V. Finally, we shall propose, and try to answer, the principal arguments that are usually brought by adversaries against our opinion.

Chapter

(n) Grand Dictionnaire de Physique, under the word Electricité, from which, with a few changes,

we have excerpted this whole Dissertation.

[p. 143]

## CHAPTER I

On the notions preliminary to the question of electric virtue.

447

Notion I. An electric machine is composed, first, of a glass globe, whose diameter can be larger or smaller; second, of a wooden wheel, by whose means a rotary motion is impressed on the glass globe, which a dry hand rubs; third, of an iron tube, which has communication with the glass globe through very thin plates of brass; fourth, of silk cords, which hold the iron tube suspended horizontally; fifth, finally, of a stool of resin made in the shape of a cake, on which a man can easily and conveniently be placed standing on his feet. This machine is represented quite exactly by Fig. LVII.

448 Notion II. A body actually electric is a body toward which all very light bodies go, and from which they come back, such as ground tobacco, very thin leaves of brass, the little feathers of birds, etc. For electric virtue is usually manifested by attractions, repulsions, sparks, inflammations, agitations, etc.

Electric virtue betrays itself also by a blue flame, which is excited with a crackling from the electric body. We speak here of that species of electricity which we shall hereafter call total and perfect. Notion III. Of bodies, some are electric in themselves, and others by communication. Sealing wax (commonly lacre), amber, alum, diamond, crystal, and especially glass are bodies electric in themselves.

Metals, however, and living bodies are bodies electric by communication.

449 Notion IV. Bodies electric in themselves manifest their virtue whenever they are rubbed with cloth, or paper, or a dry hand. Bodies electric by communication, however, receive a perfect electric force whenever they have communication, through an iron wire or a hempen cord, with bodies electric in themselves and in act. Notion V. Bodies electric in themselves acquire no electric virtue, or as good as none, by communication; and conversely, bodies electric by communication acquire no electric virtue, or as good as none, by friction. Notion VI. All the bodies of this world without exception are, in all likelihood, electric either in themselves or by communication.

T                                  Chapter

[p. 144]

## CHAPTER II

On the principal electric experiments. 450

In this Chapter we shall only report, historically, the principal experiments which are usually made by means of the electric machine, and to them we shall subjoin, by way of observations, the less principal and, as it were, secondary experiments.

451 Experiment I. Let a circular motion be impressed by means of the wheel on the glass globe, while meanwhile it is rubbed with a dry hand. Let a tube made of white iron (commonly oja de lata), which has communication with the glass globe through some thin plates of brass, be suspended horizontally by means of silk cords. The iron tube will receive so great an electric force that you will at once see a little blue flame leaping out with a crackling from its bosom if you bring near it your finger, or a key, or, in a word, any body electric by communication.

452 Observations. I. The same iron tube, suspended by means of hempen cords, receives either no electric force or very little, however great the motion of rotation with which the glass globe is endowed. II. From an iron tube endowed with electric virtue you will excite no flame at all if you bring near it sealing wax, a little glass tube, or any other body electric in itself. III. If two hempen threads, parallel to each other, hang from an iron tube not yet endowed with electric virtue, these two threads will recede from each other and form an angle as soon as the iron tube receives electric force. Indeed, the angle made by the two threads will be the greater, the livelier the electricity of the tube. Hence these two hempen threads have the name of Electrometer.

453 Experiment II. Upon a body electric in itself, such as a cake of resin, let any animal be placed, and let this animal have communication, by means of an iron wire, with the tube of which we spoke in experiment I: it will receive so great an electric force, almost suddenly, that if you bring your finger near, a blue flame will burst out from it with a crackling, which will cause both you and it a pain so sensible that you would at once believe you had been lightly pricked with a needle.

454 Observations. I. At whatever distance from the iron tube the cake of resin is found, he who has been placed upon it will at once acquire electric virtue, provided he has communication with the electric tube through an iron wire or a wet hempen cord. II. He who is placed upon the cake of resin does not excite a flame from the electric tube with which [p. 145] he is in communication. III. If someone standing on the ground holds in his hand some metal vessel containing warm spirit of wine, and offers it to a man placed on the resin cake, this man, now electric, will set the liquor on fire as often as he tries to draw fire from it. IV. Exactly the same phenomenon occurs when the man who is now electric holds the metal vessel in his hand, and a man destitute of electric virtue tries to draw the flame.

455 Experiment III. All the lightest bodies, such as ground tobacco, the thinner leaves of gold or silver, small bird feathers, bran, etc., are now attracted toward a body endowed with electric virtue, now repelled from this body, now cling to this same body. Indeed, electric virtue manifests itself by the goings and returnings of bodies of this kind, the lightest ones.

456 Observations. I. If on the iron tube of the electric machine there is placed some metal dish containing the lightest bodies, all these little bodies will flee the iron tube as soon as the tube receives the electric virtue. II. If this same dish had been placed under the iron tube, the lightest bodies put on it would have been attracted toward the tube as soon as the tube received the electric virtue.

457 Experiment IV. Let there be a glass flask half full of water and covered on the outside with metal foil. In this flask let an iron wire be set up perpendicularly, reaching down to the bottom. Let electric virtue be communicated to this iron wire; experience establishes that if someone holds up this flask with one hand by its lower part, and with the other hand draws a flame from the aforesaid wire, both his elbows and his chest will be violently shaken (Fig. LVIII.).

458 Observations. I. Let the flask of which we speak be in communication with the electric iron tube, and if anyone, holding or even touching the lower part of the flask with one hand, draws a flame from the tube with the other hand, he will feel exactly the same shock. II. Let a good many men form a chain with joined hands. Let the first of them hold up the lower part of the flask with his hand, and the last draw a flame from the tube of the electric machine; all will be struck together, and at the same instant, with the same shock, both in the elbows and in the chest. An experiment of this kind was first made at Leiden; therefore this first experiment is commonly called La experiencia de Léyden [the Leyden experiment].

459 Experiment V. Let some part of the iron tube of the electric machine be wrapped in a rather thick paper. On a metal dish let a glass flask be placed communicating with the iron tube. Between the bottom of the flask and the metal dish let there be an iron wire; experience establishes that if someone, with the same hand with which he holds the iron wire, draws a flame from the paper wrapping some part of the electric tube, this very thick paper will be pierced with a very great crack.

460 Observations. I. If in place of the paper some bird is put,

T2 [p. 146] most certain death will be brought upon it by a few sparks drawn from its featherless head. II. In place of the flask half full of water, of which we were speaking in

Experiments IV and V, we can use a square of glass whose upper part and lower part are covered with some metal foil, extending, however, scarcely to the edges of the glass. This experiment is known under the name of the magic picture, or of Franklin’s pane.

461 Experiment VI. On the roof of some high building let a cake of resin, or of glass, be placed. On this cake let some iron rod be set up perpendicularly; experience establishes that if some cloud bearing lightning in its bosom hangs over this iron rod, sparks will be drawn from it in exactly the same way as if the rod had been in communication with the glass globe, actually being rubbed, of some excellent electric machine.

462 Experiment VII. Let the rubber of the glass globe be placed on a cake of resin: he will not only receive a sensible electric force, but will also draw a flame from the tube of the machine, now electric, to which he brings his finger. Let this last experiment not slip from your memory.

463 Observation. The same rubber, standing on the bare floor outside the cake, does not receive a sensible electric force. These are the principal experiments reported by the most distinguished men Nollet, Franklin, Beccaria, Paulian, and others, of which we shall try to give the explanation in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER III

On the Causes of Electric Virtue. 464

To assign the true causes of electric virtue: this has always been the task, this the toil, in Physics, as will appear from the following enumeration.

T H E O P I N I O N O F T H E M O R E A N C I E N T P H I L O S O P H E RS .

465

Electric phenomena gave the more ancient Philosophers no trouble at all. For they had ready at hand either some occult quality, essential and intrinsic to electric bodies, or else an innate horror of the vacuum. This last opinion prevailed in the

Schools; for very many among the ancients affirmed that the air is expelled by the electric effluvium, and that any of the lightest bodies whatever are drawn in through fear of a vacuum. This opinion ought to be refuted with laughter rather than with serious reasons.

The

[p. 147]

T H E O P I N I O N O F DE SC A RT E S .

466

Descartes treated of the causes of electric virtue expressly; for thus he speaks (o):

“From the manner in which glass was said to be generated, it is easily gathered that, besides those larger intervals through which the globules of the second element can pass in all directions, many small oblong chinks are also found between its particles, which, since they are too narrow to receive those globules, afford passage to the matter of the first element alone; and it must be thought that this matter of the first element, being accustomed to put on the shapes of all the passages it enters, is formed, in passing through those chinks, into certain thin and oblong little ribbons, as it were, which, since they do not find similar chinks in the surrounding air, keep themselves within the glass, or at least do not wander far from it, and, wound about its particles, flow with a certain circular motion from some of its chinks into others.

For although the matter of the first element is most fluid, yet because it consists of minute parts unequally agitated, it is consonant with reason for us to believe that some of its most strongly agitated minute parts continually migrate from the glass into the air, and that others return from the air into the glass in their place; but that, since those which return are not equally agitated, those which have the least agitation are driven toward the chinks to which no passages in the air correspond, and there, clinging one to another, compose those little ribbons, which ribbons for that reason acquire in the course of time determinate shapes, which they cannot easily change.

467 “Whence it comes about that if the glass is rubbed strongly enough to grow somewhat warm, they, shaken out by this motion, disperse indeed through the neighboring air, and enter also into the passages of other neighboring bodies; but because they do not find such easy ways there, they at once roll back to the glass, and draw along with them the smaller bodies in whose passages they are entangled … And what we have noted here about glass must also be believed of most other bodies: namely, that certain interstices are found between their particles which, since they are too narrow to admit the globules of the second element, receive only the matter of the first.” From what has been said it follows that Descartes admitted as so many principles the things that follow.

468 I. In any glass whatever there are larger pores and smaller pores; the latter afford passage to the matter of the first element, the former to the globules of the second element. II. The matter of the first element moves with more difficulty in the air than in the smaller pores of the glass. III. Because of this resistance of the air, the matter of the first element quickly returns into the glass from which it had come

(o) Pt. 4, Principles, art. 185. [p. 148] come out on account of the friction. IV. The matter of the first element and the

electric matter are in no way distinguished from each other. V. According to

Descartes, electric phenomena depend on a certain successive outflow of the matter of the first element from the smaller pores of the glass, and inflow of the same matter toward the smaller pores of the same glass, when it is rubbed with a dry hand.

469 Remarks. I. The things that were stated in nos. 1, 2, 3, 4 of §. 468 are laid down as principles gratuitously and without foundation. II. The outflow and inflow of the electric matter seem to be simultaneous rather than successive, as will be noted below. III. This peculiar opinion of Descartes about the electric matter evidently depends on his general system, which we have shown to be false, §§. 45 and

46. IV. For all these reasons the opinion of Descartes about the electric matter seems to us one to be rejected.

T H E O P I N I O N O F H O N O R É FA B R I .

470

Nor indeed did Honoré Fabri, who flourished in the same age as Descartes, propose a more probable opinion. For thus he speaks (p): “Amber and Spanish wax consist of much fire and of a fat juice, which consists, as it were, of filaments of melting amber: namely, those filaments are drawn out in length, and their viscosity and tenacity cannot be called into doubt … The parts of fire that are in the amber act continually on that viscous and pliant moisture, which then, by the force of heat, is rarefied and flies off in an exhalation, which is itself also pliant and viscous; hence it is drawn out into filaments, however insensible … Further, the aforesaid exhalation is emitted in the manner of a dart …

471 “Because, owing to the viscosity of the matter, the emitted thread clings to a pore, it comes about, through the violence of the impulse, that the thread, drawn out in length more than is due and greatly attenuated, either at length breaks about the middle, or indeed does not break, but after the strong tension derived from that first emission at once returns, likewise with impetus … You have an analogy in a stretched string: if it is let go, or breaks from excessive tension, its segments are drawn back toward the other extremity, to which it is fixed; hence if that segment whose extremity clings to the pore, and which is drawn back with some force toward the pore and the amber, falls upon very minute little bodies that can easily be moved, it carries them off with it and fastens them to the amber itself.” And elsewhere: “A rough body that is ductile under the hammer lacks electric force.” So, a hundred and thirty years ago, did Honoré Fabri think about electricity.

472 Remarks. In this opinion the phenomena of

(p) Vol. 4, Physics. [p. 149] of bodies electric by communication are not explained: for Father Fabri held that no

body at all, not even metals, can become electric by communication, as is manifest from his last words, already cited. II. It is not explained in this opinion whence so great an electric force arises in glass. For the author of this hypothesis affirms that sealing wax and amber are the most electric bodies of all, but in this place had not said even a single word about the electricity of glass. III, finally. In this opinion the phenomena are not explained, of which there is in this age so great an abundance that the electric machine affords an astonishing spectacle: therefore the opinion of

Honoré Fabri is to be rejected as insufficient for setting forth electric phenomena.

T H E O P I N I O N O F M R . D U FA Y.

473

The first in France who weighed the question of electric virtue with a certain order and method was Mr. Du Fay. His principal experiments are recorded in the

Memoirs of the Paris Academy of Sciences (q). He affirms that there is a twofold electricity, specifically different, namely vitreous and resinous. If there is a twofold electricity specifically different (he says), there will be a twofold electric matter specifically different; and if there is a twofold electric matter specifically different, electric phenomena will be very easily set forth, namely through the conflict of this twofold matter. Mr. Du Fay also holds that all the electric matter whirls in the manner of a vortex about the electric body, as about its proper center.

474 Remarks. I. The electric force of glass seems only to be more intense than the electric force of resin: therefore vitreous electricity and resinous electricity do not differ specifically; otherwise one would have to say that the most fervent fire differs specifically from a less fervent fire. II. There is no assignable experiment by which it is even probably intimated that some vortical motion exists in the electric matter: therefore the opinion of Mr. Du Fay about the electric matter is to be rejected as false.

## THE OPINION OF MR. DE MOLIÈRES

475

Toward the end of his Lesson XIV Mr. de Molières set forth his opinion; it is comprised under five heads, as it were. I. The electric matter does not differ from the little vortices of oil contained within any electric body whatever. II. By the rubbing of a dry hand the oily little vortices are forced to go out of the electric body into the air, and most of them dispose themselves in the manner of an atmosphere about the electric body. III. There spread themselves out in the air the

(q) Years 1733, 1734, 1737. [p. 150] the oily little vortices, and, on account of the perfect plenum that has persisted in na‐

ture from the beginning of the world, similar little vortices flow toward the electric body. IV. There are more oily little vortices in metals and in other bodies electric by communication than in glass and in bodies electric by rubbing. V, finally. From non-electric bodies there issues an insensible matter which ferments with the atmosphere of electric bodies, and from that fermentation arises the spark which we are accustomed to strike out of bodies actually electric.

476 Remarks. I. We shall demonstrate below that the electric matter is fiery; therefore this matter is distinguished from oil. II. Nothing proves that oil, a tenacious and viscous body, can be whirled and driven in such rapid little vortices. III. It is not probable that there is more electric matter in bodies electric by communication than in bodies electric per se. Indeed, experiments seem to indicate that the quantity of electric matter is very small in bodies which communication alone can render electric; for these bodies, when heated and rubbed with a rather dry hand, never give any sign of electricity. IV. The fermentation of which Mr. de Molières speaks seems to be a mere fiction: therefore his opinion is to be rejected as a hypothesis faulty in almost every part.

T H E O P I N I O N O F M R . J A L L A B E R T.

477

These things Mr. Jallabert asked to be granted him in his little work on Electricity

(r). I. There exists a certain elastic and thin fluid, filling not only this whole universe but also the pores of even the densest bodies. II. The parts of this fluid, like the parts of all fluids, tend to equilibrium, and therefore tend to fill the spaces in which some little voids are left. III. This fluid, wholly undistinguished from elemental fire, and shaken out by rubbing from the bosom of bodies electric per se, disposes itself for the most part in the manner of an atmosphere about bodies that are in a state of actual electricity. IV. This fluid is not of homogeneous density: for it is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; it is denser, e.g., in air than in water. V. A body actually electric receives from the surrounding air as many fiery particles as it supplies to it.

VI, finally. Elemental fire, of itself invisible, carries off with it the particles of the bodies from which it is forced to go out, and thus renders itself manifest.

478 Remarks. There are more things in this hypothesis consonant with the truth than foreign to it. This one thing is false, that the electric matter is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; for this matter is denser in

(r) Experiences sur l’Electricité avec quelques conjectures sur la cause de ses effets. [p. 151] in amber, glass, diamond, than in air, water, etc. Unless perhaps the distinguished

Author wishes a greater abundance of electric matter to be understood by density, which does not seem so absurd. All the other things in this hypothesis are either true or at least probable; but this opinion rests on a false foundation if it lays down as certain that the electric matter is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; therefore on this head it is to be rejected.

## THE OPINION OF MR. FRANKLIN

479

In the opinion of Franklin (s) these are the heads worth noting. I. The electric matter is specifically distinguished not only from elemental fire but also from any common matter whatever. II. There exists a repulsive force between the particles of the electric matter, and an attractive force between the particles of the electric matter and the particles of non-electric matter. III. An angular electric body very easily loses its electric matter through its angles. IV. A pointed non-electric body very easily snatches the electric matter from an electric body 10 or 15 inches distant.

480 Remarks. I. Nothing proves that electric fire is specifically distinguished from elemental fire. II. There is evidently a physical and immediate cause of electric phenomena, which we shall determine below: therefore it is not permissible to have recourse to the attractive and repulsive qualities of which Franklin speaks in his little work.

T H E O P I N I O N O F M R . N O L L E T.

481

This is the proper character of the Nolletian opinion: the simultaneous effluence and affluence, namely, of a certain most subtle matter. Thus did that most distinguished Man, who has deserved excellently of Electricity and of the whole of Physics, set forth this entire matter (t). I. The electric matter is nothing other than elemental fire, which is found more or less abundantly in absolutely all bodies. II. Every electric body, whether it has received this virtue by friction or by communication, is endowed with a certain fiery atmosphere, which extends itself to a greater or lesser density according as the electricity of the body is more intense or more remiss. III. From the bosom of the electric body fiery corpuscles continually flow out, of which an atmosphere of this kind is composed. IV. Not only from the air, but also from every surrounding body, there flows continually toward the electric

V                                                 body

(s) In the work entitled Experiences & Observations sur l’Electricité, faites a Philadelphie, translated by

M. d’Alibard.

(t) Essai sur l’Electricité, and elsewhere in various small works. [p. 152] body, e.g. toward a glass globe rubbed with a dry hand, a fiery matter which

abundantly repairs the losses that the glass globe suffers on account of the friction. V. A conflict exists between the effluent electric matter and the affluent electric matter, and from that conflict Nollet deduces the explanation of electric phenomena, as may be seen in the works which he published for this purpose.

482 Remarks. I. On account of the resistance and the elasticity of the air, some part, and that not a very small one, of the electric matter which, through rubbing and the motion of rotation, had been effluent from the bosom of the glass globe returns into the globe itself, or becomes affluent: for scarcely otherwise can it be explained why the electric virtue is livelier in cold and dry weather than in warm and humid weather. II. In the Nolletian opinion it does not seem possible to explain why a man placed in the usual way on a cake of resin cannot draw a little flame from the electric iron tube to which he brings his finger: for then a very great conflict exists between the matter going out of the electric finger and the matter flowing out of the tube, which is likewise electric: therefore not absolutely all electric phenomena are explained in the Nolletian opinion.

## THE OPINION OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED

PA U L I A N , W H I C H I S A L S O O U R S .

483

Our present Theory of Electricity rests, as it were, on two kinds of principles, of which some are received by absolutely all Physicists, while others are altogether peculiar to us. I. There is a certain electric matter. For indeed there are electric bodies: therefore there is a certain matter that confers this virtue on them. II. The electric matter is a certain most subtle and most fluid matter: for it penetrates within the densest bodies, such as metals, stones, etc. III. The electric matter is a fiery matter, since by the help of this matter spirit of wine is inflamed, a candle is lit, etc. IV. The electric matter is not of homogeneous density; for there are bodies of which some are more electric than others. V. Every electric body, whether it has received this virtue by friction or by communication, emits from its bosom fiery corpuscles, most of which dispose themselves in the manner of an atmosphere. And indeed the atmosphere of electric bodies is formed in exactly the same way in which the atmosphere of odoriferous bodies is formed; but the atmosphere of odoriferous bodies is formed by a true emission, as all agree: therefore the atmosphere of electric bodies is likewise formed by a true emission.

484 VI. As many fiery corpuscles flow toward the electric body as had flowed out of its bosom. For the glass globe does not lose its electricity after innumerable frictions and immense losses, [p. 153] which it has suffered; therefore it evidently repairs its losses. But the electric body cannot make good its losses unless as many fiery corpuscles flow toward it as had flowed out of its bosom: therefore, etc. Now as regards the principles that are peculiar to us in this matter, they are five in number.

485 I. Only some part of the fiery corpuscles going out of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand enters the iron tube of the electric machine; another part of the same corpuscles communicates itself either to the air or to the bodies standing round about on every side. For experience establishes that not only the tube of the electric machine, but also the very Rubber of the glass globe sensibly receives electric force, provided he is placed on a cake of resin.

486 II. The fiery corpuscles which go out of the bosom of the glass globe, and which do not enter the iron tube of the electric machine, render initially electric all those bodies which surround the machine on every side, even if they are not placed on resin, or glass, or anything similar, provided these bodies are electric by communication. And indeed the Rubber, placed on a cake of resin or of glass, is rendered sensibly, or perfectly, electric by the fiery corpuscles which go out of the bosom of the glass globe and which do not enter the iron tube of the electric machine: therefore by these same corpuscles the same Rubber, when placed on the floor, must be rendered imperfectly, or initially, electric: for in this situation he retains a true and ready power of receiving electricity by way of communication. And what is said of the Rubber placed on the floor, let it be said proportionally also of the bodies surrounding the machine on every side which are electric by communication and are not set on resin or glass.

487 III. Bodies perfectly, or totally, electric are surrounded by a dense atmosphere, and bodies imperfectly, or initially, electric by a rare atmosphere: for the density of the electric atmosphere is in the direct ratio of the electricity of the bodies. IV. Many fiery corpuscles going out of the bosom of the glass globe continually return into the globe itself on account of the resistance and the elasticity of the surrounding air. For that reason the electric force is livelier in cold and dry weather than in warm and humid weather; for the same reason, too, electricity is livelier in a plenum than in a vacuum. Hence it follows that to the effluence of the fiery corpuscles from the bosom of the glass globe there corresponds a certain simultaneous affluence toward the same globe, partly of the same corpuscles, partly of similar corpuscles supplied by the air and by the surrounding bodies. V. Most true, although very little sensible, is the simultaneous affluence and effluence of the fiery corpuscles. For not even in the terrestrial atmosphere is there a perfect plenum (§. 257.), which would evidently be required for that synchronous affluence and effluence of the electric matter to become physically and sensibly manifest. These things premised, let this be the conclusion.

V2                                       In

[p. 154]

488 In our opinion all the phenomena of electricity are rightly explained. This is proved by the following enumeration, namely by referring to their physical causes the principal experiments that were related in ch. II.

489 Explanation of Experiment I. From the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand and endowed with circular motion there go out fiery corpuscles, of which some enter the iron tube suspended horizontally by means of silk cords, while others communicate themselves to the air and to the bodies standing round about on every side. By this emission the iron tube suspended horizontally is rendered totally electric, while the air and the bodies standing round about are rendered only initially electric. This supposed, I reason thus. When I bring my finger, which is only initially electric, toward the totally electric iron tube, then, according to the laws of equilibrium, the dense electric atmosphere surrounding the iron tube must be carried toward the rare electric atmosphere surrounding my finger, just as the outer air is carried into a room whose inner air has been rarefied by a lighted fire. In that mixing a vehement conflict exists between the electric matter surrounding the iron tube and the electric matter surrounding the finger, and through this conflict a little blue flame is excited, leaping forth with a crackle.

490 Explanation of Experiment II. The tube of the electric machine, the iron wire which is held in the hand, and the man placed on the resin cake are three bodies electric by communication, of which the last is separated by means of the resin from the rest of the floor, which is electric only by communication: therefore, when some motion of rotation is impressed on the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand, the tube, the iron wire and the man placed on the resin cake must receive a very great electric force, and the blue flame drawn from the living body must produce a sensible pain; for who does not see that this blue flame is a true fire, and properly so called?

491 Explanation of Experiment III. We ourselves also admit a certain simultaneous effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of electric bodies, and affluence of fiery particles toward the same electric bodies. By the affluent fiery particles any of the lightest bodies whatever are attracted toward the electric bodies, and by the effluent fiery particles any of the lightest bodies whatever are repelled from the same electric bodies: therefore in our opinion the goings and returnings of the lightest bodies are rightly explained.

492 Explanation of Experiment IV. The violent shock mentioned in Experim. IV arises from the vehement collision of two fiery outflows, one of which enters through the hand that holds up the lower part of the glass flask, and the other through the hand that draws the flame from the iron wire.

493 Explanation of Experiment V. The vehement conflict of two fiery outflows, one of which has its way through the iron wire,

[p. 155] the other through the electric tube, is the cause why the very thick paper mentioned in Experim. V is pierced with a very great crack.

494 Explanation of Experiment VI. A cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a body actually electric, as will be set forth below: therefore sparks must be drawn from the iron rod treated of in Experim. VI.

495 Explanation of Experiment VII. Some part of the fiery corpuscles going out of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand communicates itself to the bodies standing about the electric machine: therefore the Rubber must receive a sensible electric force, provided he is placed on a cake of resin. And the same Rubber must also draw a flame from the iron tube to which he brings his finger: for in him the electric force is much weaker than in the iron tube.

T H E A RG U M E N T S O P P O S E D AG A I N S T O U R O P I N I O N ,

B OT H B Y T H E DI S T I N G U I S H E D N O L L E T A N D B Y OT H E RS ,

A R E A N S W E R E D.

496

Obj. I. The explanation of Experim. I in this new opinion is not conformable to the laws of sound Physics: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: if the iron tube suspended by silk cords receives electric force on account of the causes assigned, the same iron tube suspended by hempen cords must likewise receive electric force; the consequent is false: therefore the antecedent also. Proof of the sequel: the iron tube suspended by hempen cords communicates with the glass globe just as much as when it is suspended by silk cords; therefore, if, etc.

497 I distinguish the antecedent: it communicates just as much and in the same manner, I deny; just as much, and in a far different manner, the iron tube communicates, etc., I concede the antecedent and deny the consequence. The iron tube suspended by silk cords receives electric force in such a way that it retains it wholly, or almost wholly; for it is suspended by means of cords electric per se; on the contrary, the iron tube suspended by hempen cords receives electric force in such a way that it loses it in great part; for it is suspended by cords that are electric by communication.

498 Inst. 1. If sealing wax is brought toward the tube endowed with electric virtue, no spark at all is excited. This supposed, I reason thus: from this new opinion it follows that in that case a little flame with a crackle must be drawn from the iron tube: but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: sealing wax not far distant from the electric machine must become initially electric: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: any iron whatever not far distant from the electric machine becomes initially electric: therefore likewise sealing wax not far distant from the electric machine must become initially electric.

I

[p. 156]

I deny the parity: iron not far distant from the electric machine acquires a rare electric atmosphere; for iron is electric by communication: whereas sealing wax, which is electric only by rubbing, acquires no electric atmosphere, although it is not far distant from the electric machine.

499 Inst. 2. From this new opinion it at least follows that a little flame must be drawn from the electric iron tube toward which sealing wax rubbed with a rather dry hand is brought; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: sealing wax rubbed with a rather dry hand has acquired an electric atmosphere: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: it has acquired an electric atmosphere which is just as dense as the atmosphere of the electric iron tube, I concede; one which is rarer than the atmosphere of the electric iron tube, I deny the antecedent and the consequent. A little flame is not drawn except through the mixing, and the consequent conflict, of a dense atmosphere with a rare atmosphere: therefore a little flame ought not to be drawn when wax totally electric is brought toward an iron tube totally electric.

500 Inst. 3. At least in this new opinion it is not explained why a little flame is usually drawn from the electric iron tube with a certain crackle: therefore it is to be rejected as insufficient. Proof of the antecedent: the mixing of the electric matter surrounding the iron tube and of the electric matter surrounding the finger ought to take place without a crackle: therefore, etc. Proof of the antecedent: two contiguous flames mingle with each other without a crackle: therefore likewise two electric atmospheres ought to mingle with each other without a crackle. I deny the consequence. The two electric atmospheres of which we speak expel the intermediate air, which is either not dilated at all or only moderately, and therefore they expel elastic air, capable of producing a crackle: whereas two contiguous flames mingling with each other expel air too much rarefied to be able to produce a crackle.

501 Obj. 2. The explanation of Experiment II does not seem conformable to the laws of Physics: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: this explanation supposes that a man placed on a resin cake receives electric virtue at precisely the same instant, whether the resin cake is far or but little distant from the electric machine: but this does not seem conformable to the laws of Physics: therefore. Proof of the minor: according to the laws of Physics, the electric matter going out of the glass globe ought not to traverse different spaces in the same time: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: in the same real and true time, I concede; in the same sensible and apparent time, I subdistinguish: supposing that the spaces differ by some thousands of leagues, I concede; supposing that they differ by some feet, I deny, and I deny the consequence. The electric, or fiery, matter is endowed with a certain incredible velocity: this matter must therefore arrive at the hundredth foot and at the twentieth foot in the same sensible time.

502 Inst. From this opinion it follows that a man placed in the usual way on a resin cake ought to draw a flame from the electric iron tube with which he is in communication: but this

[p. 157] is false: therefore. Proof of the major: a man resting on the floor draws a little flame from the iron tube with which he does not communicate: therefore a fortiori a man placed on the cake ought, etc. I deny the consequence. The man placed on the cake is just as electric as the iron tube, and is therefore surrounded by an electric atmosphere just as dense as the atmosphere of the iron tube. Whereas the man resting on the floor is only initially electric, and is consequently surrounded by a rare electric atmosphere, while the iron tube is girded by a dense electric atmosphere: therefore, according to the principles set forth above, the latter must draw some little flame from the iron tube, but the former none. But, you will say, by what mechanism is the spirit of wine inflamed, which is mentioned in Observation III of Experiment II? I reply: the spirit of wine is inflamed in exactly the same way in which a certain little flame is drawn from the iron tube.

503 Obj. 3. In this new opinion there is no physical cause of the affluence of fiery particles toward bodies actually electric: therefore the explanation of Experiment III is not to be admitted. I prove the antecedent: before some motion of rotation was impressed on the glass globe, the electric matter which was found in the air did not flow toward the glass globe or toward the iron tube: therefore neither ought it to flow toward them after some motion of rotation has been impressed on the glass globe. I deny the first antecedent: in the lower atmosphere there is a sensible plenum, and the air is elastic. These things presupposed, I reason thus: the glass globe cannot become electric without emitting many fiery corpuscles from its bosom, and without a new motion being acquired by the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side. But all these things cannot happen without there corresponding, on account of the elastic air and on account of the sensible plenum, to the effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of the glass globe an affluence of the same, or of similar, fiery particles toward the same glass globe. What has been said of the glass globe, let it be said proportionally of the iron tube: therefore in this opinion there is a physical cause of the affluence of fiery particles toward electric bodies.

504 I deny the last consequence: in the first case the glass globe was suffering no loss, and the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side had not received a new motion. But in the 2nd case the glass globe suffers an almost immense loss of fiery particles, and the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side has acquired a new motion. But you will say: what is the physical cause of the effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand? I reply: this effluence is owed to friction joined to the motion of rotation. You will say again: for what cause, then, do no fiery particles flow out of a metal globe rubbed with a dry hand and endowed with a most vehement motion of rotation? I reply that there exists a twofold cause of this phenomenon: for I. there are far fewer

[p. 158] fiery corpuscles in metals, and in bodies electric by communication, than in glass and in bodies electric of themselves. II. Metals have somewhat rigid parts, on which friction does not impress that motion from which the effluence of fiery corpuscles arises.

505 Obj. 4. From our opinion it follows that if the iron wire mentioned in Experiment IV were enclosed in a metal flask, the shock would be much more vehement than when the iron wire is enclosed in a glass flask; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: if the iron wire were enclosed in a metal flask, the fiery outflow entering through the hand that holds up the lower part of the metal flask would be much greater than when the experiment is made by means of a glass flask; therefore from our opinion it follows, etc. Proof of the antecedent: the electric matter permeates a metal flask much more easily than a glass flask: therefore, if, etc. I deny the second antecedent, as supposing something false. The iron wire enclosed in a metal flask would not become sensibly electric; for the electric matter communicated to the iron wire would evaporate through the pores of the metal. Hence I concede the last antecedent and deny the consequence.

506 Obj. 5. In our opinion there is no physical cause of the crash mentioned in Experiment V: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the vehement conflict of two electric outflows ought not to excite so great a crash; therefore there is not, etc. I distinguish the antecedent: the vehement conflict of two electric outflows in an empty place ought not to excite so great a crash, I concede; the vehement conflict of two electric outflows which rarefy and expel the intermediate air ought not to excite so great a crash, I deny, and I deny the consequence. When we treat of sound, every difficulty will vanish entirely.

507 Obj. 6. A cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is not an electric body: therefore the explanation of Experiment VI does not hold. Proof of the antecedent: a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a watery body: therefore it is not an electric body. I distinguish the antecedent: it is a body totally watery, I deny; partially only, I concede, and I deny the consequence. A cloud bearing lightning is a body containing watery, sulphurous, bituminous, nitrous particles, etc. In the article on lightning we shall set forth by what mechanism this cloud acquires electric force.

508 Obj. 7. From our opinion it follows that the Rubber mentioned in Experiment VII ought not to draw a flame from the iron tube to which he brings his finger; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: a man placed in the usual way on a resin cake does not draw a flame from the tube with which he communicates through the iron wire: therefore likewise the Rubber placed on the cake ought not to draw a flame from the iron tube with which he has communication through the glass globe. I deny the consequence. The man placed on the cake is just as electric as the iron tube with

[p. 159] which he communicates through the iron wire: whereas the Rubber is much less electric than the iron tube, even though he is placed on a cake of resin: therefore the former must draw some little flame from the iron tube, but the latter none.

C H A P T E R I V.

Some doubts about electricity are explained very briefly.

ou will ask, I.: for what cause is the electric force weaker in humid or 509

Y          warm weather, and the same electric force livelier in dry or cold weath‐

er? I reply: in humid or warm weather the air is much less elastic than in dry or cold weather; therefore in dry or cold weather the fiery corpuscles first emitted from the bosom of the electric body must be better beaten back onto the same body than when the weather is humid or warm: therefore the electric force must be livelier in dry or cold weather than in humid or warm weather.

510 You will ask, II.: for what cause does a man initially electric draw a lively spark from the iron tube to which he brings his finger, while the same man draws a weaker flame from the glass globe to which he brings the same finger? I reply: this phenomenon seems to indicate to us that a much purer electric matter goes out of the glass globe than out of the iron tube.

511 You will ask, III.: whether the electric matter can be a present remedy against paralysis? For it is related not only that a Paralytic at Geneva was cured by

Mr. Jallabert (u), but also that many Paralytics at Montpellier were cured by Mr. de

Sauvages by means of the electric machine. I reply in the affirmative. And indeed, according to the Physicians, Paralysis is the abolition, or vehement diminution, of animal motion and of touch in some part of the body, sometimes with atrophy of the same, a weak pulse and other symptoms, arising from a relaxation of the nervous parts on account of the deficient presence, or activity, of the animal spirits, through an obstruction of the nerves that has arisen. The electric matter is a certain most subtle fiery matter, which is endowed with a most rapid motion. This fire must insinuate itself through the pores of the matter obstructing the tubules of the nerves,

X                         and

(u) Experiences sur l’électricité, by Mr. Jallabert. [p. 160] and little by little dissipate every obstruction, and consequently be a present remedy against paralysis.

512 You will ask, IV.: to what distance is the electric vapor propagated? I reply: the very great distance to which a vapor of this kind is propagated, as it were in a moment of time, may seem incredible. For Du Fay at 1256 feet, Maffei at 2220, Watson at 8000, at 10600, at 12276 feet, testify that the electric virtue was propagated along iron wires with such speed that the shock was perceived at the other extremity of the chain at almost the same instant. But we do not on that account think that a propagation of this kind is instantaneous, since Beccaria (x) discovered by most accurate experiments that the electric vapor, in traversing 500 Paris feet, takes up some sensible interval of time.

513 You will ask, V.: what are Phosphori? I reply: all phosphori are rightly regarded by the Modern Physicists as bodies electric by rubbing. Hence 1. artificial phosphorus, consisting of the sulphurous and saline parts of urine, must not only glitter in the dark, but also be kindled by the rubbing of its parts and burn the bodies in its way. Hence 2. the agitated sea, sugar shaken with a quick motion, rotten wood, the scales of fish when they begin to putrefy, etc., must emit sparks. Hence 3. certain barometers shine when they are agitated in the dark. Hence 4. you will have sparks if you rub the backs of cats against the lie of the hair (y).

Chapter

(x) Dell’Elettricismo Naturale, & Artificiale.

(y) Some phosphori are natural, others are found to be artificial. Among the natural are usually counted also fireflies (commonly alumbradores), the eyes of cats, the tongue of an irritated Viper, etc. The artificial are prepared by art, and are either dry or liquid. Dry, above all, is the Bologna stone, which is fetched from Monte Paterno near Bologna; when, after calcination, it is exposed to the air, it so drinks in the light that, carried afterwards into a darker place, it shines for some while like a lighted coal. The distinguished Homberg and Lemery knew how to prepare fluid and solid phosphori (Memoires de l’Acad. 1711 & 1715.) But we have not the leisure to give either the method of making phosphori, or more of their phenomena and a more distinct explanation of them; several authors pursue this: Regnault (Entret. Phys., vol. 2, Ent. 17.) and Ozanam (Recreat. Math. & Phys., vol. 4, bk. 1, 2.) As the account of these phenomena, this is to be noted in general: that a motion and agitation of subtle parts occurs in phosphoric observations; thus the Bologna phosphorus is agitated by the rays of light, or rather the sulphureous parts of the stone, unfolded and exalted by fire, are so agitated by the nitrous particles of the air to which it is exposed, entering through its more open passages, that they can shine out in the dark.

[p. 161]

C H A P T E R V.

On Thunder as connected with electricity.

e distinguish three things in thunder, namely the flash, the crash 514

Wand the lightning. The sudden glitter that suddenly strikes the eyes has the name of flash. A certain horrid sound booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere is called the crash. Finally, a certain kindled exhalation, which is often thrust down even to the earth with huge destruction, is called lightning. What the physical causes of the flash are we shall easily determine after we have carefully weighed whence lightning arises.

515 I say, therefore, I.: the electric matter is the physical cause of lightning.

It is demonstrated by the following experiment, which we related in Ch. II, and which it is necessary to bring forward here as proof. On the roof of some high building let a cake of resin, or of glass, be placed. On it let some iron tube be set up perpendicularly; experience establishes that if some cloud bearing lightning in its bosom hangs over this iron tube, sparks will be drawn from it in exactly the same way as if this iron tube, suspended horizontally by means of silk cords, had been in communication with the glass globe of some excellent electric machine: therefore the electric matter is the physical cause of lightning.

516 I say, 2.: bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles, etc., are the food of lightning. It is demonstrated 1. Lightning is frequent where mines of sulphur, bitumen, niter, etc., are found: therefore bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles are the food of lightning. 2. If anyone is in a place which by some miserable chance has been struck by lightning, he will breathe a foul smell of bitumen, sulphur and niter: therefore bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles are the food of lightning.

T H E A RG U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

517

Obj. 1. If the electric matter were the physical cause of lightning, it would follow that a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is actually electric; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: there is nothing that renders a cloud of this kind electric: therefore it is false that a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is actually electric. I deny the consequence. Bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous particles, raised into the atmosphere by the action of the sun, render electric the cloud which we see bearing lightning in its bosom.

X2                                  518 Inst.

[p. 162]

518 Inst. The sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles treated of here are not in a state of actual electricity; therefore they cannot render electric the cloud which bears lightning in its bosom. Proof of the antecedent: the bituminous particles, etc., which flit about in the atmosphere, undergo no friction: therefore they are not in a state of actual electricity. I distinguish the antecedent: they undergo no friction, nor do they undergo anything equivalent to friction, I deny; they undergo no friction, but they undergo something, I concede, and I deny the consequence. It often happens that bituminous particles, etc., are raised into the atmosphere when contrary winds prevail. These particles, being already warm, then undergo a very great agitation. This agitation is equivalent to a most vigorous friction, and thus they easily arrive at a state of actual electricity. But a cloud cannot contain in its bosom bitumen, sulphur and niter actually electric without its watery part becoming electric by communication. That cloud alone, therefore, bears lightning in its bosom which is actually electric; and that cloud alone is actually electric which contains bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous particles raised into the terrestrial atmosphere when contrary winds prevail.

519 Obj. 2. There are many phenomena regarding lightning which cannot be explained in our opinion: therefore it is to be rejected. Proof of the antecedent: it cannot be explained in this opinion what the physical cause of the flash is: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: in the region of the clouds there is no conflict of a dense electric atmosphere with a rare electric atmosphere: therefore. I deny the second antecedent, and I explain the proposed phenomenon: when a less electric cloud is borne into a more electric cloud, then the flash occurs by exactly the same mechanism by which the electric spark is excited of which we spoke in Experiment IV, Ch. II. I deny also the third antecedent: a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a body totally electric, and consequently a body surrounded by a very dense electric atmosphere, which renders initially electric the neighboring clouds that do not have lightning in their bosom: therefore in our opinion there is, in the region of the clouds, a conflict of a dense electric atmosphere with a rare electric atmosphere.

520 Inst. 1. From what has been said it follows that there ought to be no flash when a totally electric cloud has totally electric clouds in its vicinity; but this seems repugnant; therefore. I distinguish the major: it follows, etc., if all the clouds have the same degree of total electricity, I concede; if they have a different degree of total electricity, I deny the major, and the consequence. Let the Rubber placed on a resin cake be totally electric: he nevertheless draws a spark from the iron tube, which is also totally electric, because, namely, the electric force is much weaker in the Rubber than in the tube: therefore likewise a spark must be excited from two totally electric clouds, provided one is more or less electric than the other.

521 But, you will say, what in our opinion is the physical cause of the crash booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere? I reply: the flash

[p. 163] dilates the air contained between the more electric cloud and the less electric cloud which run against each other. This air, suddenly dilated, compresses the neighboring air; the neighboring air, endowed with an excellent elater, restores itself to its first figure, and in restoring itself excites the horrid crash which we hear booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere. From this physical explanation the following necessarily follow: I.
