There must sometimes be lightning flashes without any crash being heard; namely, when we are too far distant from the place in which the electric cloud is moving, or when the air contained between the more electric cloud and the less electric cloud has not acquired sufficient dilatation. II. Sometimes a crash must be heard without any lightning flash being seen, which happens when some thicker cloud is found between the earth and the electric cloud; for a cloud of this kind absorbs the rays of light of which lightning flashes consist.

522 III. Not rarely must we judge the sound to be, as it were, running about within the bowels of the clouds; for the sound is often reflected either from different parts of the clouds, or from different mountains and crags, etc. IV. The crash is not heard from a great distance; for sound, no otherwise than motion, that is, through running into other bodies, both becomes weaker and sometimes even perishes. V. It can easily be known how far distant from us is the cloud which holds the thunderbolt in its bosom. And indeed the light of the lightning flash is transmitted all the way to us within an insensible space of time, whereas sound runs through only 173 Paris toises within one second of time: if, therefore, four seconds of time should be counted between the flash and the crash, it will evidently be inferred from this that the electric cloud is 692 Paris toises distant from us. VI. If the crash is heard at precisely the same instant at which the flash gleams, then it will have to be inferred that the electric cloud is nearer.

523 You will ask again: When, and for what cause, is the cloud carrying the thunderbolt in its bosom broken? I reply: the cloud containing the thunderbolt in its bosom is broken then, when the wind which carries the less electric cloud against the more electric cloud is stronger, or when the electricity which thrives within the bowels of the electric cloud is more vigorous. Nor indeed will there be anyone who calls into doubt the force and efficacy of this last cause; for no one is unaware that, on account of excessive electricity, especially in wintertime, glass globes have been shattered; therefore a fortiori electric clouds must more often be broken on account of excessive electricity.

524 From what has been said the following evidently follow. I. The bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous exhalations which are found within the bowels of electric clouds, and which are the fuel of the thunderbolt, must be kindled by the electric fire. II. Of these exhalations some are thick, others thinner: the thick exhalations act on bodies whose pores are wider, and leave untouched bodies whose pores are narrower. For that reason certain thunderbolts have sometimes consumed the scabbard, leaving the sword untouched. Thin exhalations, on the other hand, act

only [p. 164] on compact bodies alone. Of exhalations of this species were formed the thunderbolts which melted the sword, leaving the scabbard untouched.

## 525 You will ask, finally: Whence does the stupendous force of the kindled ex‐

halation arise? I reply: it arises first from the very velocity of fire, which all know to be incredible; then from the very elater of the air which is found within the sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles of which the exhalation consists. Here, however, it is to be diligently noted that not every thunderbolt, or not every kindled exhalation, falls to the earth. That exhalation alone falls to which the upper clouds oppose a greater resistance than the lower clouds.

526 Obj. finally: in our opinion it cannot be explained whence the thunderstone arises; therefore there are phenomena regarding the thunderbolt which cannot be explained in this opinion. Proof of the antec.: the stone is neither the matter nor the fuel of the thunderbolt: therefore. I deny the whole argument, as supposing what is false. Whatever is related about the thunderstone is held by the more recent Physicists, men, namely, of sound mind, as old wives’ tales. The thunderstone is nothing other than a stone existing in the place to which the thunderbolt has come, and sensibly altered by the kindled exhalation. This is what we had to set forth concerning thunder. Now, however, the natural order demands that we say a few things about earthquakes, with which thunder is rightly seen to have a great analogy.

## CHAPTER VI

On Earthquakes, as Depending on Electricity.

f anyone has ever called into doubt that various tracts of the earth have at 527

I        times been shaken by violent motions, he may question the wretched peo‐

ple of Lisbon, whose most illustrious city, on account of a violent concussion of the earth, on the 1st of November of the year 1755, was not only overturned but, as it were, swallowed up. (z) But in order that we may find the physical causes of this deadly phenomenon more surely and more easily, the following seem to me necessarily to be premised. First: besides the fire which not a few Physicists admit at the center of the earth, and which for that reason they call central, there are in addition many

(z) The same misfortune was suffered by Guatemala, an illustrious City of this our America,

overturned on account of a violent concussion of the earth on the 29th of July of the year just past,

1773. [p. 165] many subterranean fires in the bosom of the same earth. Hence arise the flames which Mount Etna in Sicily, Mount Vesuvius in the territory of Naples, etc., vomit forth. II. These subterranean fires are not kept up without fuel. The common fuel of these fires, moreover, is sulphur, bitumen, niter and the other fossil bodies, most of which are electric by friction. Hence it is no wonder that mines of sulphur and of bitumen are frequent in those tracts of land beneath which subterranean fires lie hidden.

528 III. Within the very bosom of the earth sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles, already hot through the motion impressed by the electric matter which they contain, are kindled. This new motion, however, or rather this equivalent friction, is excited now by contrary winds penetrating into the inmost bowels of the earth through its huge passages, which they call aërophylacia, now by an electric spark excited within. Hence it follows that there are bodies electric per se that are inflammable, and bodies electric per se that are not inflammable. Of the first kind are all sulphureous materials, of the second kind vitreous materials. IV. There are in the bosom of the earth subterranean caves, upon which for the most part huge masses of mountains rest. V. In subterranean caves are found fire, water and air, in such a way, however, that the fire, or rather the combustible matter, namely sulphureous and bituminous matter, when kindled, occupies the lowest place, the water the middle place, and the air the uppermost place. These things being premised, and laid down as so many principles,

529 I say: By means of the principles just set forth earthquakes are explained very easily. The conclusion is proved by the following explanation. Let there be a huge subterranean cave over which some region or city lies. In the lower part of this cave let sulphureous, bituminous, nitrous materials, etc., be kindled by electric fire. Let water occupy the middle part of the same cave, and air the upper part. These things supposed, I reason thus. Things cannot be in this state without the water and the air growing hot from the subterranean fire: the water and the air cannot grow hot without being rarefied in a wonderful manner; they cannot be rarefied without striving to occupy a greater space. Therefore, in order to free themselves from those straits and extricate themselves the more easily, they will lift up their own prison, burst it asunder, and break out from it with a violent crash: what wonder, then, that the earth is at that time shaken by violent motions?

530 This was probably the physical cause not only of the violent concussion by which the City of Lisbon was overturned, and that of Guatemala, but also of absolutely all the earthquakes of which ample mention is made among the Historians. Military mines afford you sensible images of this deadly phenomenon. And indeed, if you furnish a mine with choice gunpowder and duly stop up all the larger passages, the kindled gunpowder will not merely move a certain tract of earth but will utterly overturn it: (*) therefore by means of the principles set forth, whatever pertains to earthquakes is explained rightly and very easily.

(*) See Memoir. de l’Academ. Royal, for the year 1700.

[p. 166]

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

bj. 1. This whole explanation of earthquakes supposes what is false: 531

O            therefore it is itself false as well. Proof of the antec.: It supposes

that kindled fires exist at the bottom of subterranean caves; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the minor: if kindled fires existed, air also would exist at the same bottom; but it does not exist there: therefore.

Proof of the minor: air occupies the upper part of the cave: therefore it does not exist at its bottom. I distinguish the last antecedent: all subterranean air occupies, etc., I deny; the greatest part of it, I grant, and I deny the consequence.

Just as kindled fire cannot exist in the receiver of the pneumatic machine from which the air has been exhausted, so likewise kindled fires would not exist at the bottom of subterranean caves if this bottom were altogether empty of air.

Although, therefore, the greatest part of the subterranean air is found in the upper part of the cave, there is no doubt that much air exists at its bottom.

532 Obj. 2. If earthquakes depended on the causes assigned above, it would follow that maritime places ought not to be more subject to earthquakes than places not maritime; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the maj.: in our opinion the nearness of the sea was not assigned as one of the physical causes of earthquakes: therefore maritime places ought not to be more subject to earthquakes than inland places. I distinguish the antec.: it was not assigned directly, I grant the antec.; indirectly, I deny, and the conseq. The sea supplies combustible matter to the subterranean fires: therefore maritime places must be more subject to earthquakes than places not maritime.

533 But you will say: how can it come about that, when the earth trembles, the sea then often swells? I reply: When the earth trembles, the bottom of the sea is often raised. It is no wonder, therefore, that the sea then swells; no wonder, too, that its waters run out hither and thither in both directions, not without a certain deluge of the land. Hence you will explain I. Why in an earthquake a tract of the sea, its waves swallowed up, has sometimes remained dry; for then, the subterranean caves which were under the sea being opened, the waters were drained off by so great an abyss that the tract remained dry. There is explained

II. Why the swelling and flooding of rivers has often been an effect of earthquakes. And indeed, as often as we have some great earthquake, so often the bottom of the sea is raised and its waters swell; as often as the bottom of the sea is raised, so often the waters of the rivers cannot enter the bed of the sea; and when this happens, then the river waters necessarily run out hither and thither in both directions, not without a deluge of the land.

534 You will explain III: why in certain earthquakes new islands have risen up. For then the air, dilated by the subterranean fires, so lifts up the land lying hidden under the waters that this same land comes out higher [p. 167] than the surface of the waters. This was probably the origin of certain islands which have risen up in the Archipelago and in the Atlantic Ocean.

535 You will insist 1. If earthquakes depended on the causes mentioned above alone, it would follow that mountainous places ought not to suffer more frequent earthquakes than places not mountainous; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: in our opinion mountains are not numbered among the causes of earthquakes: therefore. I distinguish the antec.: they are not numbered directly, I grant; indirectly, I deny, and the conseq. Mountainous places suffer more frequent motions for this reason, that for the most part caves are found under mountains, as we said above. Hence it is easily explained why now a greater, now a lesser tract of earth trembles. For this depends, other things being equal, on the greater or lesser depth and breadth of the cavern; for the deeper and broader the subterranean cavern is, the greater, evidently, must be the space of earth which is lifted up.

536 You will insist 2. From what has been said it follows that the same earthquake could not shake two cities without also shaking all the places in between; but this is false, for the last earthquake, which we can call that of Lisbon, either shook or overturned very many cities of Europe; and yet not all the places in between suffered some damage: therefore. I distinguish the major: without also shaking all the places in between, supposing that this earthquake depends on a single fire kindled in a single subterranean cave, I grant; supposing that it depends on several kindled fires, I deny, and the conseq. The last earthquake evidently depended on several fires kindled in different subterranean caves, which communicated with one another through sulphureous veins.

537 Obj. 3. There are many phenomena pertaining to earthquakes which cannot be explained in our opinion: therefore it is insufficient. Proof of the antec. by the following enumeration. In our opinion the following phenomenon does not seem able to be explained: earthquakes have been seen through which new springs were opened, and old springs were dried up: therefore, etc. I deny the antec., and I explain the phenomenon proposed. Earthquakes through which dikes were broken which formerly held back the waters as though shut in must have opened new springs. On the other hand, earthquakes through which new dikes were set against the flowing waters must have dried up the old springs, and turned the waters themselves aside from their former course, other passages being opened: therefore in our opinion the phenomenon proposed is rightly explained.

538 But you will say: how could it come about that in certain earthquakes waters formerly cold became hot, while in others waters formerly hot were made cold? I reply: all motions which kindle a new fire near some springs must heat the waters which were formerly cold; and no one doubts that combustible materials can be kindled by motion. But as often as the old fires are extinguished through some earthquake, whether they are extinguished through evaporation

Y [p. 168] or through any other cause whatever, so often must the waters grow cold which the fires lately extinguished used to heat. You will say again: How could pestilence proceed from certain earthquakes? I reply. In certain earthquakes bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous exhalations, etc., come forth from the very bosom of the earth, which infect the air: therefore pestilence must have proceeded from certain earthquakes.

## CHAPTER VII

On the Fluidity of Bodies, as Connected with Electricity.

hose bodies are fluid which do not resist the division of their sensi539

T          ble parts, and whose insensible parts are in continual and disordered

motion. From this description the following seem necessarily to follow. First: Fluid bodies consist of tiny particles. For if their parts were rather large and rather thick, they could not easily be moved hither and thither.

Second: For the most part the figure of the particles of which fluids consist is round. And indeed particles of this kind are easily separated one from another:

therefore they cohere among themselves either little or not at all: therefore it can be affirmed that they are for the most part round. I said for the most part; for I would not deny that some of these parts are oblong, some conical, some cylindrical, or of any other figure whatever. Third: Common fluids are penetrated by a subtler fluid, which we believe to be not distinct from the electric fire. These things premised,

540 I say I: The insensible parts of fluid bodies are always in disordered motion. Proof: if continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies is taken away, most of the phenomena of nature cannot be explained; but if this motion is admitted, these same phenomena are explained very easily:

therefore the insensible parts of fluid bodies are always in disordered motion.

Proof of the antec.: if continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies is taken away, it cannot be explained, for example, why salts are dissolved in cold water, why metals are dissolved in Stygian waters, etc.; but if this motion is admitted, the explanation of these effects gives no trouble at all, as will be plain to anyone considering it even lightly: therefore.

541 I say 2: The fire lying hidden within fluids is the cause of the continual and disordered motion by which the insensible parts of fluid bodies are agitated.

[p. 169]

Proof: the continual and disordered motion by which the insensible parts of fluid bodies are agitated is to be traced back to that body whose parts are always in disordered motion, as all Physicists acknowledge: therefore it is to be traced back to the fire lying hidden within bodies of this kind.

542 I say 3: The fire producing the continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies does not seem to be distinct from the electric fire. Proof:

The fire increasing the fluidity of bodies does not seem to be distinct from the fire producing this same fluidity; but the electric fire is a fire increasing the fluidity of bodies: therefore the electric fire is the fire producing this same fluidity. Proof of the min.: let there be two perfectly equal vessels, A and B (Fig. LIX.), which are filled with the same water. Let the water contained in vessel A be made electric, and let the water held in vessel B remain non-electric. To these two vessels let the same capillary siphon be applied in succession: experience establishes that the electric water will flow much more swiftly than the non-electric water, or, what is the same, experience establishes that the electric water will be more fluid than the non-electric water:

therefore the electric fire is a fire increasing the fluidity of bodies.

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

bj. I. If fluid bodies were always in disordered motion, it would follow 543

O           that all fluids would be sensibly hot; but this is false: therefore. Proof of

the maj.: the nature of sensible heat consists in the disordered motion of the parts of the hot body: therefore if, etc. The antec. must be roundly denied by us, who, as we shall see in the following Dissertation, defend the opposite opinion against Descartes. But for clarity’s sake I distinguish the antec.: in the disordered motion of the sensible parts, as we shall explain afterwards, I grant; of the insensible parts only of the hot body, I deny, and the conseq. The solution will be better explained when we treat of heat. But you will say: this being supposed, it can never be said that fluids are at rest. I distinguish: that they are at rest as to those same insensible parts, I grant; as to the sensible parts, I deny. Those fluids are said to be at rest whose sensible parts exist in respective rest, that is, as far as our sense is concerned.

544 Obj. 2. Fire is not in continual motion: therefore it is not the cause of the fluidity of bodies. Proof of the antec.: perpetual motion does not exist in the nature of things: therefore. I distinguish the antec.: it does not exist in the nature of things, that is, there does not exist a motion, once impressed, which perseveres constantly the same and in precisely the same degree, I grant; that is, there do not exist in the nature of things bodies which are always in some motion, now greater, now lesser, I deny, and the conseq. Thus, moreover, we explain the motion of fire, which we suppose free, and reduce it to the laws of Mechanics. First. There exist in the nature of things molecules infinitely small, or as it were infinitely small, of the first, second, third order, etc. Molecules of this kind are customarily represented by Geometers by these characters:

[p. 170]

545 Second: A molecule infinitely small of the first order is infinitely greater than a molecule infinitely small of the second order; likewise a molecule infinitely small of the second order is infinitely, or as it were infinitely, greater than a molecule infinitely small of the third order, etc.: the molecule A, for example, will whirl round in a vortex toward the molecule B (Fig. LX.) if it is endowed at the same time, and perseveringly, with a perpendicular or centripetal motion along the line A B, and with a horizontal motion, or motion of projection, along the line A C. By no other mechanism does the Moon revolve about the earth, and the planets move periodically about the Sun.

546 Centripetal force, according to the eminent Newton (a), is that by which bodies are drawn, impelled, or in any way tend from all sides toward some point as toward a center. The celebrated Newton has accordingly demonstrated that a molecule A, infinitely small of the second order, will sensibly tend, or will have a centripetal motion, toward a molecule B, infinitely small of the first order, provided these two molecules are not far distant from each other. Thus, therefore, I explain the continual and vortical motion of elementary fire. Elementary fire, or any fiery little vortex whatever, is composed of a molecule infinitely small of a higher order, about which molecules infinitely small of a lower order whirl round in a vortex, endowed simultaneously and perseveringly with the force of projection and with centripetal force. If the central molecule is a quantity infinitely small of the first order, the whirling molecules will be quantities infinitely small of the second order. If the central molecule is a quantity infinitely small of the second order, the whirling molecules will be quantities infinitely small of the third order, etc.

547 Obj. finally: If water already fluid were made more fluid through electricity, the fluidity of mercury would likewise be increased through electricity; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the minor: if the fluidity of mercury were increased through electricity, it would follow that the mercury ought to stand higher in a thermometer (of which we shall speak when we treat of cold) to which a livelier electricity has been communicated than in a similar thermometer which has acquired no electricity; but this is false, as experience establishes: therefore. Proof of the major: if the fluidity of mercury is increased through electricity, it follows that a greater quantity of fire is communicated to it; but if a greater quantity of fire is communicated to the mercury of the thermometer, the mercury must surely stand higher in the thermometer: therefore if, etc.

548 I distinguish the major: if the fluidity of mercury is increased through electricity, it follows that a greater quantity of electric and, as it were, elementary fire is communicated to it, I grant; of mixed and, as it were, usual fire, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: if a greater quantity of mixed and, as it were, usual fire is communicated to the mercury of the thermometer, the mercury must surely stand higher in the thermometer, I grant the minor; if a greater quantity of electric and, as it were, elementary fire, it must stand higher, etc., I deny, and the conseq. Elementary fire is constituted by little vortices; usual fire, on the other hand,

is

(a) Principia, bk. 1, Def. 5. [p. 171] is formed by those same little vortices, which have swept along with them bitu‐

minous, sulphureous, oily, nitrous particles, etc. On the greater or lesser dilatation depends the height of the mercury in the thermometer. This dilatation, moreover, is an effect of mixed and, as it were, usual fire, not of electric and, as it were, elementary fire: therefore the mercury ought not to stand higher in a thermometer to which a livelier electricity has been communicated than in a similar thermometer which has acquired no electricity. And so much for Electricity.

## PHYSICS

P A R T I V.

O N T H E Q UA L I T I E S O F B O D I E S.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N I 

On the Physical Nature of Sensible Quality.

## CHAPTER I

The Necessary Notions Are Set Forth First.

hat every body has qualities by which, formally, to use the word of the 549

T          Schools, it is rendered sensible, no one is unaware: but what their

physical nature is, is keenly disputed among Philosophers. For the

Scholastics, or Peripatetics, those whom they call the stricter, hold it settled and fixed that they are entities of such a nature that they can be separated by divine power from the bodily substance in which they inhere and which they render sensible to us, and can exist without it; for that reason they call them absolute accidents. The Moderns, on the contrary, are persuaded that no sensible quality is an absolute accident as the Scholastics take it, but that all of them proceed immediately from the magnitude, figure, motion, rest and texture of the corpuscles of which all sensible bodies are composed. But in order that we may proceed in the more accurate order possible, some definitions must be set out first.

[p. 172]

550 That is called sensible which, because it is formally such, so affects our sense organs as to excite sensation in us. Thus wood, because it is hard or colored, is called sensible, because, if it is applied to our sense organs, it so affects them, inasmuch as it is such, that the mind thereupon feels. From this it is inferred that a body is formally sensible by that through which it is formally of such a kind that, when applied to the external sense organs, it so affects them that the mind is thereupon determined to feel. By the name of sensible quality is understood that affection of a body by which the body is formally sensible; thus color, taste, etc., are called sensible qualities of bodies, inasmuch as through them a body formally has it that it is perceived by us through the ministry of the external senses. From this it is inferred that a sensible quality is physically placed in that by which a body formally has it that it produces in the sense organ to which it is applied a change upon which there follows in the soul a certain determinate sensation, which consists in thought.

551 The existence of sensible qualities in bodies is most certain. Those who deny absolute accidents in the Scholastic sense do not on that account deny the existence of sensible qualities: for they too acknowledge that there truly is in bodies that by which they formally have it that they change the organs of the external senses for the business of sensation and affect them in a certain way. Nerves are certain very slender little cords, as it were, which, proceeding as from a root out of the inmost substance of the brain, and also out of the membranes surrounding the brain, are spread through the whole machine of the animal, chiefly for the service of sensation. The filaments of which the nerves are composed are not altogether solid, but (as the celebrated Heister demonstrates) hollow within, so that they can accordingly be regarded as true little vessels.

552 By the name of animal spirits is understood a substance supremely fluid and most mobile, secreted in the brain. From what was said in the Logic and in the Metaphysics we are persuaded that from the change which is produced in the sense organ by the impulse of a sensible thing no sensation occurs in us unless that change is communicated to the brain. It is likewise certain that the organ of each external sense is placed in certain very slender fibers of the nerves, interwoven with a dissimilar artifice according to the specific difference of the senses, and inserted in the outer part of our body; while this part is affected by the sensible thing, sensation occurs in the mind. Thus, for example, the organ of sight is placed in that membrane of the eye which is the expansion of the optic nerves and is commonly called the retina. These things being laid down, the following assertion must be held as a fundamental principle, as it were.

553 The change of the external sense organ arising from the impulse of a sensible thing, upon which the sensation of that thing follows in the soul, is nothing else, physically speaking, than a certain motion in those fibers of the nerves which constitute the external sense organ, excited by the impulse of the thing itself. For a bodily agent does not act except through local motion, namely, only insofar as it locally moves that on which it acts. Certainly there is no bodily action which by the motion of its parts (as will be plain to anyone who considers it) is

[p. 173] not accomplished. Therefore no body, either, undergoes anything from a bodily agent except insofar as it is moved by it. But the sense organs undergo something from sensible things while they are excited by them for the business of sensation:

therefore their undergoing consists in the motion alone of the nervous fibers of which the sense organs themselves are composed.

T H E O B J E C T I O N S A R E D I S P E L L E D.

bj. 1. From our assertion it follows that that organ whose office it is 554

Oto discern all impressions, namely the brain, is endowed with a most exquisite touch; but so far is the brain from enjoying an exquisite touch that it is rather almost insensible: therefore the impressions of sensible things are not merely local motions. The argument must be answered by the Peripatetics themselves as well: for according to them the common sense resides in the brain. I distinguish the major: with a most exquisite touch, if this means that its medullary substance is of such a nature that it is able to receive the motions of all the external senses, I grant; if it means that its whole substance is capable of sensation if it is touched even very lightly by an external thing, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: the brain lacks touch, that is, its inmost substance cannot receive the impressions of all the senses, I deny; that is, there is no sensation if only its outermost part, that is, the cortex of the brain, in which there are no nerves, is touched, I grant the minor, and I deny the conseq.

555 Moreover, the argument sins by the fallacy of diction. There is, namely, an error in the word touch, which can be taken in two ways: 1. for the sensation which is excited in us by the contact of a sensory nerve with a sensible thing; 2.

for the sense by which hot, cold, moist, etc. things are perceived by us. Taken in the first way, that word touch can be referred to any species of sensation whatever, because every sensation is accomplished by contact, as the great Boerhaave expressly teaches (b); taken in the second way, touch is a particular sense, having only this in common with the other senses, that, just like them, it too is not excited in us unless the nerves which serve it in performing its office are touched by their proper object. This distinction laid down, there is no reason why the

Peripatetics should turn it into a fault in the Moderns that they reduce all the external senses to touch alone, as if, namely, they then took touch for that special sense by which heat and cold, etc., are perceived, which is altogether false.

556 Obj. 2. If the change of the external organs, that is, of the senses, arises from contact, the specific diversity of the organs is in vain; but God, Best and

Greatest, did nothing in vain: therefore. The argument can be pressed against

Aristotle himself. For in many places he teaches most openly that taste is a species of touch. In bk. 2 On the Soul he says: Taste is

(b) Praelect. in suas Inst. Med., at no. 566. [p. 174] is one of the things which are perceived by touch. To the argument I reply directly that, since the sensible bodies by which the external sense organs are changed differ very greatly among themselves, and the manner in which the sense organs themselves are affected by them is plainly dissimilar, it was not done in vain, but by the supreme counsel of the Divine Maker, and by the greatest necessity of nature, that the structure of the external sense organs themselves should also be notably diverse; from which it follows that for receiving the impressions of all sensible things and communicating them to the brain, a single organ of touch, touch being taken for a special sense, would by no means suffice.

557 Obj. 3, by insisting: whatever diversity occurs in the impressions of sensible things is communicated to the brain through the nerves, the nervous fibers and the animal spirits; but in every part of the body all these things are found, and indeed of the same nature: therefore in every part of the body there exist organs which can receive the impression, or change, of sensible things: therefore, our opinion being laid down, the sensitive power consists in touch alone, and by this one sense we perceive light, taste, etc.: therefore the remaining organs of the human body would be superfluous. I deny the min. of the argument: for the parts of the human body which serve instrumentally for performing sensations differ greatly among themselves, although each of them is composed of filaments of nerves: it cannot, therefore, be said that they are of the same nature, that is, that there is no essential difference whatever between them. I deny, therefore, that the fibers are interwoven with the same artifice in all parts of the body: for this artifice, as experience itself attests, is plainly dissimilar according to the specific difference of those parts.

558 For hence it comes about that only the corpuscles of which the species of colors consist can penetrate through the sight and move its sense organ, but not likewise the corpuscles which alone, and only they, can strike and move the hearing, and so of the rest. Therefore, although all the external organs are composed of nerve fibers, nevertheless, because their structure is plainly different, it comes about that they cannot be changed for sensation except by dissimilar things; namely, that only those nerve fibers which constitute the reticular membrane of the eye can be set in motion by the rays of light. Wrongly, therefore, does Father de Benedictis ask why, since there are nerves and fibers in the foot as in the other members, not every sensible thing is therefore discerned by us through the ministry of the foot alone. For this question is superfluous, and can best be answered by this other question: if with the hand, for example, we perform so many and such wonderful operations, such as writing, painting, sculpting, etc., because the hand is furnished with digits, muscles, nerves and fibers, why can the same operations not be done with the foot, in which digits, muscles, nerves and fibers are also found?

559 Obj. 4. If no sensation can be perceived without motion, it follows that there is no memory or sensation in those who are asleep, since

[p. 175] no impression is made by objects then absent: but this is contrary to experience: therefore. I distinguish the maj.: that there is no sensation on an external occasion (which is what the question concerns), I grant; a merely internal one, I deny, and the conseq.

560 Obj. 5. If our assertion is true, the soul feels at the very point of time at which some change is produced in the sense organ; but this cannot be, if the motion impressed on the sensory nerves must be propagated all the way to the brain in order that the soul may perceive: therefore, etc. The major is evident. For if you turn your closed eyes toward a tree, while you open them the light at once enters the eyes, and at once you see, nor does even the least little delay intervene between the change of the eye and the perception of the soul. The minor, however, is plain, because, since motion takes place in time, some interval of time is necessary for the motion impressed on the little fibers of the retina to be propagated all the way to the brain: therefore, etc. Reply: I distinguish the maj.: the soul feels at the very point of time at which the change takes place in the sense organ, that is, between the motion impressed on the sensory nerves and the perception of the soul no observable delay intervenes, I grant. None absolutely, I deny the maj., and, the min. being distinguished in the same way, I deny the conseq. If motion is propagated through a very small space with great velocity, the time in which it is propagated through that space is not perceived, or is not distinguished, by us. Thus, although it is certain (as we shall see afterwards) that sound is propagated successively and not in an instant, we can nevertheless observe no delay between the moment at which someone very near us speaks and the moment at which his voice reaches our ears. The same is also plain in the propagation of light: as soon as a candle is lit in a dark place, all objects, even distant ones, are at once seen bathed in light, although light cannot be propagated in an instant. Therefore the experiment which is objected to us proves this one thing only, that the motion is transmitted from the sensory nerves to the brain with great velocity.

561 You will insist 1. Motion is not propagated to the brain through nerves which do not reach the brain; but several sensory nerves, namely 60, which come out of the spinal marrow, do not extend to the brain: therefore, etc. I reply: I grant the maj., I deny the min. For the spinal marrow is a prolongation of the brain itself, or of the medulla oblongata, and consists of nerves extended all the way to the brain; whence it comes about that in dislocations of the vertebrae (a) of the back, the members of the body placed below the dislocation lose both the motion and the sensibility which depend on the nerves situated below the dislocation. The nerves are thus, as it were, the brain diffused into all parts of the body.

Z                                         562 You

(a) Vertebrae is the name given to bones hollowed within, flat above and below, and furnished on the outside with various processes, of which Anatomists count seven in the neck, twelve in the back, and five in the loins. They are called vertebrae because through them the body is variously bent and turned.

[p. 176]

562 You will insist 2. Men have been found who lived and felt without a brain: therefore for the sensation of the soul it is not necessary that the motion impressed on the sensory nerves be propagated all the way to the brain. Reply: I distinguish the antec.: they lived and felt without the greatest part of the brain, I grant; altogether without that whole part, I deny the antec. and the conseq. In them there was the spinal marrow, and at its beginning there could have been some special structure by which that part was fitted to discharge in some measure the office of the brain. For the rest, it is likely that those men were very stupid and dull. If, however, in some the spinal marrow too was lacking, some other part, whatever it may have been, must necessarily have taken the place of this part. Finally, that these supplementary parts were present became known from the very dissection of the corpses and from anatomical observation; it could also have happened, however, that those parts, corrupted and obliterated by the force of the disease itself, perished.

563 You will insist 3. If serpents, lizards and other animals which are marked by circular incisions are cut crosswise, the single parts of them are twisted and agitated in various ways at the prick of a needle or any other irritation whatever: and accordingly they still feel without a brain: therefore, by the analogy which exists between the bodies of man and of brute, the same must be said of man. I reply: I deny the conseq. and the parity. For the structure of the human body is one thing, that of serpents and lizards another; in these the parts of the spinal marrow can be considered as so many smaller brains. Hence it comes about that parts of the human body, when cut off, are deprived of all motion after a very short time.

564 You will insist 4. It is altogether uncertain whether motion is propagated from the sense organ to the brain by the oscillation of the nervous fibrils, or by means of the nervous fluid or the animal spirits, or in any other way whatever: therefore, etc. Reply: I allow the antec. and deny the conseq. Even if we do not investigate the manner in which that propagation of motion is accomplished, it is enough that it is established by reason and experience that some motion is excited in the sense organ which is propagated all the way to the brain by the help of the nerves while the soul feels. In the same way one must reply if anyone objects that it cannot be understood by us how it can come about that, on account of the motion impressed on the nerves, the soul, which is a simple and spiritual substance, perceives the sensible object: here we establish the fact; we do not seek the reason of the fact. Moreover, against indubitable facts objections of whatever kind have no force.

565 You will insist 5. Those who are deprived of a sense organ nevertheless feel, and, on the contrary, some lack sensation in whose sensory nerves even a strong motion is produced. Therefore, in order that the soul may feel, it is not necessary that motion be impressed on the sensory nerves. Proof of the antec.: those whose limbs have been cut off sometimes seem to themselves to feel pain in those same limbs, as happened to the girl whom Descartes mentions (c).

(c) Principles, pt. IV.

[p. 177]

Madmen and delirious persons seem to themselves to see objects which are not present, and which accordingly produce no change in their sense organs. St.

Augustine (e) relates this fact: There was a certain priest named Restitutus who, whenever it pleased him, so withdrew himself from his senses, and lay so very like a dead man, that he not only felt nothing at all of those who plucked and pricked him, but was sometimes even burned with fire applied to him without any sense of pain. I reply: by these observations our conclusion is confirmed most excellently. For in every sensation four things, as we said in the Logic, are to be accurately distinguished; two which pertain to our body, namely, the motion impressed on the sense organ by the sensible object, and the motion thence propagated to the brain; and a third, which belongs to the soul, namely, the perception of the sensible object corresponding to these motions. If the motion impressed on the sense organ is not propagated all the way to the brain, the soul does not feel, as happens in us when we sleep, and as happened in the priest Restitutus, who lay most like a dead man.

566 But if, without the action of an external sensible object, the fibers of the brain are agitated by internal causes in exactly the same way in which they are moved when a sensible object by its action on the external organ produces the same motions, then the soul has the same perceptions which it would have if the sensible object were acting on the external organ, and it does not distinguish its perceptions, produced by force of imagination, from sensations; as happens to madmen and delirious men, in whose brain irregular and more vehement motions are excited: and in this way they confuse what they imagine with what they see. In the same way it is explained why those whose limb has been cut off sometimes seem to themselves to feel pain in that same limb for a while; namely, because in those nerves which reached the amputated part of the body the same motions sometimes arise from extrinsic causes which external objects would excite if no part had been cut off.

## CHAPTER II

The Physical Nature of Sensible Quality Is Established.

hese things being supposed which were said by us in the Logic, I assert: 567

T          The sensible qualities of a natural body arise solely from the mechanical

affections of the particles of matter of which that composite consists.

Proof. The quality of a sensible body is placed in that by which

Z2                                               a

(e) Bk. XIV of The City of God, ch. 24. [p. 178] a body formally has it that it is fit to be sensible [§. 550]; but from the mechanical

affections of the particles of matter of which it is composed a body has it that it is specifically sensible (just as from their solidity it is so generically): therefore. Proof of the min.: Any natural body whatever is formally sensible by that through which it formally has it that, applied to the external sense organs, it is able to move their nervous fibers in a certain manner [§. 550.]; but any body whatever can achieve this by the very fact that it is intrinsically composed of solid corpuscles endowed with a certain magnitude and figure and interwoven together with a certain artifice.

568 And certainly the Peripatetics must affirm this very thing, unless they wish to say that we are affected in the same way, and that exactly the same sensible quality is found in a stone that has fallen on the head from a height of one foot and from the top of a very high tower, where the stone is the same and only the mechanical affection, namely the motion, is different. Finally, note that whether Grace, the light of glory, and other spiritual qualities of the soul of that kind are absolute accidents in the

Peripatetic sense, let the Theologians see. I only point out that, even if these qualities are held to be accidents of this kind, it does not on that account follow that the same must be said of sensible qualities (which the whole question concerns). For they are diverse in genus. I therefore think those are mistaken who, in order to prove that the sensible qualities of bodies are absolute entities, take refuge in the spiritual qualities of the soul and strive to demonstrate that these are of this nature; as the most celebrated Fortunato da Brescia excellently observes.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N I I 

On Tactile Qualities.

## CHAPTER I

On Heat.

he parts of a body are said to be moved in a disordered way when they are 569

T          moved singly in such a way that there is no difference of place toward which they

are not carried away. They are said to be moved with an expansive motion when they tend with their motion from the center of the body itself toward its circumference, so that, by reason of that tendency of theirs, the extension of the body is increased in every dimension unless an impediment is present. Hence the following proposition must be held as a fundamental Principle, as it were. The dilatation of a body, and the disordered motion which is excited in the parts [p. 179] within it when it conceives heat, are the principal effects of heat, and, as it were, its characteristics. For that expansive and disordered motion of the parts of a body growing hot so depends on the heat by which the body is affected, and follows it in such a way, that it depends on it and follows it no otherwise than an effect depends on its efficient cause and follows it. For when heat is posited in a body, the motion itself is also posited in it; when the former is increased, the latter too is increased; but when it is taken away or diminished, the motion also is either taken away entirely or gradually decreases and is diminished.

570 Heat, therefore, is formally placed in that entity by force of which all bodies are dilated and their internal parts are agitated in a disordered way. Henceforth, then, to speak with the most learned Boerhaave (f), I shall call heat, or fire, that thing which has in itself this property, that it penetrates all bodies, solid and fluid, and by that very fact dilates them into greater spaces. We are not pleased, therefore, with the definition of heat which is handed down by the Peripatetics, namely that heat is that by which homogeneous things are gathered together and heterogeneous things separated. For, as Malebranche excellently observes (g), heat does not gather together the parts of water; rather it dissipates them into vapors. It does not gather together the parts of wine, nor even the parts of quicksilver. On the contrary, it resolves and separates all bodies, solid and fluid, homogeneous and heterogeneous. And if there are some whose parts fire cannot dissipate, this does not happen because they are of the same nature, but because they are too thick and too solid to be carried away by the motion of the parts. Moreover, no heat will be able so to segregate a mass melted together from gold, silver and copper that even the imperfect metals remain apart from the gold and silver; nay, if different portions of gold, silver and copper are contained in a vessel and placed over the fire, after some time they are gathered by the force of heat into one mass. These things laid down,

571 I say 1. Heat does not consist in the swift, disordered and expansive motion of the parts of the body growing hot. This is against Descartes. Proof: Heat does not consist in that which is an effect of heat; but the swift, disordered and expansive motion of the parts of a body, when it conceives heat, is an effect of heat [§. 569.]: therefore. It is confirmed: it is altogether certain that heat is something entirely other than that undergoing of the sense organ upon which the sensation of heat itself follows in the mind; but the undergoing of the sense organ is nothing but a certain dilatation of the nervous fibers of which it consists, and a disordered motion of the animal spirits with which they swell: therefore heat is something other than that swift, disordered and expansive motion which is excited in the particles of a body when it conceives heat.

572 I say 2: Heat in first act, or as it is in bodies, is most fitly constituted in corpuscles extremely slight in bulk, endowed with a most rapid, expansive and disordered motion, which into the fibers of the animal body

rush,

(f) Elem. Chem., vol. 1, p. 69.

(g) Recherche de la Verité, ch. 5. [p. 180] rush, and stir them up with a similar motion. Proof by parts: 1. It is certain that heat is a body, and of such a condition that it can pervade all bodies; but heat, if it is a body, cannot pervade all bodies except insofar as it enters their pores; nor can it enter the pores and diffuse itself through the whole mass of those bodies unless heat is nothing different from corpuscles, as is evident: therefore. Second: there exists absolutely no body in the nature of things so compact that heat cannot enter its pores, as the great Boerhaave testifies (h): therefore the corpuscles of heat are so slight that the same Author, just praised, has rightly said that their subtlety, if it is referred to our imagination, is infinite.

573 Third: It is necessary that the particles of heat be moved most swiftly with a disordered and expansive motion. For it is certain that it can in no way come about that by force of heat all bodies are dilated, fluids boil, hard things liquefy, and finally the smallest parts of all things conceive an expansive and disordered motion when they grow hot, unless the extremely slight particles in which heat consists press upon the walls of the pores of the body which they enter, overcome the momentum by which its molecules adhere to one another, and therefore tear them apart and drive them in manifold directions, and at the same time prevent, as long as they are mixed with them, the parts of the body itself from returning to their former contact; but the particles of heat cannot accomplish this unless they are endowed with an expansive and disordered motion, as is self-evident: therefore.

574 Moreover: it is established that the motion is most swift; for since the said particles are extremely slight in bulk and do not act except through motion, and it is certain from what has been said that the force with which they are moved, or their quantity of motion, equals the product of the mass of each into their celerity, it remains plain that the force of those particles cannot be the greatest (such as is necessary, since they are able to dilate even the hardest bodies) unless the celerity with which they perform their motion is the greatest. The assertion is confirmed: This nature of heat being laid down, all its effects and phenomena are fitly explained. For there is explained first why heat does not pervade hard bodies as easily as fluids; for since the particles of a fluid body are loose and more ready for motion, a slight resistance has to be overcome by the corpuscles of heat in order that they may insinuate themselves into a fluid body and be dispersed through its whole mass: the opposite is to be thought of hard bodies.

575 Second: The reason why the rarefaction of bodies takes place through heat is given because, since the particles of heat are endowed with expansive motion, they cannot enter the pores of bodies without exerting force against their walls, pressing upon the parts and compelling them to recede from one another, and so to occupy a greater space. Third, the hardening and drying of mud, and on the other hand the softening of wax, by the same effect of heat, is explained: for in mud the watery and more fluid parts, which

had

(h) Elem. Chem., Tract. de Igne. [p. 181] had made it tractable, fly off and cause the other parts, earthy, more tenacious and

heavier, to come closer together and become entangled; in wax, on the other hand, the viscous particles, less liable to evaporation, are drawn apart by the vehement and varied motion; hence, being less compacted with one another, they resist less the hand that presses them. From these things, moreover, you will be able to understand and easily explain many others.

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

576

Obj. 1. Heat consists in a very swift, perturbed and expansive motion of the body growing hot: therefore. Prob. antec.: when that motion is posited and increased in a body, heat is posited and increased in it, and conversely, when that motion is removed or diminished, the heat itself too is either wholly removed or gradually decreases: therefore. Dist. antec.: and this proves only that the perturbed and expansive motion of the body growing hot is the principal effect of heat, and as it were its character, I grant; and it proves anything against our assertion, I deny.

And indeed a similar motion too, excited in the fibrils of the sensorium of touch when the sensation of heat arises in us, answers to heat in this very proportion, and yet heat is not to be placed in that motion, unless we wish to dispute about a name, as the Scholastics say.

577 Obj. 2. Fire, or heat, is often endowed with a straight motion: therefore it is not endowed with a perturbed or vortical motion. Prob. antec.: fire often shines; therefore it is endowed with a straight motion. Dist. antec.: with a straight motion incompatible with a perturbed or vortical motion, I deny; with one compatible with a perturbed motion, I grant. The same small fiery vortex can be endowed at the same time with a straight motion and with a perturbed motion. For while either the center of the small vortex, or even the whole small vortex, is carried along a straight line, the molecules placed at its circumference will necessarily whirl in a perturbed way. Is not the same globe, rolled upon any plane whatever, endowed at the same time both with motion along a straight line and with a motion of rotation about its center? Therefore straight motion is not incompatible with perturbed motion. All admit that the motion of heat can be varied according to the variety of the fuel, or of the subject on which it exerts its force, or according to the obstacles and impediments that check its motion. Thus it may happen that the motion of heat is vortical, or rotatory, but this does not prevent its being called perturbed.

For while the sulphureous particles, carried off in a whirl, spin about themselves, and some drive others, there arises a certain perturbed motion, as all agree.

578 Obj. 3. All fluid bodies, of which kind are water, air, mercury, etc., have their parts agitated with a varied and indeterminate motion, and yet they are not actually hot: therefore. I reply 1. that no fluid is wholly devoid of heat, although perhaps, compared with our body, it seems cold: namely, since the parts of the blood or of the spirits are agitated more swiftly than the particles of the fluid body.

I reply

[p. 182]

2.: that for sensible heat it is not enough that the motion of the parts of the body be varied and perturbed, but it is necessary besides that it be very swift. Hence it comes about that the parts of water, agitated with a gentle motion, produce cold rather than heat in our bodies: for they rather diminish our innate heat, or motion, than increase it.

579 Inst.: There are many things prone to motion which are not held in the number of hot things, such as nitrous things and acid liquors, which abound in copious spirit and greatly promote fermentation: therefore. Resp.: not motion alone, but a varied, perturbed and very swift motion belongs to the nature of heat. Hence acid liquors, although they promote fermentation, yet by themselves scarcely produce heat, because their particles are not agitated with that perturbed motion except when they are mixed with alkaline salts: as when spirit of niter is poured onto a fixed alkaline salt. Thus air blown out with a narrow mouth is colder, but bursting out of a wide-open mouth is hotter: for when it is expelled with the mouth contracted, it is emitted with a swift motion indeed, but a direct and not a perturbed one.

580 Obj. 4.: There are fermentations in which a perturbed motion of the parts is conspicuous without any heat, nay, with intense cold, as the most distinguished men Musschenbroek, Slare, Amontons, Guglielmini, Geoffroy and very many other physicists testify: therefore the expansive and perturbed motion of the parts of a body is not so proper an effect of heat that heat itself can legitimately be placed in it, by whose force and energy that motion is excited in bodies. I deny the conseq.: for the ebullition, or perturbed motion of the parts, even in cold fermentations, is not without heat, although, on account of the great quantity of saline substance that is dissolved in them, their heat is not conspicuous. This was observed in a certain fermentation from which, as the most distinguished Musschenbroek testifies, fumes so hot burst forth that the liquor of a thermometer applied to the fumes rose through several degrees, while meanwhile the liquor of another thermometer, immersed in the fermenting liquid itself, was depressed.

581 It is to be observed, then, that there are two kinds of fermentations: the one, namely, of those in which a sulphureous substance prevails, the other of those in which a saline one predominates. Fermentations of the first kind are called hot, because, owing to the predominance of sulphur, the corpuscles in which heat consists prevail in them. Fermentations of the second kind are named cold, inasmuch as, owing to the predominance of the saline particles that are dissolved in them, the chief place in them is held by the corpuscles in which, as we shall say, cold resides. That cold fermentations are wholly saline, or contain for the most part salt, the very experiments on cold fermentations most clearly demonstrate, as the distinguished Guglielmini observes.

582 Obj. 5.: It is manifest from experience that heat can be excited without any perturbed and expansive motion of the parts, as the author praised above testifies: therefore. Dist. antec.: without motion etc. of the insensible parts, I deny; of the sensible parts, I grant; and I deny the conseq. Heat can be present in a body

[p. 183] without any sensible motion appearing in it, because it can happen that there is not released in that body such a quantity of corpuscles of heat as suffices to agitate its sensible parts in a perturbed way. But there cannot be heat in a body without any motion whatever of the insensible parts, because heat cannot be in it unless those corpuscles in which heat consists are in it and are moved; and surely, since the liquor of a thermometer immersed in those fermentations of which the author speaks rises through several degrees, it remains plain that very fine corpuscles exist in them which, driven into motion, enter the pores of the glass and agitate the contained liquor with an expansive and perturbed motion; unless we wish the liquor itself to be dilated without anything existing to which that dilatation may be ascribed.

583 Obj. 6. The north wind is carried with a vehement motion, and yet it is cold: therefore. Secondly: waters in the whirlpools of rivers rush headlong with a perturbed and swift motion; but we observe no heat in them: therefore. To the first I reply that, although the north wind is carried with a vehement motion, yet because it is driven in a straight line it is cold, especially since it brings from the northern regions particles which can check the excited motion of the insensible parts. To the second I say: heat is not observed in the whirlpools of water because the sensible parts of the water are carried off by this motion; but for the nature of heat there is required not merely a vehement and perturbed motion of any parts whatever, but an agitation of very fine and insensible parts, which, carried off above all by the fiery particles, can penetrate other bodies and fibers and stir them with a similar motion.

584 Obj. 7: Metals and other hard bodies are sometimes hot without corpuscles affected with a tumultuous motion existing in them: therefore. I deny the antec.: For, to pass over the fact that no body, however hard, can take on heat without its extension being increased, it is manifest that metals, if they are immersed in cold water when they are extremely hot, excite in it a notable ebullition with a hissing noise: therefore very fine corpuscles exist in their pores which communicate that tumultuous motion to the particles of the water; whence it seems evident that they themselves are possessed of a not dissimilar motion.

585 Obj. finally: the white of an egg congeals into a consistent mass by the action of heat: therefore heat does not consist in corpuscles affected with a very swift, perturbed and expansive motion; for it can in no way be conceived how consistency, and hence rest of the parts, could arise from that which is moved most swiftly. Dist. antec.: it congeals in such a way that that consistency is an effect of heat per se, I deny; in such a way that it is an effect of heat per accidens, I grant; and I deny the conseq. The white of an egg acquires consistency not because the nature of heat is of itself able to bestow consistency on bodies, but because the parts of certain bodies are of such a size and figure, and woven together with such artifice, that they cannot be moved by the corpuscles of heat without becoming entangled with one another and congealing into a hard mass. Indeed the very white of the egg,

Aa [p. 184] which at first hardens by the action of heat, is wholly dissolved if the heat itself is increased: a very strong argument indeed that its consistency comes from heat not directly and of itself, but by accident.

## CHAPTER II

On Cold.

t is proper to cold to condense bodies, to make hard those that are soft, to 586

I        change very many liquors into a consistent mass, and to retard, and even wholly

to stop, the perturbed and expansive motion of the internal parts of a body. For it is necessary that the effects of heat and of cold be contrary. Hence it necessarily follows that cold formally consists in that by whose agency bodies are constricted, soft things stiffen, very many liquors pass into a hard mass, and the perturbed and expansive motion of the internal parts of a body is retarded and stopped. For cold must be placed in that from which the effects commonly attributed to cold proceed. Hence cold is not well defined by the Peripatetics as a quality that gathers together both homogeneous and heterogeneous things. For it is certain that it is not a constant effect of cold to gather heterogeneous things together. For if wine, vinegar and spirit of wine are subjected to a rather intense cold, those liquors are separated and dissolved: the watery part of the wine congeals into ice, the spirit retains its fluidity, and the tartar is precipitated. These things being laid down,

587 I say 1: Cold is not rightly placed in the rest of the parts. This is against

Descartes. Prob.: heat is not rightly explained by the motion of the parts of the body growing hot [§. 573.]; therefore neither is cold rightly expounded by the rest of the parts. Secondly: Cold cannot rightly be placed in that which is an effect of cold: but the rest of the parts is an effect of cold [§. 586.]: therefore only wrongly can cold be made to consist in the rest of the parts. It is confirmed: It is settled that cold is really distinguished from that passion of the organ of touch which the sensation of cold in the soul follows; but the passion of the organ of touch is nothing but a privation of motion in those fibers of the nerves which constitute the organ itself: therefore. Thirdly: If cold were nothing different from the rest of the parts, no body could be had that is in the least cold unless its parts were at rest as far as sense can tell: but this is altogether false, as is clear from cold fermentations: therefore. Moreover: that body will be the coldest whose parts are moved in no way at all: therefore all the hardest bodies will be the coldest, and ice itself, from which a cold exhalation bursts forth abundantly, and which is endowed with an intestine motion of its parts, [p. 185] would not be a supremely cold body. Although, therefore, a body whose parts are at rest is not hot, it is not on that account, by this very fact, to be judged cold.

588 I say secondly, with the great Boerhaave (i): cold by no means consists in the mere privation of heat. This is against very many of the Moderns, among whom the distinguished ’s Gravesande is numbered. Prob.: Since water is dilated in congelation [§. 571. ff.], if it passed into ice on account of the withdrawal of heat, the water would be dilated solely on account of that withdrawal; and hence, conversely, it would be condensed by heat, as the hypothesis of our adversaries supposes; we should have to say that water has from the efficient cause by which it is condensed that very thing, namely that it is fluid: but it is against the nature of heat that water affected by it should be reduced to a smaller space than it possesses of itself [§. 567.]: therefore water is not changed into ice for this cause alone, that it is deprived of heat; but it is converted into ice when something is added to it: therefore it does not grow cold through the mere withdrawal of heat, and consequently cold does not consist in the mere privation of heat. Hence, by the very fact that a body is not hot, it cannot be judged cold, unless other things are equal.

589 I say 3: Cold, even in its cause, is something real and positive. Prob.: For if cold is neither motion nor the privation of heat, as we have already demonstrated, it certainly remains that, since it is opposed to heat, it too, just as heat does, consists in a positive entity. Secondly: It is proved from an observation of the distinguished ’s Gravesande (k). Let snow be taken, mixed in equal parts with sea salt, contained in a vessel, and surrounding a glass filled with water. If this mixture is placed on the fire, at the moment at which it melts, that is, at which its heat is increased, it does not, as other bodies do, communicate heat to the water, but the water is converted into ice. No other reason can be given for this phenomenon except that the corpuscles of heat which penetrate that vessel and dissolve the snow drive something positive out of the snow into the water, which makes the water change into ice: therefore cold consists in something positive.

590 I say 4: Cold in first act consists in corpuscles extremely slender in bulk, and these slender corpuscles are the most subtle primitive particles of salts, but chiefly of niter. The first part can be proved aptly enough from what we have said about heat. The second part is established by experience; for the most subtle particles of every salt contribute to producing cold in bodies, and cold increases or decreases according to the greater or smaller quantity of them, as the Florentine Academicians testify; for all salts placed round a vessel containing water assist its congelation. The most subtle parts of salt, therefore, even though they are few, seem to penetrate through the pores of vessels, to put the fire to flight, to fix the parts of the water, and hence to be those very

Aa 2                                corpuscles

(i) Elem. Chem., vol. 1, p. 73.

(k) Elem. Phys., §. 2460 ff. [p. 186] corpuscles in which we have said that cold consists. That the nitrous particles hold the chief place is argued by that very intense cold which is produced by means of niter. For the often-praised Musschenbroek found that, when a thermometer made with mercury was immersed in snow onto which spirit of niter had been poured, the mercury descended below the mark that indicates the cold of ice. He found also that very strong spirit of vinegar, immersed in the same snow, passed into ice. But that water does not pass into ice even if niter is added to it, the cause is that, for this to happen, the niter would have to be resolved into its primitive corpuscles; but it cannot be so dissolved by water, as all admit. From this, therefore, it does not follow that niter is not the cause of congelation, nor that cold does not reside chiefly in its particles; since we have placed cold not in any corpuscles whatever, but in the primitive corpuscles of salts.

591 Nor can I pass over in silence the celebrated experiment performed by the Florentine Academicians: namely, that just as the heat of a fire, or of the sun, collected in a mirror and reflected onto a nearby thermometer, rarefies the liquor of that same thermometer and forces it to rise higher, so, if ice is substituted in place of the sun, the liquor of the thermometer descends and is condensed; but in the first case, even according to our adversaries, certain corpuscles come out from the fire which rarefy the spirit of wine enclosed in the thermometer: therefore certain corpuscles must come out of the ice which, collected by the mirror, are reflected onto the thermometer and condense its liquor; and consequently cold must not be made to consist only in the absence of heat, as, among others, Mr. de Ratte (l) tries to show, not noticing that the experiments he brings forward to weaken our opinion prove against himself.

592 What of the fact that on our opinion the phenomena of cold are explained excellently? Writers report that in the Ukraine, a province of Poland, the cold is very keen, and far more intense than in Normandy, a province of France, although the respective situation of the places on the terrestrial globe is the same. The river that washes Peking, the royal city of the Chinese, congeals about the month of November within a single day with such force of cold, and hardens so, that for the space of four months it sustains carriages and huge weights; yet that Chinese river has the same respective position on the terrestrial globe as the Tiber at Rome holds, in which this force of cold does not prevail.

593 Hence it must be said that certain winds are colder than others, which carry saline and nitrous exhalations with them and, filled with them and mixed with them, pervade the pores of bodies and produce the aforesaid effects. On our opinion one understands also why certain streams flow most freely in wintertime, but in summertime congeal into the hardest ice: for it has been observed that the banks of those streams abound in a great deal of niter and in saline particles, which particles indeed

are

(l) L’Encyclopédie, s.v. Froid. [p. 187] are dissolved by the summer heat and flow down into the waters of the stream and are mixed with them. Besides what we have said [§. 201] about ice, it must now also be said that water is dilated while it passes into ice because the primitive parts of water are of such a texture that the likewise primitive corpuscles of niter, and of the other salts by which congelation is effected, cannot be mixed intimately with them, as is required for hardening water, without a great effervescence taking place. The expansive force of ice, therefore, says the often-praised Musschenbroek (m), arises from very subtle corpuscles flitting in the atmosphere, mixed with the water, effervescing with it, and fixing it into a firm and solid mass.

594 Against our opinion very many arguments are usually opposed, which are easily answered. I shall propose to you only one. Experience shows that water is felt as cold if the heat of the water falls short of that heat by which our sensorium is affected: therefore cold does not consist in frigorific corpuscles, but only in a diminution of heat. I deny the conseq.: For that water appears cold to us which is less hot than the organ of touch, because, since the motion produced in the parts of the water by the corpuscles of heat that are in it is more remiss than that with which the nervous fibers of touch are then endowed, the watery particles themselves, applied to those fibers, retard and stop their motion, and at the same time condense and constrict them; in a word, they excite in them that passion which the sensation of cold in the soul accompanies.

595 Moreover, this objection either is worthless or certainly proves that heat too consists in the mere diminution of cold. For indeed, just as that body appears cold to us which is less hot than our sensorium, so, as experience witnesses, that body shows itself hot to us which is affected with a weaker cold than the sensorium itself. We call tepid (says the distinguished Boerhaave) (n) that which enjoys the same heat as the human body; hot, when it exceeds the heat of our body; cold, what is less hot.

596 It will not be superfluous here, the occasion being given, to point out for your benefit that the use of cold drink can be most pernicious and most wholesome according to the diverse condition of our body. If anyone has grown heated by rather vehement exercise, or by any other agitation of the body, he must avoid above all whatever could bring on a cooling, inwardly or outwardly. That sudden death has not rarely had its origin in the imprudent use of cold baths in these cases, the most learned physician Lancisi (o) testifies. For cold, when impressed, constricts the solid parts of the animal body and condenses the fluid ones, and the effect can be such that the action of the solid parts and the motion of the fluids are too greatly diminished. Hence the whole machine of the body can be thrown into the greatest disorder. Hence arise obstructions in the canals, and

very

(m) Comment. in Experim. Acad. del Cimento, pt. 1, p. 137.

(n) Praelect. Academ. in suas Instit., on the sense of touch, no. 483.

(o) Bk. 2, De mortibus subitaneis. [p. 188] very frequent impediments in the secretions of the humors, and from diminished

or wholly suppressed transpiration there ensue innumerable kinds of diseases, and even death itself.

## 597 From the abuse of cold drink its use too is understood. Namely, if there is

excessive extension and relaxation in the fibers, and atony of the nerves, in these cases cold drinks are most usefully applied. This being so, it ought not to be a wonder that the most distinguished Hoffmann published two little works, of which one is entitled On Cold Drink, Most Hostile to the Life and Health of Men; the other, however, On the Wholesome Drinking of Cold Water.

o remedy the defect of touch in exploring the heat and cold of bodies, 598

T         the more recent Philosophers invented that instrument which is com‐

monly called the Thermometer, or thermoscope, which we use as a criterion for discerning the degree of heat and cold in bodies. There are several forms of it, and as it were species. Its first invention is attributed to Cornelis

Drebbel, a Dutchman; Sanctorius afterwards brought it to a better condition; the

Florentine Academicians added greater perfection, after whom they are named

Florentine thermometers. All these are constructed with most highly rectified spirit of wine. The mercurial thermometer was invented by Daniel Fahrenheit, and is therefore called the Fahrenheit Thermometer. The most distinguished

Réaumur found a method of making thermometers of spirit of wine which correspond to one another by so constant a law that, placed in the same spot, they mark the same degree of heat. We do not wish to dwell on explaining the construction of the thermometer. It has been explained most clearly in his periodical sheets (p) by our fellow American Don José Ignacio Bartolache, Doctor of
