♎             ♏           ♐            ♑           ♒         ♓

and Libra,      Scorpio,   the Archer,   the Goat,   the Jar,   Pisces.

721 The use of the Zodiac is contained in these points: I. As the equator measures the diurnal motion, so the middle of the Zodiac, or ecliptic, measures the periodic motion of the stars, and chiefly of the sun; for the periodic motion is said to be completed when an entire revolution under the ecliptic is completed by the Stars. II. The eclipses of the Sun and Moon take place under this same circle. III. It causes the inequality of days and nights; for neither are the days equal among themselves, nor these to the nights, for the reason that the Sun is carried along in the ecliptic. IV. The constant alternation of the seasons, of which one succeeds another in turn in every yearly course, depends on the position of the ecliptic. V. The ecliptic is the boundary of the latitude of the Stars; for the latitude of a star is the arc of the circle (which is therefore called the circle of latitude, and is a greatest circle) drawn through the poles of the ecliptic and through the centers of the Stars themselves, intercepted between this center and the ecliptic itself. VI. The longitudes of the stars are numbered in it: for the arc of the ecliptic, proceeding from the beginning of Aries in consequentia, or according to the series of the signs, comprehended as far as the circle of latitude, is the longitude of the star.

722 The Meridian is the circle described from the two points of true rising and setting, or those in which, at the time of the equinox, the Sun rises and sets, which again are called cardinal, and passing through the poles both of the world and of the horizon, or the points Zenith and Nadir, and therefore cutting the horizon at right angles; when the Sun reaches it in its ascent, it makes midday. Hence all those points of the Sphere have the same meridian which are not distant from one another except along a straight line drawn from one pole of the world to the other; on the contrary, those places obtain a different one which are distant from east to west, or vice versa: so that the meridian changes while we travel from east toward west, or vice versa, but not at all when we proceed from north to south, or conversely. As many meridians, therefore, are really reckoned as there are vertical points that can be designated from east to west. Yet from one we take the beginning, which is named the first, so that from it the rest come into the count, the reckoning being made from West to East. This is fixed by some in one place, by others in another. The French had fixed it in the last of the Canary Islands, which is called the Island of Ferro, before the more recent Astronomers of that Nation established the first meridian in the Astronomical Observatory of Paris itself, as is customary today. We give the use of the meridian circle briefly.

Ff 2                                       723

[p. 226]

723 I. It divides the Heaven into two hemispheres, the Eastern and the Western. II. It measures the greatest altitude of the Stars above the horizon, for a star is raised above the horizon until it reaches the Meridian; then, receding from it, it is depressed: it is said to culminate when it reaches it. III. Throughout the whole year it determines the point of midday and of midnight: for it bisects all those circles which the Sun runs through by its diurnal motion. The other offices of the meridian, known to Astronomers, we pass over: for we go through these things not as Astronomers but by the office of Physicists.

724 The Colures are two greatest circles which, while they pass through the poles of the world, divide each other there at right angles, and divide the equator, and likewise the ecliptic, into four by an equal partition. The colure of the equinoxes is drawn through those points of the Zodiac in which, when the Sun is there, the equinoxes occur, namely through the beginnings of Aries and Libra. The colure of the solstices is drawn through the solstitial points (so called because the Sun, on reaching them, seems in some manner to stand still, or to make a station, that is: for some days not to change its declination from the equator at all), namely through the beginning of Cancer and of Capricorn.

725 The use of each colure consists in these points. I. They determine the four cardinal points of the Zodiac, namely those in which, when the Sun is placed there, the turnings of the seasons are brought about: in Aries the vernal, in Capricorn the winter, in Cancer the summer, in Libra the autumnal. Hence three signs correspond to each part of the year: to spring Aries, Taurus, Gemini, etc. II. As the colure of the equinoxes defines in the Zodiac those two points while the Sun occupies which day is equal to night, so the colure of the solstices marks two others in that same circle, in which, when the Sun is there, now the longest day and the shortest night, now conversely the longest night and the shortest day take place. III. As the colure of the equinoxes divides the signs of the Zodiac into six northern ones: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, and as many southern ones: Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, the Goat, the Jar, Pisces; so the other colure separates the ascending signs, which are contained from the beginning of Capricorn to the first degree of Cancer, from the descending ones, or the rest, etc.

726 The Tropics are two lesser circles in the Sphere, at which, when the Sun reaches them, it does not run out further either to the north or to the south, but turns back to the Equator. They are also usually called Solstitial, because they are drawn through the solstitial points of the Zodiac: hence one is called the tropic of Cancer, the other the tropic of Capricorn. These circles are distant from the equator 23 deg. and about 30 first minutes, from each other 47 deg., from the nearer pole 66 deg. and about 30 first minutes. Their use is distinguished as threefold. I. They bound the path of the Sun. II. They define the longest and the shortest day on an oblique horizon. III. They close the torrid zone and begin the temperate.

727 The Polar circles are twin, likewise lesser circles; they have their name from the poles toward which they are moved, the one being of the arctic, the other of the antarctic, yet as far

[p. 227] removed from these as the tropics are from the equator, namely 23 deg., about 30

first min. These circles, together with the tropics and the equator itself, are commonly called parallels, because all of them stand apart from one another by an equal interval at every point of their circuit. The use of the polar circles is: I. That the stars enclosed within the arctic circle never set for those to whom the sphere is either oblique or parallel, and those comprehended within the antarctic never rise. II. By their interposition the temperate Zones are distinguished from the frigid. All these things will be understood more clearly by inspecting some armillary sphere.

## CHAPTER II

On the threefold position of the Sphere.

n a threefold situation the sphere can be viewed, namely in the right, the 728

I       oblique and the parallel, according as the position of the equator with respect

to the horizon is different. The sphere is right when the equator stands perpendicularly over the horizon and cuts it at right angles, so that its poles are set in the horizon. Those who dwell under the equator are said to have this position; where, therefore, throughout the whole year the days are equal to the nights. The sphere is oblique in which the equator is inclined to the horizon obliquely, or at unequal angles. Those enjoy this whose latitude, or distance from the equator toward one or the other pole computed on the meridian of the place, does not reach 90 degrees, that is: all those who dwell between the equator and the poles; for them, therefore, the days are unequal to the nights.

729 The sphere, finally, is called parallel in which the equator keeps parallelism with the horizon. This position of the sphere is had by those whose vertex coincides with one of the poles of the world, and so whose latitude equals 90 deg., or by those who live under the poles: for those who dwell under it there is in the yearly course only one day and one night, each bounded by as great an interval of time as the Sun takes in traversing six figures of the Zodiac; for since their horizon and the equator coincide, six signs of the Zodiac stand perpetually above the horizon, and as many lie hidden below it; for that reason it is necessary that the Sun shine upon them above the horizon for as long a time as is demanded for it to run through six signs of the

Zodiac, and again lie hidden below the horizon for as great an interval of time as is required for it to be moved through as many lower signs, that is, the space of 6

months.

730 Although, however, night as well as day ought to be circumscribed for them by the space of six months, yet for them the day is extended longer, while the night is on the contrary diminished, namely on account of the very refraction [p. 228] which the solar rays undergo, by far the greatest, while they pass through the exceedingly dense atmosphere of those places; whence it comes about that the Sun seems to shine above their horizon for some days, although it is depressed below it. Indeed the

Dutch who wintered in Nova Zembla in the year 1597 report that the Sun disappeared on the 4th day of November and was visible again on the 24th day of January, and so had anticipated the reckonings of astronomical calculation by an interval of about six days.

731 Moreover: since long-lasting twilights are drawn out for them, so that for about two months the rising of the Sun is as it were forestalled by the one, while the other lasts so long after the setting of the Sun, therefore the darkness of night holds them for no more than about two months. Nay, as Wolff observes (d), this darkness of two months is tempered, for more than half of that space of time, by the splendor of the Moon.

## CHAPTER III

The systems of the world are briefly set out.

y the name of system Philosophers here understand the order, or disposi732

B          tion, of this universe and of its principal parts, adapted to explaining the

motions and the celestial phenomena. Three systems have hitherto been celebrated in the Schools, both astronomical and physical, and they still flourish. It is fitting, therefore, to go through each of them briefly.

733 I. The Ptolemaic, so called from Claudius Ptolemy. His system makes first air, then fire, surround the earth, which is placed in the middle of the universe; it then constructs seven solid Heavens, one for each Planet, concentric with the circle of the world, in this order: that in the 1st, that is, in the highest of all, Saturn runs its course, in the 2nd Jupiter, in the 3rd Mars, in the 4th the Sun, in the 5th Venus, in the

6th Mercury, in the 7th the Moon. Above these Heavens, finally, it places the firmament with the fixed stars, which he called the primum mobile, because he thought that by its motion the orbs of the lower Planets are carried from east to west in the space of 23 hours, 56 minutes, 4 seconds.

734 II. The Tychonic system, constructed by Tycho Brahe. This, leaving the earth as the center of the universe, together with the immobile atmosphere, sets the Moon in the first place around it, then the Sun; around this, as the center of the remaining

Planets, he placed Mercury, Venus, Mars, then Jupiter with the four Satellites discovered by Galileo, and at length Saturn with its two attendants; finally he

(d) Elem. Geograph. §. 131. [p. 229] he added on top of all these the firmament, concentric with the earth.

735 III. The Copernican system took its name from Nicolaus Copernicus, after the thirty years’ study which he spent on illustrating this hypothesis. According to it the Sun is set immobile in the center of the world; he holds that around it Mercury moves nearest, then Venus, next the Earth with the Moon circling about it, afterwards Mars, then Jupiter, and finally that Saturn revolves; beyond all the Planets, and indeed at an almost immense distance, he places the Sphere of the fixed Stars, wholly destitute of all motion. To the single Planets, the Sun alone excepted, which he therefore strikes out of the number of the Planets, he assigns a periodic motion, namely under the Zodiac, following the series of the signs.

736 To the Earth he assigns a threefold motion, namely: first, that of turning about its own axis from west to east, by which the Copernicans mean to explain the alternation of night and day; for once this motion is supposed, the Sun seems to us to be whirled from east to west, and the earth always presents another face to the Sun to be illuminated: this motion he calls diurnal, because it is completed in the interval of one day. The second he calls periodic, in the great orb around the Sun under the ecliptic, by which motion the earth so advances through the signs that the Sun appears to us to be in the sign which it covers, and hence, while the earth is in the northern signs, the Sun appears to us to dwell in the southern ones, and the reverse: this motion he names annual, as it is completed in the space of one year.

737 Lastly he establishes the motion of parallelism, by which the axis of the earth itself, in its revolution around the Sun, always remains parallel both to the axis of the world itself and to itself: by this motion the Copernicans unfold the phenomena of the alternation of the seasons of the year. To explain this matter, moreover, they also adopt such an inclination of the earth’s axis to the plane of the ecliptic that it makes with it an angle of 66 degrees, 30 minutes. “In this very age of ours (says the distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry) (e) very many men eminent in piety and religion, some even distinguished by the Purple, are freely permitted to hold with Galileo and with Copernicus, provided they do not call it a certain and undoubted System, but make it a hypothesis convenient for the uses of Astronomy, as was provided by the Decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office in the year 1620.” Thus far he. (Fig. LXX sets the Copernican System before your eyes.)

Chapter

(e) Praelect. Theolog. vol. 1, Praelect. 1, On the Workmanship of the World, p. 130, Venice edition, year 1742.

[p. 230]

C H A P T E R I V.

A judgment on the systems of the world.

say: the Copernican System, as a mere hypothesis for explaining the mo738

I       tions of the Stars and the phenomena, seems much more suitable than the

Ptolemaic and the Tychonic. We show this first in general. For the hypothesis of Copernicus is not opposed to Physics and Astronomy as the Ptolemaic system is. For who could understand, in the latter, how the primum mobile carries away all the lower spheres from east to west, while these nevertheless enjoy that motion in such a way that, by a contrary reckoning, they at the same time advance daily from west to east according to the series of the signs under the Zodiac? For if the surfaces by which these spheres touch one another, namely the convex surface of the lower and the concave of the upper, are smooth, it will come about that the upper imparts no motion to the lower sphere, and so the former can revolve without carrying the latter along with it; but if they are made rough, so that their projecting parts fit into one another, it is clearly evident that one and the same motion will be effected both of the upper and of the lower spheres, as Gassendi rightly argues (f).

739 The phenomena clearly show that the Ptolemaic system agrees very little with Astronomical observations. For it has been found that Mercury and Venus are seen by us from the earth now at the sides of the Sun, now above it. But in this hypothesis they ought always to appear below the Sun and nearer to us. Not to speak of the awkward position of the fixed stars, since they are all set fixed in one surface, whereas it is manifest among Astronomers that they are located in different planes, some more remote than others.

740 Second: the Copernican hypothesis is more orderly, and weaves together the position and disposition of the celestial bodies in a neater series; for in it none of the primary Planets cuts the orbit (g) of another, as in the system of Tycho; then the revolutions of all the Planets are performed about the same center, namely the Sun, contrary to what happens in the Tychonic. Moreover, the hypothesis of Copernicus, by attributing motion to the earth while meanwhile the Sun and the fixed stars stand in their places, explains the phenomena of the Heaven much more simply and from fewer principles than

(f) Phys. sect. 2, bk. 1, ch. 1.

(g) The orbit of a Planet is the name given to that curved line, returning into itself, which it de‐

scribes in its periodic motion. [p. 231] than the Tychonic does; for in the latter all the globes contained in the celestial spaces, the terraqueous one excepted, are set in motion, and indeed in such a way that each completes its circuit in the interval of 24 hours, so that for that reason they must be moved with an almost incredible velocity: therefore the Copernican hypothesis is to be preferred (Ax. II, §. 32).

741 For this reason it is much easier, and much more apt, for Astronomical observations and for constructing demonstrations: so that the Tychonian Astronomers too make use of the Copernican hypothesis to complete their observations and to carry out the construction of their tables. Nay, as the most distinguished Serry observes (h), it was once adopted by the Church herself for the emendation of the Roman Calendar.

742 The diurnal motion, indeed, by which the earth itself is turned from west to east, brings it about that the Sun, the Planets themselves and the fixed Stars seem to us to revolve from east to west; hence the alternation of day and night follows; for, as all who know the nature of motion are forced to admit, since all things which appear to us to be moved in place are perceived in this way because either they themselves really change their place, or the spectator proceeds in the opposite direction while those bodies are unmoved, according to that line of Virgil (i):

743 We are borne forth from the harbor, and lands and cities fall away, therefore it is necessary that all the phenomena of the diurnal motion appear to us in just the same way, whether the diurnal revolution toward the West is attributed to the Stars themselves, or the motion in the opposite direction, namely toward the East, is said to belong to the earth and to our eye, the Sun and the stars not being moved from their place. But it will be enough to have hinted at these things.

744 The Tychonians frame their chief argument against the Copernican hypothesis from the Sacred Scriptures. They contend, namely, that the doctrine of Copernicus is opposed to their words, inasmuch as these manifestly teach that the Sun moves, but that the earth stands still. Thus Genesis 19: The sun was risen upon the earth. Psalm 92: He hath established the world which shall not be moved. Ecclesiastes ch. 1: But the earth standeth for ever. The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place; and Josue ch. 10 (when the Leader of the Jews commanded that the Sun should not move over against Gabaon): So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down the space of one day. Isaias ch. 38: And the sun returned ten lines by the degrees by which it was gone down. And from these very many conclude that the Copernican system, which asserts the motion of the earth and the rest of the Sun, seems to be opposed to the authority of the Holy Scriptures.

745 But the Copernicans, distinguished alike in learning and in reverent piety toward the Divine word, reply that their opinion in no way conflicts with these testimonies. For they say that these and other words of the kind must be understood not in the literal, physical, proper and absolute sense, but only in the popular, optical, improper

Gg                                                and

(h) In the place cited above.

(i) Aeneid, bk. III, v. 72. [p. 232] and according to appearance. They answer that Divine Scripture tempers itself to the capacity of the common people. The reason they give for asserting this is that “God (as the distinguished Muratori says (k)), speaking through his Scriptures, did not have this aim, to feed men’s vain curiosity about things not necessary to know, about the elements of the world and about bodies, but to hand down things truly useful for attaining eternal happiness. For He does not speak in the learned words of human wisdom, but lowers Himself to the use of those expressions which, although they are recognized as less accurate and as improper when weighed in the balance of human wisdom, yet set forth some useful and salutary truth more conveniently to an unlearned people.” For the rest, they profess that they do not wish to depart from the common ways of speaking, and that they will speak in accommodation to what appears by the testimony of the senses: The Sun rises; it is raised to the point of midday; it declines toward the West, etc.

746 The distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry too, after adducing the testimonies of Sacred Letters cited above, rises up thus against the adversary of the Copernican hypothesis (l): “Do you wield the censor’s rod on account of those few little words of Scripture? Why not rather, if you are a Theologian, until the Church condemns the ingenious System, bend the words of Scripture cited to a convenient sense? So that those words which are paraded in favor of the immobile stability of the earth may be understood only of firmness, consistency and duration, in no way excluding local motion: for Divine Wisdom is also said to have established the Heavens, or the sky above, Prov. 8, though motion according to Ptolemy’s System is in no way at odds with that firmness of the heavens: while those which are brought forward from Sacred Letters in favor of the mobility of the Sun were said not according to the truth of the thing, but according to the opinion of the common people and the common manner of speaking, so that the Sacred Writers might accommodate themselves to the understanding of an unlearned people: which we have made manifest by so many other examples; and in this very one which is especially objected, about Josue, it is most certain, namely that it was said according to the opinion of the common people, if the whole narration of the deed is attended to more diligently. Move not, O sun, says Josue, toward Gabaon: and yet, since the earth is a small mass in comparison with the Sun, and Gabaon on that same globe of the earth is as a most minute point, what, I ask, is the Sun commanded, that it should not move toward Gabaon? Could the huge globe of the Sun so correspond to this point as either to move or to stand still over against it? Josue therefore alluded to the common judgment of the eyes, for to our eyes the Sun appears as a disk to be measured by two palms at most, running over a small space of the sky.

747 “It is added in the historical narration: So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven: but the celestial orbs, being spherical (if we wish to speak exactly), as they lack extremities, so also they lack a middle; and no middle can be devised in a circular path

or

(k) De moderamine Ingenior. ch. 22. (l) In the place cited above. [p. 233] or line. That, therefore, must be interpreted according to the understanding of the

common people: that that place of the heavens seems to them the middle which is equally distant from the East and the West. The narration is finally closed with these words: there was not before nor after so long a day. Has then no longer day ever shone in the whole world? But it is well ascertained by those who travel through the regions situated under either Pole that the Sun shines longer there and that longer days occur: nay, it is most certain that this very thing is proved by a demonstrative and most evident reasoning by those skilled in Astronomical Science. The narration, therefore, was accommodated to the Jewish people, to whom the effects of the Sun in the polar regions were unknown.

748 “Unless we say this, and confess that the Sacred Writers, in these formulas of speech concerning the motion of the Sun and the stability of the Earth, spoke according to the custom of the common people, there is danger lest, with equal license and an equal abuse of the Divine Scriptures, some morose exactor of the Sacred

Words should set about demonstrating this very system of Copernicus and Galileo on the mobility of the Earth, which most of the more recent Theologians brand with their inconsiderate censures. For since the world is so often said in Sacred Letters to be set upon its cardines [poles, hinges]: 1 Kings ch. 2: For the poles of the earth are the Lord’s;

Proverbs 8: He had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the poles of the world; and since cardines, if we wish to speak strictly, denote a turning and movable thing set upon them, which is revolved and turned upon them: what, I ask you, will follow from this, except that the earth is movable and turning, which, set upon its hinges, is revolved and driven by a fixed law? All the more because in Job ch. 9, v. 6, God is said to move the earth out of its place; which the morose exactor of words will want to have been said without figure and katalexis (a certain manner of speaking accommodated to the common people).” Thus far the distinguished Serry.

749 But let these things be said in passing, not so that we may hold the system of

Copernicus and Galileo as ratified and fixed, since we said from the very beginning that we adopt it only as a mere hypothesis for explaining the phenomena.

## APPENDIX

What is to be thought of the influence of the Stars?

ublicly debated is the question whether the stars concur in producing the 750

P        effects observed on the earth, or, as it is commonly put, whether they influ‐

ence sublunary things. The Sun chiefly, and the Moon, seem to some to share a communion of effluvia with our earth: an argument which they extend from these two Stars to the rest; nor are they content to say that the stars act on sublunary things through heat and light, but they think that various other influences

Gg 2 [p. 234] are exerted upon the earth, while they attribute different specific properties to the Stars: that the Moon, being exceedingly moist, excites the humors on the earth; that Saturn is cold; Mars dry and hot, etc.; so that, accordingly, the rising of some brings on rain, that of others induces drought, etc. It is not our pleasure to pursue these and more things of the kind any further: we shall set forth our view of the influence of the Stars in brief. Wherefore the conclusion follows.

751 Apart from the action of light we acknowledge no other influence of the stars upon the earth: except, however, the Sun, which by its heat, sensible enough, warms our earth, and also the Moon, which, if not by heat or cold, yet certainly by its weight upon the atmosphere beneath it, can press upon our globe variously according to its varying position. For, in the first place, certain substantial effluvia, moist, dry, etc., cannot be transmitted from the stars to the earth; for what cause can be adduced by which such effluvia should be propelled through the longest spaces beyond the atmosphere of their star, which extends only some miles? Certainly about terrestrial effluvia all agree that they by no means run out beyond the atmosphere into the region of the Moon: then, even if effluvia were thrust out, what can be imagined that would direct them to our earth rather than to some other space and celestial body? Finally, if the Moon, in which our adversaries place the greatest force, scattered its effluvia spherically, then, since these diverge from one another the more, the further they recede from the lunar body, and at so great a distance as the Moon has from the earth can and must be spread very far apart, those effects which are attributed to the influence of the moon can by no means be produced by so stingy and meager a dew of effluvia.

752 It is shown, secondly. The action of light can be the cause of all the effects; for light consists in the rectilinear pressure of the ethereal substance, propagated all the way to us. Therefore a different motion of the smallest particles can be excited, namely a vehement, varied and perturbed one; and once this motion is posited, one effect follows, and when it ceases, again another, without any need to have recourse, in order to explain the moisture of the nights, to I know not what outflowings of the Moon. Wherefore, when we see the whole of nature cherished and propagated, plants growing up, grain turning yellow, fruits ripening, in a word, generations, alterations and augmentations promoted; when we experience the seasons of the year recurring with a fixed regulation, and more particular changes of the air, often very diverse, taking place according to the concurrence of other causes, it is necessary that we attribute these things to the action of the Sun; but to the Sun acting in no other way than by its light and the heat consequent upon it.

753 Hence, although there is in the other stars a force of striking and agitating the slender fibrils of the optic nerves, and so, since particles thinner than these fibrils and more apt for motion are contained in the air, water and earth, a force of agitating and moving these particles, and consequently of producing some effects (how far these will fall under sense, each will judge from the almost immense distance of the fixed stars, and from the

[p. 235] faint light of the planets), nevertheless none at all is to be ascribed to them except in proportion to their light, whose action must be held as demonstrated.

And since the light of the Sun alone is stronger than the light of all the stars together, therefore the cause of all these effects is chiefly to be attributed to it. But if it should perhaps be observed that the temper of the air is not the same whenever the Sun darts its rays upon the earth in the same way, this is to be referred not to the other heavenly bodies, but to some peculiar condition, at that time, of the air or of the earth. From these things it follows:

C O RO L L A RY I .

754

Judicial astrology is to be repudiated as a most empty imposture, unworthy of a

Philosopher, both because it is reproved by the Sacred Scriptures, condemned by the Councils of Braga and Toledo, censured by the Fathers, and forbidden by the authority of the Supreme Pontiffs and by the canon and civil laws, and because it is hissed off with laughter by all the wise. Certainly that division of the

Heaven into 12 houses, on which the horoscope is founded, or the figure of the celestial configuration that exists at the moment of birth, is a fiction. Moreover, neither do the same fates befall all who are born under the same star, as is plain from the example of the twins Esau and Jacob, who had the most different propensity and fortune; nor do those who experience similar fates enjoy the same horoscope, as is manifest: since many perish together by shipwreck, fire, plague, or battle, although they were brought into the light at the most different times. Not to mention that the whole supposition of this art, taken from the septenary number of the planets and from the situation of the celestial houses, is false. The first is shown by the satellites of Jupiter and Saturn, indeed even by the single one of Venus; the second, because the constellations to which they gave the name of the 12 Signs of the Zodiac, in whose order they hold that their

12 houses are found in the Heaven, have long since already receded 30 degrees from their original place. But there is no leisure to dwell on trifles.

C O RO L L A RY I I .

755

Aeroscopic astrology, or that which foretells storms and changes of the air from the stars, is to be rejected by the Philosopher: for this art is confirmed neither by any reason nor by experience; for soothsayers of this kind posit certain properties in the planets: Saturn cold and dry, Venus a hot and moist planet, etc., which suppositions are not philosophical conjectures but fabulous ones; for why should one be hot, another moist, when all are opaque masses not much unlike our earth? By experience they cannot establish their art; [p. 236] for this rests on frequently repeated observation, whereas the astrologers neither have nor can have an observation in which, from a similar position of the stars, a similar event has followed in sublunary things: since it is certain from the astronomers that the same aspect of the same stars does not return within many millions of years; and even if such a position had returned, it would have been unknown, as regards all the stars, to those unskilled men, since until the past century they were ignorant of the secondary planets.

756 Nor do predictions that sometimes come true do anything for a presumption of truth; for who is there, says Cicero, who, hurling darts all day long, does not sometimes hit the mark? Besides the fact that the far more numerous false ones carry very great weight toward detracting from the astrologers’ credit, there are innumerable examples of this. Thus in the year 1524, on account of great conjunctions of the planets in Aquarius, entire and certain deluges were predicted, yet the year was most serene; in the year 1586, winds and storms on account of conjunctions of all the planets, although the whole year was passed in calm. Certainly the astrologers themselves do not agree among themselves in their predictions: hence a certain Frenchman bought himself so many calendars that for each single day he could choose one conformable to the heavens, whereby it came about that he said his calendar was conformable to the heavens the whole year round; and although these prophecies are sometimes inserted in calendars, it is by no means proved that this is done by the counsel of the wise, or that credence is given by them to these follies, since one will hardly find in the whole world a learned astronomer who does not indignantly reject this simplicity, unworthy of a learned man, as Amort says. (m)

757 These things, namely, are done so that custom may be served, not otherwise than as physicians themselves accommodate themselves to the phlebotomic table, whose foundation is nothing other than the numerical order of the days counted from the new moon, which has no force at all. Certainly Amort says: the table for the letting of a vein, which is usually in calendars, is only for boys, rustics, and the simple common people. On account of the same inefficacious relation of numbers, the opinions about critical days and climacteric years are to be counted among fables.

C O RO L L A RY I I I .

758

Effects are falsely, and with excessive credulity, attributed to the Moon. Thus the

Moon is believed to corrode stones by a certain peculiar force; the bones of animals are thought to be full of marrow while the Moon is waxing, but empty of marrow while it is waning, and almost filled with blood. Lobsters, oysters, and many other fish are judged to be fuller at the new or the full moon than at the half moon. But these things are deservedly placed among things rashly spread abroad; for it is most likely, says the distinguished Rohault

(n)

(m) Phys. Partic., pt. 1, q. 10. [p. 237] (n), that the heat of the sun in the space of many years can torrefy and consume these

stones, which are consumed by fire in a few hours; and when this happens, it ought to seem no wonder at all if the moisture of the air reduces these stones, just as it does lime, to powder. Similarly, he continues, it is falsely thought that the bones of animals are full of marrow while the Moon waxes and empty while it wanes; for when he had observed this for more than 25 years, he always found some bones full of marrow and others empty, both while the Moon was waxing and while it was waning.

759 Wherefore another cause is to be assigned: it is most likely that the bones of certain animals are empty of marrow either because the animals have lacked nourishment or because they have been worn out by labor. Falsely too, and wholly against experience, has it been believed that the Moon, according to her various phases, fills out or thins lobsters, oysters, etc. If the bodies of fish sometimes seem diminished, this happens either from a lack of nourishment, or because they are too much agitated, the waves being stirred up by a storm, or even by their own exertion; which will seem most likely to those who know that the fish caught in the Strait of Calais, where the water is most agitated, are generally less full than those caught near

Boulogne, where the sea rests somewhat more tranquil. Finally, the other effects are to be attributed not to a moist influence of the Moon, but to the constitution of the atmosphere present at the time, filled, namely, either with excessive moisture or with other noxious effluvia.

## DISSERTATION II

O N T H E E L E M E N TA L E A RT H .

## CHAPTER I

On the Nature of the Earth.

760

As we are about to treat of the nature of the Elements, the Earth first presents itself to us; for it is she that, as Pliny says, receives us when we are born, nourishes us once born, and, once we are brought forth, sustains us. Let the conclusion therefore be:

761 The earth is in all likelihood a body composed of coarser particles, less apt for motion, affected for the most part with an irregular figure. Proof: from the fact that this seems to agree best with the inertia, gravity, and

(n) Phys., pt. II, ch. 27. [p. 238] and solidity of the earth. Further: since the earth is dissolved with the greatest

difficulty by the force of fire, and its particles cannot be blown off into the air, they must be coarser; and since, united together, they make a consistent and fixed mass and shut off the passage of light, they are in all likelihood of an irregular figure, such as to be variously entangled with one another and to form winding passages. Finally, since the earth is held to be, as it were, the basis and foundation of the other miscible bodies, and since the hardness, fixity, solidity, and gravity of bodies is derived in great part from the earth, it is fitting that its particles be not only coarser and more entangled with one another, but also less apt for motion.

## REMARK

762

Descartes composes the earth from parts of the third element, namely from striated corpuscles entangled among themselves and twisted together [§.

44.]. Gassendi, with the Epicureans, would have it made up, like the other firm and dry bodies, of little rings and hooked atoms mutually adhering to one another. Fr. Regnault asserts that the particles of earth are branching, such as do not transmit light and make a consistent mass. The distinguished da Brescia says that we cannot divine with certainty of what figure the primitive corpuscles of earth are. It is probable, he then adds, that the primitive particles are affected with a cubic figure: since this, as Plato says, possesses the firmest and safest bases, and therefore seems most proper to those corpuscles which are destined by nature to constitute a dry, inert, and fixed body. On this, however, we determine nothing certain.

## CHAPTER II

On the Figure, Situation, and Magnitude of the Terraqueous

Globe. 763

We here contemplate the Earth as a mundane body, which is usually called the orb, or the terraqueous globe. The Earth, then, is a mundane body compacted of earth and water, with a fiery fluid interspersed here and there, into a vast mass, surrounded on every side by air, the common habitation of men and of brutes. Under the name of earth there comes here first of all the heap of solid and coarser bodies of various kinds: sand, clay, fat earths of diverse colors, stones, salts, etc.: a heap which is found in the Earth, [p. 239] as no one, unless he were ignorant both of history and of narratives, would deny. By water is understood that fluid and moist substance which God, Best and Greatest, in the first creation separated from the solid and dry, and gathered into the sea, which occupies a great part of the terrestrial surface.

764 That fire is diffused through the interior parts of the earth is plain, both from the fact that it is contained in mixed bodies, and from hot springs, the heat of mines, various exhalations, and fire-vomiting mountains. That the body of the Earth is compacted into a vast mass, no one is unaware; and it has its compaction and firmness from the cause of gravity, by which, namely, its parts are compressed and driven together on every side. But this is more difficult to resolve: into what figure this mass has been compacted: whether, namely, it holds a spherical one? Or a spheroidal one; and this, whether depressed at the poles and raised at the equator, or, on the contrary, rising at the poles and sinking at the equator.

765 Physicists endeavor to demonstrate that the Earth is spherical as regards sense, and physically. First, from the very eclipses of the Moon; for she suffers an eclipse because she enters the shadow of the Earth, and divides it just as if she were a plane parallel to the base of that shadow: since, namely, the Moon revolves around the Earth. But the shadow of the earth in all the lunar eclipses observed hitherto through so many centuries has always appeared round: therefore. Secondly, because all appearances, celestial as well as terrestrial, are explained most aptly and without error under a spherical figure of the Earth, as is plain in artificial globes and spheres. Thirdly, because those who travel see the summits of mountains and the tops of towers sooner than their bases, and that equally in every direction. We have said that the Earth is round in the physical sense, not the mathematical. Very high mountains in no way hinder its figure from being spherical as regards sense, for the earth, as Seneca says, is to the mountains as a huge ball to a hair. Nor does the flatness of the plains stand in the way, when the earth seems to us to stretch out into a plane: for this comes partly from its magnitude, partly from the visible horizon, which, relative to the whole globe, is a very small part and has no sensible curvature.

766 Hence the figure of the Earth, spherical as regards sense, is not hindered either by the opinion of Newton, Huygens, ’s Gravesande, and others, who think that the terraqueous mass is not formed like a sphere but presents the figure of a spheroid swelling under the equator and sinking at the poles; or by the hypothesis of both Cassinis, of Maraldi, Mairan, Eisenschmidt, and many more, by which a figure oblong toward the poles and depressed under the equator is attributed to the Earth. For besides the fact that the arguments set out above establish a round figure for the Earth in the physical sense, it is certain that neither of these opinions is greatly opposed to the physical and sensible roundness of the Earth.

767 For that excess of the greater diameter over the lesser is so slight that nothing prevents their being held as physically equal diameters, and hence the terraqueous mass as physically spherical. Newton

Hh [p. 240] indeed holds that the greater diameter of the Earth is to the lesser as 230 to 229, and hence that the earth would be higher under the equator than under the poles by 17 miles and a sixth part. Huygens, on the other hand, establishes almost the same ratio of the diameters, namely that of the number 578 to 577; and if this ratio is then worked out in miles by the rules of proportion, as is usually done, it will be plain that the excess of the greater semidiameter of the Earth over the lesser does not equal even 7 miles; and so slight a difference leaves the Earth, at any rate as regards sense, spherical.

768 Nor does the argument for the first opinion, taken from the daily motion of the Earth, prove anything; from this revolution the patrons of this hypothesis think it follows that the parts, by a greater centrifugal force under the equator than toward the poles, recede farther from the axis of the Earth, and so are more elevated under the equator than under the poles, and form the spheroidal mass of the Earth. It does not, I say, prove anything: for, granting the motion of the Earth about its axis, it does not evidently follow that the parts about the equator swell out and are compressed toward the poles: for the mass of the Earth is not soft but firmly compacted, nor does it seem conformable to experience that a sphere revolved about its axis should be changed into a spheroid compressed at the poles of the revolution, with whatever speed it be turned.

769 As regards the situation of the Earth, the common opinion is that it is placed in the very center of the universe, at least as regards sense. For although, by the Copernican hypothesis, the Sun is set in the center of the universe and the Earth is turned in the great orb around the Sun, yet in the judgment of the astronomers the semidiameter of the great orb, if it is compared with the semidiameter of the starry heaven, as it were vanishes, and brings it about that the Earth is distant from the center of the universe by no sensible interval.

770 The reasons, moreover, that establish this situation of the Earth are these. The first, because at either equinox the time during which the Sun stays above the horizon exactly equals the time during which it stays below the horizon. The second, because to us who exist on the surface of the Earth, whatever region at last we may inhabit, the stars always appear of the same magnitude, whether at their rising, or at their setting, or in the middle of the heaven, provided there are absent vapors, mists, and exhalations, which impede the sight and change the figure of bodies. The third, because in whatever part of the earth, setting aside the hindrances of mountains and valleys, we always see half of the heaven: thus of the 12 signs of the Zodiac, 6 are perpetually seen above the horizon, and of stars diametrically opposite, such as are, more or less, the Eye of the Bull and the Heart of the Scorpion, when one rises on the eastern horizon, the other sets on the western.

771 The magnitude of the Earth, if it is compared with the starry heaven, is so slight that it stands to it just as a point. Its absolute magnitude, however, is altogether uncertain. Indeed, in determining the magnitude of one degree of the great circles of the terraqueous orb, authors disagree very much among themselves. Hence it is no wonder if they dissent in establishing the magnitude of the Earth: since from the value of one degree

[p. 241] is gathered the value of the periphery of a great circle, and hence the quantity of the diameter and of the semidiameter, as well as of the convex surface, and finally the solidity, as geometers know. It is not possible to bring forward many measures here; I submit one or two, worked out, nearly, to the more common calculation. The diameter of the Earth contains nearly 1720 German miles. The surface, nearly 92,880,000 square miles. The solidity, nearly 26,563,680,000.

One celestial degree contains 25 common leagues of France: and a common league contains 2400 geometric paces.

## CHAPTER III

On Certain Terrestrial Bodies, and First on Petrifications.

cannot fail to make mention of a certain kind of terrestrial bodies, 772

I       namely of shells, oysters, and other testaceous bodies, which occur

among the strata of certain mountains. On their origin the opinion of physicists is threefold. Woodward derives this phenomenon from the universal deluge, namely: when all the lands were covered by the waters, then indeed rocks, marbles, metals, all bodies were divided into minute particles and molecules; thus divided, they were carried confusedly hither and thither by that force of the waters, but toward the end these bodies, immersed in the water, were precipitated according to the laws of gravity: hence it came about that those marine testaceous shells, being somewhat heavier, sought the part that belongs to rocks, stones, and the like, among which they are found even today for this very reason. The second hypothesis, which Leibniz recently defended, asserts that the sea was once in all those places in which shells and oysters are found, but that the sea itself has at present receded from those places, leaving the bodies there.

773 The third holds, with Lazzaro Moro, that testaceous bodies are found among the strata of mountains because the mountains themselves, together with those bodies, were once cast up from the bottom of the sea by the action of subterranean fire. It is not my pleasure at present to sift and weigh these hypotheses, which demand a fuller discussion. It will be enough to hint at this one thing: that there is not one and the same cause and origin, universally, of the oysters and testaceous bodies of this kind found in mountains and in more prominent places. It does not seem, indeed, to stray from likelihood that those marine spoils which the investigators of Nature find here and there on the surfaces of mountains, or at no great depth,

Hh 2 [p. 242] are to be traced chiefly to the deluge, and to seas at some time spread over those places, as a knowledge of History and Geography will show.

774 But those which are not rarely discovered in deeper caverns were, I think, deposited there by earthquakes, often violent ones: for in this way, the earth being shaken, the mountains burst asunder, and swallowed up, the spoils of animals could be buried together, and in the course of a long time be converted into stones, that is, be petrified. But if they are of the kind of marine spoils, these were carried there, together with a part of the sea, through subterranean passages made and hollowed out in these motions of the earth, where the water, having dried away in the length of time, and having been diffused into the strata of the earth or driven off into vapors, deposited spoils of this kind.

775 Finally, that spoils of one kind are found in one mountain and those of another kind in another, I judge is not to be taken in a precise sense; nor, because spoils of one kind have hitherto been found chiefly in one place, must it be said that those of another kind do not lie hidden there or cannot be found. These things having been briefly surveyed in general, we must say something about the magnet. For this stone, on account of its excellent virtue and utility, is both held in admiration and valued at a high price; so that it might accordingly seem shameful for those who inquire into the secrets of nature to make no mention of it at all. Let it, then, be:

C H A P T E R I V.

What Is to Be Thought of the Force of the Magnet?

he magnet has its name and origin from Magnesia, a province of 776

T          Macedonia, where it is dug up; but according to some, from Magnes, a

shepherd, who is said to have first discovered it on Mount Ida, when the iron tip of his staff adhered to a stone of this kind, which is now called a magnet. It is a stone not unlike iron, showing a blackish color, heavy, pregnant with iron; since indeed, when subjected to fire, it exudes steel, and moreover it is dug out of iron mines. Its force, which is called magnetic and is still wrapped in many difficulties, is reduced chiefly to three heads: to its direction, to the attraction of a magnet or of iron, and to the communication of its virtue. The directive force consists in this, that a magnet suspended in the air sets itself toward the meridian of the place and turns its southern pole toward the northern pole of the Earth, as also happens in the magnetic needle. However, this direction toward the pole is not constant everywhere; for now by more, now by fewer degrees, according to the diversity of regions, more or less, now hither now thither (that is, now toward the east, [p. 243] now toward the west) the nautical needles decline; indeed, after a notable time they sometimes change their direction in the same place; and this affection is called declination.

777 To this also pertains another affection of the same, which is called inclination, various indeed, but constant, by virtue of which a magnet, or a magnetic needle freely suspended in equilibrium, preponderates toward one side and is inclined, by this law: that the inclination is more or less notable according as the tract of the earth is more remote from or nearer to the equator; for under it a perfect equilibrium is had. The attractive force is that by which a magnet draws to itself either another magnet or iron; with this difference, however, that a magnet snatches iron to itself by either of its sides, but draws a magnet to itself by one side and repels it by the other. Finally, the force communicative of itself is that by which it imbues steel or iron with the same virtue in which it is itself strong: namely, the directive and the attractive. These things set out, we inquire into the cause of these phenomena: in which altogether obscure matter we shall lay down whatever may have an appearance of likelihood and may in some fashion expound the said effects to the understanding. Before we carry this out, a preliminary hypothesis is laid down.

778 We think it not incongruous to say either, with Gilbert, that the whole terraqueous globe itself is a certain huge magnet, which that author therefore called the terrestrial magnet; or, as Fr. Zucchi holds with many others, that the nucleus of the earth itself is a true magnet.

779 This is explained, 1: because iron implements acquire a magnetic force from mere contact and application to the earth: especially if they have stood erect upon the earth for a rather long time. Hence tongs and similar iron instruments, which are usually kept standing erect beside hearths for handling the fire, acquire a force for attracting little steel needles. So too iron rods which have remained a long time, especially in the line of the meridian plane, acquire a conversive force toward the pole. Secondly, because magnetic needles suspended by a thread are inclined toward the globe of the earth just as they are observed to be inclined toward a magnet.

780 So that for this reason the tonic nisus of the magnet, or of verticity, is not toward the celestial poles but toward the terrestrial ones: hence the magnetic force resides in the terrestrial globe. Thirdly, in mines, rocks, and quarries there appear, amid huge stones, lines traced like fibers, extended very far from south to north and disposed parallel to the terrestrial axis. From this it is gathered, in all likelihood, that the magnetic force, having slipped into those tracts through effluvia, determines that disposition from pole to pole. From these, now, is deduced:

Corollary.

[p. 244]

C O R O L L A R Y.

781

From the magnetism of the terraqueous globe it is concluded that certain effluvia, having gone out from one pole of the Earth, travel around the Earth toward its other pole, and there, entering into it again, go out through the other pole of the world; and thus a perpetual circulation of effluvia of this kind is set up in the Earth, not otherwise than a perpetual circulation of subterranean water, together with the terrestrial surface, is said to be carried on from pole to pole: although the cause by which it comes about that the fluid bursting forth from the bowels of the earth is borne from one pole toward the other still escapes the industry and intelligence of physicists, and must be deduced elsewhere, at the proper time, from mechanical principles. Moreover, these effluvia are indeed communicated also to other bodies existing in this globe, but chiefly to those which are most earthy, such as the magnet and iron, in which an apt disposition of the particles and pores offers itself both for receiving and for emitting them.

782 And just as in the terraqueous globe itself the said effluvia constantly go out from one pole and, carried around the Earth, enter again into the other pole, so too the magnet, like a little orb, has its effluvia, namely a vortical atmosphere, which enter at one of its poles and go out from the other, and indeed always by the same law; this is shown excellently by the iron filings into which a magnet is plunged, which stand erect toward the poles and, in places more remote from the pole, are inclined.

Then the very disposition of the particles of the magnet can prove this, since they are inclined more to one side than to the other, and are so disposed that they can afford ingress through one side but not, in turn, egress; that such a disposition of the parts can come about is plain from this, that while the magnet was being formed in its mine, the magnetic matter, crossing the earth from one pole to the other along lines parallel to the axis and returning in a perpetual circuit, could fit the passages of the magnet in such a way as to press down their interior little hairs toward that side to which it was carried.

783 The distinguished Helvétius holds, with Mr. Du Fay, that the pores of magnets are furnished within with little hairs, and that these are so laid down and bent that their points incline toward the north poles of the magnets. Those little hairs, therefore, do not delay the motion of the magnetic matter from the pole of ingress, that is, the one which the effluvia enter, to the pole of egress, that is, the one through which they burst out, since they are bent toward that side; but they resist the return of the same matter through the same passages, since they are inclined toward the opposite side with the greatest difficulty, or not at all. These things laid down, let the conclusion be:

784 I say 1. The directive force of the magnet seems to be traced to most subtle effluvia bursting out from one pole of the Earth and breaking in through the other.

The directive force of the magnet is, namely, that by which the magnet turns itself toward each pole of the world. But this is fittingly traced [p. 245] to the effluxes set forth in the said manner; for these, moving thereafter through the same passages of the magnet which they had made for themselves in the mine, accordingly set the magnet, by the rule of their own motion, along lines parallel to the axis of the earth, as is gathered from what was said a little before. Indeed, since it is plain that no body can perpetually incline toward its due point except by the contact of another body driven toward the same point, as Helvétius rightly says, it is evident that there are fluids spread closely around the Earth which are driven, in the direction of their motion, from the southern pole toward the northern.

785 Certainly this is shown manifestly also from the fact that if an iron needle, not yet imbued with magnetic force, is placed on a pivot in a nautical box, it will be seen in equilibrium, parallel to the horizon; but when the needle has been rubbed on a magnet and has obtained the directive force, then in northern places the part of the needle directed toward the north is depressed somewhat below the horizon, so that a little ball of wax must be added to the southern point of the needle to restore the equilibrium. At the Equator, or at an equal distance from either pole, the needle is not depressed at all. Once the Equator is crossed toward the south, the northern part of the point is raised and the southern is depressed. All of which certainly confirm, not in vain, the efflux and the influx, and the circulation, of the effluvia around the surface of the Earth.

## SCHOLIUM I. 786

The   phenomenon    of  magnetic    declination is fittingly expounded in our

Hypothesis. For it is certain that the parts of the terrestrial globe are very heterogeneous, and that various veins of iron occur here and there; indeed, in the same place not only the mountains, but also the rocks and the other parts lying hid under the earth or the sea, are now more copiously endowed with magnetic veins, now, whether because a certain tract has been shaken by a motion of the earth and the situation of its parts changed, or by excavations, or in some other way, are sparsely interspersed with veins of this kind. What of the fact that in the bowels of the lands magnets in some places lie hidden deep under the earth, and elsewhere cling in the summits, the bowels, and the roots of mountains; that the said veins of iron are frequently altered, diminished, and twisted, either by earthquakes, or by subterranean fires, or by floods of subterranean waters, or by diggers; and indeed that the air itself and the corpuscles diffused in it perhaps drive the magnetic effluvia somewhat out of their straight motion?

787 Therefore from these causes a varied declination of the same needle and magnet can occur even in the same place, so that in places not far distant from each other it is very notable, and in one it inclines toward the East, in another toward the West. In confirmation of this there serves the experiment reported by

Kircher and Jansonius: namely, that at Naples, after the notable conflagration of

Mount Vesuvius, a notable change of the magnetic declination was continually observed.

Scholium

[p. 246]

## SCHOLIUM II

788

The phenomenon of inclination is also explained: for, magnetic effluvia being supposed to burst forth from the earth, it is no wonder that the needle inclines toward the terrestrial globe along that part along which the stronger and more copious effluvia flow out, namely in the northern parts along one of its parts, in the southern along the other, and this the more, the nearer the regions are to the north or to the south pole. Nor is it any wonder that the needle under the Equator, where, namely, neither effluvia prevail and the place stands off from the poles by an equal interval, keeps a perfect equilibrium, free of all inclination.

## SCHOLIUM III

789

From these principles it is illustrated why the magnet, outside the mine, on the surface of the Earth, has a situation contrary to the situation which it held in the mine; for if the magnetic outflows are conceived to enter through the southern pole of the earth, they must also enter the southern pole of the magnet turned toward the same part of the earth while it is still in the mine: but since the effluvia flowing from south to north along lines parallel to the axis in the interior of the earth return on its surface from the northern pole to the southern, the magnet, drawn out of the earth, must be disposed in a contrary situation for receiving those outflows, and its southern pole must be turned toward the northern pole of the Earth, whence the effluvia are supposed to burst out.

790 I say 2. The attractive force of the magnet is derived not from the impulse of air coming in behind, but from the motion of the atmosphere surrounding the magnet, in all likelihood by the same mechanical manner of acting as the approach of homogeneous bodies. The first part is plain. In a vacuum both the attraction of iron to the magnet and its adhesion take place: indeed, iron is seized more quickly by the magnet when the receiver has been exhausted.

Therefore the attractive force cannot be traced to the action of the air. Besides, if the magnetic effluvia have such force as to expel the air between the iron and the magnet, and so to disturb the equilibrium of that column with the other columns of air, how should I think it can happen that in that intermediate space there is a lesser resistance, compared with the air pressing on the iron and the magnet from behind? Since into the place of the air there succeeds a stronger body (namely, the effluvia excluding the air).

791 The second part is demonstrated. To explain the attractive force of the magnet it is necessary that a reason be given why poles of the same name, whether one southern and the other southern, or two northern, repel each other [p. 247] not only in the magnet but also in the magnetic needle; then why poles not of the same name, namely one southern and the other northern, approach each other; and finally why iron is snatched by a magnet from either side. But these things are conveniently explained by the force of the magnetic atmosphere. For if, as we laid down above [§. 781 ff.], the internal configuration of magnets and the structure of their pores is such that the smallest molecules, laid down and bent like little hairs, incline with their tips toward one pole of the magnetic body, e.g. the northern, it will come about, this contexture of the parts being supposed, that the fluid running into the southern pole can freely pervade it and be carried flowingly over the surface of the little hairs, no force being brought upon them; whereas the parts of the subtler fluid that have slipped into the northern pole will bring force upon the tips which occupy and line the paths of the little hairs. Wherefore, if one magnet is placed toward another in such a way that the northern pole of the former faces the southern pole of the latter, then, since the atmospheric fluid of the one is driven in the direction which the inflection of the little hairs has in the other, the most subtle parts of the fluid will pass along the very surface of the little hairs with no force and impression, or the least, made upon them.

792 But when those poles of the magnets are joined from which the subtler torrent of atmosphere bursts forth, then indeed the molecules of this fluid flowing out of the pole of the one will be unable to enter the pores of the like pole in the other magnet, since the points of the little hairs are stretched out and so resist: hence, force being brought upon these paths, they will strive to repel the magnet into which they rush. But if those poles of the magnets into each of which the surrounding fluid breaks in are placed not far from each other, then, besides the fact that the directions of the magnetic fluid oppose each other, repulsion must follow from this, that the twin atmospheres do not coalesce into one in such a way that all the other fluid interposed is removed and so an approach follows; and although an entrance lies open to the effluvia through each of these poles, yet because each is supposed to be endowed with such a habit of pores that only the magnetic fluid can enter through them, the commingling of the atmospheres and their conjunction, in a manner, into one vortex (other heterogeneous fluids being excluded) is for that reason impeded: hence it will come about that the magnets do not approach each other, but are repelled by the opposite directions of the effluvia on either side. The same is to be thought of the magnetic needle.

793 Finally, that iron not yet imbued, as they say, with magnetic virtue is snatched to the magnet, at whatever pole it is placed, we assert on this ground: that the structure of this metal and the conformation of its paths seem adapted for receiving and transmitting the magnetic effluvia, in such a way indeed that these can penetrate more freely through its interior surface and be carried flowingly along, no force being brought upon the walls of the pores: whereby it will be brought about that the other fluids interposed in the space between the magnet and the iron are removed; and these being moved away, since, the most subtle fluid being spread around the bodies, along that part

Ii [p. 248] nothing resists, it follows that by its pressure the iron is urged toward the magnet.

794 The assertion is confirmed by an exposition of the phenomena; and first a reason is given why, besides iron or steel, no other bodies are drawn by the magnet: namely, because such is the disposition of the pores in iron, and the configuration of its parts, as in a body homogeneous with the magnet, that the effluvia penetrate it more easily than the other bodies: hence, while the torrent of effluvia crosses the pores of the iron in greater abundance, the resistance in the intermediate space is diminished, and, this being removed, these bodies are joined by the forces of the pressing fluid.

795 From this likewise the reason is drawn why a magnet, if it is clothed with steel or iron, or, as they say, armed, with well-polished steel plates placed around it, attracts far more strongly and holds fast what it has attracted: for the effluvia seem to flow more easily through steel than through air, and therefore a more abundant supply of them then bursts into the iron that is to be attracted, which before wandered more freely around the sides of the magnet and were less collected. Secondly: our opinion explains more aptly why smaller magnets sometimes sustain greater weights, whereas larger ones are often weaker, indeed why some have a portentous force; for magnets often consist of notably heterogeneous parts, through which the effluvia are not transmitted so copiously, and which accordingly possess a slight atmosphere, by whose help the attraction is effected; on the contrary it can happen that a magnet, however small, compacted of purer parts, has for its bulk a great surrounding atmosphere.

795 Thirdly: on our opinion being laid down, the motion of flight and repulsion is expounded more fittingly for Physics than in the opinion of the others, who refer this to opposite vortices but attribute attraction to the air. It can scarcely be conceived, indeed, or said, that the air between two poles of egress is not driven out when two magnets are set near each other; and yet attraction does not follow this repulsion of the air, the attraction which they say comes about when the intermediate air is expelled to the sides, and the air coming in from behind drives these two magnetic bodies toward each other, where the resistance is less.

797 I say thirdly: The magnetic force communicated to iron or steel is to be derived from magnetic outflows. For magnetic force is communicated to iron or steel when these bodies are rubbed on, or applied to, the pole of a magnet or of its armature; and it consists in this, that the iron or steel directs itself toward the poles of the world and attracts other iron. But this force without doubt proceeds from magnetic outflows; for while a nautical needle is rubbed on the pole of a magnet or of its armature, those outflows rush into the needle and incline its little fibers, or hairs, to one side, according as the iron has been drawn along the magnet, so that they form for themselves two poles in the iron or the needle, one of ingress and the other of egress, not otherwise than they are in the magnet itself; which gains likelihood from the fact that these pores are interchanged by drawing the magnet in the contrary direction: therefore.

[p. 249]

798 That this can come about by the help of effluvia is fittingly shown; first of all from the fact that the little fibers of iron are softer and more flexible than those of the magnet, as the diversity of their texture suggests. Then this very thing is explained by the analogy of mercury entering into a rod of gold; for it is understood just as easily that the mineral effluvium of the magnet enters into iron and confers magnetism on it, as that the effluvium of mercury enters into gold and whitens it. What of the fact that, just as the mercury imbibed by gold is separated from it by fire, so the magnetic force is said to be removed from magnetic iron by fire?

## REMARK

799

By no means fictitious is the circulation of the magnetic effluvia around the

Earth, and their egress from one of its poles and ingress into the other: for what is said fittingly for explaining the phenomena of nature is not forthwith to be deemed fictitious, if it is not destitute of foundations that afford likelihood.

Certainly for no other reason is the nautical box of no use in the places nearest the pole than because the magnetic outflows, bursting from the pole almost perpendicularly, direct the needle itself no more to one side than to another; which the Dutch report that they experienced on their voyage.

800 Nor is a similar gyration around the magnet itself fictitious; for if we ascribe an atmosphere to all other bodies, we should surely deny it preposterously to the magnet. However, the effluvia are driven to perpetual motion by a most subtle universal fluid; but by what mechanism this is accomplished remains to be taught; and toward this circuit around the magnet they are, as it were, determined by the very disposition of the pores and parts in the magnet, which are apter for receiving them than any other bodies whatever, and indeed on one side better accommodated for letting them in, on the other for emitting them. Both points are suggested and expounded by the analogy of the juices in plants, which insinuate themselves through fibers and do not return through the same, and by their perennial circulation through little canals. Many more things about the magnet are handed down by Kircher, Gaspar Schott, Lana Terzi, Wolff,

Musschenbroek, and many others.
