## DISSERTATION III

O N WA T E R A S A N E L E M E N T.

## CHAPTER I

On the Nature of Water.

he nature of water is made by Gassendi, with the Epicureans, to consist 801

Tin smooth and round particles, which are slippery and separated by frequent little voids. Others claim that the atoms of water are cubic, because water can scarcely be compressed. Descartes thinks they are oblong and rounded.

802 I say: Water is more probably a substance consisting of parts that are oblong, rounded, flexible, slippery, voluble, little entangled with one another, and oval, that is, endowed with an egg-shaped figure.

803 For, this nature of water being supposed, the phenomena and all the properties belonging to water can be fittingly accounted for. Thus fluidity is deduced from slipperiness and volubility; from which likewise is derived the force of dissolving bodies that cohere more loosely. The force of moistening flows from flexibility and from the oblong and rounded figure; for thus the particles easily insinuate themselves into the little pores of bodies, roll around the more prominent parts on their surface, and adhere to them. The force of washing off dirt is also understood from these things; and this washing is done more conveniently when the body to be washed is prepared with a viscous matter, such as soap: for since dirt is generally fatty, it adheres more easily to the viscous matter, and then the water purges away the dirt together with the viscous matter.

804 The force of lubricating and of flowing off depends on smoothness and on the rounded figure, on account of which water runs off easily from polished and clean bodies, such as glass, or from fatty ones, as happens with the feathers of birds. Quick and swift evaporation is derived from particles little entangled. Gravity, from density, etc.; from which also arises its aptitude for passing into ice, beyond other liquors which are composed of finer particles: hence too it is that water is rarefied in a wonderful manner, but can scarcely be compressed, since its parts, touching one another immediately and rolled over one another, cannot be joined more closely. Finally, the lack of odor as well as of taste in water proceeds from its flexibility and volubility; for flexible and voluble particles, or molecules, run over the organ of taste and of smell with a gentle motion, and do not strike its papillae and fibrils with any edge. The reason of the other properties too will easily be deduced from that structure and conformation of the parts.

Scholium.

[p. 251]

## SCHOLIUM

805

In order to constitute the nature of water, insofar as it is a fluid substance, it is first of all required, as is clear (from what was said on fluidity), that its parts be divided and dissociated from one another and touch one another in few planes. The distinguished Helvétius judges that an oval figure of the aqueous molecules agrees better with all the effects which they produce; for these, he says, “will not touch one another except along the smallest surfaces, and accordingly they can be carried flowingly by the least force; and yet they will congeal into ice, because the interstices placed between them are smaller than those which would be given if the parts of water enjoyed a spherical figure. Moreover, the parts of water endowed with this figure can accomplish the dissolution of bodies more easily, because their extremities are finer than their middle part.

Finally, water must be insipid and odorless, because the extremities of its parts are blunter.” Thus he.

## CHAPTER II

On Springs, Rivers, and the Other Waters. 806

The origin of springs and rivers is what we chiefly weigh here, and on it there is a twofold opinion. Of the Moderns, some trace their origin from the sea, others from rains and melted snows. The first teach that the waters of the sea are carried through subterranean passages into the mountains and the other places in which the sources of springs are found, and that, having deposited in them their saltness and bitterness, they then leap forth through hidden passages and fissures. The latter contend that the part of the waters which falls down in rains and is drunk in by the earth penetrates through the fissures and chinks of rocks and of mountains, is received and collected in certain cavities of them and in reservoirs, from which the waters then flow down little by little through certain narrow outlets and give origin to springs, from which rivers are derived. What is to be thought in this controversy our conclusion establishes.

807 Springs and rivers arise not from the sea, by a hidden route penetrating the earth and thence welling out, as if by a road made for it, but from rains, melted snows, and vapors. The first part is proved. If springs arose from the sea, the sea waters would have to deposit their saltness and bitterness, and to ascend, as it were of their own accord, to that height above the mountains at which [p. 252] we observe springs welling forth. But neither seems capable of being maintained; for in this way the sea water would lose its saltness and bitterness insofar as it deposited, or left behind, its salty and bitter particles in those windings which the adversaries posit; but this cannot happen: for one of two things must follow: either that at length, in the course of time, those ways and passages are obstructed by the adhering salt, or this other, that the salt is scraped off and carried away by the water coming upon it, and so the waters burst forth from the springs filled with a more potent salt, or with a greater quantity of it.

808 The other cannot be reconciled with the principles of Hydrostatics: for from these we hold it as certain that water in communicating tubes, of whatever figure and perimeter at last, does not keep equilibrium unless it has obtained the same height in them, that is, has set its surface in each tube physically parallel to a horizontal line. But the places of very many springs are higher than the surface of the sea. Therefore the sea water cannot ascend to the height from which springs well forth.

809 The second part is proved: Springs and rivers are had when vapors, rains, and melted snows are given; when these are taken away, they perish; when these are increased or diminished, they are increased or diminished. For it is proved by constant experience that those regions abound in springs in which it often rains and snows; whereas very few rivers are interspersed in those in which rain is rare; none in those on which no rain and snow ever falls. Then it has been found by experience that when rains last rather long the springs swell, and even after the rains have ceased the rivers still remain higher; that in dry weather springs are diminished, and in a long drought they disappear entirely.

810 Thus the distinguished Mariotte attests that in the year 1681, which had been very dry in France, the waters of very many springs were dried up: and he confesses that he learned by his own experience and observation that after a long drought, when the rains came on, the less deep wells received water and rose first, the deeper ones more slowly: an evident indication that a moderate rain, sufficient for replenishing the first, does not suffice for the second.

811 There is added the testimony of the same Mariotte, and also of Halley; the former of whom, having made a calculation, found that the quantity of water falling from the heavens in the places lying around the Seine (*) is far greater than that which flows from that river into the sea in the same time. Halley, on the other hand, concerning the quantity of the vapors which, chiefly by the force of the Sun, ascend daily from the Mediterranean Sea (the same is true of other waters), found, having made the trial, that their quantity is so great that the waters which daily flow into it from the Ebro, the Tiber, the Nile, and the other rivers scarcely equal one third part of that which is likewise raised into vapors from the sea itself each single day.

He

(*) The Seine, a river of France.

[p. 253]

812 He relates, moreover, that on the island of St. Helena, often at night on the summit of a mountain exceeding the surface of the sea by 2400 feet, he experienced so great a condensation of vapors even in clear weather that within not many minutes it had so wetted the optical glasses that they had to be wiped, and were otherwise little fit for astronomical observations. The paper, too, on which he was writing was so quickly wetted by the falling dew that the ink was diluted by the dew: whence one may understand how great a quantity of vapors is condensed on the very lofty summits of mountains.

813 Wherefore, if we join the condensed vapors with rains and melted snows, there will be water enough to feed all springs. Besides, diggers testify from their own experience that huge reservoirs of rain and snow waters are spread out beneath the earth: of such hydrophylacia Kircher enumerates four altogether memorable: one, the chief of Asia, in the Kingdom of the Mogul; another, of Europe, under the Rhaetian Alps; the third in Africa, under the Mountains of the Moon; the fourth, among the American ones, between Peru and the Kingdom of Chile. Nor does that text of Ecclesiastes, ch. 1, stand in the way: all the rivers run into the sea . . . unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return. For it suffices that the sea waters are condensed into vapors and resolved into rain or snow for it to be truly affirmed that the rivers go out from the sea.

814 Of waters there are diverse species and properties, according to that saying of Pliny: waters are such as the earth through which they pass, understanding not only earth strictly so called, but also juices, and minerals, and in general all subterranean things from which the water flowing through can take up something. Hence the origin of hot springs, of thermal baths, and of other healthful waters. From similar causes some waters and springs are metal-bearing; and very many rivers furnish gold to the washers of their sand, while, having flowed past veins and channels teeming with gold, they carry down very minute particles.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N I V

ON THE ELEMENTS OF AIR AND FIRE,

## AND ON THE SUBLIME BODIES, OR

## METEORS, AND ALSO ON PLANTS

## CHAPTER I

On the Nature of Air.

hat a subtle fluid is spread round the Earth has already been said 815

T           above; this fluid, though invisible, is nevertheless perceived from vari‐

ous effects, and is necessary for producing very many motions and changes in nature and for prolonging animal life; we designate it by the name of air. Many things about it we have indicated in the course of the Physics, from which its properties and forces are more than sufficiently understood; here, as in its proper place, we briefly inquire into its nature. Let the conclusion therefore be:

816 Air is an aggregate of subtle particles loosely cohering, flexible with a certain rigidity, which compose a fluid altogether different from the aggregate of vapors and terrestrial exhalations.

817 That the molecules of air are subtle and minute appears from this, that they readily insinuate themselves into the pores of bodies, which is chiefly noticed by those who attempt experiments by means of the air pump. That they cohere loosely, and hence that air is porous, is taught by its fluidity; then by its impurity, since it in some manner saturates itself with the particles of other bodies, which it receives into its pores, and on account of which it very often shows itself malignant to the animal body. Its flexibility together with rigidity is evident from its elasticity, in which it is constantly and very greatly powerful: hence Descartes conjectured that air is a very rare body, like soft little feathers; Guglielmini thinks it is an aggregate of spirals twisted spherically and filled with ether, which can penetrate into their cavity only through the narrow openings of the convolutions.

818 That the aërial fluid is different from vapors and terrestrial exhalations, and hence that air consists of particles of its own proper kind, [p. 255] is evident above all from this, that it is established that vapors and exhalations ascend, but that they cannot be raised unless they are thrust out by a heavier body; so that accordingly around the globe of the Earth some other body, distinct from vapors and exhalations, which is air, must necessarily be admitted. Moreover, it is ascertained that air enclosed in a metal vessel, and even very strongly compressed, persists unchanged, which is not at all true of vapors. Finally, its elasticity is proportional to its density, and it occupies spaces which are reciprocally proportional to the compressing weights, which does not belong to vapors and exhalations.

819 The properties of air are fluidity, gravity, compressibility, and finally elasticity.

And as regards this last, it is certain that compressed air exerts it in any directions whatever; for in whatever place a vessel full of compressed air is pierced, the air will burst out continuously; and it bursts out inasmuch as it strives to dilate itself in every direction. It is further to be observed that the spring of compressed air equals the force by which it is compressed; for it is compressed until the force by which it resists the pressure has become equal to the compressing force: for then, on account of the equilibrium, the compression is ended; and therefore the elastic force of the lower air equals the weight of the upper air in the atmosphere.

820 Air, together with the terrestrial vapors and exhalations spread round the

Earth, is called the atmosphere of the Earth; about its height there is no agreement among Philosophers. Nollet, having weighed all the trials that have been made by means of the barometer, says that the height of the terrestrial atmosphere cannot be less than 6 French leagues, nor can it exceed 15 or 20 leagues, and hence that the height of the atmosphere lies between these measures.

821 The ancient Philosophers divided the whole air into three spheres, or regions; the first and supreme they called that which is nearest to the lunar orbit, filled with no exhalations at all, or with very subtle ones; the lowest was held to be that which, girding the terraqueous globe most closely, is occupied by thicker and heavier exhalations: whence it is denser than the rest and more misty, and moreover now hot, now cold, according as it is regarded by the Sun now directly, now obliquely: the middle is that which is conceived as situated between the two. Hence it is deduced:

C O RO L L A R Y.

he nature and origin of the winds are to be inquired into here, since they 822

T          seem to be nothing other than air flowing with force, or its force running

toward one quarter, or a more agitated motion, so that between wind and air, as Seneca says, there is no other difference than between a lake and a river. Their origin is various. The Sun, first of all, acting on the air, excites wind, inasmuch, namely, as it brings about by its heat that the air directly beneath it is greatly rarefied, and, having become rarer,

Kk [p. 256] by that very fact becomes lighter, and hence is thrust out by the rest, which are heavier and denser, and thus, the equilibrium of the air being disturbed, wind arises.

823 Next, the Sun excites winds by rarefying vapors with its heat; similarly while, by its action, the snows with which the summits of mountains are covered melt; for then the released particles press on the air and propel it toward that very region which lies beneath the Sun, since, being rarer, it resists their dilatation less; hence at the approach of spring north winds are very frequent, and south winds at the approach of autumn, because, as the Sun draws near the tropic of Cancer, the snows lying on the northern mountains begin to melt; but on the contrary, as the Sun draws near the tropic of Capricorn, the snows lying on the southern mountains are dissolved: to which is referred another cause of the winds as well, namely the admixture of the exhalations which are rather copiously scattered in the atmosphere, and the effervescence arising thence.

824 Finally, winds can have their origin in the bowels of the earth, and burst forth from them no otherwise than from the bottom of the sea; the more probable causes of these subterranean winds are subterranean fires, copious exhalations, etc. As regards the velocity of the winds, it is various. Musschenbroek says that it is gathered from Derham’s observations that the most violent winds were driven with such rapidity that they covered 66 English feet in a second, and 45 miles in the space of an hour; and, by the same witness, they had such great force that they tore apart a stone statue 12 feet high, 5 wide and 2 thick.

825 Diverse are their properties and qualities, which arise from the diverse vapors and exhalations which the winds carry down with them, and meet in their course, and snatch away with them; so that the north wind is cold, because it carries down with it a great quantity of nitrous and cold particles; the south winds tepid and humid, because they bring hot exhalations from the torrid Zone, or from the parts nearer to it, and at the same time humid vapors from the Mediterranean Sea.

826 The diversity of the winds is manifold: besides the winds, too, which are divided variously by reason of the various quarters from which they blow, there is besides another variety, relative to the time of blowing; similarly some winds are called provincial, which prevail in certain particular places or provinces; others have their diversity from their force and swiftness, or on the contrary from a gentle breath; the former are called stormy, the latter gentle; whose names and condition there is no leisure to pursue.

## CHAPTER II

On the Nature of Fire.

say: Fire is a fluid consisting of most subtle, most hard, supremely 827

I        mobile particles. It is demonstrated by exposition. That fire is a fluid

body is plain from this, that it communicates fluidity to other bodies, as to metals, and in others also preserves their fluidity, and brings itself back to equilibrium, as we observe in a room, where the heat is at length evenly diffused. That the molecules of fire are most subtle and most hard we gather from this, that it pervades all bodies, however compact, whereas the other fluids, even supremely volatile ones, can be kept in glasses or other vessels; then from this, that, as a universal solvent, it so tears apart and dissolves almost all bodies that by no industry of ours can they be restored to their former state; whence it is proven that the greatest mobility is in fire: it is necessary too that, to effect the motions of rarefaction, dissolution, combustion, etc., the quantity of motion in fire be very great.

## SCHOLIUM

828

Fire does not consist in sulphurous and nitrous particles agitated by the subtle matter, as the Cartesians suppose; for, to pass over many things, this is plain from this, that in the focus of a burning mirror, where the fire is so great that the imperfect metals at least turn in a short time into glass, nothing of sulphur or nitre is found; nor may one take refuge in air impregnated with these corpuscles, since the same thing happens in an exhausted receiver; nor let an escape be sought in the metals, since no sulphur is extracted by the chemists from gold, flint or diamond.

C O RO L L A R Y.

829

Flame is an aggregate of little bubbles, or of sulphurous, earthy, saline, rigid and pointed particles, agitated with a vehement and confused motion by the most subtle igneous fluid, and condensed by the surrounding air, so that they are not continually dissipated. For flame, relatively to other ignited bodies, burns little, because it embraces less fire, and much foreign matter, relatively to those ignited bodies. Its conical figure arises from

Kk 2 [p. 258] this, that it cleaves the air in a single place: namely, there where the air resists more

weakly and the flame is more active, since the most subtle parts are thrust out thither.

830 The colors of flame arise from its diverse matter: the blue around the base, from an oily humor not yet well concocted and dissipated; for the purer the flame is, and the greater the quantity of little fires it contains, the whiter it is; in the middle, many earthy particles mixed with the fire produce the red color, for if a small plate is thrust into the middle of the flame, it is stained with much soot, not so at the base and the tip. That the tip of the flame whitens is owing to the purified matter of the flame: besides, a kind of down appears, as it were, round the flame, which seems to be nothing else but an attenuated humor, not well kindled, and hence mixed partly with the air, partly with the fire, no otherwise than, e.g., a drop of wine mixed with water disperses itself, as it were, into certain filaments. No one hitherto (that I have seen) has treated of fire better than Boerhaave, so often and never sufficiently praised, in the Elementa Chemiae. Consult him, if you want more.

## CHAPTER III

On Meteors in General.

eteor means the same as appearing on high; whence the things that 831

Mare called by the Greeks meteora, or more precisely metarsia, are commonly called in Latin sublimia [lofty things]. They are conveniently divided into three kinds, or classes. The first contains the aërial or aqueous ones, in which, namely, air or water predominates. The second embraces the fiery ones, in which most subtle and spirituous exhalations prevail. The third class are the luminous or emphatic meteors, in which either solely, or at least for the greater part, light and splendor fall under consideration. A meteor, universally, is said to be an imperfect mixture consisting of certain attenuated (or, as the Chemists speak, sublimated) exhalations, and formed in the upper air. Of each we shall touch on a few things, and we shall show this general definition and nature of a meteor in each one singly.

832 A cloud is an aggregate of vapors suspended on high. It arises from vapors which at the beginning are so tenuous that they are not sensible, but which then, by the accession of some particles to others, constitute larger molecules by mutual conjunction; and these, adhering to others, form a very vast cloud, so that a cloud is accordingly to be called an aggregate of minute little bubbles in which aqueous vapors consist. Mist differs from a cloud only in its degree of density and in place; for each arises from little bubbles of humid [p. 259] exhalations agglomerated together in great quantity: they differ, however, in this, that the little bubbles constituting a cloud are far wider, and hence lighter with respect to the air, than those which make a mist, so that they lie, as it were, upon them: mist is changed into clouds by the very fact that the lower air thrusts out the bubbles, rarefied and therefore made lighter and dissipated: hence it is plain why, as the Sun approaches the meridian, mists for the most part pass into clouds.

833 Rain arises from the broken little bubbles of the clouds, which are broken from several causes: namely, either on account of the excessive heat of the Sun, by which they are very greatly dilated; or if they collide with one another by the force of contrary winds; or if they are pressed against the sides of mountains; or, finally, if they are too much constricted by an intense cold of the air. The evening damp is a certain humor, like a most subtle and insensible rain, falling from on high as night comes on; and it arises from most tenuous aqueous little bubbles, which, carried on high, are broken and turn into insensible drops as soon as the air, after sunset, is seized by some cold: hence there is none in wintertime, but only in summer, and chiefly in spring and autumn, when, moreover, no wind is blowing. And when the sky is stormy and rainy, and in winter too, those thicker droplets are dissipated by the winds, or are not dilated by rarefaction into such minute ones.

834 The morning dew differs only in respect of time: for it falls a little before the rising of the Sun, because the air is then more humid, and hence those exhalations which remained over in the air concrete; wherefore the opinion of those is less true who think that dew is nothing else than the sweat of plants, continually breathing out from the orifice of their little vessels and congealed by the force of cold; for although we do not deny this transpiration, yet something else must be affirmed of dew, since it is established that linen and woolen cloths and other bodies, glass likewise, which transmit nothing of a sweat of this kind, are sensibly wetted if they are exposed to the open air at the time when the dew is falling. Hoarfrost is nothing other than dew frozen by a sharper cold; it scorches and sucks out the tenderer crops and leaves, such as the buds of vines, indeed not seldom the vines themselves; for the nutritive juice, which, thrust out from the earth, is diffused into all the fibers of the plant, is condensed by the cold of the hoarfrost: hence the texture of the little fibers is constricted and changed.

835 Hail is rain congealed by the very cold region of the air: it is made when thin flakes of vapors, liquefied by warm air into very small drops and already tending downward, meet another, cold air, and are at once coagulated and hardened by it, new coats, as it were, being thereupon added on account of the vapors which they touch in falling. Hence it is plain why it does not hail in winter: for then the clouds are too near the Earth for very many of those very minute droplets, into which the first ones turn, to be able to come together into one before they are seized by the cold; likewise why, the higher the cloud from whose resolution the hail is formed, the larger the grains of hail are.

836 Snow is produced if the little bubbles of a humid exhalation, while turning into rain, [p. 260] are frozen by cold; for the flakes of snow are nothing else than most tenuous droplets of water, which, seized by cold, are united first among themselves like threads, when they become entangled with one another in diverse ways in their descent. The figure of snow is sometimes regular, sometimes irregular; often, if it is examined with a microscope, it shows a hexagonal star, at times a lily, and not seldom a rose; which figures seem to depend on the diverse exhalations frozen together. From these things it is easily understood what honeydew, manna, and the hair of Venus, or virgin threads, which appear like spiders’ threads over hedges and grasses, are, and whence they draw their origin.

837 The fiery meteors are, first, the flash; second, thunder; third, lightning, of which enough has been said in the Electrology; fourth, Helen and Pollux, which are fires that appear to those sailing, in the lowest region of the air, and are formed from spirituous fumes, which the sea, agitated by storms, transpires, carried up little by little, gathered together and kindled. If one appeared, it was called Helen; when two were seen, Castor and Pollux. Fifth: falling and shooting stars are certain fiery globules kindled in the upper air, and so moved through it that at times they appear to us to proceed straight, at other times to glide headlong from the sky. Sixth: the licking fire, and the foolish fire, is a fat exhalation sweating out from the flesh of men or of bodies, and from fattier matter, which is kindled by compression or friction, and clings to horses or men without harm.

838 The foolish fire is a certain marshy exhalation from putrefied plants, corpses and other oily dissolved bodies, prepared by the daily heat of the Sun, which, upon the onset of friction or fermentation, is kindled, shines, and, as it were, burns. They are called foolish fires because not only do they run hither and thither by no certain law, in the manner of a foolish man, but also because they follow those who flee them, and in turn flee those who follow them; whence they are feared by simple folk, who do not understand, namely, that this happens for the reason that he who pursues the fire, both by the motion of his body and by his breath, drives the air before him, and with it the foolish fire; while he who flees from the fire draws the air after him, and with the air the foolish fire, while he yields the place left by his body to be filled by the air.

839 Seventh: nearly the same is the account of the phenomena of the aforesaid meteors, which are distinguished among themselves only by their diverse figure; for if a marshy or bituminous exhalation, gathered together with nitrous spirits and suddenly kindled in the upper air by means of fermentation, friction or compression, presents the appearance of a fiery globe, and has about it hanging flakes, as it were, and is borne with a leaping motion, it is called the Leaping Goat; if it is oblong and parallel to the horizon, the Beam; if it swells in its middle, the Dragon; if it is round and flat, the Shield; if smooth and cylindrical, the Column; if it ends in a point, the Pyramid; if it is widely dispersed and shows, as it were, kindled straws, it is named the Stubble. Eighth: the Aurora Borealis, or northern light, is

[p. 261] that glow which in the nighttime at times appears to us in the northern quarter of the sky in such a way that the sky itself seems, as it were, to burn in that part. The history of this phenomenon is extensive; since it is found everywhere among the Moderns, for brevity’s sake I adduce only what is necessary.

840 In the first place, it has its seat in the atmosphere of the Earth, like the other fiery meteors, and is produced in it; for this light has at times been seen below the clouds, as Mayer testifies: then, if it extended beyond the atmosphere, it would be very high, and hence would be seen even from places near the equator, which, however, is contrary to experience, especially since it often happens that it is seen in one place and is not observed in another a few miles distant. Wherefore we think that this light, like the remaining fiery meteors, comes from an exhalation and vapor carried on high from the earth, or from the matter of lightning and of flashes not yet well ripened, so to speak, and not yet prepared for the effects of lightning and of flashes.

841 The luminous or Emphatic meteors are: first, the Rainbow, which is a many-colored arc formed in a dewy cloud by the refraction and reflection of the Sun opposite; whence it either brings down or naturally indicates rain, but without a great flood of waters; for clouds too heavily laden are not fit for reflecting and thus refracting the rays of the Sun. The more conspicuous colors of the rainbow are: red or crimson, yellow, green, blue, and finally purple or violet; and these in the primary rainbow hold the order mentioned and are more vivid; but in the secondary the reverse, so that in its outermost part the purple shines, then the blue, etc.; which are also seen weaker and more diluted.

842 That rainbow, moreover, is called primary which reaches the eye after two refractions of the rays and one reflection, and is seen at an angle of about 42 degrees; and the secondary, that which falls into the eye after two refractions and as many reflections, at an angle of about 52 degrees. It is to be noticed that the rainbow is not seen unless the sight is between the Sun and the dewy cloud; so when you sprinkle water from your mouth toward the light let in through windows, and stand between the Sun and the drops, you behold a rainbow, of which you also have other analogies in little leaping fountains, in spiders’ webs, on the neck of a dove, in flowers or grasses sprinkled with dew about sunrise and viewed in the due situation and place.

843 Further, why the same colors seem always to be and to remain is from this, that continually other and other parts of the dewy cloud, or new droplets again and again, succeed the earlier ones in the same situation and disposition, no otherwise than in a burning taper the same flame is believed to endure, on account of other and other particles of fire continually succeeding. Second: the Halo, or crown, or area, is a colored circle, more commonly whitish, sometimes however showing the colors of the rainbow, but more obscure, which appears now and then around the Sun, more often around the Moon; it is formed in a dewy cloud placed between the star and the eye,

[p. 262] with a texture suited to a double refraction, by virtue of which the rays make with the axis, or the line drawn through the center of the star and the eye, an angle of nearly 23 degrees.

844 If the Halo is condensed ever larger and larger, it presages rain, because the clouds gradually concrete into a shower; if it is dissipated on many sides, or even on one side, it indicates winds arising either from several quarters or from one; if it vanishes wholly, it foretells fair weather, for then the clouds are dissipated by the force of heat. Third: the Parhelion and Paraselene are luminous meteors standing beside the Sun or the Moon and showing the images of those stars; for as often as a cloud apt to be resolved very soon into waters, diaphanous, too, toward the Sun, but terminated on the other side like a mirror, runs up to the Sun, not below it toward the earth, nor directly opposite, but at the sides and obliquely, either toward the north or toward the south, so often the Sun impresses its own image upon it, which, reflected thence to our eyes, represents the Sun to us in the cloud, so that the ignorant judge that twin Suns are shining. Moreover, it can happen that the image of the Sun, impressed in like manner on one cloud, induces again another image on a second cloud, and this again on another; the same is to be thought, proportionally, of the Moon.

845 Fourth: Rods are formed in the air when a straight tract of clouds shows diverse colors, for the same cause for which these are formed in the rainbow or the crown. Fifth: we call it a Chasm, a Gap, or a Pit, when on a clear night exhalations carried upward, denser in the middle and rarer in the remaining part, are placed between the light of the stars and our eye; for if they are many, they show a chasm; if fewer, a gap; if extended lengthwise, a pit or lake; since on account of the density in the middle they are less illuminated, and everything dark, although equally near and placed in the same surface, always seems more remote and more depressed, while what is bright seems nearer and more elevated. Let it suffice to have said this, in compendium, on a most copious matter.

C H A P T E R T H E L A S T.

What is to be said of Plants.

lants, by which name every kind of growth that bursts forth from the 846

P        earth is understood, are organic bodies consisting of a varied apparatus

of organic parts most wisely co-ordinated and joined together, adhering to the earth by their roots, and animated by the influx of a suitable juice going round and returning in a circuit. The wonderful apparatus of these organic bodies was investigated [p. 263] and explained by Malpighi the Italian and Grew the Englishman. Life, in a manner, and its actions are accomplished in plants by the continual motion, returning in a circuit, of the vital fluid through solid organs most wisely disposed; which motion the agitation, impulse and pressure of the ether and the air bring about, the elastic force mediating at the same time; so that on that account they are rightly called Hydraulic-Pneumatic machines; and that these may be understood more deeply, I subjoin a very brief Anatomy of them.

847 Of the parts of plants, some are fluid, others solid. The fluid part is that humor or juice which, like the blood in man, is diffused through the solid parts of the plant. This juice, and the true and genuine nourishment of plants, they say most probably to be saline, earthy and oily parts, which, prepared in the aqueous juice, attenuated, worked up, and distributed with this juice, as with a vehicle, into the whole structure of the plants, are carried round, so that the single parts can receive what is suitable for nourishing and increasing their substance. The solid parts constitute their organic body, and are: the trunk, roots, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits. The trunk, which in trees is called the bole and stock, in flowers and herbs the stalk, scape and thyrsus, in wheat and the like the straw or haulm, is, as it were, the body of the plant, which, bursting forth from the earth, rises above it and unfolds itself into branches, fronds, etc. The root is that part of the plant which, placed wholly below the earth and adhering to it, draws its nourishment for the plant. The branches, just as the limbs from the body of an animal, so burst forth from the body, or trunk, of the plant, for the most part without order, sometimes in an elegant order, and spread themselves in every direction; being of altogether the same nature as the trunk from which they arise, and furnished like it with bark, they contain pith in the middle, and are composed of the same little vessels, namely fibers, utricles and tracheae. The leaves embrace chiefly two parts: namely, the petiole, by which the leaf is attached to the plant, and the very body of the leaf.

848 The flowers are, as it were, the first offspring of the plant; in them four parts are distinguished, namely: the calyx, which is the base and support of the flower; the petals, which rise above the calyx, propagated from the dilated stalk, and consist of woody tubes, or fibers, of tracheae too, and at the same time of a manifold order of utricles; the stamens burst forth from the lowest part of the flower, various in number and figure: they consist of a filament and an attached capsule, which is made up of woody tubes, tracheae and utricles placed lengthwise: the style, finally, is that part of the flower which, occupying its center, hides and cherishes the seed of the plant in its cavity. The fruit is the last work of plants, to the producing and perfecting of which all the remaining parts are destined; it consists, moreover, of an envelope and the seed; the former differs according to the specific difference of the fruits, and is manifold, and of diverse consistency and firmness in diverse fruits; the seed pertains to the origin of plants: of which briefly.

849 That little grain, or kernel, is called the seed, from which, as from an egg, the plant germinates; four things are distinguished in it: the envelopes;

Ll [p. 264] the first, or outermost of all, is harder than the rest; when it is removed, two little skins are met, of which the exterior is thick and almost cartilaginous, the interior very subtle, so that in a dried seed it can scarcely be separated from the exterior.

After these integuments, which are called secundines, two or even more lobes come into view, enclosed in a certain thin and pellucid membrane, which is fourth in order; and they embrace, in a kind of little ditch, as it were, hollowed out on either side in the lobes, the germ of the future plant; which is nothing else than the whole plant itself that is to arise from the seed, complete in all its parts, namely trunk, or stalk, roots, branches, etc., so that the seminal plantlet lying hidden in the germ does not differ from the adult except in the size of its parts.

850 The rising from the seed, further, is accomplished in this way: when the seed is committed to suitable earth, the fibers of its membranes are gently loosened by the heat of the earth and of the Sun, and their passages are dilated; whence it comes about that the humor in which the earth abounds gradually enters them, is variously strained in them, ferments, and is made apt for nutrition: the nutritive juice, strained in the membranes, enters the substance of the lobes, where it is mixed with the specific juice of the plantlet, ferments, and takes on new parts; this juice, prepared in due manner in the lobes, enters the most subtle pores of the radicle of the germ itself and insinuates itself into its little fibers; and the radicle, nourished and increased by this juice, bursts forth outward, spreads out its hair, and by means of those filaments is inserted into the earth; the root being sufficiently increased, a more lively portion of the nutritive liquor passes into the remaining part of the germ, and, irradiating and impelling its parts, communicates motion to them; hence are evolved and unfolded the parts of the future plant, which lie hidden in the germ, rolled up and folded together among themselves; then by degrees these same parts are increased and come into view in their order: so that from this first evolution of the seed the remaining growth of the plant is easily understood.

C O R O L L A R Y.

851

There are therefore no plants that are not generated from seed. Certainly the peculiar disposition of plants, the collocation of their parts in wonderful order and distinction, the little veins, utricles and tracheae, for producing flowers and fruits of the same species, make it manifest that plants are not born from a fortuitous concourse of the elements, or from putrid matter. This very thing is shown by an experiment of Malpighi, who had enclosed earth dug out of a rather deep pit in a vessel in such a way as to cover its upper part with very delicate cloths, so that entrance into the vessel lay open to the air and the rain, but not to other very minute corpuscles carried through the air; and so he exposed it to the rays of the Sun. He found that after a very long time no herb, or sign of a plant, appeared; so that on that account he inferred that, since no seed had either lain hidden before in the earth [p. 265] dug out from deeper down, or could have fallen into the vessel through the air, plants have their genesis from seed.

852 As regards the nutrition and growth of plants, it is accomplished by the admission, elaboration and purification of a suitable juice, and by its continual circulation through the organs of the plant; for the roots draw in moisture; this, once received, ascends through the woody tubes of the plant, because it is urged upward unceasingly by the alternate dilatation and constriction of the tracheae which are interspersed among the woody tubes; and from these it is dispersed into the other parts. That the nutritive juice circulates is shown, first of all, because only in this way does it seem that the nutrition of plants can be accomplished; since indeed this cannot take place unless that which is useful, and is suitable nourishment for the plant, is separated from the useless, and this is thrust back again to those parts, so that it may be rendered fit for nutrition through a new purification and elaboration; and then it is plain from experience; for Malpighi, when the bark had been cut round in a circle and a ring-shaped portion torn away, found that the edge of the upper bark swelled notably and also increased, but that the lower obtained no increase, but only put forth buds in their season. And let these things, which have been excerpted from Fr. Klaus, suffice to have been said, so that we may put the finishing hand to the Physics, both General and Particular.

853 But if to anyone perhaps some of the things which I have brought forward in these Elements of the Newer Philosophy should seem briefer than was fitting, I would wish him to consider that I have written for Young Men alone. Many large volumes of learned men, far fuller ones, are available for the convenience of others. Nor yet would I think on that account that I have failed in my office, since I judged it more useful to make plain whatever could cause trouble to beginners, and with these Elements rather to help the American Youth than to burden them with a greater mass of disputations. For Philosophy is to be acquired both by meditation and by experiments, and it has nothing of great advantage placed in prolixity.

O. S. C . S. M . E . C . A . R .
